docs.title: phēnix
docs.text: phēnix provides a framework for defining, deploying, and managing complex cyber-physical experiments. It orchestrates virtual machines, networks, and applications to create realistic emulation environments. It runs the virtual machines and networks on minimega.

docs.title: 🚀 Getting Started
docs.text: The easiest way to get phēnix running is using Docker.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Linux environment (Ubuntu 24.04+ recommended)
  • Docker & Docker Compose

docs.title: Running with Docker
docs.text: The phēnix repository includes a docker-compose.yml file in the docker/ directory for running phēnix and its dependencies.

docs.title: 1. Clone the Repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/sandialabs/sceptre-phenix.git
cd sceptre-phenix/docker

docs.title: 2. Start Services
docs.text: The docker-compose.yml file allows you to either build from source or use a pre-built image.

docs.title: Building from Source (Default)
docs.text:
This is the recommended method for development.

docker compose up -d --build

docs.title: Using Pre-built Images
docs.text:
To use the pre-built image from the registry instead of building from source, run:

docker compose up -d --pull always

This will pull the latest images specified in the image key for each service (e.g., ghcr.io/sandialabs/sceptre-phenix/phenix:main and ghcr.io/sandia-minimega/minimega:latest) and skip the build step.

Each GitHub release attaches SPDX JSON software bills of materials (SBOMs) of the phenix and JIT UI images and of the Debian package, listing the packages and Go modules each one contains.

To build the image with Podman instead, run podman build -f docker/Dockerfile -t phenix . from the repository root. See podman/README.md for running phēnix and minimega as a Podman pod.

docs.title: 3. Check Status
docs.text:
After starting the services with either method, view the logs to see the initialization progress:

docker compose logs -f

Once phēnix is up, docker compose ps shows the phenix container as (healthy). To also check that phēnix can reach minimega and its store, and has enough disk space, run:

docker exec phenix phenix healthcheck --ready

See Health Checks for more. To check the configuration without the server, run docker exec phenix phenix doctor (see Doctor).

Note

The Docker image includes the user apps from the sceptre-phenix-apps repository.

docs.title: 4. Open the Web UI
docs.text: phenix ui listens on port 3000 on all interfaces (--listen-endpoint, default 0.0.0.0:3000), and the Compose services use the host network. Open http://<host>:3000 in a browser, and see Using the Web UI. The image that docker-compose.yml builds, and the image on GHCR, have web UI authentication disabled. See User Authn/Authz to enable it.

docs.title: Installing Without Docker
docs.text: To run phēnix without Docker, install the Debian package. Download the .deb from a GitHub release, or build it with ./scripts/build-deb.sh on a Debian or Ubuntu host (the build itself uses Docker, and puts the package in build/deb/). To build from source (Go 1.24+ and Node.js 24+), see the repository README.

docs.title: Accessing the CLI & Shell Completion
docs.text: With phenix running in a container, you can execute commands. For the best experience, including shell (tab) completion, you should install the provided wrapper script.

docs.title: Using the Wrapper Script (Recommended)
docs.text:
The phenix repository includes a wrapper script that simplifies running phenix commands against the Docker container and is required for shell completion to work correctly.

  1. Install the wrapper: From the root of the sceptre-phenix repository, run:

    # This command installs the `scripts/phenix-wrapper.sh` script to /usr/local/bin/phenix.
sudo make install-wrapper

    Warning

    If you previously used a shell alias for phenix (e.g., alias phenix="docker exec ..."), you must remove it from your shell profile (e.g., ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc) for the wrapper and completion to work.

  2. Enable Shell Completion: Add the completion script to your shell's startup file so it's available in new terminal sessions.

    # For Bash (requires the bash-completion package)
echo 'source <(phenix completion bash)' >> ~/.bashrc

# For Zsh
echo 'source <(phenix completion zsh)' >> ~/.zshrc

    Zsh completion needs compinit to be loaded before the source line. Frameworks such as Oh My Zsh load it for you; otherwise, add autoload -U compinit && compinit to ~/.zshrc above that line.

    Now, you can use Tab to autocomplete commands, flags, and even dynamic values like experiment and VM names. For more details, run phenix completion --help. phenix completion also supports Fish and PowerShell; see phenix completion.

docs.title: Manual Execution
docs.text:
You can also execute commands directly, but shell completion will not work.

docker exec -it phenix phenix <command>

The CLI reference lists every command and flag.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
This page is for you if you use only a keyboard, a screen reader, speech input or browser zoom, or if you need more contrast or less motion.

The project's target for changes to the web UI is WCAG 2.2 level AA. Its browser tests scan most pages with axe-core: the main UI with the A, AA and AAA rules (which include 7:1 contrast for text), and Builder with A and AA rules in both of its themes.

docs.title: Keyboard
docs.text:
• Skip to main content is the first link on every page, so press Tab at the top of a page to reach it. The Builder editor starts with a second one, Skip to diagram canvas.
  • A tooltip shows when you move focus to its control, not just on hover. That's how an icon-only button in the navbar gives its name.
  • The Resources and Admin menus in the navbar are buttons. Enter opens one, Tab moves through its links and Esc closes it.
  • When a dialog or a menu closes, focus goes back to what opened it.
  • In a table, Tab stops on each sortable column heading, and Enter or Space sorts by it.

Builder, the VM consoles, the config editor and the minimega console have keys of their own.

docs.title: Screen Readers
docs.text:
• Each page has its own title, with the most specific part first, for example bennu - Experiment - phēnix.
  • A failure notification is an alert, so your screen reader reads it when it opens.
  • The refresh button in the navbar tells you when a reload failed or the data may be out of date.
  • The screen of a VM is a picture, so a screen reader can't read it. The console page reads out each change of a VM's connection, such as web: Connected.
  • In Builder, use your screen reader's focus mode (forms mode in JAWS) for the keys of the canvas. Builder reads out what each change did. A device or a switch has the facts of its info tooltip, and what the checks found, as its description.

docs.title: Zoom and Narrow Windows
docs.text:
phēnix is laid out for desktop browsers, not phones. Browser zoom works like a narrower window:

  • From 1024 to 1399 pixels wide, the navbar links and menus show only their icons, with their names in tooltips. Below 1024 pixels, a menu button holds them, with their names.
  • In Builder, the side columns stack and the page scrolls (see Side Columns). They also stack when you enlarge only the text.

docs.title: Themes and Contrast
docs.text:
• The main UI has one theme, which is dark. The project's rule for it is a text contrast of at least 7:1.
  • Builder has a Theme of its own: System, Light or Dark (see Themes). With a Windows contrast theme, Builder draws the lines and the selection on the canvas in your system colors.

docs.title: Motion
docs.text: The web UI follows your device's setting for reduced motion: animations and transitions stop, and a loading spinner stays on screen but doesn't turn. Builder also has Reduce motion in Builder settings (off by default), for when your device doesn't ask.

docs.title: Text Size
docs.text: Besides browser zoom, the minimega console has Text size buttons (10 to 24 pixels), and a VM console shows the VM's screen at 50% to 200% with Actual in its View panel. Builder has zoom buttons on its canvas, and Node icon size in Settings.

docs.title: Builder
docs.text:
You can use Builder with only a keyboard, or with a screen reader. It has a command palette, and you can change its shortcuts.

  • The diagram, the toolbar and the header counts are each one Tab stop. The arrow keys, Home and End move between the toolbar buttons and between the counts. On the diagram, the arrow keys move between nodes (see Keys on the Canvas).
  • To add and connect nodes without a pointer, use Nodes & Objects and the Inspector header, or type connect or group in the command palette.
  • To find a node without moving through the canvas, use Go to node in the command palette.
  • The cards of the drafts page are one Tab stop for each tab (see Selecting with the Keyboard).
  • A few shortcuts are a key with no Ctrl or ⌘, such as N and ?. If speech input or your screen reader presses them by mistake, turn off Single-key shortcuts (see Single-Key Shortcuts).

docs.title: VM Consoles
docs.text:
A VM console sends every key to the VM, Tab included. To move focus out of the console, press Ctrl+] and then Tab (see The Keyboard Chord).

The terminal that SCORCH opens for a component and the minimega console work the same way: Ctrl+], then Tab or Shift+Tab, leaves the terminal.

docs.title: The Config Editor
docs.text:
On the Configs page, the name of a config is a button: Tab to it and press Enter to open the viewer.

In the editor window, Tab stops on the line numbers and then on the text. On the text, press Enter to type, and Esc to stop typing so that Tab moves on. With Vim Mode on, the first Esc leaves insert mode, so press it a second time.

docs.title: The Command Line
docs.text: phēnix colors statuses, warnings and errors in its output, and the text is the same without the colors. To turn them off, pass --color off or set NO_COLOR (see Colors).

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Using the Web UI: the navbar, tables and notifications.
  • Builder Reference: every Builder shortcut.
  • VMs: the console page and its keyboard chord.
  • Settings: the color setting and --color.

docs.title: API
docs.text: The phēnix web UI is built entirely on top of a REST API served by the phēnix daemon. That same API is available for external tooling and automation, such as CI/CD pipelines (see Workflow) or custom scripts.

docs.title: Interactive API Docs (Swagger/OpenAPI)
docs.text:
Browsable, interactive API documentation is generated from the project's OpenAPI (Swagger) specification, and is available in two places:

  • On this documentation site: swagger.html (linked from the gear icon in the footer) is a static snapshot of the API docs, rendered from the openapi.yml spec at the time the docs were published.

  • On a running phēnix server: every phēnix instance also hosts its own copy of the same interactive API docs at the /docs/ path:

    http://<phenix-host>:<port>/docs/

    For a default local installation, this would be:

    http://localhost:3000/docs/

    Note

    <port> defaults to 3000 and comes from the ui.listen-endpoint setting. See Settings for details on configuring this.

    Because it's built into the phēnix binary/image itself, /docs/ on a running server is always in sync with the version of phēnix you're running, whereas swagger.html reflects the spec as of the latest docs release.

    The raw spec is at /docs/openapi.yml, with info.version set to the server's build, which authenticated /api/v1 responses also carry in an X-Phenix-Version header.

The API docs are organized by tag (Configs, Experiments, Virtual Machines, Hosts, Applications, Topologies, Disks, Users, Workflow, Jobs, Events, etc.) and document every route, including request parameters, response schemas and status codes, including the websockets and the routes outside /api/v1 (health, features, version and /webshark/).

Info

The underlying OpenAPI spec is maintained at src/go/web/public/docs/openapi.yml in the sceptre-phenix repository, and is rendered to static HTML with Redoc as part of the phēnix build: container images, Debian packages, this site, and binaries built with make build all use the Redocly CLI version pinned in scripts/api-docs.sh. Run make api-docs to render it locally.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
If UI/API authentication is enabled (see User Authn/Authz), API requests must include an auth token generated from the Users page (in the Admin menu) of the web UI, passed as the X-Phenix-Auth-Token header, which must carry the token as Bearer <token>:

X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer ******

A token in an Authorization header is ignored.

A browser link can pass the token in a token query parameter instead, without Bearer. An API request without a token gets 403, and a request with a malformed, expired or signed-out token gets 401. The API reference introduction gives the full rules.

See Generating User Authentication Tokens for details.

curl -s -H "X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer $TOKEN" http://localhost:3000/api/v1/experiments

docs.title: Status Codes
docs.text: A role without the permission a route needs gets 403 (or 404 on a few routes, so they don't reveal another user's job, console or capture token). An unknown path under /api/v1 gets 404, and a wrong method gets 405. With authentication disabled, every request acts as global-admin. With --base-path, the Location headers of new jobs and configs include the base path.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Errors are JSON with a message, the underlying cause, and a code (match on the code, since the message may change). Some add a metadata or details object.

code Statuses Meaning invalid_request 400, 405, 413, 415, 416, 422 The request cannot be acted on as sent. unauthorized 401 No valid session. forbidden 403 The role may not make the request. not_found 404, 410 The thing does not exist, or is hidden from the role. conflict 409, 412, 423 At odds with the current state, such as a stale revision. rate_limited 429 Too many requests. Retry-After says when to try again. unavailable 502, 503, 504 The server or minimega cannot serve it now. Try again later. internal other 5xx The request failed in the server. broken_disks 400 A disk or CD-ROM image of a VM is missing or has a broken backing chain, so the start was refused. details.disks lists them. See Disk Check Before a Start. 
{"message": "job not found", "cause": "", "code": "not_found"}

The exceptions are the health routes (application/health+json), the /webshark/ routes (WebShark's own format), and a failed websocket handshake (plain text).

docs.title: Response Encoding
docs.text: JSON, YAML and plain-text responses are gzip-compressed when the client sends Accept-Encoding: gzip. Downloads are never compressed.

docs.title: Paging
docs.text: The experiment, VM, disk, job, experiment VM and experiment file lists take pageNum (from 1) and perPage together, and return that page with a total that counts the whole list. Without both, they return everything.

docs.title: Query Parameters
docs.text: Boolean and enum query parameters are strict. A boolean takes true or false (also 1, t, 0 and f), and an enum only the values the API docs list. Anything else, even an empty value or a bare ?name, gets 400 (invalid_request) with the accepted values. Leave a parameter out to get its default.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
Single-file downloads (experiment files, disk images, files in a mounted VM, tunneler builds, saved captures and the server's log files) can be resumed. Each download route also answers HEAD, and every response carries Accept-Ranges: bytes, a strong ETag and Last-Modified, so Range, If-Range and If-None-Match work as usual (206, 200 for a changed file, 304).

curl -C - resumes with Range alone, so check such a download against its checksum. Experiment files and disk images have a checksum route that returns the SHA-256 (202 until it's computed).

URL='http://localhost:3000/api/v1/experiments/my-exp/files/router_eth0.pcap'
curl -C - -o router_eth0.pcap -H "X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "$URL?path=captures/router_eth0.pcap"
curl -s -H "X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "$URL/checksum?path=captures/router_eth0.pcap"

Zip downloads that phēnix builds as it sends them, and the CSV and JSONL downloads of a netflow capture, can't be resumed. The file of a finished background job, such as its zip of experiment files, can (GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}/artifact). A reverse proxy must pass Range, If-Range and the ETag through unchanged and must not compress downloads, or resuming won't work.

docs.title: Revisions and Conditional Requests
docs.text:
Every stored config has a metadata.revision that changes on each write (see Revisions). GET, POST and PUT on a config return it as a strong ETag, "r<revision>", and as a number in X-Phenix-Revision. Send the ETag back in If-Match on a PUT or DELETE to write only if nobody changed the config since you read it; otherwise you get 412 with the current revision in metadata.revision. Without If-Match, a write replaces the config whatever its revision. If-None-Match on a GET answers 304 while the config is unchanged.

curl -si -H "X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  http://localhost:3000/api/v1/configs/topology/demo | grep -i '^etag'
# ETag: "r42"

curl -s -X PUT -H "X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-yaml' -H 'If-Match: "r42"' \
  --data-binary @demo.yaml http://localhost:3000/api/v1/configs/topology/demo
# 204 with ETag: "r43", or 412 if someone saved the config after you read it

docs.title: Freshness
docs.text: Every authenticated response carries X-Phenix-Seq, and every message on the /ws websocket carries the same number in seq. It only increases within one phenix ui process, so a client can use it to order lists and live updates. Responses with state read from minimega also carry X-Phenix-Observed-At (when it was read), and X-Phenix-Stale: true when it is older than normal, such as while an experiment starts or stops.

docs.title: Streaming Endpoints
docs.text:
• GET /experiments/{exp}/vms/{name}/captures/{interface}/stream streams a running packet capture as pcap, over HTTP or a websocket.
  • GET /webshark/streams/{token}, outside /api/v1, streams the same pcap with a capture token as its only credential.
  • GET /console/{pid}/ws attaches a websocket to a minimega console.

The server closes a /ws client that falls too far behind with close code 1013 and the reason client too slow; reconnect and reload, as the web UI does. When phenix ui shuts down, it closes every websocket with close code 1001, and new websockets, consoles and jobs get 503 with Retry-After until it stops.

docs.title: Background Jobs
docs.text:
Long operations run as background jobs. The route that starts one answers 202 with the job and a Location: /api/v1/jobs/{id} header to follow. The experiment name all in POST /api/v1/experiments/all/start and POST /api/v1/experiments/all/trigger starts such a job for every experiment you may start or trigger.

Some of these routes take an Idempotency-Key header, so a retry returns the first job instead of starting another (see Retrying a request that starts a job).

docs.title: Health Endpoints
docs.text: GET /healthz and GET /readyz, at the server root and without credentials, report the server's health. See Health Checks.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
The phēnix API can be used to integrate phēnix with external systems. Known integrations include:

  • Workflow - deploy a topology directory with phenix workflow apply, or drive experiment topology/scenario updates from a git-based CI/CD pipeline reacting to push events.
  • Builder - create, edit and publish drafts, convert legacy diagrams, and manage packages, icons and templates under /api/v1/builder/.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • phenix admin: create users, roles and API tokens.

docs.title: Apps
docs.text: phenix apps provide a means of modifying an experiment topology, cluster networking, hardware-in-the-loop devices, etc. in a layered, scripted, and codified manner. phenix itself includes four (4) default apps that get applied to every experiment by default. In addition to the default apps, it is possible to apply user apps to an experiment using a scenario configuration. Non-default apps can also be disabled at startup, either through the phenix experiment create command or in the scenario file. This allows apps to execute their running stage only when manually triggered by the user.

docs.title: Default Apps
docs.text: App Description ntp provides/configures NTP service for experiment serial configures serial interfaces in VM images startup configures guest operating systems at startup using disk injection or C2 vrouter customizes Vyatta/VyOS and minirouter routers, including setting interfaces, ACL rules, etc.

docs.title: Disable Default Apps for a VM
docs.text:
To keep a VM managed by phenix and minimega without applying the built-in default apps, set the phenix/default-apps node annotation to false in the topology:

disable default apps for one VM
spec:
  nodes:
    - annotations:
        phenix/default-apps: false
      general:
        hostname: custom-vm
      # remaining node configuration omitted

This skips the ntp, serial, startup, and vrouter apps for that node during every lifecycle stage. User apps configured in a scenario are unaffected. Omit the annotation, or set it to true, to retain the default behavior.

To set it on every VM of an experiment without editing the topology, add the annotation when you create the experiment (see Adding Annotations).

docs.title: startup App
docs.text:
The startup app generates scripts that configure supported guest operating systems when an experiment starts. These scripts configure settings such as the hostname, time zone, and network interfaces. Scenario metadata for the app can also add settings such as Windows domain membership.

By default, phēnix injects the generated scripts into the VM's first drive. For images where disk injection is unavailable or intentionally disabled, phēnix can instead send and execute the scripts through minimega command and control (C2).

docs.title: Scenario Configuration
docs.text:
The startup app accepts per-host metadata in a scenario for domain membership and Windows automatic logon. The hostname, network interfaces, and routes come from the topology. The time zone of Linux, RHEL, and CentOS guests is always set to Etc/UTC. DNS servers also come from the topology unless Windows domain_controller.ip overrides the first network adapter's DNS server.

The supported metadata is:

Metadata Guest OS Fields Result domain_controller Linux, RHEL, or CentOS domain, username, password Joins the guest to the domain with realm join. domain_controller Windows domain, ip, username, password Uses ip as the first network adapter's DNS server, then joins the domain. auto_logon Windows username, password, and optional local Configures automatic logon.

A host with no domain_controller metadata does not join a domain. If domain_controller is set and one of its fields is missing, pre-start fails with an error that names the host and the field.

docs.title: Linux Domain Join
docs.text:
The Linux guest must provide the realm command and any packages required to join its domain.

Linux domain join scenario
apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v2
kind: Scenario
metadata:
  name: linux-domain-join
  annotations:
    topology: example
spec:
  apps:
    - name: startup
      hosts:
        - hostname: linux-client
          metadata:
            domain_controller:
              domain: example.test
              username: administrator@example.test
              password: change-me

docs.title: Windows Domain Join and Automatic Logon
docs.text:
When domain_controller and auto_logon are used together, omit local or set it to false to use a domain account for automatic logon.

Windows domain join scenario
apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v2
kind: Scenario
metadata:
  name: windows-domain-join
  annotations:
    topology: example
spec:
  apps:
    - name: startup
      hosts:
        - hostname: windows-client
          metadata:
            domain_controller:
              domain: example.test
              ip: 192.0.2.10
              username: administrator
              password: change-me
            auto_logon:
              username: student
              password: change-me
              local: false

docs.title: Windows Local Automatic Logon
docs.text:
auto_logon can also be used without domain_controller to configure an existing local account for automatic logon. The app does not create the account.

Windows local automatic logon scenario
apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v2
kind: Scenario
metadata:
  name: windows-local-logon
  annotations:
    topology: example
spec:
  apps:
    - name: startup
      hosts:
        - hostname: windows-client
          metadata:
            auto_logon:
              username: student
              password: change-me

Warning

Scenario metadata stores these passwords as plain text. Protect scenario files and replace the example credentials before use.

docs.title: C2 Startup Script Delivery
docs.text:
There are two ways to enable C2 delivery for a VM:

  • Set the node annotation phenix/startup-via-cc to true. This explicitly uses C2 and removes only the disk injections generated by the startup app. Other injections configured on the node are unaffected.
  • Set inject_partition: 0 on the first drive. This disables disk injection for the drive and automatically uses C2 for the generated startup scripts. Other files configured for disk injection are still skipped.

The annotation is useful when the disk supports injection but you want startup configuration to run through C2 instead:

explicit C2 startup delivery
spec:
  nodes:
    - annotations:
        phenix/startup-via-cc: true
      type: VirtualMachine
      general:
        hostname: host-00
      hardware:
        os_type: linux
        drives:
          - image: ubuntu.qc2

Like phenix/default-apps, you can also add this annotation to every VM of an experiment when you create it (see Adding Annotations).

For a disk layout that cannot be injected into, such as an LVM-based image, set the injection partition on the first drive to 0:

automatic C2 startup delivery
spec:
  nodes:
    - type: VirtualMachine
      general:
        hostname: host-00
      hardware:
        os_type: linux
        drives:
          - image: ubuntu-lvm.qc2
            inject_partition: 0
Node configuration Startup script delivery Annotation omitted or false, first drive partition omitted or nonzero Disk injection First drive inject_partition: 0 C2, selected automatically phenix/startup-via-cc: true C2, selected explicitly Only general.snapshot: false None; phēnix injects files only into a snapshot, and this setting alone does not enable C2

Warning

C2 delivery requires the miniccc agent to be installed and configured to start in the guest. Linux, RHEL, and CentOS guests must provide bash, and Windows guests must provide PowerShell.

The startup app does not generate scripts for router nodes or nodes with phenix/default-apps: false.

docs.title: Skipping Hostname Changes
docs.text: Set the node annotation phenix/startup-set-hostname: false on a Topology node to keep the guest's existing hostname while still applying timezone, network interface, and domain configuration.

docs.title: Windows Node Annotations
docs.text:
The Windows startup script also reads these node annotations:

  • phenix/domain-controller: set to true on a Windows domain controller. The script then waits until the Active Directory domain services of the VM are ready before it continues.
  • phenix/windows-rearm: set to true to stop the Windows licensing prompt (slui.exe) each time the script runs. On the first run, the script also disables the WLMS service and rearms the Windows license with slmgr.vbs /rearm.

docs.title: Port Forwards
docs.text:
Set the node annotation phenix/startup-autotunnel to a list of port forwards for the startup app to create in the post-start stage. Each entry is a string (put it in quotes) in one of these forms:

  • sport: forward local port sport to port sport of the VM.
  • sport:dport: forward local port sport to port dport of the VM.
  • sport:dhost:dport: forward local port sport to port dport of dhost, as the VM reaches it.

A dport of VNC forwards to the VNC console of the VM. Other forwards need a miniccc agent that is active in the VM when the post-start stage runs. If the agent is not active, phēnix does not create the forward. phēnix creates these forwards as the user bot, so you must activate them in your tunneler. phēnix reads this annotation even when phenix/default-apps is false.

port forwards for one VM
spec:
  nodes:
    - annotations:
        phenix/startup-autotunnel:
          - "8080:80"
          - "5901:VNC"
      general:
        hostname: web-01
      # remaining node configuration omitted

docs.title: ntp App
docs.text:
The ntp app configures experiment VMs to use a NTP server in the experiment.

There are two ways to configure the NTP app:

  • By specifying a VM node in the Topology with the label ntp-server, with the value for the label being the interface name to use as a destination IP for NTP clients. This method will result in all VMs with an os_type of linux, rhel, centos, or windows, and all nodes of type Router, in the Topology being configured for NTP.
  • By setting defaultSource in the ntp app metadata in Scenario. This method requires all VMs to be configured as NTP clients be listed in the hosts attribute.

If any node has the ntp-server label, phēnix uses the label method and ignores the ntp app metadata.

For a Vyatta or VyOS router, the vrouter app also writes the NTP server into the router configuration. With the label method, it uses the address of the labeled node's interface on the MGMT VLAN (in any letter case), not the interface that the label names. If the labeled node has no interface on that VLAN, the router uses the app metadata. With app metadata, a router listed in hosts must set client: ntp; another value causes an error.

docs.title: NTP Scenario Options
docs.text:
These are only needed if not using the VM label method as explained above.

  • defaultSource: NTP server to use if no label is specified in topology
    • hostname: hostname of NTP server in the topology to use as the source
    • interface: interface name from which IP will be extracted to configure clients. Note that this name must be the name of the interface in the phenix Topology.
    • address: IP address to use as the NTP server. This takes precedence over other configs, and can be used to configure an external NTP server (e.g. hardware clock).
  • hosts: list of hosts to configure NTP options for, including clients and server. Each host must set client or server. If a host sets both, phēnix uses client.
    • client: what NTP service is used by the client, and thus what configuration file will be changed. Available options are ntp, chrony, systemd, and windows.
      • ntp: /etc/ntp.conf, for the ntp daemon (sudo apt install ntp)
      • chrony: /etc/chrony/chrony.conf, for chronyd (sudo apt install chrony). Recommended for VMs that may not be able to reach the NTP server immediately at startup — the config is tuned to retry aggressively and step the clock quickly once the server becomes reachable.
      • systemd: /etc/systemd/timesyncd.conf, for systemd-timesyncd
      • windows: /phenix/startup/25-ntp.ps1, which will configure Windows NTP using w32tm
    • server: what NTP service is used by the server. Available options are ntpd and chronyd. If unset, the NTP server won't be configured.
      • ntpd: /etc/ntp.conf, for the ntp daemon
      • chronyd: /etc/chrony/chrony.conf, for chronyd. Default path is for Debian/Ubuntu — other distros may use /etc/chrony.conf.
    • source: Override source options for this client VM. Available options are the same as defaultSource. For a server, source sets its upstream NTP server. Without it, the server uses its own clock; a server does not use defaultSource.

docs.title: NTP Label Example
docs.text:
Example of the ntp app using a VM label in a Topology. Note that with this option, the NTP VM must be configured manually via an inject or other method.

ntp example scenario using VM label
spec:
  apps:
    - name: ntp
ntp example topology using VM label
spec:
  nodes:
    - general:
        description: Network Time server
        hostname: ntp
      labels:
        ntp-server: eth0  # this tells ntp app to use eth0 on this VM
      hardware:
        drives:
          - image: bennu.qc2
        os_type: linux
      network:
        interfaces:
          - address: 172.17.0.11
            gateway: 172.17.0.1
            mask: 24
            name: eth0
            proto: static
            type: ethernet
            vlan: example
          - address: 172.16.1.14
            mask: 16
            name: mgmt
            proto: static
            type: ethernet
            vlan: MGMT

docs.title: NTP App Metadata Example
docs.text:
Example of the ntp app using app metadata to configure the server and clients.

ntp example scenario with app metadata
spec:
  apps:
    - name: ntp
      metadata:
        defaultSource:
          hostname: ntp-server
          interface: eth0
      hosts:
        - hostname: ntp-server
          metadata:
            server: ntpd         # serve time using ntpd
        - hostname: chrony-host
          metadata:
            client: chrony
        - hostname: ntp-host
          metadata:
            client: ntp
        - hostname: systemd-host
          metadata:
            client: systemd
            source:
              hostname: other-ntp-server # use a different NTP server for this client
              interface: eth1            # address extracted from topology host|iface pair
        - hostname: windows-host
          metadata:
            client: windows
            source:
              address: 172.16.1.14  # use a specific IP instead of in-experiment host|iface
ntp example topology with app metadata
spec:
  nodes:
    - general:
        description: Network Time server
        hostname: ntp-server
      hardware:
        drives:
          - image: bennu.qc2
        os_type: linux
      network:
        interfaces:
          - address: 172.17.0.11
            gateway: 172.17.0.1
            mask: 24
            name: eth0
            proto: static
            type: ethernet
            vlan: example
          - address: 172.16.1.14
            mask: 16
            name: mgmt
            proto: static
            type: ethernet
            vlan: MGMT

docs.title: serial App
docs.text:
The serial app configures the serial interfaces of Linux VMs. It needs no scenario configuration: it reads the network interfaces of type serial from the topology (see the Interface Schema for their settings).

For each VM with an os_type of linux and at least one serial interface, the app generates a script that starts a socat process for each serial interface. The process creates a pseudo-terminal at the device path of the interface, at its baud_rate, and carries the serial traffic over UDP multicast on its udp_port. The script also adds a route for multicast traffic through the address of the interface.

The app adds the script to the VM as a disk injection at /etc/phenix/serial-startup.bash, along with the serial-startup.service systemd unit that runs the script each time the VM boots. The injections are added in the configure stage, and the files are generated in the pre-start stage. The guest must provide systemd, socat, ping, and route.

The serial app does not configure RHEL or CentOS guests, external nodes, or nodes with phenix/default-apps: false. Unlike the startup app, it never uses C2, so a VM whose first drive has inject_partition: 0 does not get these files.

serial interface in a topology
spec:
  nodes:
    - type: VirtualMachine
      general:
        hostname: rtu-01
      hardware:
        os_type: linux
        drives:
          - image: ubuntu.qc2
      network:
        interfaces:
          - name: S0
            vlan: SERIAL
            address: 10.0.0.1
            mask: 24
            proto: static
            type: serial
            udp_port: 8989
            baud_rate: 9600
            device: /dev/ttyS0

With this interface, /dev/ttyS0 in the VM is a 9600 baud serial port. Its traffic reaches the other VMs that have a serial interface in the same subnet (10.0.0.0/24) with UDP port 8989.

docs.title: vrouter App
docs.text:
The vrouter app supports the use of minimega's minirouter to include interface configuration, DHCP and DNS configuration, firewall rules, etc.

The app configures each topology node of type Router or Firewall with an os_type of vyatta, vyos, or minirouter. For Vyatta and VyOS, it generates a configuration in the pre-start stage and injects it into the router's disk. For minirouter, it sends minimega router commands in the post-start stage. The os_type linux is deprecated and gets the Vyatta configuration. The app skips external nodes and nodes with phenix/default-apps: false.

docs.title: vrouter Example
docs.text:
The following is an example of how the vrouter app can be configured via a Scenario configuration, showing all the possible options.

Warning

Some configuration sections only apply to Vyatta/VyOS and do nothing for a node marked as minirouter. See notes below or the source for more details.

vrouter example
spec:
  apps:
    - name: vrouter
      hosts:
        - hostname: rtr
          metadata:
            ipsec:
              - local: 10.0.10.2
                remote: 10.0.40.2
                peer: rtr2
                tunnels:
                  - local: 192.168.10.0/24
                    remote: 192.168.100.0/24
            acl:
              ingress:
                eth0: in-rules
              rulesets:
                - name: in-rules
                  default: drop
                  rules:
                    - id: 10
                      action: accept
                      description: Allow Incoming HTTP
                      source:
                        address: 192.168.0.0/24
                      destination:
                        address: 10.0.0.0/24
                        port: 80
                      protocol: tcp
                    - id: 20
                      action: accept
                      description: Allow Established
                      stateful: true
                      protocol: all
            dhcp:
              - listenAddress: 10.0.0.254
                ranges:
                  - lowAddress: 10.0.0.10
                    highAddress: 10.0.0.20
                defaultRoute: 10.0.0.254
                dnsServers:
                  - 10.0.0.254
                staticAssignments:
                  00:00:00:00:00:AA: 10.0.0.50
              - listenAddress: 192.168.0.254
                ranges:
                  - lowAddress: 192.168.0.10
                    highAddress: 192.168.0.20
                defaultRoute: 192.168.0.254
                dnsServers:
                  - 192.168.0.254
                staticAssignments:
                  "00:00:00:00:00:BB": 192.168.0.50
            dns:
              "1.2.3.4": foo.com
            snmp:
              listenAddress: 10.0.0.254
              systemName: edge-router-01
              location: "Lab A, Rack 2, U 24"
              contact: "network-admins@example.com"
              communities:
                - name: readonly-community
                  authorization: ro
                  trapTargets:
                    - 10.0.50.5
                - name: readwrite-community
                  authorization: rw
                  clients:
                    - 10.0.1.11
                  trapTargets:
                    - 10.0.50.5
            snat:
              - interface: eth0
                srcAddr: 192.168.0.0/24
                translation: masquerade
            dnat:
              - interface: eth1
                destAddr: 10.0.0.1
                dstPort: 80
                protocol: tcp
                translation: 192.168.0.250:8080
            emulators:
              - egress:
                  - eth0
                  - eth1
                name: comcast
                bandwidth: 400kbit
                delay: 500
                corruption: 5
                loss: 10
                reordering: 5

docs.title: vrouter Scenario Options
docs.text:
• ipsec: if present, point-to-point IPSec tunnels are nailed up between the list of given IP addresses and traffic between the given networks is tunneled. Each site needs local and remote (and peer on a VyOS router), and each of its tunnels needs local and remote.

    • local: Local IP address for IPSec connection with this peer. It must be the address of one of the router's interfaces in the topology. It must have a route to the remote address.

    • remote: Remote IP address or hostname for IPSec connection. IPv4 or IPv6 address is used when a peer has a public static IP address. Hostname is a DNS name which could be used when a peer has a public IP address and DNS name, but an IP address could be changed from time to time. A Vyatta router also uses it as the name of the peer connection.

    • peer: Name of peer connection. The peer name must be an alphanumeric and can have hyphen or underscore as special characters. A VyOS router uses it as the name of the site-to-site peer. A Vyatta router does not use it.

    • secret: pre-shared key for the connection. If it is not set, phēnix generates a random key of 32 letters and digits. A site on another router with the reverse local and remote addresses gets the same generated key. Thus set the same secret on both ends of a connection, or set it on neither.

    • tunnels: list of local and remote networks to tunnel through this point-to-point connection.

      • local: local network to tunnel to the given remote network.

      • remote: remote network to tunnel to the given local network.

  • acl: if present, access control lists (ACLs / firewall rules) are created on the router per the defined rulesets.

    • ingress: for each interface-to-ruleset mapping, apply the given ruleset to the given interface for inbound traffic. Note that the interface name used (in this example, eth0) refers to the name given to a network interface in the router's topology configuration.

    • egress: for each interface-to-ruleset mapping, apply the given ruleset to the given interface for outbound traffic.

    • rulesets: list of rulesets to create on the router.

      • name: name of the ruleset; used in the interface-to-ruleset mapping in the ingress/egress sections.

      • description: description of the ruleset in the Vyatta/VyOS router configuration.

      • default: default action to apply to traffic that doesn't match any rules.

      • rules: list of rules to apply to traffic.

        • id: integer to identify the order of the rules in the set.

        • description: description of the rule in the Vyatta/VyOS router configuration.

        • action: action to apply to traffic matching rule.

        • source: map describing what source to limit matching traffic to. If not provided, all sources are matched.

          • address: source address to limit matching traffic to. If not provided, all source addresses are matched.

          • port: source port to limit matching traffic to. If not provided, all source ports are matched.

        • destination: map describing what destination to limit matching traffic to. If not provided, all destinations are matched.

          • address: destination address to limit matching traffic to. If not provided, all destination addresses are matched.

          • port: destination port to limit matching traffic to. If not provided, all destination ports are matched.

        • protocol: IP protocol to limit matching traffic to. Must be provided; to allow all protocols, use the all keyword.

        • stateful: if true, enable established and related traffic for this ruleset.

  • dhcp: if present, DHCP is configured on the router per the provided list.

    • listenAddress: IP address on a local interface (e.g. this router) to bind this DHCP configuration to.

    • ranges: list of IP address low/high ranges to use for DHCP assignments. The IP addresses must be within the IP network of the listenAddress.

    • defaultRoute: default gateway to be included in DHCP leases.

    • dnsServers: list of DNS servers to be included in DHCP leases.

    • staticAssignments: map of MAC-to-IP assignments to use for static DHCP addresses.

  • dns: if present, map of IP-to-domain DNS entries to create on the router.

  • snmp: if present, SNMP is configured on the router.

    • listenAddress: IP address on a local interface to bind SNMP to. Defaults to listening on all interfaces.

    • systemName: a string describing the system.

    • location: a string for the system's physical location.

    • contact: a string for the system's contact information.

    • communities: a list of SNMP communities to configure.

      • name: the community string/name. This is required.

      • authorization: the authorization level for the community. Can be ro (read-only) or rw (read-write). Defaults to ro if not specified.

      • clients: a list of client IP addresses that are allowed to use this community.

      • trapTargets: a list of IP addresses to send SNMP traps to.

  • snat: if present, a list of source NAT rules to create on the router. phēnix numbers the rules from 100, in the order of the list.

    • interface: name of the topology interface that the translated traffic goes out of. This is required. phēnix stops with an error if the router has no interface with this name.

    • srcAddr: source address or network to match.

    • srcPort: source port to match, as an integer.

    • destAddr: destination address or network to match.

    • dstPort: destination port to match, as an integer.

    • protocol: protocol to match, for example tcp.

    • translation: masquerade, an address, or an address and a port in the form address:port. If it is not set, phēnix uses masquerade.

  • dnat: if present, a list of destination NAT rules to create on the router. phēnix numbers the rules from 100, in the order of the list. A rule takes the same keys as an snat rule, with these differences:

    • interface: name of the topology interface that the traffic comes in on. This is required.

    • translation: address, or address and port in the form address:port, to send the matched traffic to. This is required.

  • emulators: if present, a list of network emulator traffic policies to apply to one or more interfaces on egress. For each emulator in the list, only the name key is required, though the traffic policy will not get applied if there's not at least one egress interface defined. The delay, corruption, loss, and reordering values must be integers. A text value such as 500ms causes an error.

    • name: unique name of traffic policy for this router.

    • egress: list of interface names to apply traffic policy to on egress. The names listed should be the same names used for network interfaces in the topology. A name that is not an interface of the router is an error.

    • ingress: list of interface names to apply traffic policy to on ingress. Only Vyatta routers use it. VyOS routers ignore it.

    • bandwidth: maximum allowed bandwidth for interface and direction this traffic policy is applied to, for example 400kbit.

    • delay: fixed amount of time to add to all packets for interface and direction this traffic policy is applied to. On VyOS, the value is in milliseconds, from 0 to 65535.

    • corruption: percentage of corrupted packets for interface and direction this traffic policy is applied to, from 0 to 100.

    • loss: percentage of lost packets for interface and direction this traffic policy is applied to, from 0 to 100.

    • reordering: percentage of reordered packets for interface and direction this traffic policy is applied to, from 0 to 100.

Important

The ingress and egress setting for ACLs are from the perspective of the network segment the specified interface is connected to, not from the perspective of the interface itself. For example, if eth0 on a router is connected to VLAN EXP_01, then specifying eth0: in-rules for the ingress setting means the rules specified in the in-rules ruleset will be applied to packets "ingressing into" VLAN EXP_01. Under the hood, the rules are actually applied to packets "egressing out of" interface eth0.

Note

Currently, the ipsec, emulators, snmp, and snat/dnat metadata sections only apply to Vyatta/VyOS routers.

Note

If the host metadata has no snat rules, phēnix uses the nat settings of the router in the topology. For each ethernet interface named in in that has proto: static, phēnix masquerades the network of that interface out of the out interface. Scenario snat rules replace the topology nat settings, and dnat rules do not change them.

Note

Currently, the stateful setting for ACL rules only applies to Vyatta/VyOS routers.

Note

Currently, the dhcp and dns metadata sections only apply to minirouter routers.

Note

Currently, the only emulator policy used is network-emulator and on VyOS routers it only applies to outbound traffic (egress).

docs.title: Router Node Annotations
docs.text:
Set the node annotation vrouter/enable-ssh on a Vyatta or VyOS router to enable its SSH service. The value is an IP address, or the name of one of the router's topology interfaces. SSH listens on that address, or on the address of that interface. If the value is neither, phēnix does not enable SSH.

Set the node annotation vrouter/vyos-password on a VyOS router to set the password of its vyos user. Without the annotation, the router keeps the password of its image. The value must be a string with no single quote (') and no control character.

enable SSH on a router
spec:
  nodes:
    - annotations:
        vrouter/enable-ssh: eth2
      type: Router
      general:
        hostname: rtr
      hardware:
        os_type: vyos
      # remaining node configuration omitted

docs.title: Additional Core Apps
docs.text:
The apps listed below are provided by the core phenix application, but are not considered default apps since they do not get applied to every experiment by default. They're more like a user app, but implemented in the core application instead of as a stand-alone executable.

scorch Scorch — SCenario ORCHestration — is an automated scenario orchestration framework within phenix soh provide state of health monitoring for an experiment tap manage host taps (typically used for external network access) for an experiment

docs.title: tap App
docs.text:
The tap app manages the creation and removal of host taps needed by experiments to access external network resources. This includes creating the tap in a network namespace (netns) to avoid interface address collisions with other experiments, connecting the netns with the system network to enable external network access, and modifying iptables to allow external network access from the tapped experiment VLAN.

Note

Host taps can also be used to access VM network resources directly from the host the VM is running on. This is an advanced topic that will be documented soon.

In order for a tap to have access to experiment VMs in the tapped VLAN, it must have an IP address on the same subnet as the rest of the VMs in the VLAN. Attempting to tap multiple experiments could fail if the VLANs being tapped are using the same subnet, so the tap is put into a netns to provide isolation and avoid address collisions.

With the tap in a netns, however, it no longer has a path to external networks via the system's default netns. To remedy this, a veth pair is used to connect the tap's netns with the default netns. A very small (/30) IP subnet is used for the veth pair, and phenix manages the selection and tracking of the subnets used for each pair to avoid collisions.

With the veth pair in place, packets from the experiment VLAN can now be routed externally with the help of IP masquerading in both the tap's netns and the default netns.

Warning

This has not been fully tested against all the possible iptables firewall configurations. If you experience problems with external access, it may be due to a more restrictive iptables configuration than we've tested with.

By default, the host taps are created during the experiment's post-start stage. The optional stage metadata option can be used to instead create the taps during the pre-start stage, which is useful when other apps or VMs need the taps to already exist when the experiment starts. Valid values are pre-start and post-start; when unset, it defaults to post-start to preserve backwards compatibility.

The taps are created on the experiment host running the fewest VMs, the first by name among hosts with equally few, so every run places them the same way. Each tap must name a different VLAN. When externalAccess.enabled is true, ip must be an address in CIDR form, such as 172.20.5.254/24.

The following is an example of how the tap app can be configured via a Scenario configuration, showing all the possible options.

Note

The externalAccess.firewall portion of the tap configuration has not been implemented yet.

tap app example
spec:
  apps:
    - name: tap
      metadata:
        # the experiment lifecycle stage to create the taps in -- valid values
        # are 'pre-start' and 'post-start' (will default to 'post-start' if not
        # provided)
        stage: post-start
        taps:
            # the bridge to add the tap to (will default to the experiment's default
            # bridge, 'phenix' unless changed, if not provided)
          - bridge: phenix
            # the experiment VLAN to tap
            vlan: MGMT
            # IP address to use for host tap -- VMs on the tapped VLAN would use this
            # address as their gateway if they need external access (and it's enabled
            # below)
            ip: 172.20.5.254/24
            # IP subnet to use for veth pair between host and tap's network
            # namespace when external access is enabled (will default to a /30
            # subnet that is not already in use by any other running experiment if
            # not provided; if this subnet is in use, the next unused subnet of
            # the same size is used)
            subnet: 10.213.47.8/30
            externalAccess:
              # defaults to false
              enabled: true
              # this section is planned, but not implemented yet
              firewall:
                # default action to take if none of the rules below match a packet
                default: drop
                rules:
                    # action to take if a packet matches this rule
                  - action: accept
                    description: Only allow web access
                    source:
                      # can also use `addresses` to specify a list of addresses
                      address: 172.20.5.0/29
                    destination:
                      address: 10.0.0.0/24
                      # can also use `port` to specify a single port
                      ports: [80, 443]
                    # can also use `protocols` to specify a list of protocols
                    protocol: tcp

docs.title: User Apps
docs.text:
phenix user apps are stand-alone executables that phenix shells out to at different stages of the experiment lifecycle ( configure, pre-start, post-start, running, and cleanup). When phenix encounters an app in an experiment scenario that isn't a default app, it checks to see if an executable exists in its current PATH in the form of phenix-app-<app-name>. If the executable exists, phenix shells out to it, providing the current lifecycle stage as an argument and providing the experiment metadata, spec, and status as a JSON string over STDIN.

Note

There will always be three (3) top-level keys available in the JSON passed to a user app over STDIN: metadata, spec, and status. For the configure and pre-start stages, the status value will be null or otherwise ignored. The spec value will be experiment schema. phēnix also adds hosts (the schedulable cluster hosts) and vms (the experiment VMs that minimega reports), and leaves each out when it is empty.

Tip

You can run phenix util app-json <exp-name> to see an example of what the JSON that's passed to a user app looks like.

Note

The runtime hosts that a user app gets have no diskusage field. phēnix does not measure the disk usage of the hosts for user apps. A user scheduler gets the disk usage of the schedulable hosts.

Tip

You can also get this JSON from the REST API with GET /api/v1/experiments/{name}/apps/input.

The user app can modify the experiment at will, then return the updated JSON over STDOUT and exit with a 0 status. If the user app encounters an error, it should print error messages to STDERR and exit with a non-zero status. Logs written to STDERR must be single-line JSON objects containing level and msg fields to be fully integrated into the phēnix centralized logging system. A type field with a phēnix log type, such as SCORCH, sets the log type of the record. phēnix does not accept the AUDIT or SECURITY type from an app. A field with the same name as a phēnix field, such as time or app, gets the proc_ prefix.

Note

phenix will only process updates to the spec value for the configure, pre-start, and cleanup stages, and will only process updates to the status value for the post-start, running, and cleanup stages. More specifically, it will only process updates to status.apps.<app-name>, which can be anything the app wants it to be (e.g. a simple string, an array, or a map/dictionary).

Note

It is possible for the execution of app stages to be canceled by the caller. In the case of user apps, phenix will send a SIGTERM to the user app process and wait a maximum of 10 seconds for the process to exit gracefully before killing the process with a SIGKILL.

Note

phēnix won't start an app's running stage (a Scorch run, for example) while that app is still running a stage. If phēnix stops partway through, phenix ui clears this when it starts again, so you don't need to restart the experiment to run the app.

docs.title: Available User Apps
docs.text:
The sandialabs/sceptre-phenix-apps repo is home to some user apps that have already been created by the community, including the following:

App Link Description caldera caldera source Deployment and orchestration of MITRE Caldera in an experiment helics helics source Aids in the generation of HELICS broker start scripts and injects them into the appropriate nodes in an experiment ignition ignition source Configures an Inductive Automation Ignition Gateway 8.3 SCADA master at experiment start mgmt_tap mgmt_tap source Creates a tap on the management network of an experiment, allowing a user to copy files to and from VMs connected to that network mirror mirror source The mirror app configures cluster-wide packet mirroring for specific VLANs to a specific interface on a predefined node using GRE tunnels. It is written in Golang. ot-sim otsim source Aids in the generation of config files for OT-sim protonuke protonuke source Configures the protonuke traffic generator scale scale source Specialized phenix application designed for high-volume simulations sceptre sceptre source Core functionality for SCEPTRE, including generating configs for field devices (bennu), SCADA systems, and other systems. wind-turbine wind_turbine source Deprecated in favor of the wind_turbine plugin of the scale app. Aids in the generation of wind-turbine-specific OT-sim config files wireguard wireguard source Configures Wireguard on VMs

In addition, this repo also contains some generic library/utility code for making custom user app development easier. See the README for additional details.

docs.title: mgmt_tap App
docs.text:
The mgmt_tap application creates tap interfaces on the management network of an experiment, enabling file transfer and remote access to virtual machines within the experiment. Unlike the tap app, it is a user app, so its phenix-app-mgmt_tap executable must be installed. The mgmt_tap:

  • Creates taps on the configured VLAN (defaults to MGMT) on all compute hosts in the experiment
  • Automatically assigns sequential IPs from a configurable subnet
  • Removes taps during cleanup phase

The following is an example of how the default mgmt_tap app can be configured via a Scenario configuration.

mgmt_tap app default example
spec:
  apps:
    - name: mgmt_tap

This creates tap interfaces on all hosts with IPs 172.16.0.1/16, 172.16.0.2/16, etc. on the MGMT VLAN.

The following is an example of how the mgmt_tap app can be configured via a Scenario configuration with optional settings subnet and vlan.

mgmt_tap app optional example
spec:
  apps:
    - name: mgmt_tap
      metadata:
        subnet: 10.0.0.0/24
        vlan: INTERNAL

This creates tap interfaces with IPs 10.0.0.1/24, 10.0.0.2/24, etc. on the INTERNAL VLAN.

The optional bridge setting names the bridge to create the taps on. It defaults to the default bridge of the experiment.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A very contrived example of a simple user app, which changes the disk image used for every node in the experiment topology, is in A Minimal User App.

Tip

Additional information on runnable reference user apps can be found in the Examples section.

  • phenix experiment apps: list the apps that a scenario can use.
  • phenix experiment trigger: run a stage of an app by hand.
