docs.title: Bridge Mode
docs.text: phēnix uses Open vSwitch (OVS) bridges managed by minimega to connect VMs to virtual networks. The bridge mode setting controls how phēnix names the default OVS bridge assigned to each experiment.

docs.title: manual (Default)
docs.text:
In manual mode, the bridge name for an experiment comes from the default bridge name supplied when the experiment is created — the --default-bridge flag on phenix experiment create, the Default Bridge Name field in the UI's Advanced Options section, or the defaultBridge key in a workflow file. It is a property of the experiment, not of the topology it uses. If no bridge name is provided, phēnix falls back to the shared default bridge named phenix.

This means that unless you explicitly assign a unique bridge name when creating an experiment, all experiments using manual mode that have no custom bridge name configured will share the same phenix bridge.

docs.title: auto
docs.text:
In auto mode, phēnix automatically assigns each experiment's own name as its default bridge name. This gives every experiment a unique bridge without any manual configuration, and the Default Bridge Name field is hidden in the UI's experiment creation form because it would have no effect.

Warning

Because OVS bridge names are limited to 15 characters, experiment names must be 15 characters or fewer when using auto bridge mode. phēnix will return an error if you attempt to create or update an experiment with a longer name while auto mode is active.

When an experiment stops in auto mode, phēnix deletes the bridge named after the experiment on each of its hosts, unless another running experiment uses it. minimega keeps an OVS bridge that it did not create. In manual mode, phēnix leaves bridges alone.

docs.title: Bridge Names and Topologies
docs.text: The experiment's default bridge is applied to every node interface in the topology that does not name a bridge of its own. An interface that explicitly sets a bridge other than phenix in the topology keeps that value, in both manual and auto mode. Bear this in mind when using auto mode for isolation: topology-pinned bridges are left untouched and can still be shared between experiments.

docs.title: Bridge Name Collisions
docs.text:
Two experiments may not share the same default bridge name unless that name is the shared phenix bridge. Creating or updating an experiment whose default bridge is already claimed by another experiment fails with:

experiment <other-experiment> already using default bridge <bridge-name>

Because auto mode derives the bridge name from the (necessarily unique) experiment name, this collision cannot occur in auto mode.

docs.title: Why Bridge Mode Matters
docs.text:
Giving each experiment a unique bridge name has two important benefits:

  1. Network isolation — Experiments sharing the phenix bridge are kept apart by VLAN alone. Giving each experiment its own bridge adds a second layer of separation, so a VLAN misconfiguration or overlapping VLAN range cannot bridge traffic between two experiments on the same host.

  2. Netflow capture — phēnix's netflow feature only works for experiments that have a bridge name other than the default phenix bridge. Using auto mode (or manually specifying a unique bridge name per experiment) is therefore a prerequisite for per-experiment netflow capture.

docs.title: Configuring Bridge Mode
docs.text: Bridge mode is a global setting applied at the phēnix server level. It can be set in three ways, listed from highest to lowest precedence:

docs.title: 1. Command Line Flag
docs.text:
--bridge-mode is a global flag accepted by any phēnix subcommand, but it is only consulted when an experiment is created or updated. Passing it to phenix exp start or any other subcommand has no effect, because the bridge name was already fixed when the experiment was created.

# Run the UI server in auto mode; every experiment created through it gets a
# bridge named after the experiment.
phenix ui --bridge-mode auto

# Create a single experiment in auto mode from the CLI.
phenix experiment create my-exp -t my-topology --bridge-mode auto

docs.title: 2. Environment Variable
docs.text:
export PHENIX_BRIDGE_MODE=auto
phenix ui

docs.title: 3. Configuration File
docs.text:
Add bridge-mode to the phēnix configuration file (see Settings & Configuration for file locations):

bridge-mode: auto

docs.title: Example Workflow
docs.text:
The following shows how to start the phēnix UI server in auto mode so that all experiments automatically receive unique bridges:

phenix ui --bridge-mode auto

With the server running in auto mode, creating a new experiment requires the name to be 15 characters or fewer:

# Works — name is within the 15-character limit
phenix experiment create my-exp -t my-topology

# Fails — name is too long for auto bridge mode
phenix experiment create my-very-long-experiment-name -t my-topology

docs.title: Relationship to Netflow
docs.text:
The netflow feature captures network flows from the OVS bridge used by an experiment, but it explicitly excludes the shared default phenix bridge to prevent flows from multiple experiments being mixed together.

Setting bridge mode to auto is the simplest way to satisfy this requirement across all experiments. Alternatively, in manual mode you can specify a unique --default-bridge name per experiment at creation time:

phenix experiment create my-exp -t my-topology --default-bridge my-exp-br

See the Netflow page for more details on enabling and using netflow capture.

docs.title: Settings Reference
docs.text: Setting Key Environment Variable Default Description bridge-mode PHENIX_BRIDGE_MODE manual Bridge naming mode for experiments. auto uses the experiment name as the bridge name; manual uses the user-specified bridge name, or phenix if not specified.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• VLANs: VLAN aliases, ranges and the VLANs page.
  • GRE Mesh: carry VLANs between cluster hosts over GRE tunnels.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
phenix currently supports six (6) different configuration file types:

  1. Topology
  2. Scenario
  3. Experiment
  4. Image
  5. User
  6. Role

A Workflow file (apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v0) is not a stored config: phenix workflow apply sends it with each apply (see Workflow).

Typically, users will create Topology and Scenario configuration files by hand (or a topology with the Builder), while the rest will be generated by phenix using available commands. However, it is possible to create all configuration file types by hand if necessary.

Tip

Configuration files can also be created, viewed, edited, and deleted via the Web-UI (see Web-UI section below).

Configuration files are versioned using a header section based heavily on what Kubernetes does. Each configuration file will have a header section that looks like the following:

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Topology
metadata:
  name: foobar
spec:
  ...

In the example above, the kind field represents the type of configuration file (e.g., Topology, Scenario, Image). The apiVersion field represents the version the spec section conforms to (currently there is only v1 for all configuration types except Scenario, which is v2), and the spec section will contain the actual details for the configuration type based on the configuration schema. Note that, at least in the header section, keys are camel-case and begin with a lowercase letter, while values are camel-cased but begin with a capital letter.

Info

Throughout the documentation, we mention creating configurations manually. When we say this, we mean passing a YAML or JSON configuration file of any type to the phenix config create command.

phenix config create, phenix config apply and phenix config diff take files only: each argument is a .json, .yaml or .yml file, and a directory is an error. To read every file of a directory, give dir/* in a shell, such as phenix config create configs/*. The shell replaces dir/* with the files of the directory before phēnix starts. A subdirectory in the match is an error, so use dir/*.yml when the directory has one. Use dir/*.yml when the directory also holds files that are not configurations. The commands refuse a Builder document (see Builder documents and phenix config create).

The first time phēnix runs with a new store, it also creates each config that it finds below <base-dir.phenix>/configs (by default /phenix/configs). It sets BRANCH_NAME to the name of the folder that holds the file, and skips a file that parses but is not a valid config. A file that does not parse stops the start with an error.

A config name can contain only letters, digits, _, @, . and -.

The metadata section can also hold annotations: text values by key, such as the topology and scenario annotations of an Experiment. The exception is builder-doc, a map of digest, id and path that names the Builder diagram of a Topology (see The builder-doc annotation).

docs.title: Revisions
docs.text:
Every stored config gets metadata.created, metadata.updated and metadata.revision, a number that increases each time the config is written. phēnix sets these itself and ignores them in what you send.

metadata:
  name: foobar
  created: "2026-10-14T09:12:44-06:00"
  updated: "2026-10-14T09:30:02-06:00"
  revision: 42

If someone else saves the config while you're in phenix config edit, your save is refused with <kind/name> changed while you edited it, so run phenix config edit again.

docs.title: Applying Files
docs.text:
phenix config apply creates the configs in the given files that aren't stored yet, and updates the stored ones that are different. phenix config diff prints a unified diff first and changes nothing. Both ignore the fields phēnix sets, such as the revision.

phenix config diff ./configs/*
phenix config apply ./configs/* --dry-run
phenix config apply ./configs/*

apply skips User configs, and can't update the config of a running experiment. diff exits with 0 when nothing differs, 1 when something does, and 2 when it can't compare a config.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
The Topology configuration is one of the core configuration types for phenix, as it describes a network topology to be deployed in minimega that can be used by one or more experiments to be executed.

A topology is comprised of one or more nodes, which can either be a VM (external: false - the default) or an external node (external: true), each including system descriptions and configurations, as well as any networking settings required to connect all of the nodes in a topology together. This configuration becomes the basis for most of the minimega commands later created in the relevant minimega startup script (at least for internal VMs).

Topologies can also include other topologies, using the includeTopologies key. This feature allows users to include common components from an existing topology. These includes can come from either the phēnix store (by name) or from a file path to a topology on disk. Included topologies are merged into the including topology.

# ...
includeTopologies:
- /phenix/topologies/foo.yml
- bar-from-store
nodes:
# ...

phēnix looks for each name in the store first, then for a file at that path. It adds the nodes of each included topology after the nodes of the including topology. A hostname that is in both is an error, and so is a topology that includes itself through other topologies. A topology needs nodes, includeTopologies, or both.

docs.title: Default Settings
docs.text:
If left unmodified or unset, the following are the default settings for each node:

  • external will be set to false
  • memory will be set to 512MB
  • vcpus will be set to 1
  • cpu will be set to Broadwell
  • vm_type will be set to kvm
  • snapshot will be set to true
  • no network settings will be included
  • an interface without a bridge uses the default bridge of the experiment (phenix unless the experiment sets another)

docs.title: Required Values
docs.text:
Each topology must have a unique name, which should be lowercase and not include spaces. In addition, each node in the topology must:

  • have a specified type — the available types are defined in the schema
  • have a unique hostname (phēnix ignores letter case when it compares them)
  • have an OS type (os_type) of centos, linux, minirouter, rhel, vyatta, vyos, windows, or other
  • have a disk image assigned

Warning

Hostnames must be between 2 and 63 characters long, can only contain alphanumeric characters and hyphens, and cannot begin or end with a hyphen. Hostnames should not be used as a FQDN. The 2-character minimum comes from guest operating systems: VyOS and Windows both reject 1-character hostnames.

docs.title: Optional Values
docs.text:
Optional values for a node in the topology configuration can include:

  • static network configurations
  • specific memory values (e.g., 1-16GB)
  • specific VCPUs values (e.g., 1-4)
  • additional disk storage
  • file injections (and main disk inject partition)
  • labels, which are typically used by phēnix apps (for example the ntp-server label of the ntp app)
  • annotations, such as phenix/default-apps (see Disable Default Apps for a VM)
  • routing ruleset(s)
  • delay triggered by user, timer, or c2 (command and control)
  • deletions, advanced, overrides, and commands (see the node schemas)

Warning

If not specified, the default disk partition to inject files into is 1. This will fail for a disk that is using LVM. In order to use a disk image that's using LVM, set inject_partition: 0 on the first drive to force phēnix to skip disk injections but still snapshot the base image. The startup app will automatically deliver its generated scripts through C2; other files configured for injection are still skipped. See C2 Startup Script Delivery for the requirements and configuration options.

Note

On Windows nodes, injection and deletion paths match existing files regardless of case. The inject partition must be NTFS, and the minimega host needs lowntfs-3g; without it, minimega silently falls back to a case-sensitive mount.

docs.title: Delay Start
docs.text:
It is possible to delay the start of a VM with the delay value. There are three options available to set, but only one option can be set:

  1. user is a boolean value and when set to true the VM will require a manual start either through the phēnix UI or command line (the latter can be by phēnix or minimega commands).

  2. timer is a Golang duration string such as 30s, 5m, or 1h30m. A timer that is not a duration is rejected.

  3. c2 requires minimega command and control. Note in the example below that the hostname AD1 will be delayed starting until the VM host-00 has started and checked in with minimega command and control. It is possible to have multiple hostnames included. useUUID is an additional boolean value setting, per hostname, that will watch for the UUID instead of the hostname to register with minimega command and control.

Note

If one or more VMs are set with a delayed start, the UI will display a blue tag in the Delay column next to the Screenshot column. The tag will indicate what type of delay was set. Once all the delayed VMs have started, the Delay column will no longer be visible. For a timer delay, the tag and the VM details card show the time until the VM starts, for example starts in 4m 12s.

While VMs wait for a delayed start, the summary at the top of the running experiment page shows a blue tag, for example 2 delayed VMs waiting, next to the Running status. When a VM waits for a timer, the tag also shows the time until the next VM starts, for example 2 delayed VMs waiting, next starts in 4m 12s. The VMs tile of the summary also shows the number of delayed VMs. To see the tiles, click Details in the summary.

Note

If phenix ui restarts while timer or c2 delayed VMs are still waiting, it picks them back up. If minimega no longer has a delayed VM, the experiment is marked interrupted and its post-start apps don't run. Restart the experiment to run them.

docs.title: Network Address Translation (NAT)
docs.text:
For nodes of type Router or Firewall with an os_type of vyatta or vyos (or the deprecated linux), the vrouter app can configure basic source NAT to masquerade packets from one or more networks out a specific interface. For example, assume a router has three interfaces — eth0, eth1, eth2. eth0 is connected to the Internet, while eth1, eth2 are connected to networks that use private IP space. To masquerade packets from eth1, eth2 out eth0 the following configuration could be used.

network:
  nat:
    - out: eth0
      in:
        - eth1
        - eth2

out and each in entry are interface names of the node, not networks. The app masquerades the network of each in interface whose type is ethernet and proto is static. It uses this nat list only when the vrouter app metadata for the node has no snat rules.

docs.title: External Nodes
docs.text:
There may be cases where an experiment includes external devices (hardware in the loop) that should still be included in the topology for the purposes of the State of Health network diagram, state of health reachability checks, or for use by custom user apps. External nodes can be included in the topology by marking them as external: true. Among other things, this will prevent them from being deployed as a VM in minimega. The configuration schema for an external node in the topology is defined in the external node schema.

Danger

Do not use external: false for internal nodes that should be deployed in minimega. Instead, don't include the external configuration key at all. This is a quirk of how we internally decide which node schema should be used (via oneOf).

An external node still requires a type, general.hostname, and (if you want it to show up connected to anything in the topology graph) a network section, just like a regular node. However, the external_node schema is intentionally simpler than the schema used for minimega-deployed nodes:

  • there is no drives key (external nodes have no disk image to snapshot or inject files into)
  • there is no routes, ospf, or rulesets support, and phenix ignores injections, delay, advanced, and commands (the schema accepts them), since none of those apply to a device that phenix doesn't deploy or control
  • network interfaces only support the flat set of fields shown in the external_node schema (name, proto, address, mask, gateway, vlan). There's no oneOf between static/dhcp/serial interface types like there is for minimega nodes
- type: HIL
  external: true
  general:
    hostname: plc-01
    description: Physical PLC on the test bench
  hardware:
    os_type: linux
  network:
    interfaces:
    - name: eth0
      vlan: EXP-1
      address: 192.168.10.50
      mask: 24
      proto: static

docs.title: Special and Edge Cases
docs.text:
• Not deployed, not monitored by C2. External nodes are never started in minimega and never run miniccc, so they're excluded from the automated State of Health checks (network config, listening ports, processes, CPU load, etc.) that rely on C2. Their IP address(es) are still gathered from the topology, though, so they can be used as the src or dst of a testCustomReachability entry to ping-test connectivity to/from the external device.
  • skipHosts doesn't apply. Since external nodes are already skipped from C2-based monitoring, the SoH skipHosts setting has no effect on them.
  • Interfaces on the MGMT or MIRROR VLANs are ignored in the graph. The SoH topology graph builder skips any interface whose VLAN is MGMT or MIRROR (case-insensitive) when drawing connections, regardless of whether the node is external or a regular VM.
  • vlan can be omitted, but then the node won't be connected to anything. If an external node's interface doesn't specify a vlan, or the interface is left off entirely, the node will still appear in the SoH topology graph as an isolated node with no lines connecting it to anything else.
  • Getting a line drawn in the graph. To have phenix draw a line between an external node and other nodes in the SoH topology graph, give the external node a network.interfaces[].vlan value that exactly matches the vlan value used on the interface(s) of the node(s) you want it connected to (the VLAN name acts as the shared switch/interface node in the graph). It doesn't matter whether the matching nodes are VMs or other external nodes — any two nodes sharing a VLAN name will be connected in the graph.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A contrived, four node example — three VMs and a router — is given below, and is driven by the topology schema described here.

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Topology
metadata:
  name: foobar
spec:
  nodes:
  - type: VirtualMachine
    general:
      hostname: host-00
      snapshot: true
    delay:
      user: true
    hardware:
      os_type: linux
      drives:
      - image: ubuntu.qc2
    injections:
      - src: foo/bar/sucka.fish
        dst: /data/sucka.fish
      - src: /foo/bar/sucka/fish.sh
        dst: /data/fish.sh
    network:
      interfaces:
      - name: IF0
        vlan: EXP-1
        address: 192.168.10.1
        mask: 24
        gateway: 192.168.10.254
        proto: static
        type: ethernet
      - name: IF1
        vlan: MGMT
        address: 172.16.10.1
        mask: 16
        proto: static
        type: ethernet
  - type: VirtualMachine
    general:
      hostname: host-01
      snapshot: true
      do_not_boot: false
    delay:
      timer: 5m
    hardware:
      os_type: linux
      drives:
      - image: ubuntu.qc2
    network:
      interfaces:
      - name: IF0
        vlan: EXP-1
        address: 192.168.10.2
        mask: 24
        gateway: 192.168.10.254
        proto: static
        type: ethernet
      - name: IF1
        vlan: MGMT
        address: 172.16.10.2
        mask: 16
        proto: static
        type: ethernet
      - name: S0
        vlan: EXT
        address: 10.0.0.1
        mask: 24
        proto: static
        type: serial
        udp_port: 8989
        baud_rate: 9600
        device: /dev/ttyS0
  - type: VirtualMachine
    general:
      hostname: AD1
      snapshot: true
    delay:
      c2:
      - hostname: host-00
        useUUID: false
    hardware:
      os_type: windows
      drives:
      - image: win-svr-2k8.qc2
    network:
      interfaces:
      - name: IF0
        vlan: EXP-1
        address: 192.168.10.250
        mask: 24
        gateway: 192.168.10.254
        proto: static
        type: ethernet
      - name: IF1
        vlan: MGMT
        address: 172.16.10.3
        mask: 16
        proto: static
        type: ethernet
  - type: Router
    labels:
      ntp-server: IF0
    general:
      hostname: router-00
      snapshot: true
    hardware:
      os_type: vyatta
      drives:
      - image: vyatta.qc2
    network:
      interfaces:
      - name: IF0
        vlan: EXP-1
        address: 192.168.10.254
        mask: 24
        proto: static
        type: ethernet
        ruleset_in: test
      - name: IF1
        vlan: MGMT
        address: 172.16.10.254
        mask: 16
        proto: static
        type: ethernet
      rulesets:
      - name: test
        default: drop
        rules:
        - id: 10
          action: accept
          protocol: udp
          source:
            address: 1.1.1.1
            port: 53

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The Scenario configuration is used to define and configure one or more phenix apps (default or user) for use with a topology. In this sense, a topology can have one or more scenarios associated with it, but a scenario can only be associated with a single topology.

The scenario names its topology in its topology annotation. phēnix refuses to use a scenario without this annotation in an experiment.

docs.title: Apps
docs.text:
A phenix app can be applied to an experiment topology using a single configuration, a per-host configuration, or both. Examples could include:

  • a phenix app that adds a minimega tap to all hosts in the cluster,
  • one that injects the same file into every node in the experiment topology, or
  • one that configures a VPN between two nodes in an experiment using WireGuard.

The first two examples would involve a single configuration, while the last example would use a per-host configuration because (1) only two nodes will be modified, and (2) each of the two nodes will require different configurations (e.g., one will be a WireGuard client and the other a WireGuard server). Each configured app can contain a list of topology nodes to apply the app to, along with custom metadata for the app specific to the topology node.

docs.title: App Configuration Options
docs.text:
• assetDir: used by apps to generate absolute path to asset files when relative paths are provided in app metadata. The default is an empty string.

  • disabled: when true, phēnix skips the app at the configure, pre-start, post-start, and cleanup stages. A trigger of the running stage still runs it, and so does a trigger that names the app. A pending cleanup of the app also still runs. The default is false.

  • fromScenario: name of another scenario config to pull this app config from. This allows for defining complex app configurations in a single base scenario and referencing it from scenarios included in experiments. The default is an empty string.

  • hosts: a list of per-host configurations to apply to the experiment topology. The default is nil.

    • hostname: the name of the experiment VM to apply this per-host metadata to.

    • metadata: app metadata to apply to this experiment VM. The default is nil.

  • metadata: app metadata to apply to this experiment. The default is nil.

  • name: the name of the app being configured. There is no default value; one must be provided.

  • runPeriodically: a Golang duration string specifying how often to trigger the app's running stage. The default value is an empty string, which means the app's running stage will not be triggered periodically.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The following is an example of a configuration for a scenario named foobar, which can only be applied to an accompanying topology named foobar (while these names are the same in this example, the topology and scenario names do not have to match). Included in this scenario are apps named miniccc-injector, startup, protonuke, and wireguard. Each entry in the list of app hosts includes custom app metadata and the hostname of the topology node to apply the metadata.

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v2
kind: Scenario
metadata:
  name: foobar
  annotations:
    topology: foobar
spec:
  apps:
  - name: miniccc-injector
    metadata:
      # files to inject into each node in experiment, based on OS type
      linux:
        src: /phenix/injects/miniccc
        dst: /usr/local/bin/miniccc
      windows:
        src: /phenix/injects/miniccc.exe
        dst: phenix/miniccc.exe
  - name: startup
    hosts:
    - hostname: host-00 # hostname of topology node to apply it to
      metadata:
        domain_controller:
          domain: example.com
          ip: 10.0.0.1
          username: admin
          password: SuperSecretPassword
  - name: protonuke
    hosts:
    - hostname: host-01 # hostname of topology node to apply it to
      metadata:
        # protonuke app metadata for this topology node
        args: -logfile /var/log/protonuke.log -level debug -http -https -smtp -ssh 192.168.100.100
  - name: wireguard
    hosts:
    - hostname: AD1 # hostname of topology node to apply it to
      metadata:
        # wireguard app metadata for this topology node
        infrastructure:
          private_key: GLlxWJom8cQViGHojqOUShWIZG7IsSX8
          address: 10.255.255.1/24
          listen_port: 51820
        peers:
          public_key: +joyya2F9g72qbKBtPDn00mIevG1j1OqeN76ylFLsiE=
          allowed_ips: 10.255.255.10/32

Note

The above example includes an app named startup, which is a phēnix default app. Meaning, it is possible to configure default phēnix apps in a scenario configuration, not just user apps.

Info

See Scorch for additional information on Scenario Orchestration

docs.title: Experiment
docs.text:
Experiment configurations represent the combination of topologies and scenarios to form an experiment (it should be noted that experiments do not require a scenario).

Experiment configurations are created from an existing topology and an optional scenario, with phenix experiment create or the web UI. A configuration file holding only the header below is not enough: its spec must already hold the experiment, so phenix config create rejects it. The header of an experiment named foobar, created from a topology named foobar and a scenario named foobar (none of the names are required to match), looks like this:

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Experiment
metadata:
  name: foobar
  annotations:
    topology: foobar # this is required
    scenario: foobar # this is optional
spec:
  ...

The experiment configuration has the topology and scenario configurations embedded in it, as well as additional details like cluster host schedules for VMs, VLAN ranges, etc. The advantage of embedding the topology and scenario into the experiment is that they can be modified in the experiment without modifying the originals.

The spec of an experiment holds these fields:

  • topology and scenario: the embedded topology and scenario.
  • baseDir: the working folder of the experiment. The default is <base-dir.phenix>/experiments/<name>.
  • defaultBridge: the bridge for each interface that does not set its own. The default is phenix, and the name can have at most 15 characters. See Bridge Mode.
  • vlans: aliases, which maps each VLAN name to a VLAN ID, and min and max, the range of VLAN IDs for the experiment. See VLANs.
  • schedules: maps each VM hostname to the cluster host that runs it.
  • deployMode: all, no-headnode, or only-headnode, the cluster hosts that can run VMs. phenix experiment create copies the deploy-mode setting (see Settings).
  • useGREMesh: when true, GRE tunnels connect the cluster hosts for this experiment. Creation turns it on when the use-gre-mesh setting is on. See GRE Mesh.
  • experimentName: the name of the experiment, which phēnix sets.

From the Web-UI or the API, spec.baseDir must be a folder in <base-dir.phenix>/experiments (an update can keep a stored base directory that's outside it). phenix config create doesn't have this limit.

docs.title: Image
docs.text:
The Image configuration is used to generate VM disk images using a specific and custom version of vmdb2. Representing a disk image in a configuration like this allows for the same disk image to easily be built in different clusters without having to actually move large disk image files.

Warning

The phēnix image capability will only generate Linux based images. It will not generate Windows disk images.

Typically image configurations are created automatically by the phenix image create command, but users can also create them manually using a configuration file similar to the one shown below. This file can then be created in the phēnix store using the phenix cfg create <path-to-file> command (cfg is an alias of phenix config). A new phēnix store starts with the image configs PHENIX-caldera, PHENIX-elasticsearch, PHENIX-kali, and PHENIX-packetbeat. The Image schema lists every field.

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Image
metadata:
  name: foobar
spec:
  format: qcow2
  mirror: http://us.archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/
  overlays: []
  packages:
  - initramfs-tools
  - net-tools
  - isc-dhcp-client
  - openssh-server
  - init
  - iputils-ping
  - vim
  - less
  - netbase
  - curl
  - ifupdown
  - dbus
  - linux-image-generic
  - linux-headers-generic
  release: bionic
  size: 5G
  variant: minbase
  script_order:
  - POSTBUILD_APT_CLEANUP
  - POSTBUILD_NO_ROOT_PASSWD
  scripts:
    POSTBUILD_APT_CLEANUP: |
      apt clean || apt-get clean || echo "unable to clean apt cache"
    POSTBUILD_NO_ROOT_PASSWD: |
      sed -i 's/nullok_secure/nullok/' /etc/pam.d/common-auth
      sed -i 's/#PermitRootLogin prohibit-password/PermitRootLogin yes/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
      sed -i 's/#PermitEmptyPasswords no/PermitEmptyPasswords yes/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
      sed -i 's/PermitRootLogin prohibit-password/PermitRootLogin yes/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
      sed -i 's/PermitEmptyPasswords no/PermitEmptyPasswords yes/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
      passwd -d root

Warning

The build runs only the scripts that script_order names, in that order. A script that is in scripts but not in script_order does not run.

docs.title: User
docs.text:
The User configuration tracks phēnix UI user settings (e.g., username, password, and RBAC permissions). Typically user configurations are created automatically when a UI admin creates a new user via the UI, but they can also be created manually using a configuration file similar to the one shown below. The phenix admin commands also create users (see User Administration). password holds the bcrypt hash of the password, not the password itself.

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: User
metadata:
  name: admin@foo.com
spec:
  username: admin@foo.com
  first_name: Admin
  last_name: Istrator
  password: '<encrypted-password>'
  rbac:
    roleName: Global Admin
    policies:
    - resourceNames:
      - '*'
      resources:
      - '*'
      - '*/*'
      verbs:
      - '*'
    - resourceNames:
      - admin@foo.com
      resources:
      - users
      verbs:
      - get

docs.title: Role
docs.text:
The Role configuration is used to represent a named set of RBAC permissions that represent a user's role in the UI. When a new user is created, the role that user should have is specified, and using that role name the appropriate RBAC permissions are copied from the role configuration into the user configuration.

There are nine (9) default role configurations that get created automatically: the eight described under built-in roles, and Disabled, which allows nothing. An example role configuration is shown below for completeness.

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: global-admin
spec:
  roleName: Global Admin
  policies:
  - resourceNames:
    - '*'
    - '*/*'
    resources:
    - '*'
    - '*/*'
    verbs:
    - '*'

Resource names are matched with the same Kind/name or experiment/vm shape as the resource they belong to, and a * never crosses the /, which is why this role lists both * and */*. See Resources.

docs.title: Config Table
docs.text:
The Configs component will initially load with a table presenting all the available configuration files. It is possible to filter in two ways:

  1. There is a pull-down selector, which will allow filtering on a specific Kind of config. Choosing All kinds puts every kind back in the table.
  2. A separate Find a Config field will allow filtering on Name (if you have filtered on Kind, it will be limited to that kind of config).

Clicking on the X next to the Find a Config field will reset both filters.

The totals strip above the table counts the configs of each kind. Click the count of a kind to filter on that kind. Click the Configs total, or the count of the kind again, to show all kinds. The Kind selector shows the same filter.

The In Use column shows an icon for a topology or scenario that an experiment uses. An experiment uses the topology or scenario that its topology or scenario annotation names. This includes experiments that are not running. Hold the pointer on the icon to see the names of the experiments. For the other kinds of config, the column is empty.

Select the check boxes of one or more configs to download them (two or more come as configs.zip) or delete them all with the buttons above the table.

docs.title: View a Config
docs.text:
There are two ways to view a specific config:

  1. Clicking the name of the config entry will open a modal to view the config. It is possible to select text and copy from this modal. However, it is not possible to edit the config directly in this view. Instead, there is an Edit button, which will open an editor. It is also possible to download a copy of the config. A topology or scenario name on the Experiments page opens its config in this viewer, too. The annotations of the config show next to its title. Above the text, the viewer shows the kind, name, creation time and update time of the config. Use the YAML and JSON buttons to change the format of the text. Use Wrap lines to wrap long lines, and Copy to copy the text. The viewer of an experiment config has a button next to its title that opens the experiment page. The viewer of a topology or scenario lists the experiments that use it.
  2. Selecting the Edit button for a given config will open the editor window. It is possible to edit the config in this window and save the update to the phēnix store. The config will be validated against the schema, and if invalid, an error will be presented.

docs.title: Topologies with a Builder diagram
docs.text: A topology with a Builder diagram has the tag builder, and its Edit button opens the Builder, not the editor window, for a role with builder use. Other roles see an alert (see From the Configs page). For a role with builder use, the tag is a link into the Builder, and the viewer of a topology has an Open in Builder or Import into Builder button. A topology with a diagram from the old Topology Builder has the tag builder legacy, and its Edit button opens the editor window.

docs.title: Create a Config
docs.text:
There are two ways to create a new config:

  1. Selecting the Upload button located to the far right of the search field will allow you to upload a file from disk. It is possible to drag and drop in the upload modal or click the upload icon to open a file browser.

    Note

    Only files with the extensions .yml, .yaml, and .json will be allowed. Any file uploaded will be validated against the schema for a given kind of config, and if invalid, an error will be presented.

  2. Clicking the + button next to the search field will present an editor window where it is possible to create a new file in place. A basic template is provided based on the kind of config selected (see next section for documentation on the editor window features). Once editing a config is completed, clicking the Create button will post it server-side where it will be validated, similar to file upload. If invalid, an error will be presented.

docs.title: Editor Window
docs.text:
The editor window allows direct editing of an existing or new config file.

  • To use the editor from the keyboard, see Accessibility.

  • It is possible to edit a file as YAML or JSON by selecting the relevant radio button under File Format.

  • It is also possible to set keybindings to the Vim editor by enabling them with the sliding selector under Vim Mode.

If someone else saved the config after you opened it (see Revisions), the Config Changed dialog lets you reload it (and lose your edits), overwrite anyway, or cancel and keep editing.

docs.title: New Config
docs.text:
The editor window for creating a new config will allow editing the filename in a text field to the left or within the config editor directly. Similarly, use the pull-down selector to the left to select the kind of config or within the config editor.

Selecting the Create button will post the new config server-side for validation and addition to the store. Choosing the Exit button will leave the editor window; nothing will be saved.

docs.title: Existing Config
docs.text:
Changing the name in an existing config is only available through the editor window.

Selecting the Save button will post any updates server-side for validation and addition to the store. Selecting the Exit button will leave the editor window; nothing will be saved.

Save asks you to confirm first. The editor of a running experiment has no Save button. If you changed the text, Exit asks you to confirm that you want to lose your edits.

docs.title: Delete a Config
docs.text:
Selecting the delete icon will delete a config. A confirmation dialog will be presented to confirm the selection. Once the config is deleted, it cannot be restored to the store. If an experiment config is deleted, the corresponding experiment will no longer be presented in the Experiments tab.

From the command line, phenix config delete all [kind] deletes every config, or every config of one kind, except the config of a running experiment. Add --dry-run to see what it would delete:

phenix config delete all topology --dry-run

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Phēnix supports environment variables in its configuration files. When the CLI reads a config file, such as with phenix config create <file>, it replaces each environment variable placeholder with the value of that variable. Placeholders can be in the format ${VAR} or ${VAR:default}, where VAR is the environment variable name, and default is an optional default value to use if the variable is not set. If the variable is not set and no default is provided, the command stops with an error and changes nothing. Write ${VAR:} for a variable that can be empty. A $VAR without braces is not a placeholder. Write $${VAR} to keep the text ${VAR} in the config.

Note

For a config sent to the REST API or the web UI (POST /configs, PUT /configs/{kind}/{name} and the workflow endpoints), with a JSON or YAML body the server fills in only ${BRANCH_NAME}. It stores every other placeholder as written, so a client cannot read the server environment through a config. Of these, only the workflow endpoints take variables, in the variables part of a multipart/form-data request; the server then also fills in the placeholders from the variables and their defaults (see REST API). POST /configs and PUT /configs/{kind}/{name} do not: a client fills in the other placeholders before it sends a config. The Builder fills in no placeholders. A ${BRANCH_NAME} in these requests is filled in also when the stored config holds it as text. For POST /configs and PUT /configs/{kind}/{name}, the value is the BRANCH_NAME variable of the server, or empty text when it is not set. Write $${BRANCH_NAME} to keep the text.

Example config before parsing environment variables:

- name: foobar
  metadata:
    baz:
      ip: ${HOST:localhost}

After parsing with HOST=172.1.3.37:

- name: foobar
  metadata:
    baz:
      ip: 172.1.3.37

Or if HOST env variable isn't found, the default is used:

- name: foobar
  metadata:
    baz:
      ip: localhost

docs.title: Variable Sources
docs.text:
These commands read config files and fill in their placeholders: phenix config create, phenix config apply, phenix config diff, phenix experiment create with a file for -t or -s, and phenix workflow apply. phenix experiment create also fills in a topology file that includeTopologies names by a path, and so does the server for phenix workflow apply. A command gets the value of a variable from the first of these sources that has it:

Source Description -e, --env -e NAME=value sets a variable. -e NAME copies the value of NAME from the shell. Repeat the flag for more variables. If a name is given more than once, the last value is used. --env-file An env file of NAME=value lines. Repeat the flag for more files. A later file overrides an earlier file. A relative path starts at the working directory. phenix workflow apply reads .env in the topology directory when no --env-file is given. The shell The environment of the command, without the variables whose names start with PHENIX_. Those variables hold the settings of phēnix. Name one with -e NAME to use it. A variable whose name is not a valid variable name, for example 1A, is not used. 
phenix config create topology.yml -e HOST=172.1.3.37
phenix config apply configs/* --env-file site.env -e NODES=3

A command reads every file and checks every variable before it changes anything. It stops, and changes nothing, in these cases:

  • A placeholder has no value and no default.
  • No file uses a variable that -e sets. This is usually a typing mistake.
  • A value or a default contains a line break.

The command replaces the text of a placeholder before it reads the YAML or JSON. Thus a placeholder in a comment is also filled in, and a value can change how YAML reads a line. Put a placeholder in quotes when its value can contain : or #.

phēnix does not have the Docker Compose forms ${VAR:-default} and ${VAR:?error}. For phēnix, the default of ${VAR:-3} is the text -3. The command logs a warning for a default that starts with - or ?.

The log shows the name and the source of each variable that a file uses. It shows the values only with --log.level debug. Debug records can thus hold secrets, also in the log file.

Warning

In earlier releases, a variable that was not set became an empty string, and the CLI used every shell variable. A config that relied on this now stops the command. Give the placeholder a default, such as ${VAR:}, or name a PHENIX_ variable with -e.

docs.title: Env Files
docs.text:
An env file holds one variable on each line:

# Blank lines and lines that start with "#" are skipped.
SITE=lab
NODES=3
export IMAGE=ubuntu.qc2
MOTD="  the quotes keep the spaces  "
  • A line is NAME=value, with no space before the =. A name starts with a letter or _, and continues with letters, digits and _.
  • export before the name is permitted.
  • A value in single or double quotes is the text between the quotes. The closing quote must be the last character of the line.
  • Any other value is the text as written, a # included, without the spaces and tabs at the end of the line.
  • Nothing in the file is expanded: ${OTHER} and \n stay as written. For a workflow, the server fills in a ${BRANCH_NAME} that a value carries.
  • When a name is on more than one line, the last line is used.
  • Any other line is an error that names the file and the line.

docs.title: Environment variables using Docker
docs.text:
If phēnix is running in a docker container (or docker compose), environment variables can be passed into the compose file and/or via args in any CLI calls to phēnix, e.g.

environment:
  HOST: ${HOST}

or

docker exec -it -e BRANCH_NAME=foobar phenix phenix exp create foobar -t topo -s scenario

Tip

Configs sent by phenix workflow apply, or to the /workflow/configs/{branch} and /workflow/apply/{branch} API endpoints, don't need -e BRANCH_NAME: phēnix sets BRANCH_NAME to the workflow branch name itself. The API endpoints keep their other placeholders as written unless the request sends variables, and phenix workflow apply sends its variables with each config (see Variables). The command also copies the topology directory's phenix-injects/ to <base-dir.injects>/<name> (by default /phenix/injects/<name>), so configs can reference injected files as /phenix/injects/${BRANCH_NAME}/<file>. See Workflow.

docs.text:
• phenix config: every config command and flag.
  • Schema: the full schema of each config kind.
  • Experiments: create and start an experiment from your configs.
  • Apps: the apps that read topology fields and scenario metadata.
  • Workflow: deploy a directory of configs with one command.
  • Builder: draw a topology as a diagram.
  • User Administration: users, roles, and policies.

docs.title: Deprecations
docs.text: This page lists each deprecated part of the phenix command line, settings and configs, and the part to use instead. A future release will remove each deprecated part.

docs.title: How phēnix Shows a Deprecation
docs.text:
A deprecated part continues to work until its removal. When you use it, phēnix writes one warning to standard error, as in this example:

phenix: warning: phenix settings get -f/--format is deprecated and will be removed in a future release; use phenix settings get -o/--output instead.

The warning does not change the output or the exit code of the command. The --help output and the CLI reference do not show deprecated flags and commands.

docs.title: Deprecated Command Line Parts
docs.text: Deprecated Use instead Notes phenix settings get -f/--format phenix settings get -o/--output The two flags take the same formats. phenix settings list -f/--format phenix settings list -o/--output The two flags take the same formats. phenix experiment trigger-running <experiment name> [<app name> ...] phenix experiment trigger <experiment name> running [<app name> ...] The trig alias is also deprecated. phenix experiment trigger <lifecycle> <experiment name> [<app name> ...] phenix experiment trigger <experiment name> <lifecycle> [<app name> ...] phēnix reads the old order only when no experiment has the lifecycle as its name.

docs.title: Deprecated Settings
docs.text:
phēnix continues to read these settings keys from the config file and from their environment variables. When a key is set and its replacement is not set, phenix ui uses the key and writes the warning to standard error.

Deprecated Use instead Notes unix-socket-gid (config file), PHENIX_UNIX_SOCKET_GID (environment) ui.unix-socket-gid, PHENIX_UI_UNIX_SOCKET_GID The --unix-socket-gid flag of phenix ui sets ui.unix-socket-gid.

docs.title: Deprecated Config Values
docs.text:
phēnix continues to accept these values in a config. When it reads one, it writes a warning to the log.

Deprecated Use instead Notes os_type: linux on a Router or Firewall node of a Topology os_type: vyatta, vyos or minirouter The vrouter app configures the node as a Vyatta router.

docs.title: Flags That Are Not Deprecated
docs.text:
These flags are aliases of -o/--output. They are not deprecated.

Flag Same as phenix settings get --json, phenix settings list --json, phenix settings db list --json -o json phenix util app-json -p/--pretty -o json phenix util role-table -p/--pretty -o markdown

Do not use an alias together with an -o value that gives a different format. phēnix refuses that command line.

phenix config get -p/--pretty is not an alias. JSON output is always indented, so the flag has no effect. It stays so that existing scripts work.

phenix workflow apply --name is also not deprecated: it's the same flag as -b/--branch-name. If you give both, use the same value.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• CLI Reference: the current commands and flags.
  • Settings: the current settings keys and their environment variables.
  • Configuration: the fields of each config.
  • Logging: the log that gets the warning for a deprecated config value.

docs.title: Disks
docs.text:
The Disks page (in the Resources menu) lists the disk images phēnix knows about:

  • the images with a known extension (.qcow2, .qc2, .qcow, _rootfs.tgz, .hdd, .iso) in the minimega files directory and the folders under it (see Images in Folders)
  • every image an experiment's topology names, wherever it is
  • the images those are backed by

Disk images are built from the command line. See Virtual Disk Images Management.

docs.title: The Disks Table
docs.text:
Size on Disk is how much room the file takes now, and Virtual Size is how large the disk looks to the guest. The Type column marks an old format version or a format problem (see Image Format Versions).

In Use marks an image that a running VM holds open. A base image isn't in use just because VMs run off images built on it, so you can still snapshot it.

The list reloads on its own when the minimega files directory changes, and the header's refresh button makes the server inspect every image again. phēnix inspects images with qemu-img, which the phēnix container image includes. Without it, phēnix asks minimega instead, which lists fewer images.

docs.title: The Details Card
docs.text:
Click a row, or go to /disks?disk=<full-path>, to open the image's details card.

The health tag at the top is OK, Warning (such as an old format version, an image outside the files directory, or a bad inject partition) or Error (a broken backing chain, or an image that qemu refuses), and a Problems box lists each problem. Besides the format and partitions, the card shows the image's backing chain, the listed images built on it, each experiment that uses it (running or stopped) with its VMs, and its running clones. Its Actions section adds Commit, Rebase and Resize to the table's actions.

The Inject flag marks the partition phēnix injects files into (the inject_partition of the VM's first drive). The card warns when that partition doesn't exist, or holds no file system phēnix can write to.

docs.title: Images in Folders
docs.text:
A topology names an image in a folder by its path within the minimega files directory (image: win/10/win10.qcow2) or by its full path. The list leaves out:

  • hidden files and folders, and lost+found
  • the files, tmp and miniccc_responses folders of an experiment, which the experiment's Files tab manages
  • minimega's own saved folder and transfer_* files

Symlinked folders aren't followed. An image the list leaves out is still listed when a topology names it, but phēnix doesn't act on it.

docs.title: Images Outside the Files Directory
docs.text:
A topology can also name an image anywhere else phēnix can read it, such as /data/vms/win10.qcow2. The list shows it by its full path with a warning icon. phēnix won't change these images, so every action, Download included, is disabled: to manage one here, copy it into the minimega files directory and point the topology at the copy.

minimega doesn't copy such an image to the other cluster nodes, so every node that may run a VM with it needs the same file at the same path. In the Docker Compose setup, a path outside /phenix also needs the same mount in the phēnix and minimega containers.

Warning

With minimega's -abssnapshot flag, which the Docker Compose setup turns on, minimega cannot launch a snapshot VM from an image outside its files directory on a cluster of more than one node. Keep such images in the files directory.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: A disks permission names an image by its file name, such as win10.qcow2, so one name covers the files of that name in every folder. A role sees an image outside the files directory only when it may also get an experiment whose topology uses the image, or when the image backs an image the role sees. See User Administration for the rest.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Snapshot creates a new image backed by this one, Commit writes the image's changes into its backing image, Rebase moves it onto a different backing image, and Resize changes the virtual size of the disk. A few limits:

  • An image that a running VM holds open can only be cloned or downloaded.
  • Snapshot, Commit and Rebase work on VM images only, and Commit needs a backing image to commit into.
  • Commit, Rebase and Resize refuse an image whose backing chain leaves the files directory, or has a vmdk, qed or external data file in it. An unsafe Rebase doesn't check the chain.

Snapshot, Clone and Rename ask for a new name, relative to the image's own folder. The folder must already exist, and no action replaces an existing file. A snapshot is always a qcow2 image, while a clone or a renamed image keeps its format: phēnix adds the image's extension to a name that has none (.qcow2 for a .qc2 image), and refuses a name with the extension of another format (a .qcow image can also take .qcow2 or .qc2). Since minimega uses the name, it can't have white space, control characters, or any of ", ', `, \, #, *, ?, [, ], {, }, $, or ,.

Warning

phēnix doesn't check whether other images are built on the one you rename, so you'll need to rebase them onto its new name. A delete refuses an image that other images or experiments use, unless you click Delete anyway, and images backed by a deleted one can no longer be used. Check Built on this image on the details card first.

docs.title: Cloning in the background
docs.text: A clone copies the whole file, so it runs as a background job that you can watch or cancel from the jobs menu or the Clone jobs section of the details card. The new image shows up in the list once the copy is done.

docs.title: Uploading an Image
docs.text: Click the upload button to open Upload a Disk. Closing the dialog doesn't stop the upload, and uploaded images land at the top of the minimega files directory.

docs.title: Broken Backing Chains
docs.text:
A VM can't start from an image whose backing chain is broken: a file in the chain is missing, the chain loops back on itself, or it has more than 64 images. The table marks such an image with a Broken chain tag, and the tag's tooltip names the problem.

phēnix checks every VM disk's backing chain before a start, and refuses the start when a file is missing (see Disk Check Before a Start).

To repair the image, do one of these:

  1. Restore the missing backing file at the path that the tag names.
  2. Point the image at a copy of the missing backing file with Rebase and Change reference only selected. A rebase without this option must read the missing file, so it fails.
  3. Change the topology to use a different image.

From the command line, --unsafe does the same as Change reference only:

phenix disk rebase kali-lab.qc2 ro_kali-copy.qc2 --unsafe

docs.title: Image Format Versions
docs.text:
Before a start, phēnix also reads the format and version of each image in a backing chain, since qemu refuses some images and some old formats can cause problems:

Image What phēnix does qcow2 version 3 (compat=1.1), raw Starts the VM. qcow2 version 2 (compat=0.10) Starts the VM. phenix doctor warns. qcow version 1 Starts the VM with a warning. Some qemu builds cannot open this format. qcow2 or qcow version 1 with the old AES encryption Refuses the start. qcow2 with LUKS encryption Refuses the start. qcow2 of a version later than 3, or with feature bits qemu does not know Refuses the start. qcow2 that qemu marked as corrupt Refuses the start when the VM writes to the image (snapshot: false). Otherwise starts the VM with a warning. qcow2 that qemu did not close cleanly Starts the VM with a warning. qcow2 with zstd compression or extended L2 entries Starts the VM. phenix doctor warns when the local qemu-img is too old for them. vmdk, qed, or qcow2 with an external data file Starts the VM with a warning. phēnix does not check past this image.

With experiment.disk-check set to warn, a refused start is a warning instead. The details card gives the command to fix each image, and A Start Fails on an Image Format covers the commands.

docs.title: Downloading an Image
docs.text:
Only images in the minimega files directory can be downloaded. An interrupted download resumes from the browser's downloads list as long as the image hasn't changed, so stop any VM that writes to the image first. From a shell, curl -C - resumes a download the same way:

curl -C - -o win.qc2 -H 'X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer <token>' \
  'https://<phenix>/api/v1/disks/download?disk=win.qc2'

To verify a download, compare its sha256sum with the checksum that the API returns for the image, or that phenix disk checksum <disk> prints.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
The phenix disk commands do the same actions as this page, and don't need a running phenix ui. Give a disk as a path relative to the minimega files directory, or as an absolute path in it. See phenix disk for every command and flag.

# The images of one experiment, inspected again
phenix disk list --experiment my-exp --refresh

# What the details card shows
phenix disk details win10.qcow2

# A qcow2 snapshot backed by win10.qcow2
phenix disk snapshot win10.qcow2 win10-lab.qcow2

# Show what a delete would do, without deleting
phenix disk delete win10.qcow2 --dry-run

Add --force to phenix disk delete to delete an image that other images or experiments use.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• phenix disk: every disk command and flag.
  • Doctor: checks backing chains, image formats and leftovers without the UI.
  • VMs: backing images, snapshots and disk commits of a VM.

docs.title: Doctor
docs.text:
phenix doctor checks your phēnix configuration, the host and minimega, and it doesn't need phenix ui to be running. Reach for it when the server or an experiment won't start, when a setting seems to have no effect, after an upgrade, and before you report a bug.

# Only the checks that warn or fail, without the settings list
phenix doctor -p -x

# In the Docker deployment
docker exec phenix phenix doctor -p -x

Run it as the same user, and with the same flags and environment, as the phēnix command you're checking. doctor changes nothing: it opens the store read-only, sends minimega only commands that change nothing, and binds no port. The only files it writes are the ones every phēnix command creates, and temporary files for the inject-partitions check. The phenix doctor CLI reference lists every flag.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
--skip takes any check or group name from the Checks tables, such as on a host without minimega:

phenix doctor --skip minimega,images

--timeout is 3 seconds by default. When it runs out, a slow check such as disk-chains warns, and minimega and openvswitch fail. To give them more time:

phenix doctor --timeout 30s

Check a host from a script. --strict makes a warning exit 1 too, and the JSON report has a hint for each warning and failure:

if ! phenix doctor --strict -x -o json > doctor.json; then
  jq -r '.checks[] | select(.status == "warn" or .status == "fail") | "\(.id): \(.hint)"' doctor.json
fi

List the settings that aren't at their default value, and where each value comes from:

phenix doctor -o json --skip minimega,images | jq -r '.settings[] | select(.source != "default") | "\(.key)=\(.value) (\(.source))"'

docs.title: Reading the Output
docs.text:
doctor prints a header, every setting with its value and source, one row per check, and a summary. It never prints the values of ui.jwt-signing-key or ui.users. Here's the end of phenix doctor -p -x on a host where minimega isn't running:

CHECK               STATUS  DETAIL
ui.jwt-signing-key  WARN    empty, so phenix ui serves without authentication
minimega            FAIL    no answer on /tmp/minimega/minimega: unable to dial: dial unix /tmp/minimega/minimega: connect: no such file or directory (no socket there: minimega is not running, or base-dir.minimega names another directory)
filebeat            WARN    filebeat is not a program on PATH, so SCORCH starts no Filebeat, even for a component that enables it

FAIL: 1 failed, 2 warned, 55 passed, 24 skipped. Failed: minimega. Warned: ui.jwt-signing-key, filebeat. 79 passing or skipped checks hidden
  minimega: start minimega, or set base-dir.minimega to the directory that holds its socket
Status Meaning pass No problem found. warn phēnix works, but something may cause trouble later. fail phēnix, or part of it, won't work until you fix this. skip The check didn't run. The row says why.

doctor exits 1 when a check fails (or warns, with --strict), and 0 otherwise. -o json prints the same report as JSON, with a stable id and group for each check.

docs.title: Doctor and the Health Checks
docs.text: doctor checks a host without a running server. To monitor a running phenix ui, use the health checks (/healthz and /readyz).

docs.title: Reporting a Bug
docs.text:
--report prints the output in a fenced code block that you can paste into the bug report form:

phenix doctor --report

The report swaps host names, IP addresses, user names and email addresses for tokens such as <host-1>, and replaces passwords, the JWT signing key and other secrets with <redacted>. The same value always gets the same token, so a path keeps its shape, such as /home/<user-1>/images. Values that say nothing about your site, such as localhost and root, stay as they are.

Warning

Read the output before you paste it. doctor can't replace a name it doesn't know about, such as another host's name in a path.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text: The Check column is the name that --skip takes, and Group is its group. A check that can both warn and fail is in both tables. The hint in doctor's output gives the fix, often with the exact command.

docs.title: Failures
docs.text: Check Group Fails when Fix config-file, users-file config The file can't be read or isn't valid YAML. Fix the YAML at the line the row names. env (one row for each variable) env phēnix would refuse or misread a value, or EDITOR isn't on PATH. Fix or unset the variable. bridge-mode, deploy-mode, experiment.disk-check, color settings Every command refuses the value. Set a value that the hint lists. log.system.max-size settings The value is negative, so every write to the system log fails. Set a whole number of megabytes, or 0 for 100. store.endpoint files This user can't write the store file or its directory. Create the directory, or set a bolt:// path this user can write. store-file files The store isn't a whole BoltDB file. Restore a backup, or move it so phēnix creates an empty store. log.system.path, log.console files This user can't write or create the log file. Use a file or directory this user can write. base-dir.phenix, base-dir.minimega, base-dir.injects, base-dir.topologies, mount-dir dirs The path isn't a directory. Point the setting at a directory this user can use. ui.shutdown-grace-period, ui.netflow.max-size, ui.captures.max-size ui phenix ui would refuse the value. Set a whole number: seconds, or MiB for the sizes. ui.jwt-signing-key auth A development key doesn't name a user and a role. Write it as dev|<user>|<role>. ui.jwt-lifetime auth The value is under a minute, such as 24 (nanoseconds). Use a unit, such as 24h. ui.users auth An entry isn't name:password:role[:resource...], so phenix ui skips it. Fix the entry. ui.proxy-auth-header auth The value isn't an HTTP header name. Fix the name, or unset ui.proxy-auth-header. ui.tls tls Only one of ui.tls-key and ui.tls-cert is set, or they don't load. Set both to a readable key and its certificate, or neither. ui.tls-cert tls The certificate has expired or isn't valid yet. Renew it, then restart phenix ui. ui.listen-endpoint, ui.file-server-endpoint tls phenix ui can't listen on the value. Use host:port, such as 0.0.0.0:3000 (0 turns the file server off). unix-socket socket The directory is missing or unwritable, or the path is too long. Use a path in a directory this user can write. unix-socket-gid socket This user isn't root or in the group, so phenix ui exits. Use a group this user is in, run as root, or -1. server server This user can't connect to the socket of phenix ui. Run doctor as the user of phenix ui, or in its group. minimega minimega minimega doesn't answer on its socket. Start minimega, or fix base-dir.minimega. minimega-env minimega phēnix can't read minimega's -filepath directory. Mount the files directory at the same path for both. qemu-img, vmdb2 tools The program isn't on PATH, or qemu-img doesn't work. Install qemu-utils or vmdb2, or use --skip vmdb2. disk tools A phēnix or minimega filesystem is 98% full. Free up space. nbd (Linux only) tools qemu-nbd is missing, so minimega injects fail. Install qemu-nbd. openvswitch (Linux only) tools ovs-vsctl is missing, or Open vSwitch doesn't answer. Install or start Open vSwitch. ui.features features webshark is set without a WebShark build, so phenix ui won't start. List only vm-mount. ui.logs.minimega-path features The path isn't a regular file. Set it to minimega's log file.

docs.title: Warnings
docs.text: Check Group Warns when Fix config-file config There is no config.yaml. phēnix creates it if it can write its config directory. config-keys config A key isn't a phēnix setting, such as a typo. Rename or remove it. phenix settings list shows the valid keys. config-paths config The search path has more than one config or users file. Merge them into the first one, which phēnix reads. settings-file config phenix settings set would write a file phēnix doesn't read, or can't. Use a YAML config file this user can write. scenario-hosts config A scenario app names a host that isn't in the topology. Fix the names with phenix experiment edit <experiment>. env (one row for each variable) env A PHENIX_* variable is empty, unknown, or overridden by a flag. Fix or unset the variable. env-overrides env A PHENIX_* variable overrides a different config file value. Unset the variable, or change the file to match. proxy-env env A proxy is set, and NO_PROXY doesn't cover phenix ui. Add the named hosts to NO_PROXY and no_proxy. log.level, log.system.max-size, log.system.max-backups, log.system.max-age settings phēnix can't use the value, so it falls back to a default. Set a value from the hint. minimega.read-connections settings The value isn't a number from 3 to 64. Set a whole number from 3 to 64. store-file files One of the store's two meta pages is corrupt. Back up the store while phenix ui is stopped. store-owner files Another user owns the store file. Run phēnix as the store's owner. store-root files This user has its own store, but /etc/phenix/store.bdb exists. Use sudo -i, or set store.endpoint to bolt:///etc/phenix/store.bdb. store-fs files The store is on a network filesystem, or is mostly free pages. Move or compact the store. secret-files files Other users can read a file that holds a secret. chmod 600 the file. inject-sources files The source file of a node injection doesn't exist. Put the file there, or change the injection src. base-dir.phenix, base-dir.minimega, base-dir.injects, base-dir.topologies, mount-dir dirs The directory is missing, relative, or unusable by this user. Create it with access for this user, or use another one. base-dir.builder-templates dirs The directory is unusable, or phenix ui skips a template file. Fix the directory or file. The phenix ui log says why. ui.jwt-signing-key auth The key is empty (no sign-in) or a development key. Set a long random secret to require sign-in. ui.users auth A role is unknown, or the list is empty with sign-in on. Fix the role, or change the default user's password. proxy-jwt auth phenix ui listens on every address, but doesn't verify proxy JWTs. Listen only where the proxy reaches, such as 127.0.0.1:3000. ui.proxy-auth-header auth With no sign-in or a dev key, phenix ui ignores the header. Set ui.jwt-signing-key, or unset ui.proxy-auth-header. rbac-users auth A user's role is missing, or a role names deleted items. Fix the role on the Users page or with phenix config edit. ui.tls-cert tls The certificate expires within 30 days, or doesn't name this host. Renew it with the right names, then restart phenix ui. ui.listen-endpoint tls The endpoint has no port. Use host:port, such as 0.0.0.0:3000. unix-socket socket The path is relative, or holds a non-socket or another user's socket. Use an absolute path in a directory this user can write. unix-socket-gid socket No group has the id (as root), or a deprecated key sets it. Use an existing group in ui.unix-socket-gid, or set -1. server server No phenix ui answers, or its version or modes differ. Start phenix ui, or match its version and modes. stuck-status server The store shows runs in progress that nothing is running. Start or restart phenix ui. ui-limits (Linux only) server phenix ui uses over 80% of its open files limit. Raise LimitNOFILE= or --ulimit nofile, then restart it. minimega-env minimega -filepath is relative or read-only, -base differs, or the mesh fails. Use an absolute -filepath, and match base-dir.minimega to -base. experiment-files minimega <base-dir.phenix>/images isn't minimega's -filepath. Make the two the same directory. minimega-limits (Linux only) minimega Open files, or memory and swap, are too low for the VMs. Raise the limit, or stop VMs. state-drift minimega The store and minimega disagree on which experiments run. Stop the experiment, or clear the namespace. vlans minimega Two experiments pin a VLAN ID, or one can't get its VLANs. Change the pin, or stop the other experiment. bridge-trunk (Linux only) minimega A mesh bridge has no trunk or tunnel, so nodes can't connect. Add a trunk, or set use-gre-mesh. schedule-hosts minimega An experiment schedules a VM on a node not in the mesh. Fix the schedule, or add the node to the mesh. cc-clients minimega A VM's miniccc client is missing after 5 minutes, or mismatched. Inject a matching miniccc. filebeat tools filebeat isn't on PATH, so SCORCH starts no Filebeat. Install Filebeat if your SCORCH components use it. disk tools A phēnix or minimega filesystem is 90% full. Free up space. kernel-modules (Linux only) tools The running kernel's modules are missing, or a reboot is pending. Reboot into the installed kernel. nbd (Linux only) tools The nbd module isn't ready, or no /dev/nbdN is free. Run modprobe nbd max_part=10 as root. openvswitch (Linux only) tools Permission is denied, or ovs-vswitchd or its module isn't running. Run doctor as root, or start Open vSwitch. image-build (Linux only) tools phenix image build lacks a program, root, a loop device, or keyring. Install what the row names, and build as root. image-configs tools An overlay directory of an image config doesn't exist. Create it, or phenix image remove <config> --overlays <path>. disk-chains images An image has a broken backing chain. Restore the backing file, or rebase the image. disk-formats images An image's format is old or unsupported, or qemu-img is too old. See Image Format Versions. writable-images images A VM with snapshot: false writes to a shared or backing image. Set snapshot: true, or give each VM its own copy. leftovers images Deleted experiments or stopped VMs left files, mounts, taps or mirrors. Remove each one with the command in the hint. disk-space images A filesystem of images or minimega has under 10% or 5 GiB free. Delete unused images and leftovers. image-locks (Linux only) images A qemu process holds an image of a stopped experiment open. If nothing needs it, kill <pid> or qemu-nbd -d /dev/nbdN. inject-partitions images inject_partition names a partition minimega can't write, or one needing repair. Use the suggested partition, or repair it as the hint says. scenario-apps apps A scenario uses an app or SCORCH component that isn't installed. Install it, or add it to PATH. app-runtimes apps An app isn't executable, lacks its interpreter, or has Windows line ends. chmod +x, install the interpreter, or dos2unix. tunneler-download features downloads/tunneler isn't a directory. Make it a directory of phenix-tunneler builds, or remove it. ui.features features A feature is unknown, is missing what it needs, or is minimega-captures, which has no effect. List only vm-mount. minimega-captures features doctor can't read the minimega version. Use a minimega build that gives a version, such as minimega 3.4.0. ui.logs.minimega-path features Missing or unreadable file, or unset while minimega logs to a file. Set it to minimega's log file.

docs.title: Example Applications
docs.text:
The sceptre-phenix repository contains complete, runnable reference implementations for Go and Python applications.

These examples demonstrate best practices for:

  • Lifecycle Management: Handling configure, pre-start, post-start, etc.
  • Configuration: Parsing the experiment JSON from STDIN.
  • Logging: Implementing the App Contract (JSON on stderr).
  • Error Handling: Capturing panics and exceptions as structured logs.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
To run the examples, you first need to clone the main repository and install the development dependencies:

# 1. Clone the main repository and navigate into it
git clone https://github.com/sandialabs/sceptre-phenix.git
cd sceptre-phenix

# 2. Install dependencies for Go and Python examples
make install-dev

docs.title: 🐍 Python Example
docs.text: The Python example demonstrates how to use the phenix_apps library to build robust applications with structured logging and error handling.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# Run the app (simulating the 'running' stage)
make -C examples run-python

docs.title: 🐹 Go Example
docs.text: The Go example demonstrates how to build a lightweight app using the Go standard library and core phenix packages.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# Build and run the app (simulating the 'running' stage)
make -C examples run-go

docs.title: A Minimal User App
docs.text:
Below is a very contrived example of a simple user app that changes the disk image used for every node in the experiment topology. Assuming the name of the executable for this app as phenix-app-image-changer, it could be applied to a topology by including a scenario in an experiment that includes an experiment app named image-changer. This example demonstrates best practices, including using the phenix_apps logger to produce structured JSON logs on stderr.

Unlike the runnable Python example, this app does not use the AppBase class of the phenix_apps library. It reads the lifecycle stage and the experiment JSON itself, as User Apps describes, and it calls configure_logging() itself. phēnix sets PHENIX_LOG_FILE=stderr when it runs a user app (see phēnix Apps Environment Variables), and configure_logging() then writes the logs to stderr as JSON.

import json
import sys
from phenix_apps.common.logger import configure_logging, logger

def main():
    # Write JSON logs to the place that PHENIX_LOG_FILE names.
    # phēnix sets it to 'stderr' when it runs the app.
    configure_logging()

    # The first argument is the lifecycle stage (e.g., 'pre-start')
    try:
        stage = sys.argv[1]
    except IndexError:
        logger.error("Lifecycle stage argument not provided.")
        # Raising an exception is preferred over sys.exit()
        # phēnix will capture the non-zero exit code.
        raise ValueError("Missing stage argument")

    # Read the experiment JSON from stdin
    try:
        experiment = json.load(sys.stdin)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        logger.error("Failed to decode experiment JSON from stdin.")
        raise

    logger.info(f"Executing stage: {stage}")

    # Only modify the spec in the 'pre-start' or 'configure' stage
    if stage in ["pre-start", "configure"]:
        try:
            spec = experiment['spec']
            for node in spec['topology']['nodes']:
                hostname = node.get("general", {}).get("hostname", "unknown")
                logger.info("Processing node", hostname=hostname)
                for drive in node['hardware']['drives']:
                    original_image = drive['image']
                    drive['image'] = 'm$.qc2'
                    logger.debug(
                        "Changed image for node",
                        hostname=hostname,
                        from_image=original_image,
                        to_image=drive['image'],
                    )
        except (KeyError, TypeError) as e:
            logger.exception("Failed to parse experiment spec to change image.")
            raise

    # Print the (potentially modified) experiment JSON to stdout
    # This is how the app returns its changes to phēnix.
    print(json.dumps(experiment))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        main()
    except Exception:
        # phēnix will capture the non-zero exit code from the raised exception
        # and log any messages written to stderr.
        sys.exit(1)
