docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: For experiments spanning multiple minimega hosts, see GRE Mesh to trunk experiment networks between hosts with --use-gre-mesh, including the physical network MTU requirements.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
Click on the Experiments tab. This will display all available experiments that the user has access to view or edit.

Click a topology or scenario name to open it on the Configs page. Besides start, stop, restart and delete, the Actions column has shortcuts to the experiment's State of Health and SCORCH runs.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
This will display a list of all available experiments:

phenix exp list

Add -o json or -o yaml for JSON or YAML output.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
Click the stopped button (or the play button in the Actions column) to start the experiment, and the started button (or the stop button) to stop it. While the experiment starts or stops, a progress bar shows what step it's on, such as Launching VMs 12/40.

To Click the status button Or the button in the Actions column Start a stopped experiment Stop a running experiment Restart a running experiment

The start dialog has the same options as phenix exp start: a dry run that does everything except call minimega, treating minimega errors as warnings, and a VLAN range for this start only. Run the apps' running stage on its schedule (on by default) runs the running stage of each app that has runPeriodically in the scenario, as a background job that ends when the experiment stops.

The stop dialog has the same options as phenix exp stop. Keep the injection snapshots keeps the VM disk snapshots that phēnix deletes after a stop otherwise. Force the stop marks the experiment stopped even if minimega cannot kill its VMs. A notice then tells you to clear those VMs in minimega yourself.

The restart button stops the experiment and starts it again, as phenix exp restart does. Its dialog has the stop options and the start options, without the dry run. Before the stop, phēnix checks the disk images: a missing image refuses the restart, and the experiment keeps running. If the start fails after the stop, the experiment stays stopped. A restart needs the permissions to stop and to start the experiment.

To start, stop, restart or delete several experiments at once, check them in the table, then click Start, Stop, Restart or Delete above the table. phēnix tells you which experiments it will skip, and offers to retry any that fail.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
phenix exp start <experiment-name>

Or ...

phenix exp stop <experiment-name>

Or ...

phenix exp restart <experiment-name>

Optionally, you can use the --dry-run flag to do everything except call out to minimega. --vlan-min and --vlan-max set the VLAN range for just this start.

While phenix exp start runs, the Experiments page of the web UI shows the experiment as starting after a page refresh. phēnix refuses a second start of the experiment until the first start ends.

The web UI also shows how far a start or a stop is: the phase, the step and the percent that is done. While phenix exp stop runs, the page shows the experiment as stopping after a page refresh.

After an experiment stops successfully, phēnix deletes the VM disk snapshots created for file injection. To keep these snapshots for debugging, use --keep-injection-snapshots or its -K shorthand:

phenix exp stop --keep-injection-snapshots <experiment-name>

phenix exp restart accepts this option too. In the Web-UI, the stop and restart dialogs have it as Keep the injection snapshots.

If minimega can't kill the experiment's VMs (because it isn't answering, for example), the stop fails and the experiment stays running. Try again once minimega answers, or mark the experiment stopped anyway with --force (-f), or Force the stop in the Web-UI, and clean up its leftover VMs in minimega yourself:

phenix exp stop --force <experiment-name>

See the phenix experiment CLI reference for every subcommand and flag.

Note

For a list of global flags supported across all phenix subcommands, see Global Flags.

docs.title: Disk Check Before a Start
docs.text:
Before minimega launches any VMs, phēnix checks their disk images, on every kind of start (Web-UI, command line, API, phenix workflow apply, and the bulk Start and Restart of VMs). It follows each qcow2 image's backing chain down to its base, and skips external VMs and VMs with do_not_boot: true. A CD-ROM image (advanced.cdrom) or a drive image with the .iso extension only needs to exist.

If a file is missing, a backing chain is broken, or qemu can't open an image (an encrypted image, for example), the start is refused and the experiment stays stopped. See Broken Backing Chains and Image Format Versions. The error names the VM, disk and file:

Error: unable to start the foo experiment: qemu cannot open 2 disks on 1 VM: 2 errors occurred:
    * VM host-01: disk kali.qc2: backing file /phenix/images/ro_kali.qc2 is missing

The Web-UI shows the same thing in an error message:

An old or unusual image format, or a file phēnix can't read, only causes a warning (in the server log for a start from the Web-UI or the API).

The setting experiment.disk-check sets how strict the check is: error (the default) refuses the start, warn starts the experiment and turns each problem into a warning, and off skips the check. phenix exp start --dry-run and --treat-mm-errors-as-warnings also turn every problem into a warning.

phēnix only checks the files on the head node, so an image that only a compute node has will usually refuse the start. Copy it to the head node, or set experiment.disk-check to warn.

A restart runs the check before it stops the experiment, and refuses the restart if the start would be refused. With a user app in the scenario, this early check only warns, and the check at the start can still refuse it. The bulk Start and Restart of VMs check only the selected VMs that minimega launches again: a VM with a broken image fails, and the other VMs start.

docs.title: VLAN In Use at a Start
docs.text: A start fails when minimega has given one of the experiment's pinned VLAN IDs to another alias. In the Web-UI, the error has a Show the conflict link that opens the VLANs page with the details of that ID.

docs.title: The Running Experiment Page
docs.text: Click a running experiment's name to open its page, then click Details to see a summary of the experiment and the Apps box, which shows the status of each app and lets you trigger app stages. The stop and restart buttons next to the search box open the same dialogs as the Experiments table.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
Click the + button to the right of the filter field.

Enter Experiment Name and Experiment Topology, the remaining selection are optional. In this example, bennu is an example topology and is not included by default. You will need to create your own topology(ies), or draw and publish one, with its experiment, in the Builder.

Click Create Experiment, or Create and Start to start it right away.

Advanced Options sets the Deployment Mode (no-headnode, only-headnode or all cluster hosts), the VLAN Range, a workflow branch, and annotations. Default Bridge Name only shows when the bridge mode isn't auto.

docs.title: Purely via the Web-UI (Uploading Topo/Scenario Files)
docs.text:
You can create an experiment entirely through the Web-UI using custom topology and scenario files without needing to use the CLI:

  1. Upload Configurations on the Configs Page:

    • Navigate to the Configs page in the Resources menu.
    • Click the Upload button to upload your topology file (.yaml).
    • (Optional) Click Upload again to upload your scenario file (.yaml).
    • Verify that your uploaded configurations appear in the table (e.g., topology/my-topology and scenario/my-scenario).

  2. Create Experiment in Experiments Tab:

    • Navigate to the Experiments tab.
    • Click the + button to open the creation dialog.
    • Enter an Experiment Name.
    • Select your uploaded topology from the Experiment Topology dropdown.
    • (Optional) Select your uploaded scenario from the Experiment Scenario dropdown.
    • Click Create Experiment to create the experiment.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
You can create an experiment using either saved configuration names from the phēnix store or direct file paths to topology and scenario configuration files (.yaml).

# Using stored configuration names
phenix experiment create <experiment-name> -t <topology-name>
phenix experiment create <experiment-name> -t <topology-name> -s <scenario-name>

# Using direct file paths for topology and scenario
phenix experiment create <experiment-name> -t /path/to/topology.yaml
phenix experiment create <experiment-name> -t /path/to/topology.yaml -s /path/to/scenario.yaml

# Specifying a base directory and disabled apps
phenix experiment create <experiment-name> -t /path/to/topology.yaml -s /path/to/scenario.yaml -d </path/to/dir/> --disabled-apps "app1,app2"

An experiment can't be named all, minimega or __phenix__ (in any letter case), or . or ... From the Web-UI and the API, the base directory (spec.baseDir) must be a folder in <base-dir.phenix>/experiments. The command line has no such limit.

See phenix experiment create in the CLI reference for every flag.

docs.title: Adding Annotations
docs.text:
You can add annotations to an experiment when you create it, without editing its topology or scenario:

Annotations Web-UI (Advanced Options) Command line (repeatable) API (POST /experiments) On every VM Annotations for Every VM --node-annotation key=value node_annotations On the experiment Experiment Annotations --annotation key=value annotations

Annotations for every VM are node annotations that apps read, such as phenix/default-apps and phenix/startup-via-cc. They go into the experiment's own copy of the topology, not the topology config. A VM that already has the annotation keeps its own value, and external nodes are skipped.

Experiment annotations go into the experiment's metadata for apps to read, such as the phenix.workflow/tags pairs that SCORCH records with each run. You can't set topology or scenario.

# For every VM, deliver startup scripts over C2 and create a port forward from 8080 to its port 80
phenix experiment create my-experiment -t my-topology \
  --node-annotation phenix/startup-via-cc=true \
  --node-annotation 'phenix/startup-autotunnel=["8080:80"]' \
  --annotation phenix.workflow/tags=team=red

In the Web-UI, Add annotation offers the annotations that phēnix's own apps read, or a Custom annotation with any key and value.

In VM annotations, true, false and JSON lists or objects keep their type, and phēnix rejects a value of the wrong type for an annotation its apps read.

To change one VM's annotations after the experiment is created, use the Annotations section of its details card.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: The experiment must be stopped before it can be deleted; its trash can icon is disabled while it runs. Click the trash can icon next to the experiment to delete it.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
An experiment must be stopped before it can be deleted:

phenix exp stop <experiment-name>
phenix exp delete <experiment-name>

Alternatively, the -f/--force flag can be used to automatically stop a running experiment before deleting it, similar to docker rm -f, even when minimega cannot kill its VMs, which are then left for you to clear by hand:

phenix exp delete -f <experiment-name>

Using all instead of a specific experiment name will delete all stopped experiments (or, when combined with --force, all experiments regardless of whether they are running).

A delete from the Web-UI or the API doesn't remove a base directory outside <base-dir.phenix>/experiments. phēnix logs a warning instead.

See phenix experiment delete in the CLI reference for every flag.

docs.title: Schedulers
docs.text:
A scheduler picks the cluster host for each VM of a stopped experiment and writes its choices to the experiment's schedules section. At start, minimega places any VM that has no host. Schedulers only run when you ask for one, or when a user app does (exit code 101). You can also set a single VM's host on the Stopped Experiment page.

Scheduler What it does isolate-experiment Puts all VMs on one empty host (the first VM's host if it's empty, else the empty host with the most free memory). Replaces the hosts you set. round-robin Spreads the VMs that have no host evenly over the hosts. subnet-compute Keeps VMs whose first interface is on the same VLAN on the same host while it has free memory, and starts each new VLAN on the host with the least committed memory.

round-robin and subnet-compute keep the hosts you set. To add your own scheduler, put a program named phenix-scheduler-<name> on phēnix's PATH, and phēnix runs it as the scheduler <name>.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: The experiment must be stopped; click on the experiment name to enter the Stopped Experiment component. Click the Schedule button to the right of the start button. The menu tells how many VMs have a host, and lists the schedulers of the server. Click a scheduler, then confirm. See Schedulers for what each one does.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
The list of available schedules can be found by running the following command.

phenix experiment schedulers

Then apply the desired schedule with the following command.

phenix experiment schedule <experiment-name> <algorithm>

A user scheduler (phenix-scheduler-<name>) gets a JSON object on STDIN: the experiment spec (spec) and the schedulable cluster hosts with their disk usage (hosts). To see this JSON, run the following command. The command stores nothing.

phenix util scheduler-json <experiment-name>

The REST API gives the same JSON at GET /api/v1/experiments/<experiment-name>/schedule/input.

docs.title: Scheduling Limits
docs.text:
• A built-in scheduler must finish in 45 seconds. A user scheduler (phenix-scheduler-<name>) must finish in 2 minutes. If a scheduler does not finish in time, phēnix stops it and stores no schedule. The web UI and the REST API then show error 504.
  • If the experiment changes or starts while phēnix schedules it, phēnix keeps that change and stores no schedule. The web UI and the REST API then show error 409. Schedule the experiment again.
  • The web UI and the REST API lock the experiment while they schedule it. You cannot start or change the experiment until the schedule is complete.
  • If the cluster has mesh peers and no peer answers, phēnix stores no schedule. The web UI and the REST API then show error 503. Make sure that minimega runs on the compute nodes, then schedule the experiment again.
  • A schedule can have warnings. phēnix stores the schedule and shows each warning. The web UI shows them in a notice, phenix experiment schedule logs them, and the REST API puts them in warnings. A built-in scheduler gives a warning in these conditions:
    • A VM is set to a host that is not a schedulable cluster host. round-robin and subnet-compute keep that host. isolate-experiment puts the VM on a different host.
    • The VMs on a host need more memory or more CPUs than the host has. The warning gives the committed value and the available value.
  • The capacity checks include the VMs that have do_not_boot set, because you can boot these VMs later.
  • subnet-compute puts a VM that has no interfaces on the host that has the most VMs of the experiment. If that host does not have sufficient memory, it uses the next host.

docs.title: Triggering App Lifecycle Stages
docs.text: You can manually trigger an app lifecycle stage for an experiment without stopping and restarting it.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
The phenix exp trigger command runs one app lifecycle stage on demand:

phenix exp trigger <experiment-name> <lifecycle> [<app-name> ...]

Where <lifecycle> is one of the following stages, or its shorthand:

  • configure (or config)
  • pre-start (or pre)
  • post-start (or post)
  • running (or run)
  • cleanup (or clean)

Providing no app names triggers the stage for every app in the experiment. Use all instead of an experiment name to trigger the stage in every experiment. The running stage is skipped for experiments that are not running.

The stage runs in the command's own process, so press Ctrl+C to stop it.

Examples:

Trigger the running stage for all apps in an experiment:

phenix exp trigger my-experiment running

Trigger the running stage for a specific app:

phenix exp trigger my-experiment running soh

Trigger the configure stage for all experiments:

phenix exp trigger all configure

To stop triggers that phenix ui is running (from the Web-UI or the REST API), use --cancel, with app names to stop only those. With no app names, it also stops the scheduled runs of the running stage from a start.

phenix exp trigger my-experiment --cancel soh

docs.title: API
docs.text: POST /api/v1/experiments/<experiment-name>/trigger?apps=<app,...>&stage=<stage> runs one stage for the apps that apps names. The stage value is one of the stage names above, or its shorthand. Without stage, the request runs the running stage. The request returns before the apps run. The /ws websocket reports the progress of each app. With all as the experiment name, the stage runs in every experiment as a background job. DELETE on the same path cancels the triggers of the apps in apps, or of all apps.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: On a running experiment's page, click Trigger or an app tile in the Apps box to open the phēnix Apps dialog. The page header is collapsed by default. To see the Apps box, click Details. The browser keeps this choice. Select a stage in the Stage list. The default stage is running. Select the apps, then click Trigger Apps. The running stage does not offer the apps that phēnix runs itself, such as ntp. The dialog shows a warning for each other stage, because the stage can change the running experiment. The configure stage rewrites the experiment spec.

docs.title: trigger configure vs. reconfigure
docs.text:
phenix exp trigger configure and phenix experiment reconfigure both re-run the configure lifecycle stage, but they serve different purposes and are not interchangeable:

phenix exp trigger <experiment-name> configure phenix experiment reconfigure Use case Manually re-run a specific app's (or apps') configure hook on demand, e.g. for debugging Re-apply configuration after editing an experiment's stored topology, scenario, or deployment settings Targets specific apps Yes, via [<app-name> ...] No, always applies to every app Validates the experiment config No Yes Runs registered config hooks No Yes Guards against running experiments No Yes (refuses to run if the experiment is running)

Use phenix experiment reconfigure after changing an experiment's stored settings. Use phenix exp trigger <experiment-name> configure for targeted, on-demand re-invocation of one or more apps' configure hooks, such as when debugging an app.

docs.title: Deprecated Command
docs.text:
The phenix exp trigger-running command, and its trig alias, are deprecated and will be removed in a future release. Use phenix exp trigger instead. The deprecated command:

phenix exp trigger-running my-experiment [<app-name> ...]

Is equivalent to:

phenix exp trigger my-experiment running [<app-name> ...]

The old argument order, phenix exp trigger <lifecycle> <experiment-name>, is also deprecated (see Deprecations).

docs.title: VLAN Aliases
docs.text: Topologies refer to VLANs by alias, such as MGMT or EXP-1, which is mapped by phēnix to a numerical VLAN ID.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
On a stopped experiment, click the VLAN IDs button. The menu lists each alias with its VLAN ID. Enter an ID from 1 to 4094, or 0 to let minimega pick an ID when the experiment starts. Then click Save VLAN IDs.

Before saving, phēnix checks the IDs against the rest of the cluster and lists any conflict, such as an ID that another experiment has pinned (see Conflict Check Before a Save).

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
The phenix vlan alias command can list and change VLAN aliases.

# List VLAN aliases of every experiment
phenix vlan alias

# List VLAN aliases of a single experiment
phenix vlan alias <experiment-name>

# Print the VLAN ID of a specific alias for an experiment
phenix vlan alias <experiment-name> <alias-name>

# Pin the alias to a VLAN ID
phenix vlan alias <experiment-name> <alias-name> <vlan-id>

# Clear the pin, so minimega gives the alias an ID at the start
phenix vlan alias <experiment-name> <alias-name> --unpin

To pin or unpin an alias, the experiment must be stopped. phēnix refuses a pin when another experiment or a minimega namespace already uses the ID, or when minimega blacklists it. Add --force to pin it anyway. See VLANs for the other phenix vlan commands.

For example, if the MYVLAN alias of my-experiment maps to VLAN 105:

$ phenix vlan alias my-experiment MYVLAN
105

A running experiment reports the VLAN IDs minimega assigned when it started. A stopped experiment has no ID for an alias unless one was set explicitly, so most alias lookups will fail until the experiment starts.

docs.title: Experiment Files
docs.text: The Files tab of an experiment (running or stopped) lists the files that phēnix, its apps and SCORCH wrote for it, wherever on the cluster they were written. They live in the experiment's files folder in the minimega files directory, which the Disks page leaves out, so this is where you manage the experiment's VM disk snapshots.

docs.title: Finding a File
docs.text: Use the All Categories dropdown to show one category, such as Packet Capture, Scorch Artifact or VM Disk Snapshot, or the Find a File box to search the names and categories of all the experiment's files.

docs.title: Opening a File
docs.text:
Click a text file's name (.json, .jsonl, .log, .txt, .yaml or .yml) to read it in the browser, up to 10 MiB. Click a capture file's name (.pcap, .pcapng or .cap, optionally gzipped) to open it in WebShark, if WebShark is installed. Download anything else. An interrupted download resumes.

You can't view, download or delete a .pcap file that a running capture is still writing. Stop the capture first, or watch it live in WebShark.

docs.title: Acting on Several Files
docs.text:
Check some files (or the heading checkbox, for every file the table shows) to get a toolbar above the table:

  • Download (N) zips the checked files into <experiment-name>-files.zip as a background job, then downloads it. If you leave the page, you can still download the archive from the jobs menu within the hour.
  • Delete (N) deletes the checked files.

Warning

Deleting a file removes it from every cluster node, and it can't be undone.

One zip download holds at most 500 files and 2 GiB in total. A file the server can't fetch is left out of the archive, and a file that grows while the archive is built is cut at the size it had. The archive is then named <experiment-name>-files-incomplete.zip, its MISSING.txt lists those files, and it only downloads after you click Download incomplete archive.

docs.title: Adding Files
docs.text: To add your own files, such as an installer or a config file, upload them through the phēnix file server (see Uploading Experiment Files from the phēnix Server, which also covers copying them into a VM). They show up in the Files tab like any other.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
The phenix exp files commands do the same things as the Files tab (see phenix experiment files). A file is named by its path relative to the experiment's files folder, as phenix exp files list shows it.

# List the packet captures larger than 1 MB
phenix exp files list my-exp --filter "packet and size > 1mb"

# Copy a file to the current folder
phenix exp files get my-exp captures/web_eth0.pcap -O web_eth0.pcap

# Print the SHA-256 checksum of a file
phenix exp files checksum my-exp captures/web_eth0.pcap

# Write several files to a local zip archive
phenix exp files archive my-exp web_eth0.pcap db_eth0.pcap -O captures.zip

# Delete files from every node (add --dry-run to see what it would delete)
phenix exp files delete my-exp web_eth0.pcap

--filter takes the same search syntax as the Files tab (see phenix experiment files list). archive has the same limits as the Files tab, and if it has to leave a file out, it still writes the archive (with MISSING.txt) and then fails.

docs.title: 1. Basic Experiment Lifecycle
docs.text:
# 1. Create experiment from topology/scenario files
phenix exp create my-experiment -t /path/to/topology.yaml -s /path/to/scenario.yaml

# 2. Start the experiment
phenix exp start my-experiment

# 3. View status and inspect VMs
phenix exp list
phenix vm info my-experiment

# 4. Stop the experiment when testing finishes
phenix exp stop my-experiment

# 5. Delete the experiment
phenix exp delete my-experiment

docs.title: 2. Updating and Reconfiguring an Experiment
docs.text:
# Reconfigure a stopped experiment after modifying underlying configuration files
phenix exp reconfigure my-experiment

docs.title: 3. Dry-Run Deployment Testing
docs.text:
# Test experiment startup logic without deploying minimega VMs
phenix exp start my-experiment --dry-run

docs.text:

  • phenix experiment files: every files command and flag.

  • VMs: work with the VMs of a running experiment.
  • Troubleshooting: what to do when a start fails.
  • Packet Captures: where the capture files come from.
  • Netflow: the recorded netflow captures.

docs.title: GRE Mesh
docs.text:
Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) is a tunneling protocol that wraps one packet inside another, so the inner packet can cross an IP network between two tunnel endpoints. Layer 2 GRE carries whole Ethernet frames, which makes two switches joined by a GRE tunnel behave as if a cable connected them. For more background, see Generic Routing Encapsulation and RFC 2784.

Use --use-gre-mesh when an experiment spans multiple minimega nodes and its virtual networks need to connect VMs on different hosts. phēnix uses minimega to connect the hosts' Open vSwitch (OVS) bridges with Layer 2 GRE tunnels. These tunnels trunk experiment VLANs across the host IP network, so VMs on the same experiment network communicate transparently across hosts, including Ethernet broadcast traffic such as ARP. Guest addresses and network membership do not need to change when VMs run on different hosts.

For example, two VMs on the same experiment VLAN can communicate even when one runs on minimega node A and the other on node B. Their Ethernet frames travel from A's OVS bridge through GRE to B's OVS bridge. The physical network carries the encapsulated traffic without needing to trunk each experiment VLAN itself. See minimega's namespace bridge documentation.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The minimega nodes must already belong to a working mesh, with IP connectivity between tunnel endpoints and GRE traffic (IP protocol 47) permitted along the path. The flag configures experiment network connectivity; VM placement still depends on the experiment's schedule and available hosts. A single-host experiment does not need GRE for communication between its local VMs.

Prepare the physical network MTU before starting experiments; see MTU and fragmentation below.

docs.title: Enable GRE
docs.text:
Enable GRE when creating an experiment (the default is disabled):

phenix experiment create my-exp -t my-topology --use-gre-mesh
phenix experiment start my-exp

For an existing experiment, stop it, run phenix experiment edit my-exp, and set spec.useGREMesh to true before starting it again. Passing the flag only to experiment start does not change this stored setting.

The Web-UI has no GRE option. REST API clients can enable GRE for a single experiment by setting use_gre_mesh to true in the POST /api/v1/experiments request body. To enable GRE for every experiment created or updated through the Web-UI or REST API, start the server with phenix ui --use-gre-mesh. CLI commands inherit an enabled server setting; --use-gre-mesh=false cannot override it. See Settings & Configuration for configuration file and environment variable alternatives.

docs.title: Bridge Scope
docs.text: GRE mesh setup applies to the experiment's default bridge. Interfaces assigned to other bridges explicitly in the topology need their own connectivity arrangements. Bridge Mode explains how phēnix selects the default bridge; --bridge-mode auto gives each experiment its own bridge and can be combined with --use-gre-mesh at creation.

docs.title: MTU and Fragmentation
docs.text:
The physical network needs a larger MTU than the guests to accommodate the encapsulated Ethernet frame and IP/GRE headers. For 1500-byte guest MTUs, a host IP MTU of 1600 provides headroom for ordinary GRE over IPv4; additional encapsulation may require more. Configure sufficient MTU/frame size across all host interfaces, routed hops, and physical switch ports carrying the tunnels. phēnix does not configure these for you.

An undersized path can cause fragmentation, reduced performance, or dropped packets even when small pings succeed. If increasing the physical network MTU is not possible, reduce guest MTUs to leave room for encapsulation. See the OVS tunneling guide and RFC 7588 for details.

docs.title: Verify Connectivity
docs.text:
Confirm that the communicating VMs actually run on different minimega hosts and share an experiment VLAN. On each host, ovs-vsctl show should show GRE interfaces attached to the experiment's default bridge. Check the configured remote endpoints and verify that the host network can reach them.

Test both small and full-size packets between guests. For a Linux guest with a 1500-byte IPv4 MTU, for example:

ping -M do -s 1472 <peer-guest-ip>

The 1472-byte payload plus IPv4 and ICMP headers makes a 1500-byte guest IP packet. This checks guest connectivity at that size, but does not prove the outer GRE packets avoided fragmentation. Inspect traffic on the physical interfaces or fragmentation counters on the hosts to verify that separately.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• VLANs: VLAN aliases, ranges and the VLANs page.
  • Troubleshooting: when VMs on different nodes cannot reach each other.

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text:
A running phenix ui server answers two health endpoints that need no credentials, so Docker, systemd, Kubernetes or a load balancer can tell whether phēnix is up.

# Liveness: is the phēnix process up?
curl -s http://localhost:3000/healthz

# Readiness: can phēnix run experiments right now?
curl -s http://localhost:3000/readyz

phenix healthcheck does the same from the command line. It exits 0 when the server answers 200, and 1 otherwise:

phenix healthcheck                 # liveness, prints e.g. "pass (200)"
phenix healthcheck --ready         # readiness, listing each check that is not passing
phenix healthcheck --ready -o json # the whole response body
phenix healthcheck --url https://phenix.example.com/readyz --timeout 10s

phenix healthcheck builds the URL from the ui.listen-endpoint, ui.tls-key and ui.tls-cert settings, so it can't see a value you only gave as a flag to phenix ui. In that case, pass --url or set the matching PHENIX_UI_* environment variables. If phenix ui won't start at all, use doctor instead.

docs.title: The Endpoints
docs.text:
• /healthz (liveness) checks that the server is up and the store can be read. Restarting phēnix may fix a failure, so the Docker and Podman health checks use it.
  • /readyz (readiness) also checks minimega, the mesh, qemu-img, WebShark, free disk space and the websocket broker. A failure usually means something phēnix depends on is down.

Both answer GET and HEAD at the server root (or <base-path>/healthz with --base-path), not under /api/v1. A proxy that requires its own sign-in on every path must exempt them, or your monitors must probe the phēnix port directly.

Each endpoint answers 200 with a status of pass or warn (something needs a look, but phēnix works), and 503 with fail. The body is application/health+json, with each result in checks keyed component:measurement, such as disk:utilization.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
Check Endpoints Warns when Fails when uptime both never never store both listing configs takes over a second the store cannot be read minimega /readyz minimega takes over a second to answer, the namespaces cannot be listed, or the mesh has fewer nodes than it has had since phēnix started minimega does not answer qemu-img /readyz qemu-img is missing or broken never webshark /readyz, only when WebShark is installed the WebShark build is gone never disk /readyz a filesystem is at least 90% full a filesystem is at least 98% full websocket /readyz the broadcast queue is at least 75% full never go /readyz never never

disk checks the minimega files directory, the phēnix base directory and the directory that holds the store. To leave checks out, pass their names to ?exclude=, repeated or comma-separated:

curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/readyz?exclude=disk&exclude=qemu-img' | jq .status

Anyone who can reach the server sees each check's status and measurements. The output fields, which name paths, hosts and errors, are only in answers to authenticated requests. A probe that cannot set a header can pass ?token=<token>, but proxies and access logs often record the full URL, token included.

docs.title: Docker and Podman
docs.text:
The phenix service in docker/docker-compose.yml runs phenix healthcheck every 30 seconds, and only starts once the minimega service is healthy. podman/pod.yml gives the phenix container the same check as a liveness probe.

docker compose ps                              # the STATUS column shows (healthy)
docker exec phenix phenix healthcheck --ready  # minimega, store, disks, ...

The images don't set a HEALTHCHECK themselves. If you start your own container to run phenix ui, add the check yourself:

services:
  phenix:
    image: ghcr.io/sandialabs/sceptre-phenix/phenix:main
    command: ["phenix", "ui"]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "phenix", "healthcheck"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 60s

docs.title: Kubernetes and Podman Probes
docs.text:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 3000
  initialDelaySeconds: 60
  periodSeconds: 30
  timeoutSeconds: 10
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /readyz
    port: 3000
  periodSeconds: 30
  timeoutSeconds: 10

With TLS, add scheme: HTTPS. To probe from inside the container instead, use exec: {command: [phenix, healthcheck]}, as podman/pod.yml does.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• phenix healthcheck: every flag of the command.
  • Troubleshooting: fixes for common problems.

docs.title: Hosts
docs.text:
The Hosts page (in the Resources menu) lists the nodes in the minimega mesh and how busy each one is.

Load, RAM Used and Disk Used turn yellow at 65% and red at 85%. Load is measured against the host's CPU count, so a load of 4 is green on an 8-CPU host and red on a 4-CPU host. Disk Used is for the disks that hold the phēnix and minimega base directories, and is measured at most once a minute.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
phenix host list shows each node's CPUs, load, memory, VMs and network traffic, and doesn't need a running phenix ui. See phenix host.

phenix host list

# Each node with the fields of GET /api/v1/hosts
phenix host list -o json

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• minimega: how phēnix uses the minimega cluster.
  • Scheduling an Experiment: choose which host runs each VM.

docs.title: Virtual Disk Images Management
docs.text:
Disk images are built only with the command line binary. The Disks page of the web UI lists the images the phēnix server has, both in the minimega files directory (and its folders) and wherever a topology points to them. It can snapshot, clone, rename, download, upload and delete the images in the files directory; images outside it are listed but not changed.

Click the In use count above the table to show only the images in use. Click it again, or click the X beside the search box, to show all images.

If the file of an image is a symbolic link (symlink), the Disks page shows Symlink to and the target of the link under the name of the image. The details card of the image also shows the target. A relative target is relative to the folder of the image. The table of phenix disk list shows the target after the path, for example link.qc2 -> win/win10.qc2.

Before it deletes an image, phēnix checks for images that it backs and for experiments that use it. If it finds any, the Disks page lists them, and you can cancel or select Delete anyway.

docs.title: Listing disk images
docs.text: phenix image list

docs.title: Creating a disk image
docs.text:
The vmdb2 utility is required -- in path -- to create the disk images. This utility is included with the phenix Docker image.

phenix image create <image-name>

The phenix image create --help will output:

Create a disk image configuration

  Used to create a virtual disk image configuration from which to build
    an image.

    When specifying the --size option, the following units can be used:

    M - Megabytes
    G - Gigabytes

Usage:
  phenix image create <image name> [flags]

Examples:

  phenix image create <image name>
  phenix image create --size 2G --variant mingui --release noble --compress --overlays foobar --packages foo --scripts bar <image name>

Flags:
  -l, --components string    List of components from the mirror to download packages from (separated by comma)
  -c, --compress             Compress image after creation (does not apply to raw image)
  -f, --format string        Format of disk image (default "qcow2")
  -h, --help                 help for create
  -k, --kernel-args string   List of parameters which grub will pass to the Linux kernel (e.g. 'net.ifnames=0','consoleblank=0'); separated by comma). Warning: each comma starts a new parameter, so a value with a comma, such as console=ttyS0,115200n8, is split, which can make the build fail.
  -m, --mirror string        Debootstrap mirror (must match release) (default "http://us.archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu")
      --no-virtuals          Don't add virtual filesystem mounts to chroot before executing scripts when running vmdb2 (default is 'false')
  -O, --overlays string      List of overlay names (include full path; separated by comma)
  -P, --packages string      List of packages to include in addition to those provided by variant (separated by comma)
  -R, --ramdisk              Create a kernel/initrd pair in addition to a disk image
  -r, --release string       OS release codename (default "noble")
  -T, --scripts string       List of scripts to include in addition to the defaults (include full path; separated by comma)
  -s, --size string          Image size to use (default "10G")
      --skip-default-pkgs    Skip default packages typically included in all builds
  -v, --variant string       Image variant to use (default "minbase")

The vmdb2 configuration file can be read by running the following command:

phenix cfg get image/<image-name>

docs.title: Building a disk image
docs.text:
Building a disk image requires an existing configuration in the store (i.e., the create command should be run first to create a configuration); running phenix image build --help will output:

Build a virtual disk image

  Used to build a new virtual disk using an existing configuration; vmdb2 must
  be in path.

Usage:
  phenix image build <configuration name> [flags]

Examples:

  phenix image build <configuration name>
  phenix image build --very-verbose --output </path/to/dir/>

Flags:
  -c, --cache           Cache rootfs as tar archive
      --dry-run         Do everything but actually call out to vmdb2
  -h, --help            help for build
  -o, --output string   Specify the output directory for the disk image to be saved to
  -v, --verbose         Enable verbose output
  -x, --very-verbose    Enable very verbose output, additionally writes output log file to <image name>.log

docs.title: append
docs.text:
The disk image management tool will allow you to add packages, overlays, and scripts to existing configurations using the append command. Command usage is:

phenix image append <configuration-name> [flags]

Flags are for the overlays, packages, and scripts that you want to append.

docs.title: create-from
docs.text:
Run this command if you have an existing configuration that you would like to use as the base to create a new configuration from. The usage involves referencing the existing configuration, the new configuration name, and then additional packages, overlays, and scripts.

phenix image create-from <existing-configuration> <new-configuration> [flags]

Flags are for the overlays, packages, and scripts that you want to add to the new configuration.

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
phenix image delete <image-name>...

You can give more than one name. If one can't be deleted, the command keeps going with the rest, then exits with an error that lists each failure. Add --dry-run to see which configurations it would delete.

A name can contain the wildcard *, which matches zero or more characters. Other characters, such as ? and [, match only themselves. Put quotation marks around a pattern. If you do not, zsh stops with "no matches found", and bash can change the pattern to the names of local files.

phenix image delete 'cm-*' --dry-run
phenix image delete 'cm-*'

Before phenix deletes the configurations that a pattern selects, it shows their names and their count. The pattern '*' selects all image configurations. Another pattern that selects no configuration is an error.

An alternative could be to use the configuration management tool.

phenix cfg delete image/<image-name>

docs.title: remove
docs.text:
The remove command will allow you to remove any packages, overlays, and scripts from an existing image configuration.

phenix image remove <configuration-name> [flags]

Flags are for the overlays, packages, and scripts that you want to remove.

docs.title: update
docs.text:
This update command is used to update the script on an existing image configuration. The path to a script is tracked in the code. The image configuration gets updated with the script in the path; if no changes were made no harm. If the path no longer exists, phenix will leave the configuration alone.

phenix image update <configuration-name>

The scripts keep their order. update doesn't add or remove scripts or change packages or overlays; use append or remove for that.

docs.title: Kali Image
docs.text:
The Docker image for phenix includes everything needed to build a Kali image. If phenix is installed locally, the following will be needed to create and build a Kali image.

To build a Kali release on a non-Kali (but still Debian-based) operating system, the following steps must be taken to prepare the host (Debian-based) OS first. These steps are based on the official Kali documentation located at:

https://www.kali.org/tutorials/build-kali-with-live-build-on-debian-based-systems/.

  1. Download and install the latest version of the Kali archive keyring package. At time of writing, the latest version was 2020.2.
wget http://http.kali.org/kali/pool/main/k/kali-archive-keyring/kali-archive-keyring_2020.2_all.deb
sudo dpkg -i kali-archive-keyring_2020.2_all.deb
  1. Next, create the debootstrap build script for Kali, based entirely off the existing Debian Sid build script. Note that the following commands will likely need to be run as root.
cd /usr/share/debootstrap/scripts
sed -e "s/debian-archive-keyring.gpg/kali-archive-keyring.gpg/g" sid > kali
ln -s kali kali-rolling

At this point, you should be able to build a Kali release with phenix image.

docs.text:

  • Image: the Image config that a build reads.
  • Disks: manage the built images from the web UI.
  • Troubleshooting: when a build fails.

docs.title: Background Jobs
docs.text: Some things take too long for a single web request: acting on lots of VMs at once, zipping up experiment files, or cloning a big disk image. phēnix runs these as background jobs on the server. You get an answer right away, and the job keeps going even if you close the browser tab or lose your connection.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: The background jobs menu in the header lists your jobs and their progress, and lets you cancel them, download what they produced, and dismiss them.

docs.title: What runs as a job
docs.text:
Kind Started by vms.action bulk actions in the VM table (see VM Multi Action) files.archive downloading several experiment files (see Experiment Files) disk.clone cloning a disk image (see Disks) experiments.start, experiments.trigger starting or triggering all experiments through the API experiments.periodic starting an experiment through phenix ui when an app in its scenario has runPeriodically (see Starting / Stopping Experiments)

An experiments.periodic job runs the apps' running stage on schedule until the experiment stops or someone cancels the job. VM snapshots, starting a single experiment and SCORCH runs aren't jobs.

docs.title: Job status
docs.text:
phēnix runs a few jobs at once for each user and queues the rest. A job is queued, then running, and ends as succeeded, partial (some items failed or were skipped), failed or canceled. A failed or skipped item has an error that says why, and when trying it again may work, the web UI offers Retry failed.

If you cancel a running VM action job, it doesn't start any more VMs and stops after the ones in progress finish. A canceled archive or clone job stops at once and leaves no file behind.

Jobs only live in the memory of the phenix ui server. A finished job is kept for one hour, or until you dismiss it, and the archive of a files.archive job is deleted with it. A cloned disk image stays. Restarting the server loses every job and cancels the running ones (see Stopping the Server).

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
phenix job follows and cancels the jobs of the running phenix ui server, for every user. It can't start jobs: commands such as phenix vm restart do their work in the phenix process itself. See phenix job for every flag.

# Running and queued jobs of one experiment
phenix job list --experiment my-exp --active

# One job and the outcome of each item
phenix job get j0f3a9c2e81b4d7a6

# Cancel a job
phenix job cancel j0f3a9c2e81b4d7a6

# Wait at most 10 minutes for a job to finish
phenix job wait j0f3a9c2e81b4d7a6 --timeout 10m

phenix job wait exits 0 if the job succeeded, 2 if it ended partial, and 1 otherwise.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Route Does GET /api/v1/jobs lists jobs, newest first; filter with ?experiment=, ?kind= and ?active=true GET /api/v1/jobs/{id} returns one job with every item and its result POST /api/v1/jobs/{id}/cancel cancels a job DELETE /api/v1/jobs/{id} dismisses a finished job and deletes its file GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}/artifact downloads the file the job produced (see Downloads)

A route that starts a job answers with the job and its Location, as Background Jobs in the API page describes. When the queue is full, it answers 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After.

docs.title: Retrying a request that starts a job
docs.text:
If a client loses the answer, it can't tell whether the job started. To retry safely, send an Idempotency-Key header (1 to 255 printable ASCII characters, such as a UUID) and reuse it for each retry. A retry by the same user with the same key, body and query gets the first answer again and doesn't start a second job; the same key with a different body or query gets 422. Keys are kept for an hour, and a server restart forgets them.

# One key per request, reused for each of its retries
KEY=$(uuidgen)
curl -X POST -H "X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: $KEY" \
  -d '{"action": "restart", "vms": ["web", "db"]}' \
  http://localhost:3000/api/v1/experiments/my-exp/vms/actions

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: phēnix features a centralized logging system that aggregates logs from the core daemon, internal Go services, and external user applications.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The logging architecture is designed to be centralized. The phēnix core acts as the aggregator, capturing stderr from all running applications, parsing the output as JSON, and ingesting it into the centralized logging system.

graph TD
    subgraph "phēnix core"
        Core[phēnix Daemon]
        Plog[plog Package]
        FileLog[File Logger]
        ConsoleLog[Console Logger]
        UILog[UI Logger]
        Config[Viper Config]
    end

    subgraph "Go Apps"
        GoApp[Go Application]
        GoSlog[slog JSON Handler]
    end

    subgraph "Python Apps"
        PyApp[Python Application]
        PyLog[Python Logger]
        PySink[phēnix Stderr Sink]
    end

    Config -->|Watches config.yaml| Plog
    Core -->|Uses| Plog

    Plog -->|Write JSON/Text| FileLog
    Plog -->|Write Text| ConsoleLog
    Plog -->|Publish| UILog

    GoApp -->|Log| GoSlog
    GoSlog -->|JSON via Stderr| Core

    PyApp -->|Log| PyLog
    PyLog -->|Log| PySink
    PySink -->|JSON via Stderr| Core

    Core -->|ProcessStderrLogs| Plog

docs.title: CLI Verbosity (--log.level)
docs.text:
You can temporarily increase or decrease log verbosity for any command by using the global --log.level flag.

phenix <command> --log.level=<level>

This is useful when troubleshooting because it only affects that command invocation.

docs.title: Available Levels
docs.text:
phēnix supports the following log levels for --log.level:

  • debug: Most verbose output for troubleshooting.
  • info: Default level. Normal operational messages.
  • warn: Warnings and errors.
  • error: Errors only.
  • none: Suppress all standard log output.

Note

Level names are case-insensitive (for example, DEBUG and debug are equivalent).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Use higher verbosity to inspect behavior while running a command:

# Run the UI with debug logging for this invocation
phenix ui --log.level=debug

# Show only warnings and errors while listing experiments
phenix exp list --log.level=warn

# Keep command output quiet unless an error occurs
phenix config get --log.level=error Role/vm-admin

To change the default level for all future commands, use settings:

phenix settings set log.level debug

To revert and use the configured default again for subsequent commands:

phenix settings unset log.level

docs.title: The App Contract
docs.text:
All applications (Go or Python) running under phēnix must adhere to the following contract to ensure their logs are correctly parsed and displayed in the UI:

  1. Output: Logs must be written to stderr.
  2. Format: Logs must be single-line JSON objects.
  3. Required Fields:
    • level: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR
    • msg: The log message string.
  4. Optional Fields:
    • time: Timestamp (RFC3339 or similar). phēnix keeps it as proc_time.
    • traceback: For exceptions/panics (string).

Tip

Check out the Example Applications for complete, runnable reference implementations in Go and Python.

docs.title: Python Apps
docs.text:
Use the phenix_apps.common.logger. AppBase configures it to output JSON to stderr; an app that doesn't use AppBase calls configure_logging() first.

Important

For fatal errors, raise an exception (e.g., ValueError, RuntimeError) instead of calling sys.exit(1). The AppBase class wraps execution in a try/except block and will automatically catch the exception, log the traceback as structured JSON, and exit cleanly.

from phenix_apps.common.logger import logger

def my_func():
    try:
        logger.bind(custom_field="value").info("Starting operation")
        # ... code ...
    except Exception:
        # Automatically captures traceback and formats as JSON
        logger.exception("Operation failed")

docs.title: Go Apps
docs.text:
Use log/slog with a JSON handler.

import (
    "log/slog"
    "os"
)

func main() {
    logger := slog.New(slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stderr, nil))
    slog.SetDefault(logger)

    slog.Info("Application started", "app", "my-app")
}

docs.title: phēnix Core
docs.text:
Use the phenix/util/plog package for logging within the core application.

import "phenix/util/plog"

func MyFunc() {
    // Always provide a LogType enum for UI filtering
    plog.Info(plog.TypeSystem, "System initialized", "version", "1.0")
}

The log types are AUDIT, SECURITY, SOH, SCORCH, PHENIX-APP, ACTION, HTTP, MINIMEGA and SYSTEM. Web handlers log AUDIT records with the phenix/web/audit package rather than with plog directly (see Audit Events).

docs.title: HTTP Request Logging
docs.text: To view detailed HTTP request logs (method, path, status, duration), start the UI with the --log-requests flag.

docs.title: Logs Page
docs.text:
The Logs page (in the Admin menu) shows the system log, oldest first, and follows new entries as the server logs them.

On the Logs page, select a log message to open its details. The details show the level, the time, the type, the message text, and each key=value field in a list. Use Copy to copy the full message. Use Previous and Next to go to the adjacent messages in the filtered list.

docs.title: Downloading Log Files
docs.text: The Download menu gets the whole log files. phēnix log is the system log file (log.system.path), without its rotated files. minimega log is the file that ui.logs.minimega-path names, which the phenix ui server must be able to read, so in a container deployment, mount minimega's log into the phēnix container. The API serves the same files at GET /logs/files/{name}.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
The phenix logs commands get the same data from the running phenix ui server. By default, phenix logs shows the entries of the last hour.

# The entries of the last 10 minutes
phenix logs --since 10m

# The log files and whether the server can read them
phenix logs files

# Write the minimega log to a file
phenix logs download minimega -O minimega.log

docs.title: Audit Events
docs.text:
The web API logs an audit event, a record of type AUDIT, for each security-relevant action. The fields follow the Elastic Common Schema (ECS) as flat dotted keys, so you can ship the system log file to Elasticsearch as it is.

A success logs at INFO with event.outcome success. A refusal or a failure logs at WARN with event.outcome failure: a refusal by the user's role adds denied to event.type and says why in event.reason, and a failure puts the error in error.message. An audit event never holds a password or a token. A request refused before its permission is checked, such as one with a malformed body, isn't audited, unless it was refused for its token (see Refused Tokens).

A few things to know when you read these events:

  • A resumed download is audited once.
  • An action run as a background job is audited when the job finishes, as the user who started it, with phenix.job.id. A bulk VM action is audited once for each VM.
  • A workflow apply with dryRun=true has phenix.dry_run true and event.type info.
  • A request over the Unix socket, such as one from phenix workflow apply, has phenix.auth.method unix-socket and Global Admin in user.roles.
  • A request with a capture token is audited as the user the token was given to, with the route's template as url.path, so the token is never logged.

docs.title: Refused Tokens
docs.text:
A request that the API, the file server or a health probe refuses for its credentials is audited as a request-auth failure, with one of these event.reason values:

Reason The request had missing no token, on a route that needs one malformed a token or X-Phenix-Auth-Token header that does not parse invalid a token with a bad signature, or one that names no user expired a token past its expiry revoked a token its user no longer holds, after signing out or deleting it unknown-user, no-role a token naming a user that does not exist, or whose role cannot be read proxy-user-mismatch a proxy user header that names another user than the token

user.name is the user the token names, when its signature was checked. With proxy-jwt the signature isn't checked, so that user goes in phenix.auth.claimed_user instead. Only the first refusal each minute from a client address for a given reason is audited, and the next audited one counts the skipped ones in phenix.suppressed.

docs.title: Where Audit Events Go
docs.text: Audit events always go to the system log file (log.system.path), whatever log.level is. The console and the Logs page follow log.level and ui.logs.level, so with either set to warn you'll only see refusals and failures there. On the Logs page, choose AUDIT in the Type filter and search for a field, such as event.action=disk-delete or user.name=alice. Actions you take with the phenix CLI aren't audited, other than those that phenix workflow apply sends through the Unix socket.

docs.title: Shipping Audit Events with Filebeat
docs.text:
Filebeat (7.17 or later) can ship the audit events from the system log file, with their own @timestamp, using an input like this:

filebeat.inputs:
  - type: filestream
    id: phenix-audit
    paths:
      - /var/log/phenix/phenix.log
    parsers:
      - ndjson:
          target: ""
          overwrite_keys: true
          expand_keys: true
    processors:
      - drop_event:
          when:
            not:
              equals:
                type: AUDIT
      - rename:
          fields:
            - from: msg
              to: message
            - from: level
              to: log.level
          ignore_missing: true
      - drop_fields:
          fields: [time]
          ignore_missing: true

Troubleshooting

For common logging issues and solutions, please see the Troubleshooting page.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Settings Reference: every log.* setting.
  • Doctor: checks the log settings without a running server.

docs.title: minimega Integration
docs.text: phēnix uses minimega as its underlying network and virtual machine emulation backend. The phenix mm command provides direct access to send commands to minimega or attach to minimega's interactive console from the phēnix host. For full details on minimega's command set and capabilities, consult the minimega Documentation and the minimega API Reference.

docs.title: Command Line Usage
docs.text:
Send commands, or attach, to minimega

  Sends a command to minimega and prints the response, or attaches to the
  interactive minimega console. Exits non-zero if minimega reports an error.

  Flags must come before the minimega command. Everything after the first
  minimega argument, including arguments that start with "-", is passed to
  minimega unchanged, and arguments are quoted for minimega as needed. A
  single argument is sent as-is, so a whole command written in minimega's own
  syntax can be passed as one quoted string.

Usage:
  phenix mm <minimega args>... [flags]

Aliases:
  mm, minimega

Examples:

  phenix mm vm info
  phenix mm -n <experiment name> vm info
  phenix mm -n <experiment name> cc exec ls -a
  phenix mm -n <experiment name> "vm info"
  phenix minimega -a -n <experiment name>

Flags:
  -a, --attach             Attach to minimega console instead of sending commands
  -h, --help               help for mm
  -n, --namespace string   Default minimega namespace to use

Note

For a list of global flags supported across all phenix subcommands, see Global Flags.

docs.title: Sending Commands to minimega
docs.text:
You can execute non-interactive minimega commands directly through phenix mm.

# View minimega cluster host status
phenix mm host

# Display minimega VM information across all namespaces
phenix mm vm info

# List active VLANs in minimega
phenix mm vlans

phenix mm flags, and any global flags, must come before the minimega command. Everything after the first minimega argument is passed to minimega unchanged, including arguments that start with -, so phenix mm cc exec ls -a runs ls -a rather than treating -a as the --attach flag.

phēnix quotes each argument for minimega as needed, so empty arguments and arguments containing spaces, quotes, or # arrive intact. A single argument is sent as-is instead, which lets you pass a whole command written in minimega's own syntax as one quoted string, such as phenix mm "vm info".

If minimega errors or the minimega daemon is unreachable, phenix mm will exit with a non-zero status and record the error in the phēnix log.

You can also send a minimega command through the REST API with POST /api/v1/minimega/commands, just like phenix mm. Of the built-in roles, only Global Admin can do this, and each command is audited as minimega-command.

docs.title: Namespace Scoping
docs.text:
When working with experiment-specific VMs or VLANs, use the --namespace (-n) flag to target a specific minimega namespace. Each running experiment has a minimega namespace with the same name as the experiment.

# Execute minimega commands within the 'my-experiment' namespace
phenix mm --namespace my-experiment vm info

# Check the network connections of VMs in the 'my-experiment' namespace
phenix mm -n my-experiment .columns name,vlan,bridge,tap,ip vm info

With shell completion enabled, --namespace completes the names of running experiments, and phenix mm completes minimega commands using suggestions from the running minimega.

Warning

Specifying a namespace that does not exist will cause minimega to create it.

docs.title: Attaching to the minimega Console
docs.text:
The --attach (-a) flag opens an interactive minimega console session, allowing real-time interaction with the minimega shell.

# Attach to the global minimega console
phenix mm --attach

# Attach to the minimega console scoped to a specific experiment namespace
phenix mm -a -n my-experiment

To exit the attached console session, type disconnect or press Ctrl+D.

Warning

Typing quit in the console stops the minimega daemon itself, not just the console session. minimega asks you to enter quit a second time to confirm.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
If the phēnix server is started with phenix ui --minimega-console (or PHENIX_UI_MINIMEGA_CONSOLE=true), Console in the Admin menu opens a minimega console in the browser.

Your console keeps running while you visit other pages or reload. It ends when you press Ctrl+D or type disconnect, when you log out, or shortly after you close the last tab that has it open. Click Start a new console to get a new one, or Reconnect if the connection was lost.

The toolbar above the terminal has these controls:

  • State: The connection state: Connecting, Connected, Ended, or Connection lost.
  • Namespace: The experiment whose minimega namespace the console uses. "All (no namespace)" uses no namespace. Running experiments are first in the list. A change starts a new console in the namespace that you select, and then ends the old console. The page asks you to confirm first. If the new console does not start, the old console stays.
  • Commands: A menu of common minimega commands, and a link to the minimega API Reference. The page erases the text on the command line, and then types the command that you select. It also enters commands that only read data. You must enter commands that change data, such as vm start, yourself.
  • Search: Finds text in the output. Press Enter for the next match and Shift+Enter for the previous match.
  • Text size: Makes the text smaller or larger. The browser keeps the size for the next visit.
  • Clear, Copy all, and Download: Clear the terminal, copy all of the output, or download the output as a text file. The terminal keeps approximately the last 10,000 lines of output. If the output has more lines, the page tells you that the copy or the file has only the last lines.
  • End console: Ends your minimega command line after you confirm. minimega and its experiments continue to run.

Keyboard shortcuts:

Action Linux and Windows macOS Copy the selected text Ctrl+Shift+C Cmd+C Paste Ctrl+Shift+V Cmd+V Search the output Ctrl+F Cmd+F Clear the terminal, as Clear does Ctrl+L Ctrl+L Scroll the output up or down one page PageUp or PageDown PageUp or PageDown Scroll to the top or bottom of the output Shift+Home or Shift+End Shift+Home or Shift+End Show the previous or next command Up or Down Up or Down Search the command history (reverse search) Ctrl+R Ctrl+R Move the focus out of the terminal Ctrl+], then Tab or Shift+Tab Ctrl+], then Tab or Shift+Tab

When you enter quit, the page shows a warning. The page does not stop the command, and minimega asks for a second quit. quit with a delay, such as quit 10, stops minimega with no second request.

If the connection to the console stops, the page tries to connect again after 1, 2, 4, 8, and 15 seconds. Select Reconnect now to try immediately, or Cancel to stop.

docs.title: minimega Command and Control (miniccc)
docs.text:
phēnix and its applications rely on minimega's command and control infrastructure (miniccc) running inside experiment VMs to execute commands, transfer files, and monitor VM health.

  • VM Execution: phēnix apps run scripts and commands on VMs via cc exec.
  • File Operations: Files are sent to VMs using cc send.
  • State of Health: Health metrics are collected via C2 probes (e.g., ip addr, systemctl, pgrep).

docs.title: Daemon Configuration and Socket Access
docs.text:
By default, phēnix connects to minimega via a UNIX domain socket.

Setting Default Description --base-dir.minimega /tmp/minimega Base directory for minimega runtime state. MM_SOCKET_PATH /tmp/minimega/minimega Path to the minimega command socket. MM_FILEPATH /phenix/images Base directory for minimega disk images. --deploy-mode — Deploy mode for minimega VMs (all, no-headnode, only-headnode).

docs.title: 1. Debugging Experiment VMs
docs.text:
When troubleshooting virtual machine or network deployment issues, use phenix mm to inspect minimega's internal state:

# Check detailed VM status and tap interface mappings
phenix mm -n my-experiment vm info

# Inspect recent minimega log entries (the log ring must first be enabled,
# for example with `phenix mm log ring 1000`)
phenix mm log ring

docs.title: 2. Monitoring Cluster Hosts
docs.text:
In multi-node minimega deployments, use phenix mm to verify cluster connectivity and host status:

# Verify health of all minimega headnodes and compute nodes
phenix mm host

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• phenix mm: send commands to minimega through phēnix.
  • Hosts: the cluster hosts in the web UI.
  • Doctor: checks that phēnix can reach minimega.
  • Troubleshooting: fixes for minimega problems.

docs.title: Experiment Netflow
docs.text:
The minimega platform supports netflow capture, wherein flows through an Open vSwitch bridge can be parsed into an ASCII format and forwarded to a remote endpoint for additional consumption.

phēnix extends this capability by making the minimega netflow ASCII format available for streaming over WebSockets for experiments. The only requirement for enabling netflow for an experiment is that the experiment be configured to use a bridge name that is not the default phenix bridge. This can be done automatically for all experiments by enabling auto bridge mode, or per-experiment via the UI by expanding the Advanced Options section when creating a new experiment and providing the Default Bridge Name setting.

Note

The Default Bridge Name field is only shown when the server is running in manual bridge mode. In auto mode the bridge name is always the experiment name, so the field is hidden.

This can also be done via the CLI by providing the --default-bridge, -b option when using the phenix exp create subcommand.

Warning

As mentioned above, the experiment netflow capability will not work if a default bridge name is not explicitly specified for an experiment. This is to prevent network flows across multiple experiments from being captured.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Running experiments will have a green network icon to the right of the VM search box that, when clicked, will start netflow capture for the non-default bridge the experiment is configured to use for all VM network interfaces.

Once enabled, the icon will turn red (to signify it can be stopped), and the Netflow tab of the running experiment will be updated with a table of netflow data from minimega as it streams in. Until the first line arrives, the tab shows Waiting for netflow lines from the running capture. The start and stop of each capture get their own rows.

To stop netflow capture for the experiment, click the red network icon. A capture also stops when the experiment stops.

docs.title: Recorded Captures
docs.text:
phēnix records every capture to the experiment's files as netflow/<id>.txt, where <id> is the capture's UTC start time. Each line is one flow as minimega sent it (the 6 is the IP protocol number):

2026-10-28T09:30:12-06:00   1.5s    6   10.0.0.1:1234   <-> 10.0.0.2:443    2   2048

You can view, download and delete the file in the experiment's Files tab, but stop the capture before you delete it.

The Download captures button above the Netflow table lists the recorded captures and downloads each one as text (<exp>-netflow-<id>.txt, the lines unchanged), CSV (.csv, one row per flow) or JSONL (.jsonl, one JSON object per flow per line). CSV and JSONL use Elastic Common Schema field names: event.start and event.end (UTC, RFC 3339), event.duration (in nanoseconds), source.ip, source.port, destination.ip, destination.port, network.transport (the protocol's IANA name, such as tcp, when it has one), network.iana_number, network.packets and network.bytes. Lines that don't parse as a flow are only in the text download.

Each capture records at most ui.netflow.max-size megabytes, 100 by default (see Settings Reference). A capture that hits the limit stops recording and is marked Truncated, but keeps streaming to the Netflow tab. One that a server stop cut off is marked Interrupted.

Recorded captures are never deleted automatically, not even with the experiment. To clean up, remove <base-dir.phenix>/images/<exp>/files/netflow/ on the host.

On a busy bridge or a slow disk, the host can drop netflow datagrams before phēnix reads them. Raise net.core.rmem_max on the host (for example sysctl -w net.core.rmem_max=4194304) to give phēnix a larger receive buffer.

Warning

Captures are not authenticated. A host that can reach the phēnix server's UDP ports can add lines to a capture, or fill it to its size limit. Limit who can reach those ports.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
The phenix exp netflow commands do the same, through a running phenix ui:

phenix exp netflow start my-exp
phenix exp netflow status my-exp
phenix exp netflow stop my-exp

# list the recorded captures, then download one as CSV
phenix exp netflow captures my-exp
phenix exp netflow download my-exp 20261028T153012.345Z --format csv -O flows.csv

Without -O, the download goes to standard output. See phenix experiment netflow for all of the options.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Packet Captures: capture the packets themselves, not just the flows.

docs.title: Experiment Packet Captures
docs.text:
An experiment capture records the traffic of a running experiment on all of its hosts. minimega merges this traffic into one capture file on the head node. phēnix starts, stops, and lists experiment captures. It can also show a running capture live in WebShark.

To capture the traffic of one VM interface, see Packet Capture.

docs.title: How a Capture Works
docs.text:
Each host adds one Open vSwitch mirror to each bridge that the experiment uses. The mirror selects the frames that come into the bridge from the experiment's VM, container, and host taps. It does not select tunnel or trunk ports. Thus the capture records each frame one time, on the host where the frame came into the bridge. This is also true across a GRE mesh or a VXLAN mesh.

Each host sends its frames to the head node. The head node merges the frames in timestamp order and writes them to one file in the experiment's files directory. The file shows in the Files tab of the experiment, and it stays there after the capture stops.

An experiment capture also works on the default phenix bridge. Unlike netflow, it does not need a bridge of its own.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A minimega build with experiment captures on every node of the mesh, relays included. minimega on the head node refuses a start when a mesh node runs a minimega version without experiment captures.
  • Synchronized clocks on all hosts. Use chrony or PTP. The head node puts the frames of different hosts in order by their timestamps. A clock offset changes that order.
  • A running experiment.
  • The permissions that Permissions gives.

phēnix uses the capture commands of minimega 3.4.0 only when the minimega on the head node gives version 3.4.0 or later. With an older minimega, phēnix refuses experiment captures and starts VM interface captures in the pcap format. phenix ui asks the head node for the minimega version when it starts, and again every 10 seconds until minimega answers. It keeps the first answer. After you upgrade minimega, restart phenix ui. phenix doctor shows that version.

docs.title: Capture Options
docs.text:
Option Web-UI field CLI flag REST field Default VLANs VLANs --vlan (one for each VLAN) vlans all VLANs of the experiment BPF filter BPF filter (optional) --filter filter no filter Snaplen Snaplen --snaplen snaplen 1600 Format Format --format format pcapng File name File name (optional) --name name <exp>[-<vlan>]-<YYYYmmdd-HHMMSS>.pcapng
  • VLANs: Give the VLAN aliases of the experiment, such as EXP_1. phēnix does not compare the case of the letters. An empty list captures all VLANs.
  • BPF filter: Each host applies the filter in its kernel. The filter can hold letters, digits, spaces, and the characters . : / [ ] ( ) & | ! < > = + - * ,. Quotes, backslash, and # are not permitted. The filter can have a maximum of 1024 bytes.
  • Snaplen: This is the number of bytes of each frame that the capture keeps, from 14 to 65535. In the CLI and the REST API, 0 keeps 1600 bytes.
  • Format: pcapng or pcap (classic pcap). See Formats.
  • File name: phēnix writes the file to the experiment's files directory. It changes each character other than letters, digits, ., _, and - to _. It sets the extension to .pcapng or .pcap to match the format. The default name has the VLAN alias only when the capture has exactly one VLAN. If a file or a running capture already has the default name, phēnix adds -2, -3, and so on. phēnix refuses a name that a running capture writes, or that a file in the files directory has.

The ui.captures.max-size setting sets the maximum size of each capture file, in megabytes. The default is 10240 (10 GiB). 0 sets no limit. The setting also applies to VM interface captures. Restart phenix ui after you change it. See Settings.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
pcapng records the host and the bridge of each frame. Each host and bridge is a different interface in the file. The file also records the filter, the snaplen, and the drop counts of each host. Wireshark, tshark, and WebShark show this data.

Some tools can read only classic pcap. For these tools, select pcap. Or convert a pcapng file with editcap -F pcap in.pcapng out.pcap.

docs.title: Start a Capture
docs.text:
1. Open the running experiment.
  2. Click the Capture all experiment traffic button. It is to the right of the netflow button. The Captures tab has the same button.
  3. In the dialog, set the options. Leave VLANs empty to capture all VLANs.
  4. Click Start capture.

To capture one VLAN, click a network in the Network column of the VM table. Then click Capture VLAN <alias>…. The same dialog opens with that VLAN selected.

The dialog shows the warnings of the mirror budget before you start. If VLANs is empty and a host and bridge of the experiment has 32 mirrors, the dialog disables Start capture. If you select VLANs, the dialog shows a warning instead. phēnix refuses that start only if those VLANs use that bridge. The note Frames from hardware behind a trunk are not captured. tells you about a limit of the capture.

After the start, a message shows the capture ID and the budget warnings. phēnix asks for no confirmation to start or to stop a capture.

A user who does not have experiments/captures create does not see the button or the menu item.

docs.title: Captures Tab
docs.text:
The Captures tab lists the experiment captures. The tab label shows the number of running captures. The tab reads the list again every 5 seconds while it shows. It also reads the list when a capture starts or stops. While a capture runs and another tab shows, the page reads the list every 30 seconds.

Column Value ID The ID that minimega gives the capture Status The state of the capture Scope The VLANs and the filter, or the error of a failed capture Started The start time Size The size of the file Packets The packets in the file Drops The packets that the hosts dropped Actions The actions for the capture

minimega gives these states:

  • starting, running, stalled, and stopping: minimega writes the file. A capture is stalled when a host sends no data for 10 seconds.
  • stopped: The file is complete.
  • full: The file reached its maximum size.
  • failed: The capture stopped because of an error. The Scope column shows the error.
  • orphaned: A host lost its connection to the head node and stopped its part of the capture.

A capture that you stop stays in the list as stopped. It stays until you delete its file or the experiment stops. phēnix keeps this list in memory, so a restart of phenix ui removes the stopped captures from the tab. Their files stay in the Files tab.

Click the expand button of a capture to see a row for each host and bridge:

Column Value Host, Bridge The host and the bridge Ports The VM ports that the host captures Packets The packets that the head node wrote to the file Drops The packets that the kernel, the capture library, or a full queue dropped Lost The packets lost between the host and the head node Late The packets that came after the reorder window. The file has them out of order. Lag How far the merge on the head node is behind Skew How far the clock of the host is from the clock of the head node

A skew of more than 500 ms shows a warning. 500 ms is half of the default reorder window of minimega. With a large skew, many frames are late.

The actions of a capture are:

  • Running: Open in WebShark and Stop.
  • Stopped: Open in WebShark, Download, and Delete. Delete removes the file and asks you to confirm.
  • Failed: Delete.

Download and Delete use the experiment files. They need experiments/files get and delete.

docs.title: Live View in WebShark
docs.text:
Click Open in WebShark to open the capture on the WebShark page. WebShark must be installed. The page lists the experiment captures in the Experiment captures group, and a running capture has the label (live). The view of a running capture follows the file as it grows. Its title is, for example, exp1 capture 3 (live).

Each frame has its 802.1Q VLAN tag, because the mirror sends the frames to a trunk port.

For a pcapng capture, the page shows a display filter for each host, for example frame.interface_name == "compute1/mega_bridge_exp1". Click the copy button of a filter. Then paste the filter into the WebShark display filter box.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To start an experiment capture of all VLANs, use the following command.

phenix experiment capture start <experiment-name>

To capture some VLANs, give --vlan one time for each VLAN. The other options have the flags that Capture Options gives.

phenix experiment capture start exp1 --vlan EXP_1 --vlan EXP_2 --filter "tcp port 502" --format pcap
