                    Seconds without a hello from a neighbor before the router considers it down. Applies to interfaces
                    whose protocol is ospf.
                  type: integer
                  nullable: true
                  example: 40
                hello_interval:
                  title: "Hello Interval"
                  description: 'Seconds between OSPF hello packets. Applies to interfaces whose protocol is ospf.'
                  type: integer
                  nullable: true
                  example: 10
                retransmission_interval:
                  title: "Retransmission Interval"
                  description: >-
                    Seconds before the router resends a link-state advertisement that was not acknowledged. Applies to
                    interfaces whose protocol is ospf.
                  type: integer
                  nullable: true
                  example: 5
            rulesets:
              title: "Rulesets"
              description: >-
                Firewall rulesets for Router and Firewall nodes. An interface applies one by naming it as its inbound or
                outbound ruleset.
              type: array
              nullable: true
              items:
                type: object
                required:
                - name
                - default
                - rules
                properties:
                  name:
                    title: "Name"
                    description: 'Name interfaces use to apply the ruleset.'
                    type: string
                    example: OutToDMZ
                  description:
                    title: "Description"
                    description: 'Describes the ruleset in the router configuration.'
                    type: string
                    example: From Corp to the DMZ network
                  default:
                    title: "Default"
                    description: 'What happens to traffic that no rule matches.'
                    type: string
                    enum:
                    - accept
                    - drop
                    - reject
                    example: drop
                  rules:
                    title: "Rules"
                    description: 'Rules of the ruleset.'
                    type: array
                    items:
                      type: object
                      required:
                      - id
                      - action
                      - protocol
                      properties:
                        id:
                          title: "Id"
                          description: >-
                            Rule number, unique in the ruleset. Vyatta and VyOS routers check rules from the lowest
                            number up.
                          type: integer
                          example: 10
                        description:
                          title: "Description"
                          description: 'Describes the rule in the router configuration.'
                          type: string
                          example: Allow UDP 10.1.26.80 ==> 10.2.25.0/24:123
                        action:
                          title: "Action"
                          description: 'What happens to traffic the rule matches.'
                          type: string
                          enum:
                          - accept
                          - drop
                          - reject
                          example: accept
                        protocol:
                          title: "Protocol"
                          description: 'Protocol of the traffic the rule matches.'
                          type: string
                          enum:
                          - tcp
                          - udp
                          - tcp_udp
                          - icmp
                          - esp
                          - ah
                          - all
                          default: tcp
                          example: tcp
                        source:
                          title: "Source"
                          description: "Source address and optional port matched by this rule."
                          type: object
                          nullable: true
                          required:
                          - address
                          properties:
                            address:
                              title: "Address"
                              description: 'Source address or network the rule matches.'
                              type: string
                              example: 10.1.24.60
                            port:
                              title: "Port"
                              description: 'Source port the rule matches. Empty or 0 matches any port.'
                              type: integer
                              example: 3389
                        destination:
                          title: "Destination"
                          description: "Destination network or address for this route or rule."
                          type: object
                          nullable: true
                          required:
                          - address
                          properties:
                            address:
                              title: "Address"
                              description: 'Destination address or network the rule matches.'
                              type: string
                              example: 10.1.24.60
                            port:
                              title: "Port"
                              description: 'Destination port the rule matches. Empty or 0 matches any port.'
                              type: integer
                              example: 3389
                        stateful:
                          title: "Stateful"
                          description: "Whether the firewall rule tracks connection state."
                          type: boolean
                          example: true
            nat:
              title: "Nat"
              description: "Mappings for network address translation on this node."
              type: array
              nullable: true
              items:
                type: object
                properties:
                  in:
                    title: "In"
                    description: "Names of the internal interfaces whose networks this NAT rule maps."
                    type: array
                    items:
                      type: string
                    example:
                    - eth1
                  out:
                    title: "Out"
                    description: "External interface used by this NAT rule."
                    type: string
                    example: eth0
        injections:
          title: "Injections"
          description: 'Files phenix copies into the snapshot of the first drive before the VM starts.'
          type: array
          nullable: true
          items:
            type: object
            required:
            - src
            - dst
            properties:
              src:
                title: "Source"
                description: >-
                  File on the phenix host: an absolute path, or a path relative to the experiment directory.
                type: string
                example: foo.xml
              dst:
                title: "Destination"
                description: 'Path the file is written to in the guest.'
                type: string
                example: /etc/phenix/foo.xml
              description:
                title: "Description"
                description: 'Free-text notes about the file.'
                type: string
                example: phenix config file
              permissions:
                title: "Permissions"
                description: 'File mode for the copied file, in octal such as 0664.'
                type: string
                example: '0664'
        deletions:
          title: "Deletions"
          description: "Files to remove from the node disk before boot."
          type: array
          nullable: true
          items:
            type: object
            required:
            - path
            properties:
              path:
                title: "Path"
                description: "Path to remove from the node disk."
                type: string
                minLength: 1
                example: /etc/obsolete.conf
              description:
                title: "Description"
                description: "Human-readable description of this resource or entry."
                type: string
                example: Remove the obsolete configuration file
        overrides:
          title: "Overrides"
          description: "Minimega VM settings overridden for this node."
          type: object
          nullable: true
          additionalProperties:
            type: string
          example:
            memory: "4096"
        delay:
          title: "Delay"
          description: "Conditions that delay the node start."
          type: object
          nullable: true
          properties:
            timer:
              title: "Timer"
              description: 'Start the VM this long after the experiment starts, as a duration such as 30s or 5m.'
              type: string
              pattern: '^$|^[-+]?(0|(([0-9]+(\.[0-9]*)?|\.[0-9]+)(ns|us|µs|μs|ms|s|m|h))+)$'
              example: 5m
            user:
              title: "User"
              description: >-
                Leave the VM stopped until someone starts it from phenix or minimega. Takes precedence over the other
                delays.
              example: false
              type: boolean
            c2:
              title: "C2"
              description: 'Start the VM once each of these hosts has checked in with minimega command and control.'
              type: array
              nullable: true
              items:
                type: object
                properties:
                  hostname:
                    title: "Hostname"
                    description: 'Host to wait for.'
                    example: node-01
                    type: string
                  useUUID:
                    title: "Use UUID"
                    description: 'Wait for the host''s UUID, rather than its hostname, to check in.'
                    example: false
                    type: boolean
        advanced:
          title: "Advanced"
          description: 'Extra minimega vm config settings, each a setting name and its value.'
          type: object
          nullable: true
          additionalProperties:
            type: string
          example:
            rtc.utc: "true"
        commands:
          title: "Commands"
          description: 'minimega command and control (cc) commands phenix sends to the VM, such as exec df -h.'
          type: array
          nullable: true
          items:
            type: string
          example:
          - exec df -h
    external_node:
      title: "External Node"
      description: "Schema describing the External Node resource."
      type: object
      required:
      - external
      - type
      - general
      properties:
        external:
          title: "External"
          description: >-
            Marks a device phenix does not deploy, such as hardware in the loop. It stays in the topology for State of
            Health and apps.
          example: true
          type: boolean
          enum:
          - true
        annotations:
          title: "Annotations"
          description: "Free-form annotations associated with this node."
          type: object
          nullable: true
          additionalProperties: true
          example:
            physical: true
        labels:
          title: "Labels"
          description: "String labels used to select or group nodes."
          type: object
          nullable: true
          additionalProperties:
            type: string
          example:
            tier: endpoint
        type:
          title: "Type"
          description: 'What the device is, such as HIL for hardware in the loop.'
          type: string
          default: HIL
          example: HIL
        general:
          title: "General"
          description: "General node settings."
          type: object
          required:
          - hostname
          properties:
            hostname:
              title: "Hostname"
              description: 'Name of the device in the topology.'
              type: string
              example: ADServer
            description:
              title: "Description"
              description: 'Free-text notes about the device.'
              type: string
              example: Active Directory Server
            vm_type:
              title: "VM Type"
              description: 'Whether the device is a virtual machine or a container.'
              type: string
              enum:
              - vm
              - container
              - ""
              default: vm
              example: vm
        hardware:
          title: "Hardware"
          description: "Virtual hardware assigned to the node."
          type: object
          nullable: true
          required:
          - os_type
          properties:
            cpu:
              title: "CPU"
              description: 'CPU model of the device.'
              type: string
              default: Broadwell
              example: Broadwell
            vcpus:
              title: "Virtual CPUs"
              description: 'Number of CPUs of the device.'
              oneOf:
              - type: integer
              - type: string
              default: 1
              example: 4
            memory:
              title: "Memory"
              description: 'Memory of the device, in megabytes.'
              oneOf:
              - type: integer
              - type: string
              default: 512
              example: 8192
            os_type:
              title: "OS Type"
              description: 'Operating system of the device.'
              type: string
              enum:
              - centos
              - linux
              - minirouter
              - rhel
              - vyatta
              - vyos
              - windows
              - other
              default: linux
              example: windows
        network:
          title: "Network"
          description: "Network settings associated with this node."
          type: object
          nullable: true
          required:
          - interfaces
          properties:
            interfaces:
              title: "Interfaces"
              description: >-
                Network interfaces of the device, for the topology's network diagram and State of Health checks.
              type: array
              items:
                type: object
                required:
                - name
                properties:
                  name:
                    title: "Name"
                    description: 'Interface name, such as eth0.'
                    type: string
                    example: eth0
                  proto:
                    title: "Protocol"
                    description: 'How the interface gets its address: static, dhcp, or manual for none.'
                    type: string
                    enum:
                    - static
                    - dhcp
                    - manual
                    - ""
                    default: dhcp
                    example: static
                  address:
                    title: "Address"
                    description: 'IPv4 address of the interface.'
                    type: string
                    format: ipv4
                    example: 192.168.1.100
                  mask:
                    title: "Mask"
                    description: 'Network prefix length (CIDR bits), from 0 to 32.'
                    type: integer
                    minimum: 0
                    maximum: 32
                    default: 24
                    example: 24
                  gateway:
                    title: "Gateway"
                    description: 'Default gateway of the interface.'
                    type: string
                    format: ipv4
                    example: 192.168.1.1
                  vlan:
                    title: "VLAN"
                    description: 'VLAN (network) the interface is on.'
                    type: string
                    example: EXP-1
        injections:
          title: "Injections"
          description: "Files to copy into the node disk before boot."
          type: array
          nullable: true
          items:
            type: object
            required:
            - src
            - dst
            properties:
              src:
                title: "Source"
                description: "Source file copied into the node disk."
                type: string
                minLength: 1
                example: ./config.txt
              dst:
                title: "Destination"
                description: "Destination path for the injected file."
                type: string
                minLength: 1
                example: /etc/config.txt
              description:
                title: "Description"
                description: "Human-readable description of this resource or entry."
                type: string
                example: Inject endpoint config
              permissions:
                title: "Permissions"
                description: "File permissions to set on the injected file."
                type: string
                example: '0644'
        deletions:
          title: "Deletions"
          description: "Files to remove from the node disk before boot."
          type: array
          nullable: true
          items:
            type: object
            required:
            - path
            properties:
              path:
                title: "Path"
                description: "Path to remove from the node disk."
                type: string
                minLength: 1
                example: /tmp/obsolete
              description:
                title: "Description"
                description: "Human-readable description of this resource or entry."
                type: string
                example: Remove obsolete endpoint file
        overrides:
          title: "Overrides"
          description: "Minimega VM settings overridden for this node."
          type: object
          nullable: true
          additionalProperties:
            type: string
        delay:
          title: "Delay"
          description: "Conditions that delay the node start."
          type: object
          nullable: true
          properties:
            timer:
              title: "Timer"
              description: "Duration to wait before starting the node, in Go duration syntax such as 5m or 1h30m."
              type: string
              pattern: '^$|^[-+]?(0|(([0-9]+(\.[0-9]*)?|\.[0-9]+)(ns|us|µs|μs|ms|s|m|h))+)$'
              example: 5m
            user:
              title: "User"
              description: "Whether node start requires user confirmation."
              type: boolean
              example: true
            c2:
              title: "C2"
              description: "Command-and-control hosts whose availability can release the delay."
              type: array
              items:
                type: object
                properties:
                  hostname:
                    title: "Hostname"
                    description: "Hostname used to identify the node."
                    type: string
                    example: c2-server
                  useUUID:
                    title: "Use UUID"
                    description: "Whether to match the command-and-control host by UUID."
                    type: boolean
                    example: false
        advanced:
          title: "Advanced"
          description: "Additional minimega VM settings."
          type: object
          nullable: true
          additionalProperties:
            type: string
        commands:
          title: "Commands"
          description: "Minimega commands to run for this node."
          type: array
          nullable: true
          items:
            type: string
          example:
          - exec hostname
    iface:
      title: "Interface"
      description: "Schema describing the Iface resource."
      type: object
      required:
      - name
      - vlan
      properties:
        name:
          title: "Name"
          description: 'Interface name, such as eth0, which NAT settings and apps use to refer to it.'
          type: string
          example: eth0
        vlan:
          title: "VLAN"
          description: 'VLAN (network) the interface is on.'
          type: string
          example: EXP-1
        autostart:
          title: "Autostart"
          description: >-
            Whether the interface should come up when the VM boots. phenix itself does not act on this setting.
          example: true
          type: boolean
          default: true
        mac:
          title: "MAC"
          description: 'MAC address. minimega generates one when it is empty.'
          type: string
          example: 00:11:22:33:44:55
          pattern: '^$|^([0-9a-fA-F]{2}[:-]){5}([0-9a-fA-F]){2}$'
        mtu:
          title: "MTU"
          description: >-
            Maximum transmission unit, in bytes. Vyatta and VyOS routers apply values from 68 to 16000; other images
            keep their own.
          type: integer
          default: 1500
          example: 1500
        bridge:
          title: "Bridge"
          description: >-
            Open vSwitch bridge on the host the interface attaches to. Empty or phenix uses the experiment's default
            bridge.
          example: phenix
          type: string
          default: phenix
        driver:
          title: "Driver"
          description: 'Emulated network card, such as e1000 or virtio-net-pci. Empty uses minimega''s default.'
          type: string
          example: e1000
        qinq:
          title: "QinQ"
          description: >-
            Carry the guest's own VLAN tags inside the interface's VLAN (QinQ, 802.1ad). The guest brings the interface
            up without an address.
          example: false
          type: boolean
          default: false
    iface_address:
      title: "Interface Address"
      description: "Schema describing the Iface Address resource."
      type: object
      required:
      - address
      - mask
      properties:
        address:
          title: "Address"
          description: 'IPv4 address of the interface.'
          type: string
          format: ipv4
          example: 192.168.1.100
        mask:
          title: "Mask"
          description: 'Network prefix length (CIDR bits), from 0 to 32.'
          type: integer
          minimum: 0
          maximum: 32
          default: 24
          example: 24
        gateway:
          title: "Gateway"
          description: 'Default gateway, reached through this interface.'
          type: string
          format: ipv4
          example: 192.168.1.1
        dns:
          title: "DNS Servers"
          description: 'DNS server addresses the guest uses: one address, or a list.'
          nullable: true
          oneOf:
          - type: string
          - type: array
            items:
              type: string
          example:
          - 192.168.1.1
          - 192.168.1.2
    iface_rulesets:
      title: "Interface Rulesets"
      description: "Schema describing the Iface Rulesets resource."
      type: object
      properties:
        ruleset_out:
          title: "Ruleset Out"
          description: 'Ruleset for traffic going out of this interface, on Router and Firewall nodes.'
          type: string
          example: OutToInet
          pattern: '^[\w-]*$'
        ruleset_in:
          title: "Ruleset In"
          description: 'Ruleset for traffic coming in on this interface, on Router and Firewall nodes.'
          type: string
          example: InFromInet
          pattern: '^[\w-]*$'
    static_iface:
      title: "Static Interface"
      description: "Schema describing the Static Iface resource."
      allOf:
      - $ref: '#/components/schemas/iface'
      - $ref: '#/components/schemas/iface_address'
      - $ref: '#/components/schemas/iface_rulesets'
      required:
      - type
      - proto
      properties:
        type:
          title: "Type"
          description: 'Kind of interface: ethernet.'
          type: string
          enum:
          - ethernet
          default: ethernet
          example: ethernet
        proto:
          title: "Protocol"
          description: >-
            How the interface is addressed: static for a fixed address, or ospf for a fixed address that also takes part
            in OSPF on a router.
          type: string
          enum:
          - static
          - ospf
          default: static
          example: static
    dhcp_iface:
      title: "DHCP Interface"
      description: "Schema describing the Dhcp Iface resource."
      allOf:
      - $ref: '#/components/schemas/iface'
      - $ref: '#/components/schemas/iface_rulesets'
      required:
      - type
      - proto
      properties:
        type:
          title: "Type"
          description: 'Kind of interface: ethernet.'
          type: string
          enum:
          - ethernet
          default: ethernet
          example: ethernet
        proto:
          title: "Protocol"
          description: >-
            How the interface is addressed: dhcp to ask a DHCP server, or manual to bring it up with no address.
          type: string
          enum:
          - dhcp
          - manual
          default: dhcp
          example: dhcp
    serial_iface:
      title: "Serial Interface"
      description: "Schema describing the Serial Iface resource."
      allOf:
      - $ref: '#/components/schemas/iface'
      - $ref: '#/components/schemas/iface_address'
      - $ref: '#/components/schemas/iface_rulesets'
      required:
      - type
      - proto
      - udp_port
      - baud_rate
      - device
      properties:
        type:
          title: "Type"
          description: 'Kind of interface: a serial link, carried over the network between VMs.'
          type: string
          enum:
          - serial
          default: serial
          example: serial
        proto:
          title: "Protocol"
          description: 'Serial interfaces have a static address.'
          type: string
          enum:
          - static
          default: static
          example: static
        udp_port:
          title: "UDP Port"
          description: 'UDP port that carries the serial traffic between VMs.'
          type: integer
          minimum: 0
          maximum: 65535
          default: 8989
          example: 8989
        baud_rate:
          title: "Baud Rate"
          description: 'Speed of the serial line, in bits per second.'
          type: integer
          enum:
          - 110
          - 300
          - 600
          - 1200
          - 2400
          - 4800
          - 9600
          - 14400
          - 19200
          - 38400
          - 57600
          - 115200
          - 128000
          - 256000
          default: 9600
          example: 9600
        device:
          title: "Device"
          description: 'Serial device the guest uses, such as /dev/ttyS0.'
          type: string
          default: /dev/ttyS0
          example: /dev/ttyS0
</code></pre>

docs.title: Scorch
docs.text:
Scorch — SCenario ORCHestration — is an automated scenario orchestration framework within phēnix. It is included in phēnix as a core app. The development of the Scorch framework was motivated by the need to facilitate rigorous experimentation. Some advantages of Scorch include the ability to run many repeated scenarios on an experiment with consistency and minimal overhead. Scorch also provides the ability to efficiently capture experimental data for retrieval and analysis.

A phēnix scenario configuration file is used to define and configure the Scorch app for use on a topology. The Scorch app is meant to allow for the staging of Scorch components in sequence to execute against a running experiment. When applied to a given topology, the Scorch app will be available in the Scorch table to execute and then observe, manipulate in some cases, and review output from available components for a given stage in the Scorch pipeline.

The configuration file and most of the screenshots in the rest of this document are from an example Scorch scenario, scorch-demo.

docs.title: Scorch Components
docs.text:
A Scorch component is simply an executable available to be called by the Scorch app within phēnix. A component is expected to implement any or all of the various stages in the Scorch pipeline.

For an executable to be considered a Scorch component, it must meet the following requirements:

  1. Follow the phenix-scorch-component-<type> naming convention, where <type> is the component type used in the Scorch app configuration. An example would be phenix-scorch-component-tcpdump.
  2. Be an executable file.
  3. Be in the PATH of the user running phēnix.

Scorch runs the executable for each component type that is not a built-in component. If the executable is not in the PATH, the component fails. phenix doctor lists the components in the PATH and warns when a scenario uses one that is not installed.

When the Scorch app executes a Scorch component, it will pass a number of positional arguments to the component via the command line, as well as the JSON representation of the experiment the component is to be executed against via STDIN. The positional arguments passed are as follows:

  1. run stage (configure, start, stop, or cleanup)
  2. component name (name given to component type in Scorch app configuration)
  3. run ID (integer >= 0 representing the array index of the Scorch run in the app configuration being executed)
  4. loop (integer >= 0 representing the current run loop being executed)
  5. count (integer >= 0 representing the current loop count being executed)

Scorch also sets these environment variables for the component: PHENIX_DIR, PHENIX_FILES_DIR (the files directory of the experiment), PHENIX_LOG_LEVEL, PHENIX_LOG_FILE (stderr), PHENIX_DRYRUN, and PHENIX_SCORCH_STARTTIME (the start time of the run).

Tip

To see the JSON that a component gets on STDIN, run phenix util scorch-json <exp-name> <component-name>. The command writes the arguments and the PHENIX_* environment variables of the component to STDERR (not with -o json). Use --run, --loop, --stage, and --count to select the point in the run. The command stores nothing. The REST API gives the same JSON at GET /api/v1/experiments/<exp-name>/scorch/components/<component-name>/input, with the query parameters run, loop, stage, count, replace, and runtime. During a run, the tap and break components can add taps to the experiment status that later components get. The command does not show these taps.

During component execution, the Scorch app assumes anything written to STDOUT by a component is intended to be relayed to the user. Thus, when Scorch is run via the web UI, anything written to STDOUT gets streamed to the UI for viewing. Any error messages generated by a component should be written to the log file or to STDERR unless it's to also be relayed to the user directly. Scorch writes what a component writes to STDERR to the phēnix log as SCORCH entries. A line that follows the app contract keeps its level.

The Scorch app expects a component executable to exit with a value of 0 upon completion if the component was successful, and exit with any other value otherwise. An exit value of anything other than 0 will result in Scorch halting execution of the current stage and jumping to the next appropriate stage to complete the Scorch run. In the stop and cleanup stages, Scorch still executes the other components of the stage (see Stages).

docs.title: Component and Run Settings
docs.text:
The Scorch app is configured in the metadata of the scorch app in a Scenario. Each item of components has these keys:

  • name: the name that the runs use for the component.
  • type: a built-in component, or the <type> of a phenix-scorch-component-<type> executable. It defaults to name.
  • background: if true, a component in the configure or start stage runs in the background, and Scorch continues with the next component. Scorch stops it when the run executes the same component in the cleanup stage (for configure) or the stop stage (for start). background has no effect in the stop and cleanup stages, and no effect on the break and tap components.
  • metadata: the settings of the component. Scorch applies the replacements to it before each execution.

Each item of runs has these keys:

  • name: the name of the run in the web UI.
  • count: the number of times to execute the run (default 1). Each pass executes all the stages. If a pass fails, the run stops.
  • configure, start, stop and cleanup: the names of the components to execute in that stage, in order.
  • loop: a loop to execute after the start stage and before the stop stage (see Stages).
  • replace: see Replace.
  • filebeat: see Automated Component Data Collection.

A loop has the same keys as a run, except name and filebeat. Its count is the number of times to execute the loop (default 1).

docs.title: Automated Component Data Collection
docs.text:
The Scorch app is capable of generating a configuration file for and starting an instance of Filebeat in the background before execution of each Scorch run. As each Scorch component is executed, any data it generates and collects can be configured to be automatically processed by Filebeat for indexing in Elasticsearch. At a minimum, this requires the following.

  1. Filebeat to be enabled and configured in the Scorch app configuration.
  2. A Filebeat input to be configured for each component generating and collecting data.
  3. The filebeat executable installed and in the PATH of the user running phēnix.

The filebeat block of the Scorch app has these keys:

  • enabled: if true, Scorch starts Filebeat for each run that has at least one Filebeat input.
  • config: the Filebeat configuration. Scorch adds its own settings to it: the scorch.experiment, scorch.run_id, scorch.run_name (when the run has a name), scorch.runtime and scorch.start_time fields, the logging (level warning unless logging.level is set), the registry, and the inputs.
  • expNameAsIndexName: if true, Scorch sets the Elasticsearch index to experiment-<experiment-name>.

A run can have its own filebeat block, which replaces the block of the app for that run. Scorch starts Filebeat only if the block of the app has enabled: true.

The filebeat.inputs of a component are Filebeat inputs. Scorch uses only the file name of each path, and reads that file in each loop-<loop>-count-<count> directory of the component. Thus, a component must write its data to scorch/run-<run>/<component-name>/loop-<loop>-count-<count>/ in the files of the experiment (PHENIX_FILES_DIR). Scorch sets scan_frequency to 5s, sets close_inactive to 5s unless the input sets it, and adds the scorch.itername and scorch.output_file fields. After the run, Scorch waits for Filebeat to finish reading the files, then stops it.

See the example configuration below for examples of how Filebeat and Filebeat inputs are configured in the Scorch app configuration.

docs.title: Built-in Components
docs.text:
The following Scorch component types are considered core components, in that they are included in the main phēnix repository and are available for use in Scorch app configurations by default.

Component Description break pauses the run and gives users a shell on the phēnix server until a user exits it pause pauses the run for a configured duration soh runs the State of Health app at this point of the run tap creates a minimega tap, with optional external network access, for other components

docs.title: break Component
docs.text:
The break component is comparable to a source code break point when debugging an application in that it pauses execution of the current Scorch run until a user exits the break. While the break component is running, users have access to a shell on the server running phēnix as the user running phēnix. The first user to access the shell via the terminal modal in the UI whose role may create experiments/trigger (the permission that starts a run) will have read-write access and can exit the break. Every other user whose role may get the experiment has read-only access but will get live updates as the user with read-write access uses the terminal.

The terminal has an Exit button for the user with read-write access, which exits the terminal and ends the break. Users with read-only access have a Close button, which closes the terminal window but does not exit the terminal. If the run executes in the process of phenix experiment scorch (phenix ui is not running), the shell opens in the terminal of that command.

It's possible to configure the break component in the Scorch app configuration to create a minimega tap when the component is executed. When the component exits, the tap will be deleted. In addition to the tap, external network access can also be configured (e.g., Internet access). With a tap, the shell runs in the network namespace of the tap.

Option Type Default Description tap map none A tap to create while the break runs, with the options of the tap component. readme string none Markdown text that the terminal shows (with /usr/local/bin/glow) in place of a shell.

An example of configuring a break component to create a tap and configure external network access during the configure stage is as follows. The break component can be configured to run in any stage.

spec:
  apps:
  - name: scorch
    metadata:
      components:
      - name: break-tap
        type: break
        metadata:
          tap:
            bridge: phenix
            vlan: MGMT
            ip: 172.16.33.25/16
            internetAccess: true
      runs:
      - configure: ["break-tap"]

docs.title: pause Component
docs.text:
The pause component is similar to the break component in that it pauses execution of the current Scorch run, but instead of waiting for user intervention, the pause component waits for a configured duration before continuing.

spec:
  apps:
  - name: scorch
    metadata:
      components:
      - name: pause-1m
        type: pause
        metadata:
          duration: 1m
      runs:
      - start:
        - pause-1m

The duration field accepts Go duration strings (e.g., 10s, 1m30s, 2h). If not specified, it defaults to 10s.

Option Type Default Description duration string 10s How long to pause. failStages list of stages none The stages in which the component fails after the pause, for example to test how a run handles a failure.

To use random durations, use the replace feature with a distribution specification:

spec:
  apps:
  - name: scorch
    metadata:
      components:
      - name: pause-random
        type: pause
        metadata:
          duration: "{{PAUSE_DURATION}}s"
      runs:
      - name: random-pause-run
        replace:
          "{{PAUSE_DURATION}}":
            type: int
            uniform:
              minimum: 5
              maximum: 10
        start:
        - pause-random

docs.title: soh Component
docs.text:
The soh component allows users to execute the State of Health app at scheduled times throughout a Scorch run. This is handy when, for example, other Scorch components might cause nodes in the experiment to misbehave or fail.

The component can be configured to limit which health checks are run, and can also be configured to fail if any of the health checks fail. The log level can also be configured, which will limit what logs get sent to the component's UI modal while the component is running.

The State of Health app must be configured in the scenario, and must have run after the experiment started. If not, the component fails.

Option Type Default Description checks list all checks The checks to run (see the example below). c2Timeout string the c2Timeout of the soh app The C2 timeout for this execution, as a Go duration string. failOnError bool false Fail the component if a check fails. logLevel string info The lowest level of the logs that the component shows: debug, info, warn or error.

Each stage of the component writes its check results to scorch/run-<run>/<component>/loop-<loop>-count-<count>/soh-<stage>.json in the experiment's files (for example, soh-start.json).

spec:
  apps:
  - name: scorch
    metadata:
      components:
      - name: health-check
        type: soh
        metadata:
          c2Timeout: 5s # if provided, will update the C2 timeout setting when this component runs the state of health app
          checks:       # default is to run all the following checks
            - network-config       # Ensure all nodes still have network configured per the topology. Will use `skipInitialNetworkConfigTests` setting in soh app config.
            - reachability         # Basic ICMP-based reachability testing. Will use `testReachability` setting in soh app config.
            - custom-reachability  # IP-based reachability testing (TCP or UDP). Will use `testCustomReachability` setting in soh app config.
            - files                # Ensure expected files exist in nodes. Will use `hostFiles` setting in soh app config.
            - files-absent         # Ensure files do not exist in nodes. Will use `hostFilesAbsent` setting in soh app config.
            - services             # Ensure expected services are running in nodes. Will use `hostServices` setting in soh app config.
            - processes            # Ensure processes are running in nodes. Will use `hostProcesses` setting in soh app config.
            - ports                # Ensure listeners are running in nodes. Will use `hostListeners` setting in soh app config.
            - docker               # Ensure Docker containers are up/healthy in nodes. Will use `dockerContainers` setting in soh app config.
            - custom               # Run custom tests in nodes. Will use `hostCustomTests` setting in soh app config.
            - cpu-load             # Gather CPU load stats from nodes.
            - flows                # Gather packet flows from ElasticSearch server. Requires `packetCapture` setting to be configured in soh app config.
          failOnError: true # default is false
          logLevel: debug   # default is info
      runs:
      - start: ["health-check"]

docs.title: tap Component
docs.text:
The tap component implements the exact same functionality described above in the break component for creating a minimega tap and, optionally, external network access, but allows for the tap (and external network access, if configured) to exist while other components are executed (as opposed to only existing for the duration of the break component).

Option Type Default Description bridge string the default bridge of the experiment The bridge to add the tap to. vlan string none (required) The VLAN alias to tap. ip string none The IP address of the tap, in CIDR notation. Required for external access. externalAccess.enabled bool false Give the tapped VLAN external network access. internetAccess bool false The older name of externalAccess.enabled.

The tap app section tells how phēnix creates a tap in a network namespace and gives it external network access.

An example of configuring a tap component to create a tap and configure external network access is as follows. The tap component can be configured to run in the start stage (create the tap), the stop stage (delete the tap), and the cleanup stage (delete the tap). Configuring the tap component in the cleanup stage ensures that the tap is deleted even if preceding stages or components fail or if the SCORCH run is cancelled.

spec:
  apps:
  - name: scorch
    metadata:
      components:
      - name: tap-inet
        type: tap
        metadata:
          bridge: phenix
          vlan: MGMT
          ip: 172.16.33.25/16
          internetAccess: true
      runs:
      - start: ["tap-inet"]
        stop: ["tap-inet"]
        cleanup: ["tap-inet"]

NOTE: In deployments where minimega is running in a container on the headnode, and Docker networking is in use (e.g., the minimega container is not configured to use host networking), users will need to execute the following commands if access to the minimega tap created by the tap (or break) component from the Docker host is required.

ovs-docker add-port phenix TDN minimega
docker exec -it minimega ovs-vsctl add-port phenix TDN
ovs-vsctl add-port phenix temp-tap tag=<vlan-ID> -- set interface temp-tap type=internal

The above commands assume the name of the minimega container is minimega. The name of the local tap created (in this case, temp-tap) can be whatever, but the value for the VLAN tag must match the numerical ID of the VLAN that's mapped to the VLAN alias used in the tap (or break) component configuration. Run phenix vlan alias <experiment-name> <VLAN-alias> to print that ID.

Note

Using host networking mode for the minimega container allows for all the above nonsense to be skipped.

docs.title: User-defined Components
docs.text:
The following Scorch component types have been developed external to the main phenix repository and are available in the sceptre-phenix-apps repository, which also includes README-based documentation for each component. Most are developed in Python, and leverage common helper classes that ease the development of user components. The repository installs each component as a phenix-scorch-component-<type> executable, and also installs phenix-scorch-validate, which checks the component metadata in a scenario file before you run it.

Component Description art Runs Atomic Red Team attacks (MITRE ATT&CK techniques). caldera Executes operations in MITRE Caldera via the REST API. cc Runs commands and moves files on VMs through minimega Command and Control (miniccc). collector Collects and processes data from cyber-physical experiments and Scorch components. disruption Orchestrates and executes disruption scenarios for cyber-physical experiments. erspan Mirrors the traffic of an experiment, live, to a capture machine outside phēnix through an ERSPAN tunnel. ettercap Runs Ettercap. hoststats Collects resource utilization statistics on minimega hosts. iperf Collects network performance measurements using iperf3 or rperf. kafka Filters and exports Kafka data as a CSV or JSON file. mm Runs minimega actions: packet captures, starting and stopping VMs, and connecting or disconnecting VM interfaces. opcexport Exports data from an OPC server to Elasticsearch. pcap Collects PCAPs from VMs via minimega's capture pcap API. pipe Implements minimega pipe API. providerdata Collects and verifies data from pybennu providers, such as the RTDS or OPALRT. qos Apply Quality of Service (QoS) effects on network interfaces, including dropping packets (loss), delaying packets (delay), or limiting bandwidth (rate). rtds Collects and verifies data from the Real-Time Dynamic Simulator (RTDS), and orchestrates the starting/stopping of RSCAD cases. snort Configures and runs Snort. ssh Executes commands on a remote host and copies files from it. tcpdump Executes and collects and processes data from tcpdump. trafficgen Network traffic generation. vmstats Collects resource utilization statistics from Linux VMs in the experiment, using the vmstat command.

docs.title: Replace
docs.text:
Warning

The replace feature applies changes to the entire component metadata. Please choose placeholder names carefully!

The replace feature allows dynamic substitution of values in component metadata at runtime. Replacements are defined per-run (or loop) and are resolved once at the start of each pass of the run/loop (see count), ensuring consistent values throughout that pass of the pipeline. This can be used to parameterize components, or introduce controlled randomness into experiments.

Replacements are defined in the replace block of a run or loop. Each key is a placeholder string that will be replaced in component metadata. The type specifies how the replacement value is determined. Replaces can be 'stacked' like below, where the {{RAND1}} is defined at the run level and carries through to all subordinate loops, but {{OVERRIDE}} is overridden in each interior loop.

The value of a placeholder is one of these:

  • A list of values. Scorch selects one value at random.
  • A distribution, with exactly one of uniform (minimum and maximum, default 0 to 10), gaussian (mean and stddev, default 10 and 2) or exponential (mean, default 10). With type: int, Scorch rounds the value to an integer. Otherwise, the value is a float.

If a metadata string is only the placeholder, the string becomes the value with its type (for example, a number). Otherwise, Scorch replaces the placeholder with the value as text.

An example scorch run:

- name: scorch
  metadata:
    components:
      - name: cc
        type: cc
        metadata:
          vms:
            - hostname: testy
              start:
                - type: exec
                  args: 'echo "We have picked RAND1: {{RAND1}}, RAND2: {{RAND2}}, RAND3: {{RAND3}}, override: {{OVERRIDE}}"'
    runs:
      - name: replacey
        replace:
          '{{RAND1}}': ['foo', 'bar', 'baz']
          '{{OVERRIDE}}': ['run']
        start: [ cc ]
        loop:
          count: 2
          replace:
            '{{RAND2}}':
              type: int
              uniform:
                minimum: 10
                maximum: 100
            '{{OVERRIDE}}': ['loop 1']
          start: [cc]
          loop:
            count: 3
            replace:
              '{{RAND3}}':
                type: float
                gaussian:
                  mean: 100.123
                  stddev: 10.456
              '{{OVERRIDE}}': ['loop 2']
            start: [cc]

Would result in the following commands:

echo "We have picked RAND1: bar, RAND2: {{RAND2}}, RAND3: {{RAND3}}, override: run"
echo "We have picked RAND1: bar, RAND2: 19, RAND3: {{RAND3}}, override: loop 1"
echo "We have picked RAND1: bar, RAND2: 19, RAND3: 86.97164992182161, override: loop 2"
echo "We have picked RAND1: bar, RAND2: 19, RAND3: 114.48324331867562, override: loop 2"
echo "We have picked RAND1: bar, RAND2: 19, RAND3: 95.97843337384487, override: loop 2"
echo "We have picked RAND1: bar, RAND2: 82, RAND3: {{RAND3}}, override: loop 1"
echo "We have picked RAND1: bar, RAND2: 82, RAND3: 91.0323724023587, override: loop 2"
echo "We have picked RAND1: bar, RAND2: 82, RAND3: 96.65899272237336, override: loop 2"
echo "We have picked RAND1: bar, RAND2: 82, RAND3: 94.85640056376343, override: loop 2"

The same resolved values are used across all stages (configure, start, stop, cleanup) and all subordinate loop iterations (until they are overridden). However, each new pass of a run or loop, and each new run of the same scorch pipeline, will generate new replacement values, allowing for variability across runs.

phenix util scorch-json selects the replacement values in the same way as a run, and writes them to STDERR (not with -o json). To set a value, use --replace <key>=<value>.

docs.title: Scorch Table
docs.text:
The Scorch table, accessible as one of the tab selections within the phēnix UI, lists all possible Scorch apps available based on the experiments established in phēnix. The following columns or functions are available:

  • Experiment: the experiment name, which links to the experiment's runs page
  • Experiment Status: this reports on the status of the experiment — an experiment must be running for a Scorch app to start. The buttons next to it start or stop the experiment and open the experiment's page.
  • SCORCH Status: this will report the running or stopped status of the Scorch app itself. The buttons next to it start the first run or stop the run that is executing, and open the runs page.
  • Terminal: if the Scorch app has reached a break point, a terminal will be available — if clicked, a terminal dialog will be opened and is running on the phēnix host system
  • Find an Experiment: similar to the search fields in other tables within the phēnix UI, it is possible to filter experiment names based on terms entered here

Each button is only shown if your role permits the action it takes.

docs.title: Scorch Pipeline
docs.text:
Scorch pipelines are available from the Scorch table in the phēnix UI. The table is sorted by Experiment name by default. Only those experiments with the Scorch app configured in the scenario configuration will be listed in the table. It is possible to start or stop an experiment, as well as start or stop a Scorch run. Finally, if a terminal is available when a break point is reached in a running Scorch app, it can be accessed from the table.

The Scorch pipeline provides a graphical representation of the Scorch app, including the configure, start, stop, and cleanup stages. If the Scorch app provides output for a given step, or component, users can click into the component and receive the output. The output window opens as soon as the component is clicked and shows a loading indicator until the output arrives.

A user can access the terminal if a break point is reached by clicking on the component. As with the terminal access described above, a dialog will be presented with a terminal running on the phēnix host system.

docs.title: Runs Page
docs.text:
To open an experiment's runs page, click its name in the Scorch table, or its fire button on the Experiments table or the experiment's page.

Start all starts the runs one after another, Stop all stops the executing run and drops the ones waiting to start, and Clear all clears the status of every run that isn't running. Each run also has its own buttons:

  • Clear: forgets the statuses of the run's components, so its pipeline reads as never run
  • Cleanup: executes only this run's cleanup stage, for example to tear down what a canceled run left behind. It is shown only for a run that has cleanup components.
  • Download: the archives of the run's artifacts. Each time a run finishes, Scorch archives what it wrote to scorch-run-<run>_<start>.tgz in the experiment's files. The archive also holds a <experiment>-scorch-run-<run>-<start>.json file with the run's name, start and end times, and the phēnix and minimega versions. From the command line, use phenix experiment files get.
  • the start or stop button: starts the run, or stops it while it executes

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
For a given Scorch pipeline, there are four stages of execution:

  1. configure
  2. start
  3. stop
  4. cleanup

A Scorch component may implement any or all of the various stages, and Scorch will execute each stage inside the components in order. Each component can be configured in the Scorch app scenario configuration file (see Component and Run Settings).

Note

There is additional done stage in the UI obtained when cleanup has been completed. It is meant to report the completion of all stages in the Pipeline UI, and shows as failed when a component failed or the run's data could not be archived.

It's completely up to the component developer if and how an execution stage is implemented and handled by the component. If a component is configured in the Scorch app to be executed as part of a stage, but the component does not implement said stage, then the Scorch app will happily continue on to the next component in the stage (unless the component errors out if the current stage is not implemented, in which case the Scorch run will fail).

The following indicators are presented for each component of the Scorch app:

  • Uninitialized: a component has not yet been reached or initialized — if the component has not yet been run, all components will be identified as uninitialized
  • Running: the component is currently running and has not yet been completed
  • Success: the component has completed successfully
  • Break Point: a break component has been reached — a terminal should be accessible by clicking on the component
  • Backgrounded: a component is running in the background
  • Failure: a component has failed for some reason — reporting on the failure may be accessible by click on the component

Loops are also available within a Scorch app and are included in the configuration file. A loop supports looping within a given component through additional components. Once a loop is completed, the next component is executed. There is no limit on the number of loops or depth of them. The Scorch pipeline UI supports access to each loop and will report the depth in the pipeline's title. The first loop in the scorch-demo app is presented in the following example; clicking the return button will return the display one level up in the loop chain (or ending at the parent Scorch app). To open a loop, click the loop node in the pipeline. Scorch executes a loop after the start stage and before the stop stage.

In addition to loops, multi-run is supported within a Scorch app. Unlike loops, multi-run allows for individual Scorch runs containing four separate stages. They are not nested in each other but are independent runs. A use case for multi-run could be executing multiple independent portions of an experiment against a topology, in any order or executing a run multiple times. There are two runs depicted in the configuration below.

As described above, each component will provide a modal for output reporting. The output could either be a fairly straight forward report, nothing at all, or it include logging output for a given component in the stage. The result will be streamed as it is received if the component is currently in a running component. If the component has finished running, the output will be static. If a component has no output at all, the window closes again and says so. If the window falls too far behind a running component, it stops streaming; reopen it to see the full output.

A terminal modal is available from the Scorch table when a break point component is reached; it is also available in the Scorch pipeline. There are two types of terminal modals: read-write and read-only. If another user opens a terminal modal for a given component, it will be read-only the next time a terminal is open. The following are examples of each. In the first example, a read-only terminal, the user viewing this modal is only observing what another using is executing. In the second example, a read-write terminal, the user ran two simple commands on the phenix host system. The terminal sends Tab to the shell. To move focus out of the terminal, press Ctrl+], then Tab or Shift+Tab (see Accessibility).

If a component fails, the Scorch app will skip the remaining components involved in the current execution stage and jump to the next appropriate stage to complete the Scorch run. For example, if a component fails in the Configure stage the Scorch app will jump to the Cleanup stage, and if a component fails in the Start stage Scorch will jump to the Stop stage (skipping execution of any configured loops in either case). If a component fails in the stop or cleanup stage, Scorch still executes the remaining components of that stage, and the run fails.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
phenix exp scorch starts a Scorch run (--run, 0 by default), prints its progress, and exits with an error if the run fails. If phenix ui is running, the server executes the run, so the web UI shows it and Ctrl+C cancels it. Otherwise the run executes in the command's own process, and the web UI doesn't show it.

With phenix ui running, you can instead act on the run with one of --status, --cancel, --cleanup (runs only the cleanup stage) or --clear (see phenix experiment scorch):

phenix exp scorch my-exp --run 1
phenix exp scorch my-exp --run 1 --status
phenix exp scorch my-exp --run 1 --status -o json

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
Example Scenario using the vmstats, hoststats, tcpdump, trafficgen, snort, and break components.

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v2
kind: Scenario
metadata:
  name: scorch-demo
spec:
  apps:
  - name: mirror
    metadata:
      directGRE:
        enabled: true
        mirrorBridge: phenix
        mirrorNet: 172.30.0.0/16
        mirrorVLAN: mirror
    hosts:
    - hostname: detector
      metadata:
        interface: IF0
        vlans:
        - EXP
  - name: scorch
    metadata:
      components:
      - name: vmstats
        type: vmstats
        metadata:
          filebeat.inputs:
          - enabled: true
            type: log
            json.add_error_key: true
            paths:
            - vm_stats.jsonl
            processors:
            - copy_fields:
                fields:
                - from: json
                  to: scorch.vmstats
            - drop_fields:
                fields:
                - json
            - timestamp:
                field: scorch.vmstats.UTC
                layouts:
                - '2006-01-02 15:04:05'
      - name: hoststats
        type: hoststats
        background: true
        metadata:
          filebeat.inputs:
          - enabled: true
            type: log
            json.add_error_key: true
            paths:
            - host_stats.jsonl
            processors:
            - copy_fields:
                fields:
                - from: json
                  to: scorch.hoststats
            - drop_fields:
                fields:
                - json
            - timestamp:
                field: scorch.hoststats.timestamp
                layouts:
                - UNIX_MS
      - name: trafficgen
        type: trafficgen
        metadata:
          scripts:
            backgroundGen: /phenix/topologies/scorch-demo/scripts/background-gen.py
            malwareGen: /phenix/topologies/scorch-demo/scripts/malware-gen.py
            trafficServer: /phenix/topologies/scorch-demo/scripts/traffic-server.py
          targets:
          - backgroundClient:
              hostname: background-gen
              probability: 0.01
              rate: 10000
            duration: 30
            hostname: traffic-server
            interface: IF0
            malwareClient:
              hostname: malware-gen
              probability: 1.25
              rate: 20
      - name: break
        type: break
        metadata: {}
      - name: tcpdump
        type: tcpdump
        metadata:
          convert_to_json: true
          filebeat.inputs:
          - enabled: true
            type: log
            json.add_error_key: true
            paths:
            - '*.pcap.jsonl'
            processors:
            - copy_fields:
                fields:
                - from: json
                  to: scorch.tcpdump
            - drop_fields:
                fields:
                - json
          vms:
          - hostname: detector
            iface: eth0
      - name: snort
        type: snort
        metadata:
          configs:
          - dst: /etc/snort/snort.conf
            name: snort
            src: /phenix/topologies/scorch-demo/configs/snort.conf
          - dst: /etc/snort/rules/emotet.rules
            name: emotet
            src: /phenix/topologies/scorch-demo/configs/emotet.rules
          filebeat.inputs:
          - enabled: true
            type: log
            json.add_error_key: true
            paths:
            - snort-stats.jsonl
            processors:
            - copy_fields:
                fields:
                - from: json
                  to: scorch.snort
            - drop_fields:
                fields:
                - json
            - timestamp:
                field: scorch.snort.timestamp
                layouts:
                - UNIX
          hostname: detector
          scripts:
            configSnort:
              executor: bash
              script: /phenix/topologies/scorch-demo/scripts/configure-snort.sh
          interface: eth0
          waitDuration: 5
      runs:
      - name: baseline
        configure:
        - trafficgen
        - snort
        start:
        - hoststats
        - vmstats
        loop:
          configure: null
          start:
          - tcpdump
          - snort
          - trafficgen
          stop:
          - trafficgen
          - snort
          - tcpdump
          cleanup: null
        stop:
        - vmstats
        - hoststats
        - break
      - start:
        - tcpdump
        - trafficgen
        stop:
        - trafficgen
        - tcpdump
      filebeat:
        enabled: true
        config:
          output.elasticsearch:
            hosts:
            - es:9200
          setup.dashboards.enabled: true
          setup.kibana.host: http://kibana:5601

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• phenix experiment scorch: start, follow, cancel or clean up a run.
  • phenix util scorch-json: print the JSON that a component reads.
  • Scenario: the config that holds the Scorch app.
  • Apps: Scorch and the other core apps.
  • State of Health: the app that the soh component runs.
  • Example Applications: user apps that follow the same logging contract as a component.
  • Troubleshooting: when a run stays marked as running.

docs.title: Settings & Configuration
docs.text:
phēnix supports dynamic configuration management via the phenix settings command. A running phenix ui applies changes to the log.* settings, ui.logs.level, experiment.disk-check, minimega.read-connections and the users file at once, without restarting. It reads every other setting only at startup, and logs a warning when one of those changes:

config change takes effect only when phenix ui restarts keys="store.endpoint, ui.listen-endpoint"

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
phēnix looks for a configuration file (e.g. config.yaml, config.json, config.toml) in the following locations, in order, and reads the first it finds:

When run as root:

  • ./config.yaml (the working directory)
  • /etc/phenix/config.yaml

When run as a regular user:

  • ./config.yaml (the working directory)
  • $HOME/.config/phenix/config.yaml
  • /etc/phenix/config.yaml

It looks for users.yaml in the same locations. sudo phenix searches as the user that runs sudo, so it also searches that user's $HOME/.config/phenix.

phēnix creates the default log directory, $HOME/phenix_logs (/var/log/phenix as root), and, if it finds no config file, an empty config.yaml in $HOME/.config/phenix/ (/etc/phenix/ as root).

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
base-dir:
  minimega: /tmp/minimega
  phenix: /phenix
log:
  level: info
  console: stderr
  system:
    path: /var/log/phenix/phenix.log
store:
  endpoint: bolt:///etc/phenix/store.bdb
ui:
  listen-endpoint: 0.0.0.0:3000
  jwt-signing-key: abcde12345
  logs:
    minimega-path: /var/log/minimega/minimega.log

docs.title: Configuration vs. Data Store
docs.text:
It is important to distinguish between the System Configuration and the Data Store:

  • System Configuration (config.yaml): Configures the phēnix daemon itself. It controls how the service runs (e.g., log levels, API ports, storage backend connection strings).
  • Data Store (BoltDB): Stores the application state. It holds what phēnix manages (e.g., defined experiments, topologies, user accounts, active VM states).

Deleting config.yaml resets daemon behavior to defaults. Deleting the Data Store results in data loss (experiments, users, etc.).

docs.title: Store Configuration
docs.text: The phenix tool uses a bbolt key-value data store, a single file with no external dependencies that is only accessible on one machine. Set its path with the bolt:// store endpoint (e.g. bolt:///etc/phenix/store.bdb). phenix no longer supports the etcd:// store endpoint.

docs.title: Managing Settings
docs.text:
# View all current runtime settings
phenix settings list

# Change log level to debug
phenix settings set log.level debug

# Revert a setting to default
phenix settings unset log.level

# Reset all settings
phenix settings unset --all

phenix settings set gives the value the type of the flag of the setting. For example, log.system.max-size takes an integer, ui.jwt-lifetime takes a duration such as 24h, and ui.users takes a comma-separated list. A string setting, such as ui.jwt-signing-key, keeps the text as it is, so 0123 stays 0123. The command refuses a value that does not have the type of the setting.

phenix settings set and phenix settings unset change only the key. The comments, the key order and the other keys in the file stay. A new key goes at the end of its section. An empty section, such as {}, changes to block style when you set a key in it. When you unset a key that is not in the file, the file does not change.

Both commands write to the config file that phēnix read, and refuse to change one that isn't YAML.

docs.title: Checking the Configuration
docs.text: phenix doctor checks the configuration without a running phenix ui. It shows where each setting comes from. See Doctor.

docs.title: Configuration Precedence
docs.text:
phēnix resolves each setting in the following order (highest to lowest):

  1. Command Line Flags: Arguments passed directly to the binary (e.g., phenix ui --log.level=debug).
  2. Environment Variables: Variables like PHENIX_LOG_LEVEL. An empty variable is ignored.
  3. Config File: Settings in config.yaml (managed via phenix settings set), with users.yaml merged over it.
  4. Defaults: Internal application defaults.

A PHENIX_* variable therefore hides a value that phenix settings set writes to the config file. phenix doctor warns about each one in its env-overrides check; unset the variable to use the file's value.

docs.title: Global Flags
docs.text:
The following global flags are supported by all phenix subcommands. The CLI reference lists them with every command's own flags.

Flag Type Default Description --base-dir.builder-templates string <base-dir.phenix>/builder/templates Directory of Builder node template files that phenix ui reads at start. See Template files on the server. --base-dir.injects string <base-dir.phenix>/injects Directory that phenix workflow apply stages topology injects into. The phenix ui server reports its value to the CLI, and the flag on the phenix workflow apply command line overrides it. See Workflow. --base-dir.minimega string /tmp/minimega Base minimega directory. --base-dir.phenix string /phenix Base phēnix directory. --base-dir.topologies string <base-dir.phenix>/topologies Directory that phenix workflow apply looks up topology directory names in. See Workflow. --bridge-mode string manual Bridge naming mode for experiments (auto uses experiment name for bridge; manual uses user-specified bridge name, or phenix if omitted). A phenix ui running in auto mode makes the commands that reach it over --unix-socket use auto. See Bridge Mode. --color string auto When to color the output (auto, on, or off). auto colors only a terminal, and not when NO_COLOR is set or TERM is dumb. See Colors. --deploy-mode string — Deploy mode for minimega VMs (all, no-headnode, or only-headnode). --experiment.disk-check string error What a start does when a VM disk image or CD-ROM image is missing, or its backing chain is broken (error, warn, or off). See Disk Check Before a Start. -h, --help — — Display help information for the command. --hostname-suffixes string -minimega,-phenix Hostname suffixes to strip. --log.console string stderr Destination output for console logs in text format (stderr, stdout, or a file path). --log.level string info Level to log messages at (debug, info, warn, error). --log.system.max-age int 90 Maximum number of days to retain old log files. --log.system.max-backups int 3 Maximum number of old log files to retain. --log.system.max-size int 100 Maximum size in megabytes of the system log file before rotation. --log.system.path string /var/log/phenix/phenix.log as root, $HOME/phenix_logs/phenix.log otherwise Path to persistent system log in JSON Lines format, with one JSON object per line. --minimega.read-connections int 16 Maximum number of read-only commands that phēnix sends to minimega at the same time, from 3 to 64. phēnix keeps 2 of them for reads of the head node. --mount-dir string <base-dir.phenix>/mounts Base directory for VM filesystem mounts. --store.endpoint string bolt:///etc/phenix/store.bdb as root, bolt://$HOME/.phenix.bdb otherwise BoltDB store endpoint (bolt://<path>). --unix-socket string /tmp/phenix.sock phēnix unix socket to listen on (ui subcommand) or connect to. --use-gre-mesh bool false Use GRE tunnels between mesh nodes for VLAN trunking. See GRE Mesh.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text: phēnix colors the statuses in tables, the rows of phenix doctor, warnings and errors. Set --color, the color setting or PHENIX_COLOR to auto (the default: only on a terminal, and not when NO_COLOR is set or TERM is dumb), on (even into a file or a pipe) or off. JSON and YAML output, and phenix doctor --report, never have color.

docs.title: Settings Reference
docs.text:
Setting Key Environment Variable Default Description bridge-mode PHENIX_BRIDGE_MODE manual Bridge naming mode for experiments. auto uses the experiment name as the bridge name; manual uses the user-specified bridge name, or phenix if not specified. See Bridge Mode. experiment.disk-check PHENIX_EXPERIMENT_DISK_CHECK error What a start does when a VM disk image or CD-ROM image is missing, or its backing chain is broken. error refuses the start, warn starts the experiment and shows each problem as a warning, and off does not check the images. It applies to every start: the CLI, the web UI, the REST API, phenix workflow apply, and the bulk start and restart of VMs. phēnix refuses another value. phenix ui applies a change at once. See Disk Check Before a Start. use-gre-mesh PHENIX_USE_GRE_MESH false Enable Layer 2 GRE tunnels for the default bridge of experiments created or updated with this setting. See GRE Mesh for usage, server inheritance, and MTU requirements. phenix ui reads this setting at startup. (Restart Required) log.level PHENIX_LOG_LEVEL info Global log verbosity (debug, info, warn, error). color PHENIX_COLOR auto When phēnix colors its output: statuses in tables, phenix doctor rows, warnings and errors. auto colors only a terminal, and not when NO_COLOR is set or TERM is dumb. on and off ignore both variables. JSON and YAML output never have color. phēnix refuses another value. See Colors. log.console PHENIX_LOG_CONSOLE stderr Destination for console logs (stderr, stdout, or a file path). Uses Text/Human-Readable format. Note: Setting this to a file path will prevent console logs from appearing in docker logs. log.system.path PHENIX_LOG_SYSTEM_PATH /var/log/phenix/phenix.log as root, $HOME/phenix_logs/phenix.log otherwise Path to the persistent system log file (used by UI). Uses JSON format. This is independent of log.console and is always active. log.system.max-size PHENIX_LOG_SYSTEM_MAX_SIZE 100 Max size in MB before rotation. log.system.max-backups PHENIX_LOG_SYSTEM_MAX_BACKUPS 3 Number of old log files to retain. log.system.max-age PHENIX_LOG_SYSTEM_MAX_AGE 90 Max age in days to retain old logs. ui.logs.level PHENIX_UI_LOGS_LEVEL "" Log level for the web UI stream (defaults to log.level). minimega.read-connections PHENIX_MINIMEGA_READ_CONNECTIONS 16 Maximum number of read-only commands, such as vm info, that phēnix sends to minimega at the same time. Each command uses a connection of its own, which phēnix opens when it needs one and closes after 5 minutes without use. The value must be from 3 to 64. phēnix uses the nearest value in that range for a value outside it, and logs a warning. phēnix keeps 2 connections for reads of the head node only, and lets screenshots use at most 4 fewer than the maximum. It applies to phenix ui and to every CLI command. phenix ui applies a change in the config file at once, unless a flag or an environment variable sets the value. The Settings page of the web UI also changes it. ui.logs.minimega-path PHENIX_UI_LOGS_MINIMEGA_PATH "" Path to the minimega log file to display in the UI and offer for download on the Logs page. (Restart Required) ui.features PHENIX_UI_FEATURES "" Optional UI features to enable. Separate them with commas in the --features flag and with spaces in PHENIX_UI_FEATURES. Use a YAML list in the configuration file. The features are:
  • vm-mount: enables transferring files to and from a running VM (see Mount a VM). Set it yourself.
  • webshark: phenix ui turns it on when it finds a WebShark build, and refuses to start with webshark set but no WebShark build.
  • tunneler-download: phenix ui turns it on when the downloads/tunneler directory exists (see Downloading the Tunneler).
  • file-server: phenix ui turns it on when ui.file-server-endpoint is set.
  • minimega-captures: phenix ui turns it on when minimega supports experiment captures (see Requirements).
(Restart Required) ui.file-server-endpoint PHENIX_UI_FILE_SERVER_ENDPOINT 0 (disabled) Address (port or host:port) for the separate experiment file-upload server. A port-only value binds to 127.0.0.1. Also works with the vm-mount feature - see Uploading Experiment Files from the phēnix Server. If it is set and the address cannot be listened on, phenix ui exits with an error. (Restart Required) ui.shutdown-grace-period PHENIX_UI_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD 5 How many seconds stopping phenix ui may take to finish requests and jobs and close connections, as a whole number such as 10. 0 closes everything without waiting; a negative value, or one that is not a whole number of seconds (such as 10s or 1.5), is refused at startup. Also phenix ui --shutdown-grace-period. See Stopping the Server. (Restart Required) ui.netflow.max-size PHENIX_UI_NETFLOW_MAX_SIZE 100 Maximum size in megabytes of each recorded netflow capture, as a whole number. A capture that reaches it stops recording and is marked truncated, while the live view goes on. 0 does not record captures; a negative value, or one that is not a whole number, is refused at startup. Also phenix ui --netflow.max-size. See Recorded Captures. (Restart Required) ui.captures.max-size PHENIX_UI_CAPTURES_MAX_SIZE 10240 Maximum size in megabytes of each packet capture file that minimega writes, as a whole number. 0 sets no limit; a negative value, or one that is not a whole number, is refused at startup. Also phenix ui --captures.max-size. See Capture Options. (Restart Required) ui.unix-socket-gid PHENIX_UI_UNIX_SOCKET_GID -1 ID of a group that may write to the unix socket of phenix ui. -1 does not change the group. Also phenix ui --unix-socket-gid. The deprecated key unix-socket-gid (PHENIX_UNIX_SOCKET_GID) still works when this key is not set, and phenix ui then writes a warning to standard error. See Deprecations. (Restart Required) mount-dir PHENIX_MOUNT_DIR <base-dir.phenix>/mounts Base directory used for VM filesystem mounts created via phenix vm mount. See Mount a VM. base-dir.injects PHENIX_BASE_DIR_INJECTS <base-dir.phenix>/injects Directory that phenix workflow apply stages a topology directory's phenix-injects/ into, as <base-dir.injects>/<name>. The phēnix server's value is used unless --base-dir.injects is given; see Workflow. Use an absolute path.
