(Restart Required) base-dir.topologies PHENIX_BASE_DIR_TOPOLOGIES <base-dir.phenix>/topologies Directory where phenix workflow apply NAME looks for NAME when NAME isn't an existing path. Use an absolute path. See Workflow. base-dir.builder-templates PHENIX_BASE_DIR_BUILDER_TEMPLATES <base-dir.phenix>/builder/templates Directory of Builder node template files (*.yaml, *.yml, *.json) that phenix ui reads at start as read-only server collections. Use an absolute path. See Template files on the server. (Restart Required)

docs.title: Stopping the Server
docs.text: phenix ui shuts down cleanly on SIGINT (CTRL+C) or SIGTERM (docker stop), within ui.shutdown-grace-period seconds (5 by default). Requests in progress get the whole grace period to finish, running background jobs get the first half, and queued jobs are canceled. Every websocket closes (consoles, SCORCH terminals, VNC and port forwards). A second signal stops the server at once. docker stop kills the container after 10 seconds, so if you raise the grace period past that, raise Docker's timeout too (stop_grace_period in docker-compose.yml, or docker stop --time).

docs.title: The Settings Page
docs.text:
The Settings page is in the Admin menu.

The password and timeout settings live in the data store and take effect as soon as you save. The minimum password length is 8 to 32. From the command line, use phenix settings db edit:

phenix settings db edit Password MinLength 12

The file logging and minimega fields apply at once and save to the config file like phenix settings set. The save fails if a flag or PHENIX_ variable of phenix ui sets a log limit you changed, or if phenix ui has no YAML config file.

docs.title: Web UI Session Timeout
docs.text: Turn on Log out users after period of inactivity to log out idle users. The idle time must be at least 0.5 minutes, and the warning has to come before the idle time is up.

docs.title: phēnix Apps Environment Variables
docs.text:
Apps (phenix-apps) run as subprocesses and read their configuration from the environment. phēnix sets these itself when it launches an app:

Environment Variable Value Description PHENIX_DIR base-dir.phenix Base phēnix data directory. PHENIX_FILES_DIR experiment files directory Where the app reads and writes experiment files. PHENIX_LOG_LEVEL phēnix's own value, else DEBUG App log verbosity. PHENIX_LOG_FILE stderr App logs stream back to phēnix rather than to a file. PHENIX_DRYRUN true / false Whether the run is a dry run. PHENIX_STORE_ENDPOINT store.endpoint Data store endpoint (user apps only). PHENIX_SCORCH_STARTTIME run start time Scorch components only.

The rest are inherited from the phēnix process:

Environment Variable Default Description PHENIX_TEMP_DIR /tmp/phenix App temporary directory. MM_FILEPATH /phenix/images Base minimega file path. MM_SOCKET_PATH /tmp/minimega/minimega minimega command socket.

docs.title: miniccc (cc) Timing
docs.text:
Apps drive VMs over minimega's cc command-and-control channel. These bound how long an app waits, in seconds.

Environment Variable Default Description PHENIX_CC_POLL_RATE 2.0 Interval between cc polls. PHENIX_CC_CLIENT_GRACE 300.0 Wait for a miniccc client to register before failing. PHENIX_CC_SEND_GRACE 300.0 Wait for a file send or component start to be acknowledged. PHENIX_CC_CMD_GRACE 0.0 Wait for a command response. 0 waits indefinitely, supervised by client liveness instead. PHENIX_CC_EXITCODE_GRACE 10.0 Wait for an exit code once the response is counted. PHENIX_CC_LIVENESS_INTERVAL 10.0 Interval between client-liveness checks during an unbounded wait. PHENIX_CC_LOG_INTERVAL 10.0 Delay before the first "still waiting" log line. PHENIX_CC_LOG_MAX_INTERVAL 320.0 Ceiling for that interval, which doubles each time.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• phenix settings: view and change stored settings.
  • phenix ui: the flags of the server.
  • Logging: what the log settings do.
  • Troubleshooting: when a setting has no effect.

docs.title: State of Health
docs.text: State of Health (SoH) is a core (but not default) app meant to assist with understanding the state of a running experiment. It has many configuration options, and relies on minimega's command and control infrastructure (ie. the miniccc agent running in experiment VMs) to drive and collect the experiment health state data. See the command and control section for more details.

docs.title: User Interface
docs.text:
SoH information is presented in the UI in two places. The SoH tab in the navbar summarizes every experiment, and each experiment has its own SoH page with its topology graph and, when SoH packet capture is enabled, its network volume. To open an experiment's SoH page, click the heartbeat button in the Experiments table or next to the Running status on the experiment's page.

From the command line, phenix exp soh shows the same summary. Give it an experiment name to see each VM with its status and failing checks, and --status (running, notrunning, notboot, notdeploy or external) to see only the VMs with that status.

phenix exp soh
phenix exp soh my-exp --status notrunning

docs.title: State of Health Overview
docs.text:
The SoH tab in the navbar lists every experiment in one table, worst first, so you can see which ones need attention without opening each one.

The SoH column holds one of these verdicts:

Verdict Meaning degraded a VM that should be up is down, at least 20% of the checked hosts have a failing check, or fewer than 90% of the reachability pairs pass checks failing at least one check is failing, but the experiment is not degraded waiting for start the soh app is configured, but the experiment is not running yet waiting for first run the experiment is running, but the app has no results yet first run in progress the experiment is running, and the app is running its first checks disabled, not run yet the experiment is running, but the scenario sets disabled: true on the app and nobody has started it healthy every check the app ran passed not configured the experiment's scenario does not include the soh app

The buttons above the table filter it: All, Needs attention (degraded and checks failing), Healthy, and No SOH data (the waiting verdicts and not configured).

Expand a row to list the experiment's failing checks and the VMs that are down, or click Run SOH to start a new run. A VM marked Do Not Boot, an external device, or a VM still waiting for its delayed start doesn't count as down.

docs.title: Topology Graph
docs.text:
This tab displays a network graph of the running experiment.

The color of the node is based on the condition of the corresponding VM and could be:

  • Running
  • Not running (part of the experiment, but currently paused)
  • Not booted (part of the experiment, but marked as Do Not Boot)
  • Not deployed (part of the experiment, but flushed from minimega)
  • External / HIL (an external node, i.e. hardware in the loop, not deployed by minimega)

While the experiment is stopped, its VMs are drawn without a status color.

It is also possible to filter the graph based on nodes that are either:

  • All (the default)
  • Running
  • Not running
  • Not booted
  • Not deployed
  • External / HIL

The Refresh Network button reloads the graph data from the server. It keeps the filter you picked.

The Run SOH button triggers a new SoH run. To get the latest server-side SoH data without a new run, use the Refresh Network button.

Before the first SoH run, a note beside the buttons tells you why there are no results:

  • The soh app waits for its first run, which starts after post-start.
  • The soh app is running its first checks.
  • The scenario sets disabled: true on the soh app, so the app did not run at post-start. The Run SOH button is available. Use it to start the app manually.

The SoH tab shows the same information for each experiment in its Last Check column and on its run buttons.

The graph opens in the VLAN groups layout (the VLANs button), which puts the hosts in a box for each VLAN. Use the layout buttons above the graph to select a different layout. The page remembers the layout that you select. The graph uses the Force layout when the VLAN groups layout cannot draw it: the graph has more than 300 nodes, or the layout fails. A note above the graph tells you when the graph is too large for the layout. When a layout that you selected fails, the page does not remember it.

Hovering over a node in the graph will cause it to expand to show what operating system the node is running. An orange border around a node is indicative of the node currently having health issues (e.g., expected files, services, or processes are missing, or the node cannot reach other nodes on the network). Other virtual systems will also be represented accordingly (e.g., a router or firewall).

Clicking on the node with an orange border will produce a details modal with the current error reporting.

If there are no errors to report and command and control is enabled, the details modal will only show the current CPU load.

Note the green button in the lower right corner of the modal; this will provide access to the VNC for any running VM. When the VM is not running, access to the VNC will be disabled. Finally, if there is no SoH information to report on a given VM, it will be noted in the details modal. The following screenshot is an example of no SoH information with the VNC button disabled.

The Notes section of the modal shows the VM's notes. If your role can change the VM, the tag button edits its notes and labels, and the paintbrush button changes how the graph draws the node (fill color, stroke color and stroke style).

docs.title: Graph Layouts
docs.text: Besides the default VLAN groups, the layouts are Force (a physics simulation), Radial tree (the most central router or firewall in the middle, everything else in rings by hop distance), Layered (the core on top, VLANs under their routers, hosts below) and ELK layered (tiers like Layered, arranged by the ELK engine). The Fit button fits the whole graph in view.

docs.title: Downloading the Graph
docs.text: The Download menu saves the graph as drawn, as a PNG, an SVG, or a GEXF 1.3 file for Gephi and Gephi Lite. The PNG and SVG include a title and the legend. The GEXF file holds each VM and VLAN node with its status and SoH check results, an edge for each interface and, when network volume data is available, the traffic flows as weighted edges.

docs.title: External Devices
docs.text:
Experiments that include hardware-in-the-loop or other devices not deployed by minimega can still represent them in the topology graph by adding them to the topology as external nodes (external: true). External nodes show up in the graph with the External / HIL status color (see the legend above) and, when hovered, still show which OS type/icon was configured for them.

Because external nodes don't run miniccc, they're excluded from the automated command-and-control-based checks described in Command and Control (network config, reachability, files, services, listening ports, processes, Docker containers, custom tests, CPU load). An external node's details modal will therefore show only the reachability tests that other VMs ran to it, or no SoH information when there are none, and the VNC button will be disabled since phenix has no console access to it.

External nodes can still participate in reachability testing indirectly: their IP address(es) are read from the topology configuration, so they can be used as the src or dst in a testCustomReachability entry to verify connectivity to/from the device from another VM in the experiment.

When testReachability is sample or full, the other VMs also ping the addresses of external nodes. To stop these pings, add the external node's hostname to skipHosts. Custom reachability tests can still reach an external node in skipHosts.

Getting a line to draw to an external device

The topology graph only draws a line between two nodes when they share a common VLAN name on one of their network interfaces (the VLAN name becomes the shared switch node in the graph). To connect an external node to the rest of the topology in the graph, give it a network.interfaces[].vlan value that matches the VLAN used by the node(s) you want it connected to. Interfaces on the MGMT or MIRROR VLANs are always ignored when drawing these lines (for both external and internal nodes), and an external node with no vlan set on its interface(s) will appear in the graph as an isolated node with no connecting lines.

docs.title: Network Volume
docs.text:
This tab displays a chord graph that shows network flows between nodes using flows from Packetbeat fed to Elasticsearch; connections represent the volume of traffic between nodes.

Tip

This information is only available if the packet capture option is enabled for SoH. The tab appears only after a run of the flows check has recorded flow data.

This is an example chord graph of a Protonuke server with two clients; one of which is requesting content at a delayed interval (therefore less traffic flow).

If you hover over traffic flow, a tooltip will appear providing additional details. (In this screenshot, the mouse is hovering over the traffic for IP 192.168.100.1.)

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
Set these options in the metadata of the soh app in the Scenario. The app fails when it has no metadata.

  • disabled: Like any (non-default) phenix app, soh can be disabled at startup by setting disabled: true. In this case, health checks will not be run at experiment startup but can be triggered manually after the experiment is running through either the phenix cli or web UI (see Running the Checks Again). A disabled app also skips its configure and post-start stages, so it does not inject ICMP rules or deploy packet capture.

  • appMetadataProfileKey: since the listeners and processes one might want to monitor could be highly dependent on other apps that are configured for an experiment, it's possible to specify the listeners, processes and custom tests to be monitored in the other apps themselves, in the metadata of a host of the app, under the key specified here. The key holds listeners, processes and customTests lists, which take the same values as hostListeners, hostProcesses and hostCustomTests for that host. The default key is sohProfile.

    spec:
  apps:
  - name: my-app
    hosts:
    - hostname: server
      metadata:
        sohProfile:
          listeners:
          - :80
          processes:
          - nginx
          customTests:
          - name: web-check
            testScript: curl -s http://localhost/
            testStdout: Welcome

  • c2Timeout: a Golang duration string specifying how long to wait for the miniccc C2 client to become active in a VM. If it doesn't, SoH records the VM's remaining checks in that run as failed with the error c2 not active on host. The default is 5m.

  • c2AppearGrace: how long a C2 command can take to show up on the cluster host that has the VM's miniccc client before the check fails. 0s disables this limit. The default is 30s.

  • c2ClientGrace: how long a VM's miniccc client can be absent while a check waits for its response before the check fails as if C2 were not active. 0s disables this limit. The default is 90s.

  • c2Concurrency: the maximum number of C2 checks that one SoH run sends at a time. The wait doesn't count against c2Timeout. A value of 0 or less removes the limit. The default is 16.

  • exitOnError: a boolean representing whether the app should cause the entire experiment deployment to fail if it has any errors. The default is false.

  • startupDelay: a Golang duration string specifying how long to wait before initiating checks at the experiment starts. This can be useful when some processes are not healthy immediately at experiment start. This only delays SoH when it first runs at the experiment start. It will not delay SoH when run manually later by clicking the Run SOH button in the UI or running phenix exp trigger <experiment-name> running (or the deprecated trigger-running command) from the command line. The default is no delay.

  • hostCustomTests: If present, a map of custom tests to run on the given hosts. Each test needs a testScript and at least one of testStdout, testStderr, validateStdout and validateStderr. SoH sends the script to the VM with cc send.

    • name: name of test. Used as script name to be sent to the host. The script name is <host>-<name>. SoH replaces each run of white space with one _. Then it replaces each character other than a letter, a digit, -, _, or . with _. If this changes the name, SoH adds - and an 8-character hash, for example web-db_check-420ef7c9. Thus two test names on one host do not use the same script file.

    • testScript: the actual script (can be multiple lines) to be executed using the specified executor.

    • executor: the application to execute the testScript with (e.g. bash, powershell). The default is bash, or powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy bypass -File on a Windows VM. If the executor starts with powershell, SoH adds .ps1 to the script name.

    • testStdout: a string to look for in STDOUT from the executed script. If found, the test passes. If not found, it fails.

    • testStderr: a string to look for in STDERR from the executed script. If found, the test passes. If not found, it fails.

    • validateStdout: a script to run that will be provided, via STDIN, the STDOUT from the executed script. If this validation script exits 0, the test passes. If it exits non-zero, the test fails. This validation script should always be a bash script, even if the host is a Windows host. phēnix runs it with bash on the phēnix server, not in the VM. When both are set, validateStdout is used in place of testStdout.

    • validateStderr: a script to run that will be provided, via STDIN, the STDERR from the executed script. If this validation script exits 0, the test passes. If it exits non-zero, the test fails. This validation script should always be a bash script, even if the host is a Windows host. phēnix runs it with bash on the phēnix server, not in the VM. When both are set, validateStderr is used in place of testStderr.

  • hostFiles: a map of VMs, each specifying a list of file paths that should exist within the VM. Paths may target Linux or Windows VMs. Missing files are reported in the node's Files table in the SoH details modal and mark the node as unhealthy. The default is nil.

    hostFiles:
  linux-server:
  - /etc/phenix/startup/1_hostname-start.sh
  windows-client:
  - 'C:\ProgramData\phenix\ready.txt'

  • hostFilesAbsent: a map of VMs, each specifying a list of file paths that must not exist within the VM. SoH uses the same command as for hostFiles. A file that exists is reported in the node's Files (Absent) table in the SoH details modal and marks the node as unhealthy. The default is nil.

    hostFilesAbsent:
  linux-server:
  - /etc/phenix/startup/failed

  • hostServices: a map of VMs, each specifying a list of service names that should be running within the VM. Linux VMs are checked via systemctl, and Windows VMs are checked via Get-Service. Services that aren't active are reported in the node's Services table in the SoH details modal and mark the node as unhealthy. The default is nil.

    hostServices:
  linux-server:
  - sshd
  windows-client:
  - Spooler

  • dockerContainers: a map of VMs, each specifying a list of Docker container names/IDs that should be up and healthy within the VM. For each container, if it has a Docker healthcheck configured, its health status (healthy, unhealthy, or starting) is used to determine node health; otherwise, the container simply being in the running state is considered healthy. Requires the docker CLI to be available on the VM (Linux or Windows) and the VM's miniccc user to have permission to run it. Results are reported in the node's Docker Containers table in the SoH details modal and mark the node as unhealthy if a container is missing, not running, or unhealthy. The default is nil.

    dockerContainers:
  linux-server:
  - nginx
  - redis

  • hostListeners: a map of VMs, each specifying a list of listening ports to check for within the VM. If the port can be listening on any interface, the form :80 can be used. If the port should be listening on a specific interface, the form 192.168.1.10:80 can be used. Each address and port can contain only letters, digits, and the characters -_.%*/. The default is nil.

  • hostProcesses: a map of VMs, each specifying a list of process names to check for within the VM. On Linux, each entry is a pgrep -f pattern, which matches the full command line, for example python3 server.py. On Windows, each entry is a Get-Process name. The check passes when the VM returns one or more process IDs. Other output, for example a pgrep error, makes the check fail with an error. The default is nil.

  • hostsToUseUUIDForC2Active: a list of topology hostnames to use the minimega VM UUID for when determining if their cc agent is active. This is useful for topology nodes that are configured with snapshots disabled, preventing their hostname from getting updated when booted. Note that this configuration option also supports being set to all (e.g., hostsToUseUUIDForC2Active: all) if a user wishes to use the minimega VM UUID for all topology nodes.

  • injectICMPAllow: a boolean representing whether any existing firewall/router rulesets should have a rule added to allow ICMP between all nodes to facilitate reachability testing. See Injecting ICMP Rules for more details. If reachability tests are disabled, then this will be too, regardless of its setting here. The default is false.

  • packetCapture: if present, and its captureHosts lists at least one VM, a partially hidden packet capture infrastructure based on Elasticsearch, Kibana, and Packetbeat will be deployed for the experiment. See Packet Capture for more details. The default is nil.

    • elasticImage: path to the disk image to use for the Elastic/Kibana VM for packet capture. An image/PHENIX-elasticsearch config comes bundled with phenix and can be used to build an image to use here. There is no default for this setting; if packet capture is to be deployed it must be provided.

    • packetBeatImage: path to the disk image to use for the Packetbeat VM for packet capture. An image/PHENIX-packetbeat config comes bundled with phenix and can be used to build an image to use here. There is no default for this setting; if packet capture is to be deployed it must be provided.

    • elasticServer:

      • hostname: the hostname to use for the Elastic/Kibana server added to the experiment topology. There is no default for this setting; if packet capture is to be deployed it must be provided.

      • vcpus: the number of CPUs to assign to the Elastic/Kibana server VM. The default is 4.

      • memory: the amount of memory to assign to the Elastic/Kibana server VM. The default is 4096.

      • ipAddress: the IP address to use for the Elastic/Kibana server added to the experiment topology. The network interface this IP address is used for will be added to the MGMT VLAN. The IP address must be an IPv4 address in CIDR notation. There should also be sufficient IP addresses after the one specified here to be assigned to each of the Packetbeat monitor VMs that will be deployed, as the IP addresses assigned to them on the MGMT VLAN will increment up from this IP. There is no default for this setting; if packet capture is to be deployed it must be provided.

    • captureHosts: a map of VMs, each specifying a list of network interface names to monitor. One Packetbeat VM will be deployed for each listed VM that boots, and it monitors the interfaces listed for that VM. A listed VM that is not in the topology, is an external node, or will not boot gets no Packetbeat VM, and SoH logs a warning. The default is nil.

  • skipInitialNetworkConfigTests: by default, a set of tests will be run on each VM to ensure the VM was assigned the correct IP address and can reach its default gateway (if specified). Setting this to true will skip these initial tests, but will also disable reachability testing (including testCustomReachability). The default is false. These tests skip interfaces on the MGMT VLAN and serial interfaces. For an interface that uses DHCP, SoH waits for minimega to report the VM's address instead.

  • skipHosts: a list of VM hostnames and/or disk image names to skip health monitoring for. For disk image names, any host using the disk image as its primary image will be skipped. A disk image name ends in .qc2, .qcow2, or .qcow. An external node in the list is not a target of the ICMP reachability test. The default is nil.

  • testReachability: reachability testing is the process of making sure each VM can reach other VMs within the experiment over the network. See Network Reachability for more details. There are three options for this setting: off, sample, full.

    • off: reachability testing is disabled. This is the default.

    • sample: each VM in the experiment will attempt to ping a random VM in every experiment VLAN, its own VLAN included.

    • full: each VM in the experiment will attempt to ping every other VM in every experiment VLAN, its own VLAN included.

  • testCustomReachability: if present, a list of custom reachability test settings.

    • src: hostname to conduct test from.

    • dst: hostname and interface name (e.g. host-01|IF0) to conduct test to. A value without |, for example an IP address, is used as it is.

    • proto: protocol to use for test. Currently the options are tcp and udp. If udp is used, the udpPacketBase64 setting must be provided.

    • port: destination port to conduct test to.

    • wait: amount of time to wait for a response from the destination. If not provided, the default of 5s is used.

    • udpPacketBase64: a base64-encoded packet to send when testing using udp. This is required to generate a response over UDP to determine if the remote server is up and reachable. The given packet must be valid enough to generate a response from the server.

docs.title: Network Reachability
docs.text:
Testing network reachability for a VM requires that the VM has minimega's command and control (C2) layer active (ie., the miniccc agent is running in the VM), has the correct IP address configured, and can ping its default route if one is configured. If C2 is not active for a VM after the c2Timeout duration has passed, then SoH does not run reachability tests from the VM. Those tests, the VM's later checks and its CPU load are recorded as failed with the error c2 not active on host. Once C2 is up for a VM, the VM is queried to confirm its IP address is configured and its gateway is reachable for a maximum of the c2Timeout duration (5 minutes by default). Once all the VMs with C2 detected have their IP address configured and their gateways are reachable, reachability tests begin.

Reachability tests are run in the post-start stage and each time the running stage is triggered. Given this, if for some reason a VM comes up with its C2 agent active, but its network has to be configured manually, it will not be included in reachability tests during the post-start stage. Once the VM's network settings have been configured manually, the running stage can be triggered and the VM will be included in reachability tests this time around.

docs.title: Injecting ICMP Rules
docs.text:
The injectICMPAllow option can be used to add rules to routers/firewalls in the topology to prevent reachability tests from failing due to ACLs. When enabled, all rulesets present in the experiment (either in the topology or scenario) will have a rule prepended to the list of existing rules allowing the ICMP protocol to/from any address. To ensure this rule is applied before any other rule, the SoH app attempts to inject it with an ID 10 less than the lowest existing rule ID, or 1 if that is less than 1 (since Vyatta/VyOS orders rules by ID). If a rule already exists with an ID of 1 then injecting this rule will fail.

A check is done in the configure stage, which runs when an experiment is created or reconfigured, to see if injecting ICMP rules is enabled, and if not, any injected rules are removed from the experiment. This means the setting can be changed between runs of an experiment (e.g., using phenix config edit experiment/<name>, then phenix experiment reconfigure) and the change will be reflected accurately when the experiment is started again.

docs.title: Packet Capture
docs.text:
The SoH packet capture capability leverages minimega's tap mirroring to monitor traffic on experiment VM interfaces with Packetbeat and feed network flow data to Elasticsearch.

When enabled, an Elasticsearch/Kibana VM is added to the experiment's topology so it can be accessed via the phenix UI. Packetbeat VMs are deployed in minimega for each experiment VM that is configured to be monitored and boots, but are not added to the experiment topology so they do not clutter the phenix UI. The configure stage adds the Elasticsearch/Kibana VM, and the post-start stage deploys the Packetbeat VMs.

This capability is separate from experiment packet captures and netflow, which minimega records without extra VMs.

When packet capture is enabled, the experiment's SoH page will include a Network Volume tab that uses network flow data queried from Elasticsearch to populate a chord graph in an effort to depict how much traffic is flowing between VMs. Users/Analysts can also access Kibana using VNC via the phenix UI to do additional analysis on the network flow data that's being captured.

docs.title: Sample SoH Scenario Config
docs.text:
spec:
  apps:
  - name: soh
    disabled: false
    metadata:
      appMetadataProfileKey: sohProfile  # metadata key to look for in other apps
      c2Timeout: 5m
      exitOnError: false
      startupDelay: 5m  # only delays at experiment start (PostStart phase)
      hostCustomTests:
        host-00:
        - name: FooBarTest
          testScript: |
            cat /etc/passwd | grep root
          validateStdout: |
            count=$(wc -l)
            [[ $count -eq 1 ]] && exit 0 || exit 1
          executor: bash
        host-01:
        - name: SuckaTest
          testScript: |
            Get-Process miniccc -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
          testStdout: miniccc
          executor: powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy bypass -File
      hostFiles:
        host-00:
        - /etc/phenix/startup/1_hostname-start.sh
        host-01:
        - 'C:\ProgramData\phenix\ready.txt'
      hostFilesAbsent:
        host-00:
        - /etc/phenix/startup/failed
      hostServices:
        host-00:
        - sshd
        host-01:
        - Spooler
      dockerContainers:
        host-00:
        - nginx
        - redis
      hostListeners:
        client:
        - :502
        server:
        - :80
        - :443
      hostProcesses:
        client:
        - miniccc
        server:
        - miniccc
      hostsToUseUUIDForC2Active:
      - host-02
      injectICMPAllow: true
      packetCapture:
        elasticImage: /phenix/images/elasticsearch.qc2
        packetBeatImage: /phenix/images/packetbeat.qc2
        elasticServer:
          hostname: soh-elasticsearch-server
          vcpus: 4
          memory: 4096
          ipAddress: 172.16.200.1/16  # on the MGMT VLAN
        captureHosts:
          client:
          - IF0  # interface to monitor on "client" node in topology
          server:
          - IF0  # interface to monitor on "server" node in topology
      skipInitialNetworkConfigTests: false  # if true, testReachability will be off
      skipHosts:
      - kali.qc2  # can be an image name, in which case any host using image will be skipped
      - foobar-host  # can be hostname from topology
      testReachability: full  # can be off, sample, or full
      testCustomReachability:
      - src: host-00
        dst: host-01|IF0
        proto: tcp
        port: 22
        wait: 30s
      - src: host-01
        dst: host-00|IF0
        proto: tcp
        port: 22
        wait: 30s

docs.title: Running the Checks Again
docs.text:
The soh app runs its checks in the post-start stage and each time its running stage runs. To run them again on a running experiment:

  • click Run SOH on the Topology Graph tab, or in the SoH tab;
  • run phenix experiment trigger <experiment-name> running soh (see phenix experiment trigger);
  • add a soh Scorch component;
  • send POST /api/v1/experiments/<experiment-name>/trigger?apps=soh to the API.

To repeat the running stage on a schedule, set runPeriodically (a duration such as 5m) on the app in the Scenario. The schedule is a background job of the phēnix server that the experiment start creates (see Starting / Stopping Experiments), and it ends when the experiment stops.

A Scorch component, or a query parameter of the API request, can change one run: checks limits the run to the listed checks (network-config, reachability, custom-reachability, files, files-absent, services, processes, ports, docker, custom, cpu-load and flows), and c2Timeout replaces the app's setting. The API request also takes c2AppearGrace, c2ClientGrace and c2Concurrency. The reachability checks run only together with network-config.

docs.title: Command and Control
docs.text:
As mentioned earlier, SoH relies on minimega's command and control infrastructure (miniccc) to drive and collect the experiment health state data. Under the hood, the SoH app uses C2 to execute a test on a VM (cc exec), wait for the command to complete (cc commands), grab the STDOUT/STDERR of the command (cc responses), and compare it to an expected response.

Current tests executed on Linux VMs include the following:

  • ip addr
  • ip route
  • ping -c 1 <ip>
  • stat -c present -- <path>
  • systemctl is-active -- <service>
  • pgrep -f -- <process>
  • ss -lntu state all 'sport = <port>'
  • docker inspect --format=<template> -- <container>
  • cat /proc/loadavg

Corresponding tests for Windows VMs include the following:

  • ipconfig /all
  • route print
  • ping -n 1 <ip>
  • powershell -NoProfile -Command "if (Test-Path -LiteralPath '<path>' -PathType Leaf) { 'present' }"
  • powershell -NoProfile -Command "if ((Get-Service -Name '<service>' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).Status -eq 'Running') { 'active' }"
  • powershell -NoProfile -Command "Get-Process -Name '<process>' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Id"
  • powershell -NoProfile -Command "@(Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; Get-NetUDPEndpoint -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) | Where-Object LocalPort -eq <port> | Select-Object -First 1"
  • powershell -NoProfile -Command "docker inspect --format='<template>' -- '<container>' 2>&1 | Where-Object -Property Exception -Not"
  • powershell -command "Get-WmiObject Win32_Processor | Measure-Object -Property LoadPercentage -Average | Select -ExpandProperty Average"

SoH quotes each value, so that the VM gets the value as one argument. A path, service, container, or process value can contain spaces and quotes. minimega expands environment variables in each cc exec argument, also in quoted text. Thus, SoH does not send a check if its value has a $ before a letter, a digit, _, {, or one of *#$@!?- (for example, $HOME). Other uses of $ are permitted, for example at the end of a process pattern. minimega also replaces a value that starts with file:, http:, https:, or tar:, so SoH does not send that check. For each check that SoH does not send, the check result shows an error.

Custom tests send their script with cc send and run it with cc exec. Custom reachability tests use cc test-conn.

docs.title: SoH Run History
docs.text:
Besides the per-host results of its latest run, the soh app keeps a short history in its app status:

  • lastRun: when the last run finished
  • lastRunDuration: how long it took, in seconds
  • history: a summary of the last 20 runs, each with its time, duration, total checks, failing checks, and hostsFailing and hostsDown counts

docs.text:

  • Scenario: where the soh app and its metadata go.
  • phenix experiment soh: show the state of health from the command line.
  • phenix experiment trigger: run a stage of the app by hand.
  • Scorch: run the checks during a Scorch run.
  • Troubleshooting: a VM that has no miniccc client.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
This page consolidates common issues and their solutions when working with phēnix.

Most of the problems below have a phenix doctor check that finds them, so run it first. To report a bug, paste the output of phenix doctor --report (docker exec phenix phenix doctor --report in Docker) into the issue (see Reporting a Bug).

docs.title: Logs Not Appearing in UI
docs.text:
If your application logs are not showing up in the phēnix web UI, check the following:

  • Check the stream: Ensure your app writes logs to stderr. stdout is reserved for returning modified experiment configuration JSON to phēnix.
  • Check the format: The phēnix core expects valid, single-line JSON objects. If your app prints raw text (like Starting app...), it may be logged as a warning or error by the core but will not be indexed correctly for the UI.
  • Check the environment: Verify PHENIX_LOG_FILE=stderr is set in your app's environment (phēnix does this automatically for apps it launches).
  • Check for skipped lines: When the server logs faster than it can send to the browser, the Logs page's live view skips lines and shows a WARN entry such as 120 log lines skipped while the server was busy. The lines are still in the log file: reload the Logs page, or call GET /logs, to see them. The server also logs a WebSocket broker dropped slow clients or live log lines warning at most every 30 seconds.

docs.title: No minimega Logs on the Logs Page
docs.text: The Logs page shows minimega's log only when ui.logs.minimega-path names the file minimega logs to, such as /var/log/phenix/minimega.log in the Docker Compose setup. If the file isn't there, phenix ui waits for it without a warning.

docs.title: JSON Parsing Errors
docs.text:
If you see "malformed log entry" warnings in the main phēnix system log, it's likely because your application is writing non-JSON text to stderr.

  • Debug Prints: Ensure you are not using print() (Python) or fmt.Println() (Go) for debugging. These pollute the stderr stream. Use the structured logger.
  • Tracebacks: Ensure exception tracebacks are not being printed as raw text.
    • Python: Use logger.exception("message") inside an except block. This correctly captures the traceback as a JSON field. Standard print(e) or traceback.print_exc() will break the parser.
    • Go: Use structured logging fields for errors (e.g., slog.Error("message", "err", err)).

docs.title: Inconsistent Timestamps
docs.text: Ensure timestamps in your JSON logs are in a consistent format that phēnix can parse, such as RFC3339. The core now enforces a 2006-01-02 15:04:05.000 format for its own file logs for easier reading, but is flexible on ingest.

docs.title: Experiment Captures Are Not Available
docs.text: Experiment captures need minimega 3.4.0 or later on every node. phēnix checks the minimega version of the head node. For the disabled controls, a refused start, and a skew warning, see Experiment Packet Captures.

docs.title: Settings in config.yaml Have No Effect
docs.text:
If phēnix can't read its config file (or users.yaml), it falls back to environment variables and defaults, and prints a warning on stderr at startup (docker logs phenix in Docker):

phenix: warning: ignoring config file /etc/phenix/config.yaml: it does not parse at line 3

Fix the file at the line it names. phenix doctor also finds misspelled keys.

docs.title: Every Command Fails on a Mode Setting
docs.text:
Every command except phenix doctor and phenix healthcheck reads bridge-mode, deploy-mode, experiment.disk-check and color first, and stops on a value it doesn't know:

setting user-specified bridge mode: setting bridge mode: unknown bridge mode provided: sideways

Fix the value in the flag, the PHENIX_* variable or the config file.

docs.title: Output Shows Escape Codes Such as ^[[32m
docs.text: phēnix colors its output when --color is on, or auto and the output is a terminal, so a program that reads the output shows the codes as text. Use --color off, PHENIX_COLOR=off, NO_COLOR=1, or color: off in the config file (see Colors).

docs.title: phenix ui Fails to Start, or Ignores TLS or Users
docs.text:
phenix ui exits at startup when it can't listen on ui.listen-endpoint or ui.file-server-endpoint, or can't create its unix socket or give it the unix-socket-gid group. It starts, but not as configured, when only one of ui.tls-key and ui.tls-cert is set, a ui.users entry isn't name:password:role[:resource...], or ui.jwt-lifetime has no unit. To find which, run this as the user of phenix ui, with its settings, and read the auth, tls and socket rows:

phenix doctor --skip minimega

docs.title: Browsers Refuse the Certificate of phenix ui
docs.text: Browsers refuse a certificate that has expired, isn't valid yet, or whose DNS and IP names don't include the host users connect to (they ignore the common name). phenix doctor -p -x shows the expiry date and names in its ui.tls-cert row. Make a new certificate with that host in its names, set ui.tls-cert and ui.tls-key to the new files, and restart phenix ui.

docs.title: Requests for phenix ui Go to a Proxy
docs.text: Programs that read HTTP_PROXY or HTTPS_PROXY send their requests to the proxy. The proxy-env row of phenix doctor -p -x names each host of phenix ui that NO_PROXY or no_proxy doesn't cover. Add those hosts to both, then restart phenix ui and the apps that run in the same environment.

docs.title: A Command Ignores bridge-mode or deploy-mode
docs.text: Every command except phenix doctor and phenix healthcheck first asks phenix ui on unix-socket for its modes. If phenix ui uses bridge-mode: auto, so does the command, and if you didn't set deploy-mode for the command, it uses the one from phenix ui.

docs.title: Do Not Delete config.yaml
docs.text:
If you delete the config.yaml file while phēnix is running, the internal file watcher will break, and dynamic configuration changes will no longer apply.

To reset your configuration, use the command phenix settings unset --all instead of deleting the file.

docs.title: phenix settings set Has No Effect
docs.text: A flag or a PHENIX_* environment variable overrides the config file and hides what phenix settings set writes (the Docker deployment sets PHENIX_COLOR, for example). Drop the flag or unset the variable. phenix doctor shows where each setting comes from.

docs.title: A Command Sees Different Experiments Than phenix ui
docs.text: By default, root uses the store /etc/phenix/store.bdb and other users use $HOME/.phenix.bdb, so if phenix ui runs as root and you don't, you're looking at a different store. sudo phenix doesn't help, because it still uses the store of the user that ran sudo. Run the command from a root shell (sudo -i), or set store.endpoint to the store of phenix ui.

docs.title: Upgrading the BoltDB Store
docs.text: You don't need to delete or recreate store.bdb after an upgrade, and earlier releases can still open the store.

docs.title: The Store Is on a Network Filesystem or Has Many Free Pages
docs.text:
On a network filesystem (NFS, SMB) or a FUSE filesystem (sshfs), BoltDB's file lock or write sync can fail, so two processes can write to one store or a write can be lost. Set store.endpoint to a path on a local disk.

BoltDB also doesn't shrink the store file when phēnix deletes data. To compact a store with many free pages:

  1. Stop phenix ui and copy the store file to a backup.

  2. Compact it with the bbolt tool:

    go install go.etcd.io/bbolt/cmd/bbolt@latest
bbolt compact -o <new-file> <store-file>

  3. Replace the store file with the new file, with the same owner and mode 0600, and start phenix ui.

docs.title: Files That Hold Secrets Are Readable by Other Users
docs.text: phenix doctor warns when the group or other users can read the TLS key, the store file, or a config or users file that sets ui.jwt-signing-key or ui.users, or when the key or such a config file belongs to someone other than root or the user that runs phēnix. Run chmod 600 <file> on each file it names, and chown <user> <file>, where <user> runs phenix ui, on each file another user owns.

docs.title: An App or SCORCH Component Is Not Found
docs.text:
phēnix runs an app that isn't built in as phenix-app-<app> on PATH, and a SCORCH component as phenix-scorch-component-<type>. If the program isn't on PATH, or this user can't run it, the start or SCORCH run fails:

external user app phenix-app-foo does not exist in your path: user app not found

Install it (in Docker, in the image) or add its directory to PATH for the user that runs phenix ui, and make it executable with chmod +x <path>. If its #! line names a missing interpreter, install the interpreter, and if the line ends in a carriage return, run dos2unix <path>.

docs.title: Reserved Experiment Names
docs.text:
You can't name an experiment minimega, __phenix__, all, . or .., in any mix of upper and lower case:

cannot use 'minimega' for experiment name: reserved experiment name: it is a minimega namespace

docs.title: timeout running command
docs.text: phēnix sends most minimega commands over one shared connection, one at a time, so a command that waits for it or holds it too long fails with timeout running command. A web request that changes VMs fails with an error that includes context deadline exceeded. Either way, minimega is usually stuck or overloaded: check minimega -e version and the minimega log on the head node.

docs.title: A Start Fails on a Broken Backing Chain
docs.text:
phēnix won't start an experiment when a VM's disk or CD-ROM image, or a file in a disk's backing chain, is missing:

Error: unable to start the foo experiment: qemu cannot open 1 disk on 1 VM: 1 error occurred:
    * VM host-01: disk kali.qc2: backing file /phenix/images/ro_kali.qc2 is missing

Restore the file that the error names on the head node, or point the image at a copy of it with Rebase and Change reference only on the Disks page (or minimega's disk set-backing). A rebase without that option has to read the missing file, so it fails. You can also change the topology to use a different image. If the file is only on a compute node, set experiment.disk-check to warn (see Disk Check Before a Start).

docs.title: A Start Fails on an Image Format
docs.text:
phēnix refuses an image that qemu can't open, such as one with the old AES or LUKS encryption, a qcow2 version later than 3, or a corrupt qcow2 image that qemu must write to. It warns, but starts the VM, for a qcow version 1, vmdk or qed image, or one that qemu didn't close cleanly. See Image Format Versions for each format.

Stop each VM that uses an image before you change it. Then:

  • Upgrade a qcow2 version 2 image to version 3, in place:

    qemu-img amend -f qcow2 -o compat=1.1 kali.qc2

  • Convert a qcow version 1 image to qcow2, then point each image that it backs at the copy:

    qemu-img convert -f qcow -O qcow2 kali.qcow kali.qc2
qemu-img rebase -u -F qcow2 -b kali.qc2 overlay.qc2

  • Remove the old AES encryption, or LUKS, by writing a copy without it. Put only the passphrase in a file, with no newline at the end (use driver=qcow for a qcow version 1 image):

    printf '%s' 'kalipass' > passphrase.txt
qemu-img convert --object secret,id=sec0,file=passphrase.txt \
  --image-opts driver=qcow2,file.filename=kali.qc2,encrypt.key-secret=sec0 \
  -O qcow2 kali-plain.qc2

    Warning

    The old AES encryption doesn't check the passphrase, so a wrong passphrase, or a newline after it, gives you a copy full of random data. Examine the copy before you use it.

  • Back up and repair an image that qemu marked as corrupt or didn't close cleanly:

    cp kali.qc2 kali-backup.qc2
qemu-img check -r all kali.qc2

  • For an image that a newer qemu made and an older qemu can't open, write a copy with the newer qemu-img. The copy has no zstd compression, extended L2 entries, or external data file:

    qemu-img convert -O qcow2 -o compat=1.1 kali.qc2 kali-compat.qc2

docs.title: phēnix Cannot Reach minimega or Its Images
docs.text:
When minimega doesn't give its version on <base-dir.minimega>/minimega, phenix doctor names the likely cause: no socket (minimega isn't running, or base-dir.minimega names another directory), a stale socket file, or a user that isn't allowed to connect.

phēnix also needs to see minimega's -filepath directory to find the images minimega launches. In a container, mount that directory at the same path for both, as the Docker Compose setup does with /phenix.

docs.title: A Start Fails Because an Inject Source Does Not Exist
docs.text: minimega disk inject copies each injection source into the VM's snapshot, so a missing source fails the start with cp: cannot stat. phēnix looks for a relative source in the experiment's baseDir. Put the file there, or change the injection's src. In a container, mount the path at the same location for phēnix and minimega.

docs.title: Injects Fail With an nbd Error
docs.text:
To write injects (at a start, and for phenix image inject-miniexe), minimega disk inject connects the image to a /dev/nbdN device with qemu-nbd and mounts a partition. These errors come from that step:

Error Cause add module 'nbd' The nbd module isn't loaded, or it's part of the kernel. no available nbds found Each /dev/nbdN has a lock file in /var/lock or a process in /sys/block/nbdN/pid. no partitions found on image or desired partition N not found The nbd module has max_part set to 0, or the image has no such partition (see Injects Go to the Wrong Partition).

To fix them, as root:

  1. Load the module with partitions: modprobe nbd max_part=10. If it's already loaded with max_part=0, disconnect each device, then run modprobe -r nbd && modprobe nbd max_part=10.
  2. For a device a failed inject left behind, unmount its partition with umount <mount-point> (in <base-dir.minimega>, such as /tmp/minimega/dstImg123), then run qemu-nbd -d /dev/nbdN.
  3. Remove any lock file /var/lock/qemu-nbd-nbdN that no qemu-nbd uses.

If modprobe can't find the module after a kernel upgrade, reboot into the installed kernel. In a container, run it privileged with /dev from the host, as the Docker Compose setup does.

docs.title: Injects Go to the Wrong Partition
docs.text:
minimega disk inject writes the injects, and the startup app's scripts, into partition inject_partition of the VM's first drive (1 if unset), using the number Linux gives it: 1 to 4 for MBR primary, 5 and up for logical, the entry number for GPT. A wrong number fails the start:

Error Cause desired partition N not found The disk has no partition of that number. no partitions found on image The disk has no partition table or no partition 1, or the nbd module has max_part set to 0 (see Injects Fail With an nbd Error). A mount error, such as wrong fs type The partition is extended, or holds swap, an LVM physical volume or a LUKS volume. cp: cannot create regular file '/tmp/minimega/dstImg.../phenix/startup/20-startup.ps1': No such file or directory It isn't the system partition. On Windows, partition 1 is often System Reserved and C: is partition 2 (sandialabs/sceptre-phenix#166).

phenix doctor suggests a partition for each image, and the Disks page shows an image's partitions (see The Details Card). Set inject_partition on the VM's first drive to the partition that holds its system files:

inject into partition 2
spec:
  nodes:
    - type: VirtualMachine
      general:
        hostname: win-00
      hardware:
        os_type: windows
        drives:
          - image: win10.qc2
            inject_partition: 2

If the image has no partition that minimega can write to, such as an LVM image, set inject_partition: 0. The startup app then sends its scripts through miniccc (see C2 Startup Script Delivery), and phēnix injects no other files.

docs.title: Open vSwitch Does Not Answer
docs.text:
minimega uses ovs-vsctl to make the bridges and taps for VMs. Run phenix doctor as root, like minimega: it fails when ovs-vsctl isn't on PATH or ovsdb-server doesn't answer, and warns when ovs-vswitchd isn't running, which stops traffic on the bridges. On Debian or Ubuntu, install the openvswitch-switch package, then:

modprobe openvswitch
systemctl restart openvswitch-switch

Don't look for the experiment bridge (phenix by default) too early: minimega makes it when it launches the first VM on it.

docs.title: Low Disk Space and Leftovers of Deleted Experiments
docs.text:
phenix doctor warns when the filesystem of the images directory, minimega's -base or the minimega log has less than 10% or 5 GiB free, and names what phēnix and minimega left behind. Run phenix doctor -p -x on the head node as root, with the same store.endpoint as phenix ui, and work through its rows:

Row What to do leftovers snapshots rm <file> (no stored experiment uses it) leftovers files Copy out what you want to keep, such as captures, then rm -r <directory> leftovers mounts umount <path> leftovers taps ovs-vsctl del-port <bridge> <port>, then ip link delete <tap> leftovers mirrors ovs-vsctl -- --id=@m get mirror <mirror> -- remove bridge <bridge> mirrors @m disk-space inject dirs If no inject is running, unmount each mounted dstImg* directory, disconnect its nbd device, then rmdir <directory>

A large minimega log can fill the disk too. Rotate or delete it, for example with logrotate and its copytruncate option.

docs.title: A VM Does Not Start: Failed to get "write" lock
docs.text:
qemu locks each image it opens, so a VM won't start when another process holds its image or a backing file. phenix doctor names each qemu-system, qemu-nbd or qemu-img process that holds an image of a stopped experiment. Stop it with kill <pid>, or disconnect a qemu-nbd device with qemu-nbd -d /dev/nbdN.

A related trap: a VM with snapshot: false writes to its drive images. phenix doctor warns when such an image backs another image (the writes break it), or when more than one VM uses it. Set snapshot: true, or give each VM its own copy of the image, for example with qemu-img convert -O qcow2 <image> <copy>.

docs.title: Experiments Show as Running After minimega Restarts
docs.text:
When minimega restarts or stops, the store still marks its experiments as running. Reset the stored state, then start the experiment again:

phenix experiment stop my-exp
phenix experiment start my-exp

phenix doctor also names each minimega namespace with VMs that no stored experiment owns. Make sure it reads the store of phenix ui, then kill those VMs with minimega -e 'clear namespace <namespace>'.

docs.title: Apps or a SCORCH Run Stay Marked as Running
docs.text: If phenix ui stops in the middle of an app stage or a SCORCH run, the store keeps the app marked as running, so phēnix skips that app's running stage and SCORCH refuses a new run. Start or restart phenix ui to clear the marks of the running experiments (it also resumes their delayed VM starts). If phenix doctor names an interrupted start, stop the experiment with phenix experiment stop <experiment> and start it again.

docs.title: An Experiment Cannot Get Its VLANs
docs.text:
minimega refuses a VLAN alias for a VLAN that's in use, and stops when its VLAN range has no free VLAN. phenix doctor finds both before a start:

  • Two experiments pin the same VLAN ID: give one of them another ID with phenix vlan alias <experiment> <alias> <id> --force.
  • A stopped experiment's VLAN range has too few free VLANs, or overlaps another namespace's range: stop other experiments, or set a larger range with phenix vlan range <experiment> <min> <max> --force.

The VLANs page shows the same conflicts for the whole cluster.

docs.title: VMs on Different Nodes Cannot Reach Each Other
docs.text:
In a mesh of more than one node, each experiment bridge needs a trunk port or a tunnel to the other nodes. Add a trunk on each node, on the interface that connects the nodes (such as eth1):

minimega -e 'bridge trunk <bridge> <interface>'

Or set use-gre-mesh to true, and phēnix makes GRE tunnels between the nodes at each start (see GRE Mesh).

If phenix doctor names a VM scheduled on a node outside minimega's mesh, change the schedule with phenix experiment edit <experiment>, or connect the node to the mesh.

docs.title: minimega Runs Out of Open Files or Memory
docs.text:
minimega keeps about 5 files open for each VM, and each qemu gets minimega's limits. When phenix doctor warns that the soft limit of open files is too low, raise it, then restart minimega:

  • systemd: set LimitNOFILE=<n> in the [Service] section of the minimega unit.
  • Docker: add --ulimit nofile=<n>:<n> to docker run, or ulimits to the Compose service.

When phenix ui has more than 80% of its own limit open, raise it the same way and restart phenix ui. When the host is short of memory or swap, or the VMs ask for more memory than it has, stop VMs or give them less memory in their topologies.

docs.title: A VM Has No miniccc Client
docs.text:
phēnix needs a miniccc client in a VM when the startup app sends its scripts through miniccc, another VM waits for the client at the start, or the soh app checks the VM. If phenix doctor names a VM with no client or a client whose version differs from minimega's, copy the miniccc of the same minimega release into the image, and start it when the VM boots:

phenix image inject-miniexe <miniccc> <image>

docs.title: phenix image build Fails Before or in debootstrap
docs.text:
The build needs debootstrap, kpartx, losetup and qemu-img on PATH, loop devices it can use (and a free one), and the right to mount. Run it as root, or in a privileged container with /dev from the host.

debootstrap fails with No such script when it has no script for the release, and can't check the Release signature without the keyring the script names. Install the keyring package (debian-archive-keyring, ubuntu-keyring or kali-archive-keyring), and for a new release, a later debootstrap or a script in /usr/share/debootstrap/scripts. For Kali on a host that isn't Kali, see the Kali host setup in the phenix-image skill (skills/phenix-image/references/environment.md).

Each overlay directory of a stored image config must exist, because vmdb2 copies it into the image. Create the directory, or remove it from the config with phenix image remove <config> --overlays <path>.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Doctor: checks for many of these problems with one command.
  • Logging: where the logs are and how to read them.
  • Health Checks: check a running server.
  • Builder Troubleshooting: problems with the Builder.

docs.title: Tunneler
docs.text:
The phenix-tunneler is a small application that runs on a user's local machine to forward TCP traffic from VMs in a running experiment down to local ports. This lets a user interact with a VM directly using command line tools, instead of having to go through noVNC in a browser. A common example is using a real RDP client to connect to a Windows VM instead of interacting with it through noVNC (which enables things like copy/paste support that noVNC does not). For copy and paste in the web console, see Copy and Paste.

Traffic is proxied through the phēnix UI server over a WebSocket connection, so the local machine only needs network access to the phēnix UI.

docs.title: Downloading the Tunneler
docs.text:
Click the Tunneler button near the right-hand end of the banner at the top of the phēnix UI.

This page lists the phenix-tunneler builds on the phēnix server, with a Download link for each OS and architecture, and a Quick Start that sums up the steps below. phēnix ships these builds:

OS Architecture Linux amd64 macOS arm64 macOS amd64 Windows amd64

Download the binary that matches your local machine and make it executable (on Linux/macOS, chmod +x phenix-tunneler-<os>-<arch>).

Note

The Tunneler button, and its downloads, are only available if the phēnix server has been configured to serve tunneler binaries (a downloads/tunneler directory must exist in the directory the phēnix server runs from when it starts). This will be the case if you have a typical deployment using the Docker image.

docs.title: Starting the Tunneler Server
docs.text:
Once downloaded, start the tunneler's local proxy server with the serve subcommand, passing it the full URL to the phēnix UI:

phenix-tunneler serve https://phenix.example.com

If authentication is enabled in the phēnix UI, credentials must also be provided via one of the following flags:

  • --username (-u) -- the phēnix username to log in with. The tunneler will prompt for the corresponding password (input is hidden) and use it to log in to phēnix on your behalf.
  • --auth-token (-t) -- an existing phēnix API/JWT auth token, used in place of a username/password login. The username is parsed directly out of the token, so a separate --username isn't needed.
  • --use-cookie (-c) -- optional, only used alongside --auth-token. Sets the name of a cookie to send the auth token in, in addition to the X-Phenix-Auth-Token header, for phēnix deployments that expect the token as a cookie.
# log in interactively with a username/password
phenix-tunneler serve https://phenix.example.com --username jdoe

# use an existing auth token instead of logging in
phenix-tunneler serve https://phenix.example.com --auth-token <token>

The serve command keeps running in the foreground and needs to stay running for as long as forwarded ports should remain reachable locally. While it runs, it:

  • Connects to phēnix over a WebSocket and listens for port forward create/delete events happening across the phēnix UI.
  • Fetches the list of port forwards that already exist for the logged-in user and creates local listeners for each of them.
  • Automatically creates a new local listener any time the logged-in user creates a new port forward for a VM in the phēnix UI (see below).
  • Exposes a local Unix domain socket (at $TMPDIR/phenix/tunneler.sock) that the other phenix-tunneler subcommands (list, activate, deactivate, move) use to manage listeners while serve is running.

docs.title: Creating a Port Forward for a VM
docs.text:
With phenix-tunneler serve running locally, create a port forward for a VM from the phēnix UI:

  1. Open a running experiment and click on a VM's name in the VM table to open its details.
  2. Click the Port forward button under More actions, or the add link beside the Port forwards section. Either one requires the VM to be running with an active miniccc agent; the button's tooltip says so when it is not.
  3. Fill out the Create New Port Forward dialog:
    • Source Port -- the port to listen on locally.
    • Destination Host -- the host, reachable from the phēnix server, to forward traffic to (typically the VM's own IP address).
    • Destination Port -- the port on the destination host to forward traffic to (e.g., 3389 for RDP).
  4. Click Create.

If the port forward was created by the same user that's logged into the running phenix-tunneler serve process, the local listener is activated automatically -- no further action is needed. Port forwards created by other users show up too, but must be activated manually (see activate below) before they can be used locally.

Once a local port is listening, connect to it with whatever application is appropriate (an RDP client, a database client, ssh, etc.) and traffic will be forwarded through the phēnix UI server to the VM.

Existing port forwards for a VM are listed in the Port forwards section of the same VM details, each with the user that created it, and can be removed by clicking the trash icon next to a forward.

You can also manage port forwards from the phēnix server with phenix vm forward add, list and remove (this needs a running phenix ui). Forwards added this way are owned by global-admin, so other users have to activate them in their tunneler.

phenix vm forward add my-exp my-vm 80 --host 10.0.0.5 --source-port 8080
phenix vm forward list my-exp my-vm

docs.title: Managing Listeners from the Local Web App
docs.text: The serve command provides an option for also serving up a local web application for listing and managing listeners. It is disabled by default, and can be enabled with the --web-listen 127.0.0.1:8080 flag (the address or port can be changed if needed).

docs.title: Managing Listeners from the Command Line
docs.text: While phenix-tunneler serve is running, use the following subcommands (in another terminal) to inspect and manage local listeners.

docs.title: list
docs.text:
Show a table of all known port forwards, including their local port and whether or not they're currently listening (activated) locally.

phenix-tunneler list

docs.title: activate <id>
docs.text:
Start listening locally on the local port assigned to the given listener ID. Used to manually activate a port forward that wasn't created by the logged-in user (and therefore wasn't activated automatically).

phenix-tunneler activate <id>

docs.title: deactivate <id>
docs.text:
Stop listening locally for the given listener ID, without deleting the port forward itself.

phenix-tunneler deactivate <id>

docs.title: move <id> <port>
docs.text:
Move an existing listener to a different local port.

phenix-tunneler move <id> <port>

Listener IDs used by activate, deactivate, and move can be found in the output of phenix-tunneler list.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • phenix vm forward: manage port forwards from the phēnix server.

docs.title: User Authn/Authz in phenix
docs.text:
phenix provides three separate modes of user authentication (authn) and authorization (authz).

  • disabled
  • enabled
  • proxy

docs.title: disabled Mode
docs.text:
When in disabled mode, no user authentication or authorization occurs. Users do not have to authenticate, and all actions are allowed.

To use disabled mode, the UI should be built with VITE_AUTH=disabled (if Docker is being used to build the UI, use Docker build arg PHENIX_WEB_AUTH=disabled) and the UI server should be started without the -k/--jwt-signing-key option set.

docs.title: enabled Mode
docs.text:
When in enabled mode, user authentication and authorization occurs within phenix directly. Users have to authenticate to the phenix UI, and certain actions are prohibited based on the role assigned to the user.

To use enabled mode, the UI should be built with VITE_AUTH=enabled (if Docker is being used to build the UI, use Docker build arg PHENIX_WEB_AUTH=enabled) and the UI server should be started with the -k/--jwt-signing-key (and optionally the --jwt-lifetime) option set.

docs.title: proxy Mode
docs.text:
When in proxy mode, user authentication is expected to occur in a reverse proxy that sits in front of phenix but user authorization still occurs within phenix directly. Users authenticate to the proxy, and certain actions are prohibited based on the role assigned to the user.

To use proxy mode, the UI should be built with VITE_AUTH=proxy (if Docker is being used to build the UI, use Docker build arg PHENIX_WEB_AUTH=proxy) and the UI server should be started with the -k/--jwt-signing-key and --proxy-auth-header (and optionally the --jwt-lifetime) options set.

In addition, the reverse proxy should add a header to requests being proxied that contains the username of the authenticated user, with the name of the header matching what --proxy-auth-header is set to (for example, --proxy-auth-header=X-phenix-user).

If a user is able to authenticate to the proxy but is not yet a user in phenix, the UI shows them a sign-up page with their username. After they submit it, they are added as a phenix user and assigned the Disabled role that will deny all actions until an admin user can assign them a different role.

docs.title: Create a new user
docs.text:
There are three primary ways to create new users. A username must start with a letter or digit and contain only letters, digits, ., _, @, + and -. phenix refuses other usernames and stores no user.

  1. Choose the Create Account link off the login page and complete all fields in the Create a New Account dialogue. This will initiate a message to an administrator's account who can then activate the account, setting the role(s) and resource name(s).

  2. From the Users page in the Admin menu, click the + button to create a new user. Here the administrator will add the role(s) and resource name(s). phenix refuses a username that is already taken or a role that does not exist, and stores no user.

  3. Create a YAML or JSON file at /etc/phenix/users.[yml|json] with the following structure. When the phenix UI starts, it looks for this file and adds any users present in the file that are not already present in phenix. For users in the file that already exist, phenix ensures the user role matches what's in the file and updates it as necessary. This file is also automatically watched, so any users added to the file while phenix is running will automatically be added to phenix. An entry may end with resource names that scope the role, each after its own :. phenix skips and logs an entry whose role does not exist, and stores no user for it.

ui:
  users:
    - <username>:<password>:<role-name>[:<resource-name>...]
    - ...

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
The login page is self-descriptive. Using the Remember me checkbox will set a token to local storage so that you can remove the requirement to enter a Username and Password each time the page or site is reloaded.

If an administrator starts the UI server with the following command, authentication is enabled:

phenix ui -k <some_string>

Without the -k (or --jwt-signing-key), authentication is disabled.

docs.title: Generating User Authentication Tokens
docs.text:
From the Users page in the Admin menu, click the key icon next to the given user's name. The icon shows for your own user, and for another user only when your role has users/tokens create on them. A dialog box will pop up where you can enter in a description for the token to be created and an expiration date. This expiration date should be entered in Golang time duration. For example, 4320h is valid and represents 4320 hours or about 6 months. After clicking Create Token a token should appear with the expiration date.

This token can be used to authenticate when using the Phenix API. Specifically, you would include the following as a header in HTTP requests.

X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer ******

On the phēnix server itself, phenix admin token create prints a token for a user, signed by the running phenix ui. --lifetime takes a duration such as 12h, or a whole number of days.

TOKEN=$(phenix admin token create ci-bot --lifetime 30 --description "CI runner")

docs.title: User Administration
docs.text: The Users link in the Admin menu shows for a role with users list, or with users get on your own user, which then lists only you.

docs.title: Updating Users
docs.text: An administrator is able to click on the username on the table on the Users page to update a user. They can update First Name or Last Name, Role, Experiment Names, and Resource Name(s).

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Global Admin is the administrator level account and has access to all capabilities, to include user management. Global Admins also have access to all resources. The following table provides a high-level overview of all the available roles and their access rights.

Role Limits List Get Create Update Patch Delete Global Admin Can see and control absolutely anything/everything. E V U E V U E V U E V U E V U E V U Global Viewer Can see absolutely anything/everything, but cannot make any changes. E V U E V U Experiment Admin Can see and control anything/everything for assigned experiments, including VMs, but cannot create new experiments. E V E V V E V V E* V Experiment User Can see assigned experiments, and can control VMs within assigned experiments, but cannot modify experiments themselves. E V E V V Experiment Viewer Can see assigned experiments and VMs within assigned experiments, but cannot modify or control experiments or VMs. E V E V VM Admin Can see assigned experiments, and has full administrative control over VMs in assigned experiments. E V E V V V V V VM Viewer Can only see VM screenshots and access VM VNC, nothing else. V

Key: E - experiment resource, V - VM resource, U - user resource

E* in the Experiment Admin row means the role can delete an experiment's files, but not the experiment itself.

The built-in Builder role is for users of the Builder. It holds builder use, which gives access to the Builder and all its drafts, templates, layer sets and icons. It can also list, get, create, update and delete Topology, Scenario and Experiment configs, and can list, get, create and update experiments. Global Viewer does not have builder use. See the policies in Builder (builder) and The Builder role.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
On the phēnix server, the phenix admin commands manage users, custom roles and API tokens. The commands that change something go through the running phenix ui, as global-admin.

# Create a user (it asks for the password twice)
phenix admin user create alice --role experiment-user --resource-names 'lab-*'

# Create a custom role
phenix admin role create "Lab Viewer" --policy 'resources=experiments,vms;verbs=list,get;names=lab-*'

Use --password-stdin to pipe the password in instead.

docs.title: Manage Custom Roles Through the API
docs.text:
A Global Admin can create, update and delete custom roles through the REST API (the roles resource); the built-in roles can't be changed or deleted. You can only hand out what you hold: the caller must hold each permission that the role gives, and a policy without resource names counts as a policy for *.

To create a role, send POST /api/v1/roles with its name and policies:

{
  "name": "Lab Operator",
  "metadataName": "lab-operator",
  "policies": [
    {"resources": ["experiments"], "verbs": ["list", "get"]},
    {"resources": ["vms", "vms/*"], "verbs": ["list", "get", "update"]}
  ]
}

metadataName is optional. Without it, the config name is the name in lower case with other characters changed to -. Neither name can match another role's, ignoring case. A role can have up to 256 policies, and a policy up to 64 resources, 64 verbs and 64 resource names.

To give the role to a user, send PATCH /api/v1/users/{username} with role_name and resource_names. You must hold each permission that the role gives with those resource names; permissions the user already holds don't count.

PATCH /api/v1/roles/{name} replaces the policies of the role, and of each user's copy of it, with the complete new list (a role can't be renamed). Each user keeps the resource names they got with the role. If the old role had no policy without resource names, though, the new policies without resource names give the user no named resource: give the role to the user again to set the names. If some users can't be updated, the response is 500 with them in details.users; send the same request again.

DELETE /api/v1/roles/{name} refuses a role that a user has (give them a different role first), or one that a default user in ui.users or the development key in ui.jwt-signing-key names.

docs.text:

Verb list Desc get list of disk images Exp. Scoped no (listing one experiment's images also needs get on that experiment) Res. Scoped yes (list is filtered to only include images in scope; an image outside the minimega files directory also needs get on an experiment using it, unless it backs a listed image) Verb get Desc download a disk image Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped yes Verb create Desc snapshot or clone a disk image Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped yes (the new image's file name; the image copied also needs get) Verb update Desc commit, rebase, resize, or rename a disk image Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped yes (commit also needs it for the backing image) Verb delete Desc delete a disk image Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped yes Verb upload Desc upload a disk image Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped no

docs.title: Resource: vlans
docs.text:
A vlans resource name is an experiment name. The blacklist and the minimega namespaces that no experiment owns need the resource name *. See VLANs.

Verb list Desc get the VLAN IDs of the cluster, find free IDs, and check proposed IDs (with *, also the blacklist and the unowned namespaces) Exp. Scoped yes (list is filtered to only include experiments in scope) Res. Scoped no Verb get Desc get one VLAN ID with its VMs, or the VLANs of a specific experiment Exp. Scoped yes Res. Scoped no

A change to the VLAN pins or the range of an experiment needs experiments patch on that experiment.

docs.title: Resource: vlans/blacklist
docs.text:
Verb create, delete Desc add a VLAN ID to, or remove one from, the minimega VLAN blacklist (needs the resource name *) Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped no

By default only Global Admin has this permission.

docs.text:

docs.text: Verb list Desc get list of users Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped yes (list is filtered to only include users in scope) Verb get Desc get a specific user Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped yes Verb create Desc create a new user Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped no Verb patch Desc update an existing user Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped yes Verb delete Desc delete an existing user Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped yes
