docs.text:
Verb create Desc create an API token for another user (also needs users patch on them) Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped yes

By default only Global Admin has this permission. A user with users patch on themselves creates their own tokens without it.

docs.title: Resource: users/roles
docs.text: Verb patch Desc update user role assignments Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped yes

docs.title: Resource: roles
docs.text:
Verb list Desc get list of roles (GET /roles) Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped no Verb get Desc get a specific role by its config name or display name (GET /roles/{name}) Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped yes (the name in the request)

Add ?permissions=true to either request to also get the permissions each role gives. list also allows GET /permissions, which lists every resource and its verbs, like phenix util role-table.

Verb create Desc create a new custom role (POST /roles) Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped no Verb patch Desc update the policies of a custom role, and of the users that have it (PATCH /roles/{name}) Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped yes (the name in the request) Verb delete Desc delete a custom role that no user has (DELETE /roles/{name}) Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped yes (the name in the request)

Only the built-in Global Admin role has create, patch and delete on roles; a custom role can't get them.

docs.title: Resource: configs
docs.text:
Verb list, get, create, update, delete Desc manage store configurations (topologies, scenarios, etc.) Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped yes

Resource names are <Kind>/<name>, such as Topology/riverside-water, not the name alone. Topology/* covers every topology, and */* covers every config, User and Role configs included (a * never crosses the /). phēnix also checks create and update against the kind and name of the config in the request body. So a role scoped to Topology/* cannot create or overwrite a User or Role config. An update that renames a config or changes its kind also needs create for the new Kind/name.

The configs API never returns a User config's password hash or API tokens, and an update keeps the stored ones.

docs.title: Resource: builder
docs.text: Verb use Desc use the Builder: read and change every Builder draft, template, layer set and icon (see Builder permissions) Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped no

docs.title: Resource: settings
docs.text: Verb update Desc update phēnix system settings Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped no

docs.title: Resource: runtimeSettings
docs.text:
Verb read, update Desc read and change the runtime settings of phenix ui (/runtimeSettings), as phenix settings does Exp. Scoped no Res. Scoped no

By default only Global Admin has this permission.

docs.title: Resource: minimega/commands

By default only Global Admin has this permission.

docs.title: Resource: vms/mount

docs.title: Resource: vms/forwards

docs.title: Built-In Roles
docs.text: The following default roles are defined in phēnix as YAML resource specifications:

docs.title: Global Admin (global-admin)
docs.text:
apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: global-admin
spec:
  roleName: Global Admin
  policies:
  - resources:
    - "*"
    - "*/*"
    resourceNames:
    - "*"
    - "*/*"
    verbs:
    - "*"

docs.title: Global Viewer (global-viewer)
docs.text:
apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: global-viewer
spec:
  roleName: Global Viewer
  policies:
  - resources:
    - "*"
    - "*/*"
    resourceNames:
    - "*"
    - "*/*"
    verbs:
    - list
    - get
  - resources:
    - "vms/mount"
    resourceNames:
    - "*"
    - "*/*"
    verbs:
    - post
    - delete

docs.title: Builder (builder)
docs.text:
phenix creates this role at start if the store does not have it. If a stored builder role does not have the builder use policy, phenix adds it (see The Builder role).

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: builder
spec:
  roleName: Builder
  policies:
  # Only the config kinds the Builder reads and publishes: User and Role
  # configs hold accounts and permissions.
  - resources:
    - configs
    resourceNames:
    - "Topology/*"
    - "Scenario/*"
    - "Experiment/*"
    verbs:
    - list
    - get
    - create
    - update
    - delete
  # Read and change every draft, template, icon and layer set.
  - resources:
    - builder
    verbs:
    - use

docs.title: VLANs
docs.text:
The VLANs page (in the Resources menu) shows every VLAN ID in use in the cluster: which experiment and alias use it, and whether phēnix and minimega agree. You can also pin IDs, set ranges, edit the minimega blacklist, and release IDs that no experiment owns.

All experiments on the phēnix bridge share one pool of IDs, 1 to 4094, and they stay apart only because their IDs are different. This page shows you a clash between two experiments before the second one fails to start.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: A role scoped to some experiments sees only the IDs of those experiments. The blacklist and the namespaces that no experiment owns show only to roles with the resource name * (see Resource: vlans). When an issue involves an experiment you can't see, the page calls it another experiment.

docs.title: What the Page Shows
docs.text:
The page merges two sources:

  • phēnix has, for each experiment, running or stopped, the pinned ID of each alias (spec.vlans.aliases), the range (spec.vlans.min and spec.vlans.max), and the aliases its topology uses.
  • minimega has the ID it gave each alias in each namespace, and the cluster's blacklist.

When the two disagree, the alias shows both, phēnix first: 104 → 110. The sources are only compared for running experiments, since a stopped experiment has no minimega namespace. If phēnix can't read minimega, the page shows only the experiment specs.

An ID can be pinned (the experiment spec sets it), allocated (minimega gave it to an alias in a running namespace), blacklisted (minimega gives it to no alias), or more than one of these at once. An ID with none of these is free.

docs.title: Issues
docs.text:
Click Show issues only, or the Issues total, to see only the cards with an issue.

Kind Severity Means duplicate-pin conflict Two owners pin or use the same ID, and at least one of them pins it. pin-blacklisted conflict A pin uses an ID on the minimega blacklist. unowned conflict A minimega namespace holds IDs, but no phēnix experiment has that name. id-differs difference A running experiment pins one ID for an alias, but minimega gave the alias a different ID. minimega-only difference minimega has an alias of a running experiment that the spec does not have. range-overlap warning The ranges of two experiments overlap. It's a problem only when they run at the same time. out-of-range warning A pin is outside the range of its experiment.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
The page has three views:

  • By experiment (the default) has a card for each experiment and for each minimega namespace that no experiment owns. A card shows the experiment's status, a bar of the ID space with its range and IDs, and each alias with its IDs and issues.
  • ID space (/vlans?view=grid) shows every ID from 0 to 4095 as a cell in a 64 × 64 grid, colored by state. Drag across the grid, or Shift+click, to see a summary of a range of IDs.
  • Blacklist (/vlans?view=blacklist) lists each ID on the minimega blacklist.

docs.title: Details Panel
docs.text: Click any ID, on a card or in the grid, to open its details: each experiment that pins it, each minimega namespace that uses it, whether it's blacklisted, which experiment ranges hold it, the VMs on it (with their interface and host), and its issues. From there you can jump to the experiment's card, its VMs, its State of Health group, or its Netflow tab, or start a packet capture (Capture…) on every interface on that VLAN of a running experiment.

docs.title: Filters, Search and Links
docs.text: The search box matches an ID that a card holds or ranges over, or part of an experiment or alias name. The page keeps its state in the URL, so you can share a link to exactly what you're looking at. For example, /vlans?experiment=substation-a shows only that experiment's card, /vlans?vlan=102 opens the details of ID 102, and ?filter=issues and ?q=MGMT apply a filter and a search.

docs.title: Fixing a Conflict
docs.text:
If an experiment fails to start because minimega gave one of its pinned IDs to another alias, the error message has a Show the conflict link that opens this page on that ID (see VLAN In Use at a Start).

The cards and the details panel offer quick fixes for an issue, such as Change <alias> to <id>…, which opens the ID dialog with a free ID filled in, or Suggest a range… for a range that overlaps another.

Note

You can only change the pins or the range of a stopped experiment. Pin live IDs… is the only change you can make to a running one.

docs.title: Pinning and Unpinning IDs
docs.text:
Click Edit IDs… on an experiment's card. Type an ID from 1 to 4094 for each alias you want to pin, or 0 to unpin it. An alias with no pin gets its ID from minimega when the experiment starts. A pin outside the experiment's range is refused.

# Pin the EXP alias of my-exp to VLAN 101
phenix vlan alias my-exp EXP 101

# Unpin it
phenix vlan alias my-exp EXP --unpin

docs.title: Setting a Range
docs.text:
minimega gives an experiment's aliases IDs from its range. Click Set range… and fill in Minimum and Maximum, or click Suggest a free range to fill in the first free block outside all ranges, with one ID for each alias. Clear the range removes it. A range must hold every pin of the experiment, and a range that overlaps another experiment's range is a warning.

phenix vlan range my-exp 150 199
phenix vlan range my-exp --clear

docs.title: Pinning the Live IDs
docs.text:
When minimega gave an alias of a running experiment an ID that the spec does not pin, Pin live IDs… copies the IDs from minimega into the spec, so the next start gets the same IDs. An ID outside the experiment's range is refused.

phenix vlan pin-live my-exp

docs.title: Changing the Blacklist
docs.text:
minimega gives a blacklisted ID to no alias, which is handy for an ID that a hardware switch uses. Use Add an ID… on the Blacklist card or Add to the blacklist… in the details panel. You can't blacklist an ID that a minimega namespace already gave to an alias.

phenix vlan blacklist add 100
phenix vlan blacklist remove 100

Warning

Removing an ID from the blacklist needs a minimega that has the clear vlans blacklist <vlan> command (see sandia-minimega/minimega#1688). With an older minimega the remove buttons are disabled, so phēnix can't undo an addition. minimega also refuses to remove an ID that a VM uses.

docs.title: Releasing Unowned IDs
docs.text:
A minimega namespace can keep its IDs after its experiment is gone. Click Release <n> IDs… on its card to clear its aliases in minimega, so the IDs can go to other experiments. phēnix refuses to release a namespace that an experiment has, or whose VMs use its IDs.

phenix vlan release old-demo

docs.title: Find Free IDs
docs.text:
To find a block of free IDs:

  1. Click Find free IDs.
  2. Type how many IDs in a row you need. The default is 16.
  3. Select Any free, or Outside all ranges.
  4. Click Find <n> free IDs.

A free ID is one that no experiment in the cluster pins, no minimega namespace uses, and minimega does not blacklist. If the block is in an experiment's range, use it only for that experiment, or select Outside all ranges. To make the block the range of a stopped experiment, select the experiment, then click Set as the range of <experiment>….

phenix vlan free --count 16 --outside-ranges

docs.title: Conflict Check Before a Save
docs.text:
phēnix checks an experiment's VLAN IDs against the cluster before each of these saves:

  • Save VLAN IDs in the VLAN IDs menu of a stopped experiment (see VLAN Aliases)
  • a save of an Experiment config in the config editor
  • Save in the ID and range dialogs of this page

If it finds issues, the VLAN Conflicts dialog lists them. Click Save anyway to save, or Cancel to keep the old IDs. If the check can't run, the save goes ahead, and phēnix checks the IDs again when the experiment starts. A new pin from the ID dialog is the exception: when minimega does not answer, phēnix refuses it. To save such a pin anyway, use phenix vlan alias --force or ?force=true on the API.

To run the same check from the command line without saving anything:

phenix vlan check my-exp --alias EXP_1=101 --alias EXP_2=102
phenix vlan check my-exp --range 100-199

docs.title: Export
docs.text: Click Export, then CSV or JSON, to save the rows of the cards that the filters and search show. vlans.csv has one row for each ID of each owner, plus a row with an empty id for each alias that has no pin and no live ID. vlans.json has the same structure as the GET /api/v1/vlans response.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
The phenix vlan commands give the same data and make the same changes (see phenix vlan). The ones not shown above:

# List every VLAN ID in the cluster, with a second table of issues
phenix vlan list

# Only the rows of one experiment, or only the rows with an issue
phenix vlan list --experiment substation-a
phenix vlan list --issues

# The CSV file of the Export button
phenix vlan list -o csv > vlans.csv

# List the blacklist
phenix vlan blacklist

phenix vlan alias and phenix vlan range run the same checks as the page, and --force saves the change anyway. --dry-run checks a removal (an unpin, range --clear, release or blacklist remove) without making it.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
The /api/v1/vlans and /api/v1/experiments/{name}/vlans endpoints do the same as the page and the commands. For example, GET /api/v1/vlans?issues=true lists only the rows with an issue. The API docs list each endpoint, parameter and status under the VLANs tag.

Add ?force=true to save a pin or range change that has a conflict, or a pin when minimega does not answer.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Bridge Mode: one bridge per experiment.
  • GRE Mesh: carry VLANs between cluster hosts over GRE tunnels.
  • Troubleshooting: when an experiment cannot get its VLANs.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
The experiment must be started; click on the experiment name to enter the Running Experiment component. Within that component, click on the checkbox in the header of the first column, to the left of the Node column, to select all the VMs; its tooltip reads Select/Unselect All. Alternatively, the checkbox at the start of a VM's row can be used to select the VM. Once one or more VMs are selected, a toolbar will appear to the left of the Hosts and Labels filters, before the search text box.

Every button on the toolbar acts on all of the selected VMs at once. A button is grayed out if your role does not allow its action on every one of them. Its tooltip then names the permission, for example Your role does not permit this action (vms delete). The buttons, named by their tooltips, are:

  • start - starts the selected VMs, and resumes the paused ones
  • pause - pauses the selected VMs
  • create memory snapshot - dumps each VM's memory to the file named for it in the dialog
  • create backing image - creates a new backing image from each VM's disk
  • create VM snapshot - saves each VM's disk and memory as a snapshot
  • modify state - replaces these buttons with the modify state toolbar described below

A button skips the selected VMs its action cannot be applied to, by the same rules that disable the action in a VM's details card (see VMs). For example, start skips VMs that are already running, and every button skips a VM that is busy with another action. One dialog asks before anything happens. It lists the VMs the action will act on, and names the skipped VMs with the reason, such as The VMs web and db are not running.

start, pause, restart, shutdown, kill and reset disk state run as one background job for all the VMs, which the jobs menu shows and can cancel. The page stays usable while the job runs. When it ends, one message sums up the outcome, names the VMs that failed or were skipped, and offers Retry failed for the VMs that may work if tried again.

docs.title: Modify State Toolbar
docs.text:
The modify state button replaces the toolbar with the actions that change a VM's state. These buttons, again named by their tooltips, are:

  • redeploy - sets CPUs, Memory, Disk and Replicate Original Injection(s) for each VM, then kills and deploys it again
  • reset disk state - resets each selected VM's disk to how it was when the experiment started
  • restart - restarts the selected VMs that are running
  • shutdown - powers off the selected VMs that are running
  • kill - kills the selected VMs and removes them from the running experiment
  • close toolbar - returns to the toolbar above

Per-VM actions, including the ones this toolbar has no equivalent for, are described in VMs.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
Several phenix vm commands support selecting target VMs by label with -l / --label, or all VMs using all. When using labels, a VM name argument is not required.

Supported commands:

  • phenix vm info
  • phenix vm pause
  • phenix vm resume
  • phenix vm restart
  • phenix vm reset-disk
  • phenix vm redeploy
  • phenix vm shutdown
  • phenix vm kill

Behavior:

  • Multiple labels are supported and use OR semantics (a VM is selected if any label matches).
  • Labels support glob patterns (for example, ot-* or *-server).
  • The special label all selects every VM in the experiment.
  • Labels can be provided by repeating -l and/or as a comma-separated value.

Examples:

# Show VM info for all VMs with a label matching "ot-*"
phenix vm info <experiment-name> --label ot-*

# Restart VMs that match either label
phenix vm restart <experiment-name> -l control -l historian

# Pause VMs using comma-separated labels
phenix vm pause <experiment-name> -l control,historian

# Shutdown all VMs in the experiment
phenix vm shutdown <experiment-name> --label all

docs.title: API
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/experiments/<name>/vms/actions runs one power action (start, pause, restart, shutdown, kill or resetDisk) on several VMs as a background job:

curl -X POST -H "X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"action": "restart", "vms": ["web", "db", "fw"]}' \
  http://localhost:3000/api/v1/experiments/exp1/vms/actions

The job records each VM's outcome. A VM your role may not act on is skipped, and a VM busy with another action fails and is marked retryable. PATCH /api/v1/experiments/<name>/vms changes the settings of several VMs at once in the same way. See the API documentation for both.

docs.title: Searching for VMs
docs.text: The search text box can be used to filter the list of VMs to only apply actions to the filtered list.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
The experiment must be started; click on the experiment name to enter the Running Experiment component. Within that component, use the search textbox to find VMs by:

  • state - The keywords running,shutdown,paused,capturing can be used to find VMs in a specific state. Also, the not keyword can be used to negate search term(s) (i.e. not running)

  • ipv4 address - VMs in a specific subnet can be found by entering the subnet (i.e 192.168.1.0/30). An address with no mask (i.e. 192.168.1.5) finds the VMs that have that address.

  • other fields (i.e. name, network, host, disk, tags) - All other fields will be searched for a keyword contained within the field

  • combine search terms - Search terms can be combined by using or and keywords. Parenthesis can also be used to group search terms. Two terms with no keyword between them use and. The search applies not first, then and, then or. For example, web db or ot is the same as (web and db) or ot.

  • escape keywords - To find keywords that appear in a VM name use double quotes. For example, to find a VM named free_running, type "running". A quoted term can contain spaces. For example, "web server" finds a VM named my web server, but not a VM named web-server.

A search that the Web-UI cannot parse finds no VMs. For example, (web, web and, and "web find no VMs.

The Hosts and Labels filters beside the search box narrow the list further; see Filtering and Sorting the VM Table.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Multiple search terms

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
While the interactive search bar is specific to the Web-UI, you can view and list all VMs in an experiment (or filter for specific VMs by name or label) using the phenix vm info command:

# List details for all VMs in an experiment
phenix vm info <experiment-name>

# Display details for a specific VM in an experiment
phenix vm info <experiment-name> <vm-name>

# Filter VMs by label
phenix vm info <experiment-name> --label <label>

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
In the VM table, click a network in the Network column to open its menu. The menu has these capture items:

  • Start capture on this interface or Stop capture on this interface starts or stops the capture on that interface.
  • Start interface captures on VLAN <alias> starts a capture on each interface on that VLAN.
  • Stop interface captures on VLAN <alias> stops the captures on that VLAN. The menu shows this item only when an interface on that VLAN has a capture.
  • Capture VLAN <alias>… opens the dialog of an experiment capture of that VLAN. An experiment capture records the VLAN on all hosts into one file. See Experiment Packet Captures. When the server does not report capture support, the item is disabled and shows the reason.
  • Show capture files in the Files tab opens the Files tab with a search for the capture files of that interface.
  • Open live capture in WebShark opens the capture of that interface on the WebShark page. The menu shows this item only when the interface has a capture and the server has WebShark.

The VM must be running to start or stop a capture from the menu.

Start capture on this interface and Start interface captures on VLAN <alias> open a dialog. Select the Format, pcapng or pcap, and click Start. The capture file name ends in .pcapng or .pcap to match the format. When the server does not report capture support, the items start the captures at once in pcap format.

The menu also has these items:

  • Change VLAN… moves the interface to another VLAN.
  • Disconnect disconnects the interface from its VLAN. A dialog asks you to confirm.
  • Set link quality… opens a dialog that shapes the traffic that the VM receives on the interface. Enter a loss in percent (less than 100), a delay in us, ms, or s (such as 100ms), or a rate of 1 to 999999999 kbit, mbit, or gbit. You cannot set a rate with a loss or a delay. Clear removes the link quality from the interface. The command line equivalent is phenix vm qos (see Link Quality).
  • Show VMs on VLAN <alias> shows only the VMs on that VLAN. It puts the network name and its VLAN ID in the search box, for example "exp_1 (101)".

The VM must be running to use Change VLAN…, Disconnect, or Set link quality…. If you cannot use an item of the menu, the network shows as text. A VLAN request shows one message for all of its captures.

The Web-UI has no single control for a subnet's captures. Enter the subnet in the search box, such as 10.1.2.0/29, to list the VMs in it. Then click an address in a VM's IP column, or a tap in its Taps column, to start a capture on that interface (see Packet Capture).

The Capture all interfaces button in a VM's Actions column starts a capture on every connected interface of that VM. While the VM is capturing, the button becomes Stop all packet captures, which stops them all (see Capture All Interfaces).

To find every VM with a running packet capture, enter capturing in the search box.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To start packet captures on running VMs for a specific subnet, use the following command.

phenix vm capture start-subnet <experiment-name> <subnet>

To stop all packet captures for a specific subnet, use the following command.

phenix vm capture stop-subnet <experiment-name> <subnet>

To start packet captures on each interface on a VLAN of the running VMs, use the following command. Give the VLAN alias, such as EXP_1.

phenix vm capture start-vlan <experiment-name> <vlan-alias>

To stop the packet captures on the interfaces on a VLAN, use the following command. The captures on other interfaces continue.

phenix vm capture stop-vlan <experiment-name> <vlan-alias>

The --filter flag of these four commands limits them to the VMs that the filter matches. The filter has the syntax of the VM search box (see Searching for VMs), such as running and web. It is not a minimega filter.

The --format flag of start-subnet and start-vlan sets the capture file format, pcapng (the default) or pcap.

To stop all packet captures for an experiment, use the following command.

phenix vm capture stop-all <experiment-name>

docs.title: Stopped Experiment
docs.text:
Similar to the Running Experiment component, multiple VMs can be selected for the Stopped Experiment component. Its toolbar shows how many VMs you selected and has these buttons, named by their tooltips:

  • set to boot and set to not boot clear or set the do not boot flag.
  • make the disks persistent and make the disks non-persistent clear or set the snapshot flag.
  • reset settings to the topology values sets the host, CPUs, memory, disk, inject partition, persistence, and do not boot flag of each VM back to the values of the topology. The toolbar shows this button only when a selected VM has these values. The reset skips each selected VM that does not have these values or that already uses them.

Each button changes every selected VM. While the server works, the button spins and the toolbar tells what it does. Then a message tells how many VMs changed. A message about VMs that failed has a Retry failed button.

The Hosts and Labels buttons show only the VMs that are assigned to the hosts you check, or that have the labels you check. In addition, VMs in the Stopped Experiment component can be searched by:

  • state - The keyword dnb can be used to find all VMs with the do not boot flag set to true. Also, the not keyword can be used to negate search term(s) (i.e. not dnb)

  • ipv4 address - VMs in a specific subnet can be found by entering the subnet (i.e 192.168.1.0/30). An address with no mask (i.e. 192.168.1.5) finds the VMs that have that address.

  • other fields (i.e. VM, host, disk)

  • combine search terms - Search terms can be combined by using or and keywords. Parenthesis can also be used to group search terms. The rules are the same as in the Running Experiment component: two terms with no keyword between them use and, and the search applies not first, then and, then or.

  • escape keywords - To find keywords that appear in a VM name use double quotes. For example, to find a VM named dnb_me, type "dnb". A quoted term can contain spaces. For example, "web server" finds a VM named my web server.

A search that the Web-UI cannot parse finds no VMs.

docs.text:

  • phenix vm: the VM commands of the command line.

docs.title: VMs
docs.text: How to use and interact with VMs, from either the command line or Web UI.

docs.title: Filtering and Sorting the VM Table
docs.text:
On the running experiment's VMs tab, the Hosts, Labels and Paginate controls sit to the left of the Find a VM search box.

  • Hosts lists every cluster host running one of the experiment's VMs. Check hosts to list only the VMs running on any of them.
  • Labels lists every key=value label on the experiment's VMs. Check labels to list only the VMs that carry any of them.

Each button shows how many items are checked, and Clear hosts or Clear labels unchecks them all. The filters combine with each other and with the search box: a VM must match all of them.

docs.title: VM Actions Column
docs.text: The running experiment's VM table has an Actions column of icon buttons that act on that row's VM without opening its details card. The buttons work as they do on the VM details card.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: To open the details card for a VM, click on the VM's name from the VM table for an experiment. You can also navigate directly to the URL: /experiment/<exp>?vm=<vm>

docs.title: VM Details Card
docs.text:
The VM details card has the following:

  • the VM name and a state tag: Running, Paused, Shut down, Building, Delayed start, Error, Busy or Not booted
  • OS icon (based on hardware.os_type).
  • a do not boot tag, when the VM is flagged not to boot
  • the host the VM runs on and how long it has been up, or starts after <delay> for a VM with a delayed start
  • the VM's description from the topology, if it has one
  • Shortcut buttons for State of Health, SCORCH page, and the docs you're reading now.
  • Live, view-only console of the VM (see The Details Window). Click the screen or Open console to open the console page in a new browser tab. Clicking on Take control will enable direct interaction without opening a new tab!
  • miniccc state, vCPUs and memory, and interface count.
  • Power buttons: Start, Pause, Restart, Shut down, and Kill. Each power action runs as a background job.
  • Storage: the disk image, the backing image chain, a CD-ROM if one is inserted, and a link to the Disks page.
  • Network: interface ID, name, VLAN, IP, host interface, and a shark button to start a packet capture. There are also buttons on the top right to start and stop captures for all interfaces on the VM. See Packet Capture and Capture All Interfaces.
  • Labels: lists the VM's labels, and view/edit opens the label editor.
  • Snapshots: lists the VM's snapshots, with buttons to restore or delete individual snapshots.
  • Port Forwards: lists port forwards, with ability to delete forwards, and a add button to open the menu to create a new one.
  • Annotations: view and edit a VM's node annotations (see Adding Annotations). Changes are saved to the experiment, not to the Topology config. Changes only take effect when the experiment is restarted or an app that reads that annotation is triggered.
  • More actions, under the screenshot, holds everything else (see More Actions below).

docs.title: More Actions
docs.text:
Button What it does Redeploy Kill the VM and deploy it again, optionally with new CPUs, memory or disk Reset disk Reset the VM's disk to how it was when the experiment started, discarding changes Snapshot Save the VM's current disk and memory as a snapshot that can be restored later Screenshot Save a full-size PNG of the VM's screen in the experiment files, in the screenshots folder Backing image Create a new backing image from the current VM disk Memory snapshot Save a dump of the VM's memory for forensics tools such as Volatility Port forward Forward a port to a port on the VM through its miniccc agent Insert CD-ROM Insert an ISO image into the VM's CD-ROM drive. Reads Change CD-ROM when one is inserted Mount disk Mount the VM's filesystem to browse, upload and download files

Reset disk and Snapshot ask you to confirm first. Screenshot saves the image at once (see Save a VM Screenshot), and the other buttons open a dialog.

Note

Mount disk appears only when the vm-mount feature is enabled (see Mount a VM).

An action that the VM's state rules out or your role cannot do is grayed out, with the reason in its hover tooltip.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
There are two options for displaying the information for VMs in an experiment. First run the following command to see information for all VMs in a given experiment.

phenix vm info <experiment-name>

Or, run the following to see the information for a specific VM in an experiment.

phenix vm info <experiment-name> [vm name] [--label <label>] [--host <host>]

--host lists only the VMs running on specific cluster host(s). Press Tab after --host to complete host names.

phenix vm info my-exp --host compute1 --host compute2
phenix vm info my-exp --host compute1 --label role-web

-o json and -o yaml print the results from the API (GET /api/v1/experiments/{exp}/vms) in JSON or YAML format. These can be combined with --label and --host.

phenix vm info my-exp -o json
phenix vm info my-exp -o yaml

# Single VM
phenix vm info my-exp my-vm -o json

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
Click on the name of a running VM in a started experiment to open its details card, then click Backing image in More actions. The same action is in the VM table's Actions column. The VM must be running and have snapshots enabled.

phēnix shuts down the VM while it makes the image, and then starts the VM again. It also starts the VM again if the operation fails.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To create a backing image from the first disk of a running VM, run the following command.

phenix vm commit <experiment-name> <vm-name> [image name]

The image name must be a bare file name, with no folder and must not start with a scheme that minimega fetches, such as file: or http:. By default, the image is the base image name plus the current time. The image is written to <base-dir.phenix>/images. The VM must have its snapshot flag set.

Warning

For a VM with more than one disk, the backing image is created only for the first disk. This is a known issue that will be addressed someday. If this affects you, please open an issue on GitHub.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: Click on the name of a running VM in a started experiment to open its details card, then click Memory snapshot in More actions. Type the file name and click Create, or click Cancel to stop. The button is disabled when the VM is not running.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To create an ELF memory dump, run the following command.

phenix vm memory-snapshot <experiment-name> <vm-name> <snapshot-file-path>

A relative path is in the experiment files directory, <base-dir.phenix>/images/<experiment-name>/files. For a VM on a compute node, phēnix copies the dump to the head node from that directory only. Thus, for such a VM, phēnix refuses an absolute path outside that directory. Each memory snapshot stops after one hour if QEMU does not complete it.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
Click on a running VM in a started experiment to open its details card, then click Snapshot in More actions and confirm. The VM must be running and have snapshots enabled.

The same action is in the VM table's Actions column and in the bar of a tile in the VNC tab when in Live mode (see Live Tiles).

Once a snapshot exists, the VM card's Snapshots section lists it, and the play button next to its name restores it.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
A VM snapshot holds the disk and the memory state of a VM. For an ELF memory dump, see create a memory snapshot. To save and restore the state of a running VM, do the steps that follow.

  1. Create a snapshot of the VM. The command prints the name of the snapshot, for example web__before-update.

    phenix vm snapshot create <experiment-name> <vm-name> <snapshot-name>

  2. List the snapshots of the VM.

    phenix vm snapshot list <experiment-name> <vm-name>

  3. Restore the VM to a snapshot. Use a name from the list.

    phenix vm snapshot restore <experiment-name> <vm-name> <snapshot-name>

To delete a snapshot from every cluster node, use phenix vm snapshot delete <experiment-name> <vm-name> <snapshot-name>. The experiment should be stopped before doing this, since phēnix refuses a snapshot whose disk a running VM uses.

The VM must have its snapshot flag set and only one disk. phēnix refuses a VM with more than one disk, because a snapshot holds only the first disk (#145).

phēnix keeps the snapshot files on the cluster node that runs the VM, in <base-dir.phenix>/images/<experiment-name>/files. The list shows the snapshots on all nodes. A restore of a VM on a node other than the head node can fail if minimega on that node runs with the -headnode flag. minimega then gets the snapshot files from the head node, which does not have them (#153).

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: Click on a running VM in a started experiment to open its details card, then click Screenshot (the camera icon) in More actions. The console page has the same button in its top bar. phēnix saves a full-size PNG image of the VM screen in the experiment files, in the screenshots folder. The file name is <vm>-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>.png, with the UTC time. phēnix does not replace a file: when the name is in use, it adds -1, -2 and so on. A message shows the name of the file. The button is disabled when the VM is not running. In Live mode, the bar of a tile in the VNC tab also has Screenshot.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
The phenix vm screenshot command will save a screenshot of the VM's VNC to a file on the local system.

phenix vm screenshot my-exp my-vm

The command writes the file <vm>-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>.png, with the UTC time, in the current folder, and prints the file name. The name is the same as in the web UI. The command does not replace a file: when the name is in use, it adds -1, -2 and so on.

-O, --output-file gives the file a different name or folder. When stdout is not a terminal, the command writes the image to stdout. --size sets the longest side of the image in pixels.

phenix vm screenshot my-exp my-vm -O screen.png
phenix vm screenshot my-exp my-vm --size 800 > small.png

Note

Note that phenix vm screenshot won't save the screenshot to the experiment's files on the server. If you need to do that, use the API (POST /api/v1/experiments/<exp>/vms/<vm>/screenshots).

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
The web UI shows the screen of a VM in three places:

  • The console page (/vnc) shows one to four VM consoles in a browser tab.
  • The VNC tab of a running experiment and the VM Tiles page show live tiles.
  • The details window of a VM shows a live console.

The experiment must be started, and the VM must be running or paused and not busy with an action.

Warning

The console needs the minimega release that adds the vga column to vm info. With an older minimega, the console shows minimega is too old: vm info has no vga column, update minimega. Port forwards to the VNC port of a VM also fail. Key recordings (vnc record kb) of an older minimega do not include the key events that noVNC sends.

docs.title: Open a Console
docs.text: Click the screenshot of a VM in the VMs table, a live tile in the VNC tab, or Open console in the details window of the VM. The console page opens in a new browser tab. Each link has a real address. You can open the link in a new window or copy it. When another tab already shows the same VMs, a message tells you. Click Open another anyway to open one more tab.

docs.title: The Console Page
docs.text:
The top bar acts on the pane that has keyboard input. It shows the VM name and these controls:

  • The flask button, at the left of the VM name, opens the page of the experiment of the pane.
  • In single view, the information button at the right of the VM name opens the details card of the VM on the experiment page.
  • The VM action buttons: Pause or Resume, Restart, Shut down, Screenshot, the packet capture button, Port forwards and Mount disk. Screenshot saves a PNG image of the VM screen in the experiment files (see Save a VM Screenshot). Mount disk opens the same file browser as on the experiment page. It needs the vm-mount feature, a running VM and an active miniccc agent.
  • The packet capture button starts a capture on interface 0 when no capture of the VM runs. When minimega can write pcapng, a dialog asks for the format first. When a capture of the VM runs, the button is Stop captures and stops all captures of the VM.
  • Port forwards lists the port forwards of the VM. Each forward has Remove. Only the user that made a forward can remove it. Add port forward opens the same dialog as on the experiment page. Tunneler opens the Tunneler page in a new tab.
  • Clipboard, Keys and View are icon buttons. Their tooltips give their names.
  • Clipboard: send text to the VM (see Copy and Paste). Clear empties the text box.
  • Actions: a menu with Snapshot, Memory snapshot and Backing image, then Capture interface…, Capture all interfaces (or Stop all packet captures) and Link quality…, then Insert CD-ROM (or Change CD-ROM), then Edit labels and Edit annotations, then Redeploy, Reset disk and Kill in red. Most open the same dialogs as on the experiment page.
  • Capture interface… and Link quality… ask for the interface when the VM has more than one. A capture cannot use a disconnected interface or an interface that phēnix already captures. Link quality… then opens the same dialog as Set link quality… on the experiment page.
  • Keys: send Ctrl+Alt+Del, Esc, Tab, PrintScreen and Ctrl+Alt+F1 to F12. Hold Ctrl, Alt or Win, and release all held keys. It also shows the keyboard shortcuts (see The Keyboard Chord).
  • View: the scaling (Fit, Actual or Resize VM), the zoom of Actual (50% to 200%), the quality, the compression, View only, full screen for the pane, and Open alone in a new tab. Pane headers and Banners show or hide the pane headers and the banners of the VMs. A zoom level also selects Actual. The browser keeps these settings for each user, except View only. With View only, the console shows the VM screen, but sends no keyboard or mouse input to the VM. Resize VM needs a VM with vga virtio. To set it, add vga: virtio to the advanced settings of the VM in the topology. Linux VMs use qxl by default.
  • The layout buttons, Add VM and Full screen for the page. In full screen, the same button is Exit full screen. Add VM shows the list of running VMs that it read the last time, and reads the list again. The browser keeps the list for each user.
  • The connection state, for example Connected. Click it to see the screen size, the scaling, the encoding and the copy/paste mode. It also shows the host of the VM, its uptime, the state of its miniccc agent and its IP addresses, each with a copy button.
  • Hide toolbar, at the right end, hides the top bar. The panes then use all of the page. A Show toolbar button at the same place shows the bar again. Ctrl+] then T also hides or shows the bar (see The Keyboard Chord). The browser keeps the choice.

An action that the VM state does not allow is grayed out, and its tooltip gives the reason. An action that the role cannot do is also grayed out. Its tooltip names the permission, for example Your role does not permit this action (vms delete).

Pause, Restart, Shut down, Snapshot, Reset disk and Kill ask you to confirm. Resume does not ask. During Redeploy and Reset disk, the pane shows that the VM restarts, and the console connects again when the VM runs. After Kill, the pane shows VM killed and a link to the experiment page.

docs.title: Split View
docs.text:
The console page shows up to four VMs. The VMs can be in different experiments. Use Add VM to add a running VM, and select a layout in the top bar: One pane, Two columns, Two rows, One large pane and two stacked or Grid of four. The address of the page keeps the VMs and the layout, for example /vnc?vm=demo/web&vm=demo/db&layout=cols. The layouts are single, cols, rows, main-2 and grid.

Each pane shows the banners of its VM and a header with the VM name, the VM state, an information button, the pane number and a menu. Pane headers and Banners in the View panel hide the headers and the banners. The information button opens the details card of the VM on the experiment page. The menu has Swap with pane N, Open alone, Full screen and Close. Click a pane to give it keyboard input. That pane shows a blue ring and the Keyboard tag. When you close a pane and only one VM stays, the page shows that VM in one pane.

To open many VMs in one console page, select one to four running VMs in the VMs tab, or with the check box on each tile in the VNC tab. Then click Open N selected in split in the VNC tab.

docs.title: The Keyboard Chord
docs.text:
The console sends every key to the VM. To move the keyboard out of the console, press Ctrl+], then one more key:

Key Action Tab Move focus to the top bar. Shift+Tab moves focus to the last control of the bar. When the top bar is hidden, move focus to Show toolbar. 1 to 4 Give keyboard input to that pane. F Exit full screen. T Hide or show the top bar. Esc Cancel the chord.

Press the key in the position of ] on a US keyboard. On a German keyboard, that key is +. The Keyboard tag, the Keys menu and a message show this hint. The message shows the first time that a pane gets keyboard input in a browser session.

docs.title: Full Screen and HTTPS
docs.text: In full screen over HTTPS, Chrome and Edge send Esc, Alt+Tab and Ctrl+W to the VM (Keyboard Lock). To exit full screen, press Ctrl+] then F, or hold Esc. Over HTTP, full screen works without Keyboard Lock, and a message says Keyboard capture needs HTTPS. Firefox and Safari do not have Keyboard Lock. Paste from clipboard in the Clipboard panel also needs HTTPS.

docs.title: Copy and Paste
docs.text:
The copy/paste mode of a VM comes from its minimega setting bidirectional-copy-paste:

  • Paste as keys (the default): phēnix types the text into the VM as key presses. It types printable ASCII characters, Tab and Enter only. Before it types text with other characters, the panel lists the characters that it types as "?" (above U+00FF) and the characters that it skips (U+0080 to U+00FF). It also shows the typing time. Click Type anyway or Cancel. For text longer than 5,000 characters, the bidirectional mode is faster.
  • Bidirectional: the VM and the Clipboard panel exchange UTF-8 text in the two directions.

docs.title: Live Tiles
docs.text:
The VNC tab of a running experiment and the VM Tiles page show a live, view-only tile for each running or paused VM. A tile sends no keys and no pointer events to the VM. A paused VM keeps a still tile with the PAUSED tag. Click a tile to open its console page. Move the pointer over a tile to show its bar, with Open console, Details and the VM power actions. In Live mode, the bar also has Screenshot and Snapshot. The bar also shows when a control of the tile has keyboard focus. A disabled button tells why in its tooltip. Pause, Restart, Shut down, Kill and Snapshot ask you to confirm. Start and Resume do not ask.

  • Live tile limit sets how many tiles can be live at one time: 4, 8, 16 (the default), 24 or 32. The browser keeps the choice. A tile over the limit shows a screenshot with the Snapshot tag.
  • Snapshots turns off all live tiles, and Live turns them on again.
  • A tile is live only while at least 25% of it is on the screen. A tile that leaves the screen, or a browser tab that is hidden, disconnects after 30 seconds.
  • The server does not send screenshots of live tiles.

docs.title: The Details Window
docs.text:
The details window of a VM shows a live, view-only console with the banners of the VM. Click Take control to send keys and pointer events to the VM, and View only to stop. Open console opens the console page of the VM.

Note

QEMU allows 32 shared clients for each VM. Every console, live tile, details window, minimega recording and paste playback counts. Thus a browser tab never opens two connections to one VM. While the details window or a console pane of a VM is open, the tile of that VM in the same tab disconnects and shows its last screen.

docs.title: VM Settings for VNC
docs.text:
phēnix adds two settings to the minimega script of an experiment:

  • For each KVM VM, vm config qemu-override "-vnc unix:" "-vnc lossy=on,vnc=unix:", before the overrides of the topology. With lossy updates, the quality level of a console or a tile selects JPEG for regions that look like photos. A topology override that matches -vnc unix: no longer matches, because this override changes that text first.
  • For each Linux VM, vm config vga qxl, in place of vm config qemu-append -vga qxl. phēnix does not add it when the advanced settings of the VM set vga. minimega then shows the video card in the vga column of vm info.

Note

The phēnix host must connect to the VNC port of each VM on the compute node that runs the VM. minimega selects a random high TCP port for each VM. Make sure that the network lets the phēnix host connect to these ports on each compute node. When phēnix cannot connect, the console shows phēnix cannot connect to the VNC port of <vm> on <host> (port <n>).

docs.title: VNC Banners
docs.text:
Each pane of the console page and the console of the details window show a banner above and below the VM's screen. Live tiles show no banners. On the console page, Banners in the View panel hides them. Both banners read EXP: <experiment> - VM: <vm> unless the VM has a vncBanner annotation:

  • A string sets the text of both banners. Each newline in it starts a new line.
  • A map sets each banner apart. topBanner and bottomBanner each take a banner list of lines, a backgroundColor and a textColor. A banner the map leaves out is not shown, and disabled: true turns both off.
annotations:
  vncBanner:
    topBanner:
      banner:
        - Training range
        - Lab use only
      backgroundColor: "#007a33"
      textColor: white
    bottomBanner:
      banner:
        - Training range
      backgroundColor: "#007a33"
      textColor: white

Colors are CSS color names, such as green, or hex colors, such as #007a33. Any other color falls back to the default white background or black text. Banner text is shown exactly as written, so HTML in it appears as text.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To reach the VNC console from your computer, add a port forward to it. The vnc value forwards to the VNC console of the VM. Then use phenix-tunneler to open the forward. The command needs a running phenix ui.

phenix vm forward add <experiment-name> <vm-name> vnc

phenix vm forward list and phenix vm forward remove show and remove the forwards. A forward from the command line has the owner global-admin.

To save a PNG image of the screen of a running VM, see Save a VM Screenshot.

docs.title: Mount a VM
docs.text:
The VM Mount feature lets you transfer files to and from a running VM directly through the phēnix Web-UI. It is an optional feature that must be enabled when starting the phēnix UI with the vm-mount feature flag (see Enabling VM Mount below).

Note

Mounting a VM requires the minimega command-and-control agent (miniccc) to be installed and actively running in the VM. If cc is not active for a VM, the Mount disk button is disabled and phenix vm mount fails.

docs.title: Enabling VM Mount
docs.text:
VM Mount is disabled by default. Enable it by passing the vm-mount feature to the --features flag when starting the UI:

phenix ui --features vm-mount

The feature can also be enabled via the ui.features configuration key or the PHENIX_UI_FEATURES environment variable. See Settings & Configuration for details.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
The experiment must be started. Click on the name of a running VM to open its details card, then click Mount disk (the hard-drive icon) in More actions. The button is disabled, with the reason in its tooltip, when the VM is not running or has no active miniccc agent.

The mount browser modal lists the folders and files of the VM. Click a folder to open it. Click a file to download it from the VM to your local machine. An interrupted download resumes when retried from the browser's downloads list. Two controls below the list add a file to the open folder:

  • Upload Local File — browse to a file on your local machine and upload it into the VM.
  • Copy experiment file — copy files that already exist on the phēnix server into the VM. This option is only available when the experiment file server is enabled (see below).

Every path stays inside the VM's file system, so a symbolic link that points outside it cannot be browsed or written through. Several users can have the same VM mounted at once, and it is unmounted when the last of them closes the modal.

docs.title: Uploading Experiment Files from the phēnix Server
docs.text:
phēnix can optionally run a lightweight file server on a port separate from the main UI. This was added to support environments where the phēnix UI is only reachable on a private network but files (for example, application installers or configuration files) need to be uploaded to an experiment from a public network.

When the file server is enabled, the VM Mount modal gains the Copy experiment file option described above, allowing files that have been uploaded to an experiment to be copied directly into a VM without going through the user's local machine.

Enable the file server by passing the --file-server-endpoint flag when starting the UI:

# Bind to 127.0.0.1 on port 8080 (port-only value binds to localhost)
phenix ui --features vm-mount --file-server-endpoint 8080

# Bind to a specific interface and port
phenix ui --features vm-mount --file-server-endpoint 0.0.0.0:8080

The file server presents a simple interface for selecting an experiment and uploading a file to it. When authentication/authorization is enabled for the main phēnix UI, it is automatically enforced on the file server as well, so users must already have valid phēnix credentials to upload files. File upload permissions are included in the default Experiment Admin and Experiment User roles.

See Settings & Configuration for the ui.file-server-endpoint configuration key.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
Use phenix vm mount to mount a running VM's filesystem to a directory on the phēnix headnode. Unlike the Web-UI mount browser above, this does not require the vm-mount UI feature flag to be enabled, and the mounted filesystem is accessed directly on the headnode's filesystem rather than through the browser.

phenix vm mount <experiment-name> <vm-name>

The VM is mounted at <mount-dir>/<experiment-name>/<vm-name>, where <mount-dir> defaults to <base-dir.phenix>/mounts (see mount-dir). To use another folder, set the global --mount-dir flag or the PHENIX_MOUNT_DIR environment variable. The command prints the host path once the mount succeeds.

phenix vm mount my-exp my-vm
# VM my-vm in experiment my-exp mounted at: /phenix/mounts/my-exp/my-vm

To unmount the VM's filesystem, run:

phenix vm unmount <experiment-name> <vm-name>

Note

Mounts are automatically unmounted, and their mount directories removed, when the owning experiment is stopped or deleted, so mounts do not outlive their experiment.

docs.title: Run a Command or Copy a File
Command Line
docs.text:
phenix vm exec runs a command in a running VM through its miniccc agent. It prints the output of the command, and exits with the exit code of the command when minimega reports it.

phenix vm exec <experiment-name> <vm-name> [--] <command> [args...]

miniccc runs the command without a shell. To use pipes or redirects, run a shell. Put -- before a command that has flags:

phenix vm exec my-exp host-01 -- sh -c 'ps aux | grep nginx'

phenix vm cp copies one file into or out of a running VM. Give the VM side as <vm-name>:<absolute-path>. A path that ends with / is a folder.

phenix vm cp my-exp ./setup.sh host-01:/root/
phenix vm cp my-exp host-01:/var/log/syslog ./syslog

Both commands need the miniccc agent in the VM, and wait one minute by default (--timeout). A copy out of the VM works only for a VM on the head node, and the copy gets the permissions 0600. phēnix refuses an argument with a $ variable or a file:, http:, https: or tar: URL, because minimega would change it on the host.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
Click on the name of the network tap, or on the IP address, of a running VM in a started experiment to start a packet capture on that interface. The name of the network tap will turn green once a packet capture has started. Each interface in the VM's details card has its own shark-fin button that does the same thing.

phēnix starts the capture, or stops a running one, without asking you to confirm. A capture started from the web UI is written to the experiment's files as <vm>_<interface>_<time>_<random>.pcapng, so a restarted capture never replaces an earlier file.

It is possible to start captures on multiple network taps. Stopping the capture on one interface leaves the VM's other captures running. Use Stop all packet captures to stop them all.

The console page also starts captures, with the packet capture button of its top bar and with Capture interface… and Capture all interfaces in its Actions menu (see The Console Page).

A capture cannot be started on a disconnected interface; phēnix says Cannot capture traffic on a disconnected interface. instead of starting one.

phēnix writes the capture file in pcapng format, and the file name ends in .pcapng. When minimega cannot write pcapng, phēnix writes pcap, and the file name ends in .pcap. The network menu of the VM table can also start a capture in pcap format (see Starting/Stopping Packet Captures). To capture the traffic of all VMs into one file, see Experiment Packet Captures.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To start a packet capture, run the following command, specifying the target network interface by its name (as declared in the experiment topology, e.g. IF0) or its zero-based index.

phenix vm capture start <experiment-name> <vm-name> <iface-name/index> </path/to/out file>

The --format flag sets the capture file format, pcapng (the default) or pcap. phēnix sets the extension of the output file name to match the format. The ui.captures.max-size setting limits the size of the file (see Settings).

To stop all packet captures on a running VM, use the following command.

phenix vm capture stop <experiment-name> <vm-name>

Pass an interface name or index to stop only that interface's capture, leaving the VM's other captures running.

phenix vm capture stop <experiment-name> <vm-name> [iface name/index]

To list the running captures of an experiment, or of one VM, use the following command. phenix exp captures <experiment-name> gives the same list.

phenix vm capture list <experiment-name> [vm name]

A capture continues while its VM is paused.

Note

Stopping the capture on a single interface, Web UI or the command line, requires minimega 3.3.0 or later.

To view a capture's packets in the browser, or stream a running capture into a local Wireshark (phenix vm capture stream), see WebShark.

docs.title: Capture All Interfaces
docs.text: Capture all interfaces, in the VM table's Actions column and in the details card's Network section, starts a packet capture on every connected interface of the VM that does not already have one. It does not ask you to confirm, and writes one .pcapng file per interface to the experiment's files. The button is disabled, with the reason in its tooltip, when the VM is not running, has no connected interface, or is already capturing every connected interface. While captures run, a red Stop all packet captures button takes its place and stops them all. The Actions menu of the console page has the same item (see The Console Page).

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
Click on the name of a running VM in a started experiment to open its details card, then click Kill in the Power section and confirm. The bar of a live tile and the selection toolbar also ask you to confirm.

Note: if you stop and then start the experiment again, that VM will run again per the experiment configuration.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To kill a VM, run the following command. Add --dry-run to show the VMs that the command would kill.

phenix vm kill <experiment-name> [vm name] [--label <label>]

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: Click on the network for the desired VM in the Running Component to modify the settings. Select from a pull down what network you want to switch the VM interface you clicked on to. To revert back to previous setting, simply repeat selecting the network interface you wish to change, and select the previous network setting.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To connect a VM network interface to a different network, run the following command.

phenix vm net connect <experiment-name> <vm-name> <iface-index> <vlan-id>

To disconnect a VM network interface, run the following command.

phenix vm net disconnect <experiment-name> <vm-name> <iface-index>

phenix vm set with --interface <index>=<vlan> also connects an interface, and --interface <index>= disconnects it.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: See Set link quality… in Starting/Stopping Packet Captures. On the console page, Link quality… in the Actions menu opens the same dialog (see The Console Page).

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
phenix vm qos shows and changes the packet loss, the delay or the rate limit that minimega applies to the traffic that a VM interface receives. The experiment must run. Give the interface as an index from 0 or as its name in the topology.

phenix vm qos get <experiment-name> <vm-name> [<interface>]
phenix vm qos set <experiment-name> <vm-name> <interface> --loss 0.5 --delay 100ms
phenix vm qos set <experiment-name> <vm-name> <interface> --rate 10mbit
phenix vm qos clear <experiment-name> <vm-name> [<interface>]

A rate cannot go with a loss or a delay. set replaces the link quality of the interface. clear without an interface clears each interface.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: Click on the name of a running VM in a started experiment to open its details card, then click Pause in the Power section and confirm. The bar of a live tile, the selection toolbar and the top bar of the console page also ask you to confirm.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To pause a VM, run the following command.

phenix vm pause <experiment-name> [vm name] [--label <label>]

To resume a paused VM, run the following command.

phenix vm resume <experiment-name> [vm name] [--label <label>]

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: Click on the name of a running VM in a started experiment to open its details card, then click Redeploy in More actions. The dialog that opens lets you change the VM's CPUs, memory and disk, and whether the original injections are replicated, before it is deployed again. Its Disk menu works as described in Disk Menu, and the disk changes only when you pick a different one.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To redeploy a VM, run the following command.

phenix vm redeploy <experiment-name> [vm name] [--label <label>]

The -c, --cpu and -m, --mem flags change a value only when you set them. Without them, the VM keeps its current CPUs and memory. A new disk (-d, --disk) replaces only the first disk of the VM. The other disks do not change. The disk value is a minimega disk spec, <path>[,<interface>][,<cache-mode>], for example new.qc2,virtio. A field that you do not set keeps the value of the current first disk.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: Click on the name of a running VM in a started experiment to open its details card, then click Reset disk in More actions and confirm. The button is disabled when the VM is paused or does not have snapshots enabled, with the reason in its tooltip, such as Cannot reset disk: the VM is paused. Resume paused VMs first.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To reset the first disk to the initial pre-boot state, run the following command.

phenix vm reset-disk <experiment-name> [vm name] [--label <label>]

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: Click on the name of a running VM in a started experiment to open its details card, then click Restart in the Power section and confirm. Restart is also in the VM table's Actions column. The button is disabled when the VM is not running, with the reason in its tooltip. The bar of a live tile, the selection toolbar and the console page also ask you to confirm a restart. Restarting a selection of VMs from the table's toolbar skips the ones that are not running.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To restart a VM, run the following command.

phenix vm restart <experiment-name> [vm name] [--label <label>]

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
Click on the name of the paused VM in a started experiment to open its details card, then click Resume in the Power section.

phēnix refuses to start a VM that the topology sets to not boot (general.do_not_boot), because minimega did not launch it. To launch the VM, redeploy it.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To resume a paused VM, run the following command.

phenix vm resume <experiment-name> [vm name] [--label <label>]

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: Click on the name of a running VM in a started experiment to open its details card, then click Shut down in the Power section and confirm. Shut down is also in the VM table's Actions column, the selection toolbar, the bar of a live tile and the top bar of the console page. Each one asks you to confirm.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To shutdown a VM, run the following command.

phenix vm shutdown <experiment-name> [vm name] [--label <label>]

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
There are two ways to modify VM settings:

  1. Click on a stopped experiment to access the Stopped Component. Its VM table shows each VM's host and IP address, and lets you edit the following:

    • Host: the cluster host the VM is scheduled on
    • CPUs
    • Memory
    • Disk: the image the VM boots from (see Disk Menu)
    • Partition: the disk partition files are injected into
    • Labels
    • Boot: the do-not-boot flag
    • Persistence: Non-persistent (snapshots on) or Persistent

    Edit a setting in the row of the VM, or click the VM name to open its details card. The card has the same settings, and you can also edit the labels and annotations of the VM there. A change saves at once, with no dialog. The control spins until the server answers. If the change fails, an error message shows and the control shows the previous value. A dot next to a setting tells that its value is different from the value that the VM had when the experiment was created. Reset settings sets all of the settings back to those values. Experiments created before this version of phēnix have no saved values, so they do not show Reset settings. The card also lists the port forwards that the phenix/startup-autotunnel annotation opens when the experiment starts. To change them, edit the annotation. The Select visible columns button shows or hides the columns of the table. 1. From a running experiment, click on the VM name and then Redeploy in More actions on its details card. You are able to edit the following: * CPUs * Memory * Disk * Replicate Original Injection(s)

docs.title: Disk Menu
docs.text:
The stopped experiment's Disk column and the Redeploy dialog pick a VM's disk from the images the experiment can use on the Disks page. Images in the minimega files directory are listed by their path within it, such as win/win10.qcow2. Images outside that directory are listed by full path under Outside the standard images directory. On a stopped experiment, picking an image writes the image's full path into the topology.

  • An image whose path minimega cannot use is disabled and marked (minimega cannot use this name).
  • A warning icon marks a disk outside the files directory.
  • A red icon with a cross marks a disk whose backing chain is broken.
  • A disk the list does not hold, such as a missing image, shows as <full-path> (not listed).

The menu needs list on disks to offer other images. Without it, the menu shows only the VM's current disk.

docs.title: CD-ROM
docs.text: Insert CD-ROM in the details card's More actions opens the CD-ROM picker for a running VM. When an ISO image is already inserted, the button reads Change CD-ROM and the picker names the inserted image. The picker lists the ISO images the Disks page knows, with those outside the minimega files directory in a group of their own. If there are none, it says so and links to the Disks page, where an .iso file can be uploaded. Insert (or Change) inserts the selected image, and Eject removes the inserted one. From the command line, use phenix vm cdrom insert <experiment-name> <vm-name> <iso-path> and phenix vm cdrom eject <experiment-name> <vm-name>. minimega reads the ISO path on the cluster node that runs the VM.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
To modify VM settings, run the following command, specifying one or more of the configuration flags described below.

phenix vm set <experiment-name> [<vm-name>] [flags]

Only the flags that are explicitly provided will be applied; any setting whose flag is omitted is left unchanged. The following flags are supported:

Flag Description -c, --cpu Number of VM CPUs (1-16 is valid). -m, --mem Amount of memory in megabytes (a multiple of 512 from 512 to 131072). -d, --disk VM backing disk image. -p, --partition Partition of the first disk to inject files into. 0 turns off disk injection, so the startup app sends its scripts through miniccc. --host Cluster host to run the VM on. An empty value lets the scheduler choose the host. --annotation key=value VM annotation. May be repeated. Replaces all of the annotations of the VM. --interface <index>=<vlan> Connect the interface to a VLAN alias or ID, or disconnect it with <index>=. Running experiments only. --do-not-boot Set the do-not-boot flag for the VM. --snapshot Set the snapshot (non-persistent) flag for the VM. -L, --label-changes key=value VM label to set, in key=value form. May be repeated to set multiple labels. --append-labels Append the provided labels to the VM's existing labels instead of replacing them. -l, --label Apply the change to every VM whose label matches the provided label (supports glob patterns). Use all to select every VM in the experiment. May be repeated.

A label key or value may not hold a double quote, a backslash, $, or a control character other than a newline or tab, and may not start with file:, http:, https: or tar:. A VLAN an interface connects to may not hold white space, ' or #.

For example, to set the CPU count to 4 and memory to 2048 MB for a VM named my-vm in an experiment named my-exp:

phenix vm set my-exp my-vm --cpu 4 --mem 2048

To set the role=server labels on VMs whose existing labels matches tier=web* in the same experiment, without clearing the existing labels:

phenix vm set my-exp --label "tier=web*" -L role=server --append-labels

To set two labels on the VM my-vm and replace the existing labels on the VM:

phenix vm set my-exp my-vm -L val1=true -L val2=roger

Note

Only labels, annotations and interface VLAN connections can be modified while an experiment is running. Apps read the new annotations when the experiment starts again. To change CPU, memory, disk, partition, host, do-not-boot, or snapshot settings, the experiment must be stopped. Use --interface or phenix vm net to modify interface VLAN connections on a running experiment.

docs.title: Applying Actions to Multiple VMs
docs.text:
Note

See VM Multi Action for documentation on applying actions to multiple VMs at once.

docs.text:

  • Troubleshooting: what to do when a VM does not start.

docs.title: Using the Web UI
docs.text: This page explains the basics of using the web UI. The specific pages are described in separate sections in the documentation (Experiments, VMs, Disks, Hosts, VLANs, etc.).

docs.title: The Navbar
docs.text:
From left to right:

  • Home (the experiments page)
  • Links and Menus
  • phēnix documentation (where you are now!)
  • The refresh button
  • The background jobs menu
  • Logout or Reauthorize (depending on if proxy authentication is enabled)

Note

Some of the buttons in the navbar may not be available, due to your Role's permissions (see Roles) or a missing feature (such as WebShark or the minimega console).

docs.title: Page Freshness and Refresh
docs.text:
When navigating to a page, it will load immediately and show you the last data that was cached for that page, while loading fresh data in the background. This improves responsiveness, but can lead to confusion when data isn't what you expect.

The status of the background load is in the refresh button on the top right. It will spin while loading, show green when data is fresh, and turn more and more orange the more stale a page gets. To refresh, click the button (this eliminates the need to do a browser page refresh).

docs.title: Background Jobs Menu
docs.text: This menu shows the background jobs you started, such as bulk VM actions, file archives, or cloning a disk image (see Background Jobs for the full list). The menu lists every running or queued job and the ten most recent finished ones. Jobs keep running when you leave the page, reload or lose the connection.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Tables appear in many places in the phenix UI, such as the VMs for an experiment or experiments on the home page. They can be sorted by clicking on a column, and click again to change the sort order. Most columns are sortable, but some may not.

If a table is empty or loading, a message will be displayed, e.g. Loading disks… or No disk images found.

docs.title: Search
docs.text: Most tables will also have a search box located at the top right above the table, which will filter what is shown in the table.

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text: By default, all items in a table are shown, but you can show a limited number at a time with the Paginate toggle on the top right of a table. This preference is remembered in your browser.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A failure opens a red notification at the top of the page, which stays until you dismiss it. Successes and progress show as short messages that go away by themselves. When the server nests one error inside another, the notification lists each step on a line of its own, with the root cause last and in bold.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: If you open a page your role cannot use, the UI sends you to the first page your role can use. Buttons and menu items your role cannot use are hidden or disabled, and a disabled button says why in its tooltip. For what a role may do, see User Administration.

docs.title: Refresh Rates
docs.text:
Some pages ask the server for fresh data on their own:

What How often The Hosts page every 30 seconds The VM tiles every 60 seconds, with screenshots of only the tiles on screen Screenshots of the VMs on a running experiment's page every 15 seconds, running VMs only The State of Health overview, while a run is in progress every 15 seconds

These pages skip a refresh while the last one is still waiting, or while their browser tab is hidden.

docs.text:
