  • Accessibility: keyboard, screen reader and display notes.
  • Settings: the ui.* settings.
  • Builder: draw a topology in the browser.
  • Troubleshooting: fixes for common problems.

docs.title: WebShark
docs.text: WebShark is a build of Wireshark that runs in the browser. The phēnix UI uses it to show an experiment's packet captures, both running captures (updating live) and capture files saved in the experiment's files. If you'd rather use a local Wireshark or tshark, you can stream a running capture to it instead.

docs.title: Installing WebShark
docs.text:
The phēnix Docker and Podman images and the Debian package include WebShark in /opt/phenix/webshark. The server also looks for a webshark directory in the directory it runs from, and logs Serving WebShark when it finds one. Without it, the web UI has no WebShark tab or buttons.

To build it yourself, you need Node.js (22.22.3, 24.15.0 or 26, or a later release), npm, gzip, wget and python3. Restart the phēnix server afterwards.

git clone https://github.com/QXIP/webshark.git
sceptre-phenix/docker/build-webshark.sh webshark /opt/phenix/webshark

WebShark is licensed under the AGPL v3.0, and its Wireshark build under the GPL v2.0.

docs.title: Behind a Reverse Proxy
docs.text: If a reverse proxy serves the phēnix UI under a base path, WebShark is served under the same path and needs no route of its own. Start the server with the base path the UI was built with, e.g. phenix ui --base-path /phenix/ (only letters, digits, -, ., _, ~, % and /). WebShark's RTP audio player works only over HTTPS, in a tab of its own, so a proxy that ends HTTPS must send X-Forwarded-Proto: https or Forwarded: proto=https.

docs.title: Viewing Captures
docs.text:
Click the WebShark tab in the navbar, pick an experiment, then pick one of its running captures (by VM and interface) or saved capture files (.pcap, .pcapng or .cap, optionally gzipped). A running capture gets a red Live tag, and WebShark reloads it as it grows. Until it has packets, you'll see No packets yet. in place of WebShark.

The URL names the experiment and capture, so you can bookmark it or share it with other phēnix users. You can also open WebShark from a capture file on the experiment's Files tab, or from a capturing interface in a VM's details. To start a capture, see Packet Capture.

docs.title: Streaming a Running Capture
docs.text:
phenix vm capture stream writes a running capture as pcap (every packet so far, then each new one) until the capture stops, from whichever cluster node runs the VM. Give the interface as its index or name. On the phēnix server, pipe it into Wireshark or tshark, or save it with -O copy.pcap (it won't write to a terminal):

phenix vm capture stream my-exp my-vm 0 | wireshark -k -i -

# only the packets from now on
phenix vm capture stream my-exp my-vm 1 --from-now | tshark -i -

From your own machine, click Copy Wireshark command on a live capture in the WebShark tab. It copies a command like this one, which you must run within 5 minutes:

curl -fsSN --max-redirs 0 -L \
  'https://phenix.example.com/webshark/streams/pcs_<token>' \
  | wireshark -k -i -

Behind a sign-in proxy (a UI built with PHENIX_WEB_AUTH=proxy), add the proxy's sign-in cookie as -b 'NAME=VALUE', or use phenix vm capture stream on the server. For the API, see Streaming Endpoints (add ?from=now to skip the earlier packets).

docs.title: Capture Tokens
docs.text:
WebShark and the copied command use a capture token that can read only one capture, not your sign-in. A WebShark link's token expires 2 hours after it was last used, 12 hours after it was given, or when your session ends; if it has expired, WebShark says "not found", so open the capture again from the WebShark tab. A stream token (pcs_<random>) starts streams for 5 minutes, and a stream it started ends with your session. A token also ends when its user, experiment or capture file is deleted, and a server restart ends every token.

To stream from a machine with no phēnix sign-in, get a stream token from the API and use it in the curl command above:

curl -s -H 'X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer <sign-in-token>' \
  -d '{"vm":"<vm>","interface":<iface>,"operations":["stream"]}' \
  'https://phenix.example.com/api/v1/experiments/<exp>/captureTokens'

GET on the same URL lists your tokens, and DELETE .../captureTokens/<id> revokes one.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: WebShark loads a whole capture into the browser, so large captures (hundreds of megabytes) are slow to open, and a live capture downloads again each time WebShark reloads it. Stream large captures into a local Wireshark instead.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Packet Captures: start captures and what they cost.
  • phenix vm capture: start, stop and stream captures from the command line.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text: A topology directory holds everything phēnix needs to run an experiment: its configs, the files to inject into its VMs, and a workflow config (phenix.yml) that says whether to create, update, start or restart the experiment. phenix workflow apply deploys such a directory in one command. It runs on the phēnix host (or in the phēnix container) and talks to the running phenix ui server through its unix socket. CI jobs and scripts can call the same REST API.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Create a topology directory with a topology config, a file to inject and a workflow config:

mkdir -p /phenix/topologies/helloworld/phenix-configs /phenix/topologies/helloworld/phenix-injects
cd /phenix/topologies/helloworld

echo "hello from phenix workflow apply" > phenix-injects/motd

cat > phenix-configs/topology.yml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Topology
metadata:
  name: ${BRANCH_NAME}
spec:
  nodes:
  - type: VirtualMachine
    general:
      hostname: host-01
    hardware:
      os_type: linux
      drives:
      - image: ubuntu.qc2
    network:
      interfaces:
      - name: IF0
        vlan: EXP
        address: 10.0.0.1
        mask: 24
        proto: static
        type: ethernet
    injections:
    - src: /phenix/injects/${BRANCH_NAME}/motd
      dst: /etc/motd
EOF

cat > phenix.yml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v0
kind: Workflow
metadata: {}
spec:
  auto:
    create: ${BRANCH_NAME}
  topology: ${BRANCH_NAME}
EOF

Do a dry run, then deploy for real:

phenix workflow apply helloworld -n
phenix workflow apply helloworld
phenix experiment list

The dry run logs the plan (action=createAndStart, experiment=helloworld) and changes nothing. The real run copies phenix-injects/ to /phenix/injects/helloworld, creates the helloworld topology, and creates and starts the helloworld experiment. After you change the topology, add -f so phēnix may restart the running experiment:

phenix workflow apply helloworld -f

docs.title: Topology Directory
docs.text:
helloworld/
├── .env                # variables for the configs (optional)
├── phenix.yml          # workflow config
├── phenix-configs/     # topology, scenario and other configs
│   ├── topology.yml
│   └── scenario.yml
└── phenix-injects/     # files to inject into VMs
    └── motd

Each part is optional and a missing part is skipped, but a directory with none of them is an error.

  • .env - the variables for the placeholders in the configs and in the workflow config, as NAME=value lines.
  • phenix.yml - the workflow config. Use -c for another name, such as phenix.yaml. An older .phenix.yml is read when there's no phenix.yml, and having both is an error.
  • phenix-configs/ - one config per .json, .yaml or .yml file, subdirectories included (hidden files are skipped). Each file holds one document with a kind. Each config is created or updated, topologies first.
  • phenix-injects/ - copied to <base-dir.injects>/<name> on the phēnix host (by default /phenix/injects/<name>), replacing the previous copy. By default, symlinks inside phenix-injects/ are copied as symlinks; --follow-inject-symlinks follows them and copies targets as regular files or directories.

docs.title: Branch Name
docs.text:
<name> is the workflow branch name: the directory's name, or what you set with -b. It holds only letters, digits, ., _ and -, and starts with a letter or digit. phenix.yml, phenix-configs and phenix-injects are reserved, in any letter case: not as the branch name, and not in the top two levels of phenix-injects/.

The branch name decides where the injects go, what ${BRANCH_NAME} expands to in the configs and the workflow config, and which experiment the workflow acts on. Only -b sets ${BRANCH_NAME}; every other ${VAR} placeholder is a variable. Use ${BRANCH_NAME} in names and inject paths, as the quick start does, and you can deploy one directory under several names. A hard-coded /phenix/injects/lab-a/<file> needs -b lab-a.

The branch name is not the experiment name. The experiment name is auto.create in the workflow config. With auto.create: ${BRANCH_NAME}, as in the examples on this page, -b also names the experiment, and each branch name is a separate deployment. A fixed auto.create ignores -b. phēnix reads auto.create only when no experiment is mapped to the branch, so -b and auto.create do not rename an experiment that exists.

docs.title: The phenix workflow apply Command
docs.text:
phenix workflow apply <DIR|NAME> [flags]

A NAME that isn't an existing path is looked up under base-dir.topologies (by default /phenix/topologies/NAME).

Flag Default Description -b, --branch-name, --name the directory's name The workflow branch name. It does not rename an experiment. --name is an alias; if you give both, use the same value. -c, --config phenix.yml Workflow config file, relative to the directory unless absolute. -e, --env Set a variable: NAME=value, or NAME to copy the value from the shell. Repeat it for more variables. --env-file .env in the directory Read variables from an env file. A relative path starts at the working directory. Repeat it for more files. -n, --dry-run false Check everything, log the server's plan, and change nothing. -f, --force false Allow restarting a running experiment. --follow-inject-symlinks false Follow symlinks in phenix-injects/ and copy targets as regular files or directories.

The global flags --unix-socket, --base-dir.injects, --base-dir.topologies and --log.level also apply (see Global Flags).

The command never prompts. It runs five steps, and each log line names its step in the step field:

  1. preflight - checks that the server answers, fills in the variables, and checks that every file parses.
  2. plan - the server dry-runs everything, and the plan is logged. -n stops here, and so does a restart without -f.
  3. injects - copies phenix-injects/ into place. Nothing changes before this step.
  4. configs - creates or updates each config.
  5. apply - applies the workflow config (see Actions).

The exit status is 0 when the run completed or the dry run passed. Each apply tags the experiment, in its phenix.workflow/tags annotation, with method=workflow, dir, branch, workflow_date and the git commit.

Warning

Don't run the command from inside a topology directory you didn't write: phēnix reads its settings files (config.* and users.*) from the current directory first.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Command What it does phenix workflow apply /phenix/topologies/helloworld Deploy by path. The branch name is helloworld. phenix workflow apply helloworld Look up helloworld under base-dir.topologies. phenix workflow apply . Deploy the current directory. phenix workflow apply helloworld -b helloworld-2 Deploy a second copy under another branch name. phenix workflow apply helloworld -e MEMORY=4096 -e SITE=lab Set variables. -e overrides an env file. phenix workflow apply helloworld -e MEMORY Copy MEMORY from the shell. It then overrides helloworld/.env. phenix workflow apply helloworld --env-file base.env --env-file site.env Read the env files, and not helloworld/.env. site.env overrides base.env. phenix workflow render helloworld -e MEMORY=4096 Print the configs with the variables filled in. Nothing is sent. phenix workflow apply helloworld --follow-inject-symlinks Follow symlinks in phenix-injects/ and copy targets as regular files or directories. : "${BRANCH:?}" && phenix workflow apply ./site -b "${BRANCH//\//-}" -f In CI, deploy a checkout under its git branch name (/ isn't allowed in a branch name).

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
phenix workflow apply fills in the ${NAME} and ${NAME:default} placeholders of each file in phenix-configs/ and of the workflow config to check them. Then it sends each file as written, with the variables, and the server fills them in. The server does the same for each topology file that includeTopologies names by a path (see Included Topology Files). It does not change the files in phenix-injects/.

The command gets the value of a variable from the first of these sources that has it:

  1. -e NAME=value on the command line. -e NAME copies the value of NAME from the shell.
  2. The env files that --env-file names. Without --env-file, the command reads .env in the topology directory, if that file exists. A later file overrides an earlier file.
  3. The shell environment, without the variables whose names start with PHENIX_. Name such a variable with -e NAME to use it.

The command sends only the shell variables whose names are valid variable names, and stops when the variables are larger than 1 MiB as JSON.

For example, a topology directory can hold its defaults in .env:

helloworld/.env
SITE=lab
MEMORY=2048

A config uses the variables, and gives a default to a variable that is optional:

helloworld/phenix-configs/topology.yml (part)
    general:
      hostname: ${SITE}-host-01
    hardware:
      memory: ${MEMORY}
      drives:
      - image: ${IMAGE:ubuntu.qc2}

phenix workflow apply helloworld                      # lab-host-01, 2048, ubuntu.qc2
phenix workflow apply helloworld -e MEMORY=4096       # lab-host-01, 4096, ubuntu.qc2
MEMORY=8192 phenix workflow apply helloworld          # 2048: .env overrides the shell
MEMORY=8192 phenix workflow apply helloworld -e MEMORY  # 8192: -e copies it from the shell

The command checks every variable in the preflight step, before it changes anything:

  • A placeholder with no value and no default is an error. Write ${NAME:} for a variable that can be empty.
  • A -e variable that no file uses is an error. This finds a variable name with a typing mistake. With a workflow config, a variable that only an included topology file uses counts as used: the command does this check in the plan step, after the server dry-runs the workflow config.
  • A value or a default that contains a line break is an error.
  • BRANCH_NAME can't be set as a variable. Use -b.

The rules for placeholders, for env files and for the logs are the same for every command that reads config files. See Environment Variables for the syntax, the $${NAME} escape and the env file format.

Note

The command reads the shell environment of the user that runs it. sudo removes most of that environment, and with docker exec the shell is that of the container. Use -e, an env file, or docker exec -e NAME=value in these cases.

docs.title: Included Topology Files
docs.text:
The server reads a topology file that includeTopologies names by a path, so the command can't check its placeholders. The server fills them in with the variables of the command. It gives a placeholder that no variable sets the first of these values:

  1. The environment variable of the same name on the server, with a warning.
  2. The default of the placeholder.
  3. An empty string, with a warning.

The server logs each warning with the file, the line and the variable, and the command logs it in the plan step:

/phenix/topologies/common/net.yml line 3: no variable SITE in the request or in the server environment, and the placeholder has no default; phenix used an empty string

A warning is for one file, variable and kind. It gives the first line and the count of the other lines, for example line 3 (and 2 other lines). The server reports at most 50 warnings for each request, and then says how many it left out.

As for a config, an included topology file can be at most 5 MiB after the server fills in the variables and the branch name. A larger text is an error.

The dry run reads each topology file that the topology of the workflow config includes, for every plan. So the plan step reports a line break in an included file.

docs.title: Show the Result
docs.text:
phenix workflow render prints each config, and then the workflow config, with the variables and the branch name filled in. The text is what the server has after an apply. The command does not contact the server and changes nothing. It does not read the topology files that includeTopologies names, so a -e variable that only such a file uses is an error in render.

phenix workflow render helloworld -b helloworld-2 -e MEMORY=4096

# phenix-configs/topology.yml
apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Topology
metadata:
  name: helloworld-2
...
---
# phenix.yml
apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v0
kind: Workflow
...

The command takes -b, -c, -e and --env-file, and gives the same variable errors as phenix workflow apply, except that a -e variable that only an included topology file uses is an error. Its output can hold secrets: it shows the value of each variable that a file uses.

docs.title: Workflow Config
docs.text:
The workflow config is a phēnix config of kind Workflow. It isn't stored in phēnix; it's sent with each apply. spec: {} applies every default.

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v0
kind: Workflow
metadata: {}
spec:
  auto:
    create: ${BRANCH_NAME}
    update: true
    restart: true
  topology: ${BRANCH_NAME}
  scenario: ${BRANCH_NAME}
  vlans:
    EXP: 101
  schedules:
    host-01: compute1
  deployMode: all
  useGREMesh: false
  vlanRange:
    min: 100
    max: 200
  defaultBridge: phenix
Field Default Description auto.create unset The experiment to create when none is mapped to the branch. Unset, none is created. auto.update true Update the mapped experiment. A running one is only updated if auto.restart is true too. auto.restart true Restart a running experiment to update it, and start a new or updated one. topology the experiment's topology The topology config. Required to create an experiment. scenario the experiment's scenario The scenario config, if any. vlans VLAN alias to VLAN ID. schedules VM hostname to cluster host. deployMode the server's deploy-mode all, no-headnode or only-headnode. useGREMesh false Use GRE tunnels between mesh nodes for VLAN trunking. vlanRange.min, vlanRange.max 0 The lowest and highest VLAN IDs minimega may assign. 0 leaves that end unset. defaultBridge phenix The bridge VMs connect to by default: at most 15 ASCII letters, digits, _, @, . or -. Unless it's phenix, no other experiment may use it.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text: The config must match the Workflow schema in v0.yaml, also served at GET /api/v1/schemas/workflow/v0. An unknown key or a wrong type gets a validation error.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
An experiment is mapped to a branch when its phenix.workflow/branch annotation is the branch name; phēnix sets it on each experiment a workflow creates. The server picks one action from the experiments mapped to the branch:

Mapped experiments Condition Action 0 auto.create not set none 0 auto.create set, auto.restart true createAndStart 0 auto.create set, auto.restart false create 1 auto.update false none 1 running, auto.restart false none 1 running, auto.restart true restart (needs -f in the CLI) 1 stopped, auto.restart true updateAndStart 1 stopped, auto.restart false update more than 1 any error

auto.create is only read when no experiment is mapped, so changing it later doesn't rename the experiment. It's an error when it names an existing experiment that isn't mapped, so don't put an Experiment config by that name in phenix-configs/.

A restart runs the start's disk check first: if the start would fail, the apply fails and the experiment keeps running. After a start, the scenario's runPeriodically apps run in an experiments.periodic background job.

docs.title: Dry Run
docs.text:
A dry run (-n) runs every check and changes nothing. A real apply runs the same checks first, so a broken config never stops a running experiment. The server checks each config's schema and each topology's nodes (such as duplicate or reserved hostnames), the workflow config's schema, that the topology and scenario exist (stored or in phenix-configs/) and go together, and that the plan has no conflict.

If the plan starts the experiment, the dry run also runs the disk check. It reports problems as warnings (in warnings in the REST response) without failing; a problem that would stop the start begins with the start would fail:.

A dry run doesn't merge the topologies that an unstored topology includes, and only checks the schema of an Experiment config. So the real apply can still fail after the injects and configs are in place, but before the experiment changes.

docs.title: Validation Errors
docs.text:
When a config fails schema validation, phēnix explains each error in one line:

<item> "<hostname|name>" (line N): <what> (at <sub-path>)

When the missing key is somewhere else in the same item (usually indented at the wrong level), a hint: line follows. For example, here the second node's image is one level too high:

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Topology
metadata:
  name: helloworld
spec:
  nodes:
  - type: VirtualMachine
    general:
      hostname: host-01
    hardware:
      os_type: linux
      drives:
      - image: ubuntu.qc2
  - type: VirtualMachine
    general:
      hostname: host-02
    hardware:
      os_type: linux
      image: ubuntu.qc2
      drives:
      - interface: virtio

nodes[1] "host-02" (line 21): property "image" is missing (at hardware.drives[0].image)
  hint: "image:" is on line 19 under nodes[1].hardware, but the schema expects it at nodes[1].hardware.drives[0].image

phenix config create, the web UI's config editor and API errors (in metadata.validation) show the same lines.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
The command uses two endpoints, listed under the Workflow tag in the API docs.

Endpoint Description POST /api/v1/workflow/configs/{branch} Create or update one config. POST /api/v1/workflow/apply/{branch} Apply the workflow config and return the action as JSON.

Send the file as the body with Content-Type: application/x-yaml or application/json, plus an auth token when authentication is enabled.

The server fills in ${BRANCH_NAME} with the branch of the URL and keeps every other placeholder as written. A client fills in the other placeholders before it sends a file, or sends variables with it.

To send variables, send a multipart/form-data body with two parts: a config part with the file and its Content-Type, and a variables part with a JSON object of strings. This is what phenix workflow apply sends. The server fills in each placeholder of the file from the variables, and of each included topology file on the apply endpoint. In the file, a placeholder that no variable sets gets its default, or stays as written with a warning. A variable that no file uses is not an error. A value or a default with a line break is an error. A config or an included topology file can be at most 5 MiB after the server fills in the variables and the branch name. For a larger file, the answer is a 400. The answer of a config dry run and of an apply lists the used variables in variables and the warnings in warnings. A warning is for one file, variable and kind, with the first line and the count of the other lines. The answer holds at most 50 variable warnings, and then one that says how many it left out. The server logs each warning. The audit records name the used variables, but never their values. An apply dry run reads each topology file that the topology of the workflow config includes, for every plan, so it reports a line break in an included file.

API=http://localhost:3000/api/v1/workflow
echo '{"SITE": "lab"}' > vars.json
curl -sS --fail-with-body -X POST -F 'config=@phenix.yml;type=application/x-yaml' \
  -F 'variables=<vars.json;type=application/json' "$API/apply/helloworld?dryRun=true"

A config's kind and metadata.name can use no placeholder but ${BRANCH_NAME} and the variables that the request sends.

Query parameter Endpoint Description dryRun=true both Run every check and change nothing. pending=<ref> apply, dry run only A config you'll store before the real apply. <ref> is the pending value its config dry run returned. Repeatable. expect=<action> apply Return 409 and change nothing when the server plans another action. tag=<key>=<value> apply A tag to store on the experiment. Repeatable.

This is what the command does, minus the injects, for one topology config:

API=http://localhost:3000/api/v1/workflow
YAML='Content-Type: application/x-yaml'

# 1. Check the config
curl -sS --fail-with-body -X POST -H "$YAML" --data-binary @phenix-configs/topology.yml "$API/configs/helloworld?dryRun=true"

# 2. Plan the apply, naming the config that step 3 stores
curl -sS --fail-with-body -X POST -H "$YAML" --data-binary @phenix.yml \
  "$API/apply/helloworld?dryRun=true&pending=Topology/helloworld"

# 3. Store the config
curl -sS --fail-with-body -X POST -H "$YAML" --data-binary @phenix-configs/topology.yml "$API/configs/helloworld"

# 4. Apply, only if the plan is still the one step 2 returned
curl -sS --fail-with-body -X POST -H "$YAML" --data-binary @phenix.yml "$API/apply/helloworld?expect=createAndStart"

The apply returns its plan:

{"action":"createAndStart","experiment":"helloworld","reason":"","dryRun":false}

On the phēnix host, the unix socket needs no authentication:

curl -sS --unix-socket /tmp/phenix.sock -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/x-yaml' \
  --data-binary @phenix.yml 'http://unix/api/v1/workflow/apply/helloworld?dryRun=true'

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
With Docker Compose, run the command inside the phenix container, where the socket is:

docker exec phenix phenix workflow apply helloworld -n
docker exec phenix phenix workflow apply /phenix/topologies/helloworld -f

Keep topology directories under /phenix (the same path in the container) and pass an absolute path or a bare name. To change a setting, set its environment variable in the phenix service and recreate the container.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Two settings apply; use absolute paths for both. base-dir.injects (default <base-dir.phenix>/injects) is where injects go, and the server's value wins unless you give --base-dir.injects. base-dir.topologies (default <base-dir.phenix>/topologies) is where a NAME is looked up.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• There's no web UI for workflow apply. A CI job on another machine can call the REST API, but must get the injects onto the phēnix host itself.
  • Of the REST API, only the two workflow endpoints take variables. POST /api/v1/configs, PUT /api/v1/configs/{kind}/{name} and the web UI don't.
  • An apply dry run can reveal whether a file exists on the server; grant workflow:create only to trusted roles.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Permission denied. Your user may not have write access to the socket or the injects directory. Run as the user that runs phenix ui (usually root), or start phenix ui with --unix-socket-gid set to your group.
  • The server doesn't answer. Check that phenix ui is running on the --unix-socket path (/tmp/phenix.sock by default).
  • The server doesn't support workflow dry runs or workflow variables. Upgrade the server.
  • A variable is not set. A file has a ${NAME} placeholder with no value and no default. The error records name the variable, the file and the line. Set it with -e NAME=value or in an env file, write ${NAME:default}, or write $${NAME} to keep the text ${NAME}. Nothing changed.
  • A variable from the shell is not used. sudo and docker exec don't pass your shell environment, an env file overrides the shell, and a variable whose name starts with PHENIX_ needs -e NAME. Run phenix workflow render to see the values.
  • The run asks for -f. The plan would restart a running experiment. Nothing changed; run it again with -f.
  • The plan changed (409). The experiment was started or stopped between the plan and apply steps. Run it again.
  • The injects destination is refused. It overlaps a topology directory, or the server reports a relative base-dir.injects. Check base-dir.injects and -b.
  • A run stopped partway. The injects and stored configs stay in place, and the error says what changed. Fix the cause and run it again. Only a run that stops in apply can have changed the experiment.
  • Hidden .<name>.tmp-* or .<name>.old-* entries in <base-dir.injects>. An interrupted run left them. Remove them when no other run is active.
  • No commit tag. Git refuses a repository another user owns (common under docker exec). Add the directory to git's safe.directory.
  • No output. --log.level at warn or higher hides the plan and result; rely on the exit status.
