docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text: In about 10 minutes, you'll import a topology, arrange it, add a workstation, fix a warning, and publish a topology and an experiment. The example is Riverside Water, a small water utility with an internet edge, a DMZ, a corporate network and an OT network behind a firewall.

docs.title: The Example Lab
docs.text:
You need a phēnix server and a role that can use Builder, such as Global Admin or Builder (see Administration).

Download these files:

  • corp-services.topology.yaml
  • riverside-water.topology.yaml
  • riverside-water.scenario.yaml

Store the three configs and create the experiment riverside from them:

phenix config create corp-services.topology.yaml riverside-water.topology.yaml riverside-water.scenario.yaml
phenix experiment create riverside -t riverside-water -s riverside-water

Or, in the web UI, upload the three configs on the Configs page (see Create a Config), then create the experiment riverside on the Experiments page with the topology and the scenario riverside-water (see Create a New Experiment).

Other pages use a few more example files, which you don't need now: pump-station.topology.yaml, pump-station.builder.json, pump-station.package.yaml, riverside-water.builder.json, lakeside-treatment.builder.json and node-templates.yaml.

docs.title: Step 1: Import the Topology
docs.text:
1. Click Builder in the navigation bar. The drafts page opens.
  2. Click Import.
  3. In the Import topology or experiment dialog, select riverside-water under Source name. Leave the other fields as they are.
  4. Click Import. The dialog says "This import has 1 warning.": dns-01 and ntp-01 come from the included topology corp-services and are read only.
  5. Click Continue to editor.

A new draft named riverside-water opens in the editor. From now on Builder saves every change, and the toolbar shows the save state, for example All changes saved.

docs.title: Step 2: Arrange the Diagram
docs.text:
1. In the toolbar, open the layout menu (it says Default).
  2. Select ELK layered. Each switch moves next to its devices.
  3. Click Auto-group, then select By network. Builder puts each network in a group: CORP, DMZ, INTERNET and OT.
  4. Click Fit diagram to view at the bottom left of the canvas.

The two devices with a dashed border, dns-01 and ntp-01, come from corp-services. You can move them, but you can't change them here.

docs.title: Step 3: Add a Workstation
docs.text:
1. Under Templates in the left column, click Workstation. A device named workstation appears on the canvas, and the Inspector on the right shows its settings.
  2. In the Inspector, set Hostname to ws-03 and Description to Engineering workstation.
  3. Under Network, click Add interface. The new interface is eth0, with Interface kind set to Static or OSPF and Mask set to 24.
  4. Enter Address 10.10.20.103, Gateway 10.10.20.1 and VLAN CORP.
  5. Click Apply.

Because the VLAN names the CORP network, Builder connects eth0 to the CORP switch. The header now counts 13 devices and 16 connections and says No issues. A server that lists its disk images can also warn about an image it doesn't have, but that warning doesn't block publishing.

Tip

You can also connect a device with the mouse: drag from the + handle under the device to a switch. Builder adds the interface and, when the network has a subnet, gives it the next free address.

docs.title: Step 4: Fix a Warning
docs.text:
1. Select historian-01 on the canvas.
  2. Press Ctrl+D (⌘+D on macOS). A copy named historian-01-2 appears with an interface that isn't connected, and the header says 1 warning.
  3. Click 1 warning. The Diagram checks dialog says that eth0 of historian-01-2 has no VLAN.
  4. Click Go to beside the warning. The canvas selects the copy.
  5. Click Delete in the toolbar. The header says No issues again.

A warning like this one blocks publishing, because the experiment would fail or misbehave with it. Other warnings are only for your information (see The Editor).

docs.title: Step 5: Add the Scenario
docs.text:
To publish an experiment with a scenario, add the scenario to the diagram:

  1. Click Scenarios in the toolbar.
  2. Under Scenarios of this diagram, check riverside-water.
  3. Click Save scenarios.

docs.title: Step 6: Publish
docs.text:
1. Click Publish in the toolbar. The Publish diagram dialog opens.
  2. Under What to publish, select Topology and an experiment.
  3. Keep Topology name riverside-water. The hint says "A topology with this name exists. Publishing updates it."
  4. Enter Experiment name riverside-lab.
  5. Keep Experiment scenario riverside-water.
  6. Read Checks. It says that 11 devices, 4 switches, 4 networks and 14 connections are ready to publish. The two included devices aren't copied, because the topology includes corp-services by reference.
  7. Click Update topology and create experiment. Builder asks "Replace topology riverside-water?".
  8. Click Update topology and create experiment again.
  9. The dialog says "Published. Every stage succeeded." Click Close.

phēnix keeps no earlier version of a config, so Builder always asks before it replaces one (see Publishing).

docs.title: Step 7: Open the Result
docs.text:
• The Topology config riverside-water now has ws-03. On the Configs page, its row has the tag builder, which opens the diagram in Builder again.
  • The experiment riverside-lab is on the Experiments page, and Exp in the editor toolbar opens it. To start it, see Experiments.
  • Publishing doesn't update experiments that you made outside Builder, such as riverside.

docs.title: Step 8: Download a Picture
docs.text:
1. Click Download in the toolbar.
  2. Click PNG. The browser saves riverside-water.png.
  3. Click Close.

The same dialog saves Builder JSON, which Upload opens again, and Topology YAML, the Topology config that Publish would write. To move the diagram to another phēnix server, download a Builder package (see Import, Upload and Download).

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• To publish later edits, click Publish again with the same names.
  • To go back to an earlier version, use Draft History (see Drafts).
  • To draw more, see Diagrams and Templates and Icons.
  • If something doesn't work as this page says, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Administration: Details
docs.text:
Info

This page goes deeper than the short guide: Administration.

docs.title: Availability
docs.text:
Every phēnix server has Builder, and no setting turns it on or off. The editor is at /builder, and its API is under /api/v1/builder (see REST API).

phēnix sets no Content-Security-Policy on the application page. If a proxy in front of phēnix adds one, it must allow workers from the phēnix origin and data: images: the layout engine and Auto-group by name pattern run in workers, and custom icons are data: images.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
builder use also covers the Builder schemas that give the fields of the Inspector. The verb "*" gives use too. Any Builder user can open, change and delete any draft.

builder use gives no access to configs (see What Each Task Needs and Resource: configs). A role that limits topology names doesn't limit which Builder files its users can read (see Who Can Read a Builder File).

With authentication disabled, everyone works as global-admin with the Global Admin role, so drafts show global-admin as the user who created and changed them. Global Viewer doesn't have builder use.

Without builder use, the Configs page has no Builder links or buttons. A refused API request answers 403 with a message such as "deleting a Builder draft: user bob does not have permission", and a draft that doesn't exist answers 404.

docs.title: The Builder Role
docs.text:
Builder (builder) shows the role as YAML. It gives no access to User, Role or Image configs. Each time phenix ui starts:

  • If the store has no role named builder and no role with the role name Builder, phēnix creates it, so a deleted role comes back.
  • If the role exists, phēnix keeps its policies. If it lacks builder use, phēnix adds the builder policy to the role and to its users. Nothing else changes.

docs.title: What Each Task Needs
docs.text:
builder use alone covers drafts and snapshots, undo and redo, the libraries, the default layer set, the Inspector fields, and Upload of a Builder document from a file or pasted text. Other tasks also need:

Task Other permissions See the Published Diagrams tab configs list on the topologies it lists Open a published diagram (Open, Edit as a draft or Upload) configs get on that topology, such as Topology/riverside-water (this doesn't protect a Builder file) Import a stored config configs get on the config, and topologies list (or experiments list) on its name Import a config file, or convert a legacy Builder diagram with Upload configs get and create Upload a Builder package configs get, and create to create the configs you tick Open a topology in Builder from the Configs page configs list, and get on the topology (create to import it) See Exp, which opens the experiment of a publication experiments get on that experiment Add a stored scenario to a diagram configs list and scenarios list View, edit, create or upload a scenario in the Scenarios dialog configs on Scenario/<name>: get to view, update to edit, create to create or upload, and get and update to replace a scenario with an uploaded file See the apps of the diagram's scenario in the Inspector configs get on Scenario/<name> Download Topology YAML or a package configs get Use Publish, in the editor or on a draft card configs update Publish a topology configs create (new) or update (existing) on Topology/<name>. For a draft imported from a stored config, also configs get and topologies get (or experiments get) on that config Publish an experiment experiments and configs create (new) or update (existing) on Experiment/<name> Publish a diagram that lists scenarios configs get and scenarios list on each listed Scenario/<name>, and configs update on each scenario whose topology annotation doesn't name the topology yet See which host pins an experiment update removed experiments/schedule get (otherwise the warning only counts them) Delete a published topology configs get and delete on Topology/<name> Get drive image suggestions and missing-image checks disks list Run Preflight configs get, plus per check (a check without its permission shows as unavailable): Host capacity, hosts list. Networks, hosts list, experiments list for the VLANs of running experiments, and configs and experiments get on the named experiment. Disk images, disks list. Scenario apps, applications list, and configs get and scenarios list on each listed scenario

Import and Publish read included topologies, such as corp-services, with the user's own configs get and topologies list permissions, and warn about an include the user can't read. An import of a config file keeps each ${NAME} and ${NAME:default} as written, so Builder never shows the server's environment variables.

docs.title: The Libraries
docs.text:
No role can change these library items, Global Admin included (see The template library, Layer sets and Custom icons):

Item A change answers The five built-in templates, and the templates and collections of template files on the server 409, template.item.read-only The built-in layer set Purdue Model (ID builtin:purdue) 403, layerset.read-only (also for a delete) The icons that phēnix adds from template files 403 (rename or delete)

Any Builder user can rename or delete an uploaded icon. When someone deletes the default layer set (see Layers for new diagrams), the server has no default. A diagram keeps its own copies of templates and layers, so a library change doesn't change the diagram (see Linked templates).

phēnix logs each add, change or delete of a template, collection or layer set, each choice of a default layer set, and each upload, rename or delete of an icon, with the user name.

docs.title: Example Role
docs.text: The example role topology-designer.role.yaml has builder use, configs list and get on Topology/*, Scenario/* and Experiment/*, list and get on topologies, scenarios and experiments, and disks list. Its users can import stored configs, open published diagrams and download Topology YAML. To let the role publish, add create, update and delete to its configs policy.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Drafts, published documents and the three libraries are records in the phēnix store (the store.endpoint setting), in namespaces that start with builder.. Their limits are in Limits. The built-in templates and layer set are part of phēnix, not store records, and phēnix keeps the collections of template files in memory only.

The libraries belong to the server. When someone deletes a user account, its icons, templates and layer sets stay, and createdBy and updatedBy keep the user name.

A publish stores a copy of the diagram that never changes, the published document, which the builder-doc annotation names. After a publish, phēnix deletes the topology's older published documents that are more than one hour old. When anyone deletes or renames a topology, by any means, phēnix deletes its published documents (one less than an hour old can stay for a while, in case a publish is in progress). This never reads, changes or deletes a Builder file.

The browser keeps unsaved changes in the IndexedDB database phenix-builder, and preferences in localStorage keys that start with phenix.builder.. Logging out deletes the unsaved changes (see Logging out).

docs.title: Cleaning Up Storage
docs.text:
When phēnix starts, and every hour while it runs, it deletes the published documents that no topology references, and the stored document content that no draft or published document names. It keeps:

  • what phēnix stored in the last hour, since a publish or a save may still reference it
  • every published document, when a topology can't be read or its builder-doc annotation doesn't decode
  • a published document that it can't read, and its content
  • every Builder file

phēnix leaves a published document it can't read (a newer phēnix may have saved it) out of every list, and logs skipping unreadable builder published document with the ID. To delete it, send DELETE /builder/documents/{document} with that ID, which changes no config. The role needs configs get and delete on the topology the record names, or on */* when it names none. For If-Match, send any tag: the 412 answer gives the right one in its ETag header.

Clean up… in the Builder settings does the same at once, and also deletes each draft whose current snapshot is the last one it published, with no newer snapshot, while its topology still references what it published. The topology and its published document stay. A draft also stays when its topology was deleted or published again from another draft (it's then the only copy of its diagram), or when it changes while the cleanup runs.

A cleanup waits for a publish that is in progress. With ?dryRun=true, POST /builder/cleanup deletes nothing and tells you what it would delete:

{"dryRun": true, "drafts": ["4b0c…"], "documents": 1, "content": 2}

drafts lists draft IDs, and documents and content count published documents and stored document content. If the cleanup can't read or delete an item, the answer has a Warning header and the server log gives the reason. The answer still lists the deleted drafts.

docs.title: Template Files on the Server
docs.text:
The guide covers where the directory is and how to change it. Each file becomes a read-only server collection, in the format that the Node Templates tab downloads (see Downloading and importing templates).

phēnix reads at most 50 files directly in the directory, in name order: names that end in .yaml, .yml or .json in any case, and that don't start with .. It doesn't read subdirectories. A file must be a regular file of at most 8 MiB, as JSON or YAML, and phēnix only follows a symbolic link that stays in the directory. When the directory doesn't exist or can't be read, phēnix has no server collections and Builder still starts.

For each file it skips, phēnix logs skipping builder template file with the file and the reason. It logs builder template directory cannot be read when the path isn't a directory, and read builder template files with the counts.

The custom icons of a file go into the icon library under their names, if the library doesn't have them yet. The icon dialog shows them as from "Server". They fill at most 1,000 of the 2,000 icons; phēnix skips the rest and logs builder icon library has no room for more template file icons. When the library already has an icon of that name with a different picture, the library keeps its picture, and phēnix logs builder template file icon differs from the icon library's, which is kept.

The IDs of collections and templates come from the file name and the template name, so they stay the same across restarts. Renaming a file gives its collection a new ID, and a diagram links its copy of a template by that ID (see Linked templates).

docs.title: The builder-doc Annotation
docs.text:
The annotation is a map with up to three keys:

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Topology
metadata:
  name: pump-station
  annotations:
    builder-doc:
      digest: sha256:1c92d3b0c95588fbb20926c1e58bb0452903c4e2cb0ffbf12fcdc19f72717732
      id: fd063e784604f43e5c39cc9959501cf117b4dc2be895e92f9bb98e23f8465c4b
      path: /phenix/topologies/pump-station/pump-station.builder.json
spec:
  ...
Key What it holds digest sha256: and 64 lowercase hex digits: the published document with that content for this topology, or with path, the document the file must hold id The ID of a published document in the store, valid only for the topology that received it path The absolute path of a Builder file on the phēnix server (see Builder Documents in Files)

The map needs at least one of these keys, and no others. Publish writes digest and id, and keeps a path. builder-doc is the only annotation that is a map (an object, in JSON); all other annotations are text.

docs.title: Which Diagram a Topology Shows
docs.text:
1. The published document that the annotation names: by id, or by digest when there's no id. It must belong to this topology, and match the digest, if any.
  2. Otherwise, the Builder file at path. It must hold the document with the digest, if any.
  3. Otherwise, none. Published Diagrams doesn't list the topology, and on the Configs page its builder tag and edit button open the Import dialog with "Topology pump-station has no Builder diagram to open. Import it to make one."

The stored document comes first because Publish wrote the stored topology from it, while the file may have changed since.

docs.title: What phenix Checks
docs.text:
phēnix checks the annotation each time anyone creates or updates a Topology config, by any means, and refuses a config whose builder-doc isn't valid. With phenix config create, the log line before the error gives the reason:

$ phenix config create pump-station.topology.yaml
2026-10-01 21:52:35.595 ERR calling config hook: config validation failed: topology pump-station: builder: invalid request: builder-doc.path: must be an absolute path type=SYSTEM uuid=197b8a05-ccb3-4162-994a-c39d8ebc1dc5
Error: Unable to create configuration from pump-station.topology.yaml (search error logs for 197b8a05-ccb3-4162-994a-c39d8ebc1dc5)
Reason What is wrong value must be an object builder-doc is text, not a map property "file" is unsupported A key other than digest, id and path there must be at least 1 properties The map is empty builder-doc: digest is not a sha256 digest digest isn't sha256: and 64 lowercase hex digits builder-doc.path: must be an absolute path path doesn't start with / builder-doc.path: must be a clean path, with no ".", "..", "//" or trailing "/" path has one of these builder-doc.path: must end in .json, .yaml or .yml path has a different ending, or an ending in capitals, such as .JSON

A path can be at most 1024 bytes. phēnix doesn't look for the file when it stores the config.

phenix config edit can't delete an annotation. To delete builder-doc, send the config without it with PUT /api/v1/configs/topology/<name>, or delete the topology and create it again.

docs.title: Renaming and Copying a Topology
docs.text:
A published document belongs to one topology name. After a rename, or a copy of the config under a new name, the id and digest no longer name a document of that topology, so phēnix changes the annotation:

  • Without a path, phēnix deletes the annotation. The topology is a plain Topology config until someone publishes it again.
  • With a path, phēnix deletes the id. The path and digest stay, so phēnix reads the topology from the file, which must still hold the document with that digest.

docs.title: Builder Documents in Files
docs.text: Instead of a published document, a topology can name a Builder document in a file on the phēnix server, such as a repository you check out there. The guide has the steps (see A Builder file beside a topology).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The directory /phenix/topologies/pump-station/ holds two files:

  • pump-station.builder.json, the Builder document (the example file pump-station.builder.json).

  • pump-station.topology.yaml, the Topology config, with a builder-doc annotation that names the document:

    apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Topology
metadata:
    name: pump-station
    annotations:
        builder-doc:
            path: /phenix/topologies/pump-station/pump-station.builder.json
spec:
    nodes:
        - general:
            description: Field engineering laptop
            hostname: eng-ws-01
        - ... # the rest of the nodes

Make the config from Download > Topology YAML (see Topology YAML). Don't use the example file pump-station.topology.yaml here: its node order is different, and a draft made from the file can't update a topology that differs from what the document publishes.

$ phenix config create /phenix/topologies/pump-station/pump-station.topology.yaml
2026-10-01 21:52:35.788 INF configuration created type=SYSTEM kind=Topology name=pump-station

Its diagram opens read only (see Diagrams read from a file). phēnix keeps no copy of the file, so after a git pull the next Open shows the new diagram, but the stored Topology config doesn't change. To make it match the file again, create the config again, or publish a draft made from the file.

docs.title: Which Files phenix Reads
docs.text:
phēnix reads a Builder file only when all of these are true:

  • It's below the phēnix base directory: /phenix, or the base-dir.phenix setting (see Settings).
  • It's not below the VM mount directory: /phenix/mounts, or the mount-dir setting.
  • It's a regular file, not a directory, a device or a pipe. phēnix only follows a symbolic link whose target is a relative path that stays below the base directory and outside the mount directory, so it refuses an absolute target, such as from ln -s /phenix/topologies/a.json b.json.
  • It's at most 5 MiB.
  • It holds one valid Builder document, as JSON or YAML. The content sets the format, not the file name. A YAML file must not use anchors, aliases, merge keys or more than one document.

When the CLI creates the config from a file, phēnix fills in ${NAME} in the path from the environment. A config sent to the REST API only fills in ${BRANCH_NAME}. phēnix doesn't fill in ${NAME} in the Builder file.

phēnix resolves the path on the server that runs phenix ui, so servers that share one store each read their own file system.

phēnix only reads the file when someone opens the diagram, makes a draft from it, or publishes that draft. Published Diagrams shows a card even when the file is missing or invalid, and no config change or phenix command reads the file.

docs.title: Who Can Read a Builder File
docs.text:
Anyone whose role has configs get on the topology can open its diagram, and anyone who can list the config can see the path.

Warning

The name of a topology doesn't protect its Builder file. A user who has configs get, and create or update, on any one topology name can store a topology there with any path below the base directory, and then open the diagram of that file.

For example, a role limited to Topology/teama-* can still store teama-x with the path of a team B Builder file, and open it. A fixed layout such as /phenix/topologies/<name>/ makes the path easy to guess.

Only keep a Builder file below the base directory if each user who can create or update a topology may read it. A published document doesn't have this problem, because it belongs to its topology.

docs.title: Pinning the File with a Digest
docs.text:
Add digest beside path to accept only one document:

builder-doc:
  digest: sha256:1c92d3b0c95588fbb20926c1e58bb0452903c4e2cb0ffbf12fcdc19f72717732
  path: /phenix/topologies/pump-station/pump-station.builder.json

If the file holds a different document, the diagram doesn't open.

The digest is the SHA-256 of the document as phēnix writes it, not of the file, so sha256sum of a YAML file, or of JSON with different spacing, key order or final line break, gives a different value. Get the digest from the REST API (see Examples).

docs.title: When the File Cannot Be Used
docs.text:
Opening the diagram then fails with "Could not open the diagram of topology pump-station." and one of these sentences, which the REST API gives as message. The phēnix log says builder document file not usable, with the topology, the path and the reason.

Message Status Why "Builder file … is outside /phenix, the directory phenix reads Builder files from." 422 The path isn't below the base directory, or it's below the mount directory "Builder file … does not exist on this phenix server." 404 No file is at the path, or a part of the path is a file "phenix cannot read Builder file …." 422 phēnix has no read permission, a symbolic link isn't allowed, or the read failed "Builder file … is not a regular file." 422 The path is a directory, a device or a pipe "Builder file … is larger than 5 MiB." 413 The file is too large "Builder file … is not a valid Builder document. Upload it in the Builder to see why." 422 Upload shows the problem (see Uploading a Builder document) "Builder file … does not match the digest topology pump-station records for it." 422 The file holds a document with a different digest

docs.title: Editing and Publishing
docs.text:
A draft made with Edit as a draft from the file can update the topology under the rules in Publishing to a topology that names a Builder file. Publish never writes the file. It stores a published document and writes digest and id beside the path:

builder-doc:
  digest: sha256:4ba9ae46494bb7d2498f5119b55996f332c52c1b95d79502361afbf50707cbc3
  id: 89f0a9779c2e5892da9f7a9ae2ed5c58c564fe57ea86f50f4452f174cb68ad93
  path: /phenix/topologies/pump-station/pump-station.builder.json

The topology then shows the published document, without the File tag, and the file is out of date until you replace it. The path stays for any other phēnix server that gets this config without the published document: that server reads its own file, if the file matches the digest.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Scripts use the same REST API as the web UI, under /api/v1. The interactive API docs at /docs/ describe each route under the Builder tag (see Interactive API Docs). No single request publishes a Builder file: create a draft from the document, then publish the draft.

Each route needs builder use. These routes also need configs permissions:

Route What it does configs permission POST /builder/drafts/{draft}/publish Publish the draft. With "dryRun": true, report what publishing would change and write nothing (no If-Match needed) That of each config POST /builder/drafts/{draft}/preflight Run the preflight checks named in checks (capacity, network, disks, apps), against the named experiment, if any get, plus those of each check (see What Each Task Needs) GET /builder/sources The configs that a document can come from or publish with list POST /builder/generate Make a document from a stored config or a config file, with the import options (includes, copy, name) get, and create for a config file POST /builder/legacy Convert a legacy Builder diagram, or a Topology config file that holds one get and create POST /builder/export/topology The Topology YAML that a document would publish get POST /builder/package The Builder package of a document, with the sections in include get, and for each config in the package, get with scenarios or topologies list POST /builder/package/resolve Whether each item the package needs is present, missing, different or unknown here get, list for icons, disks list for disk images, applications list for apps GET /builder/documents The published documents (source store), and the topologies that name a Builder file (source file, with path and no id) list GET /builder/documents/{document} Read a published document get on its topology DELETE /builder/documents/{document} Delete a published topology and its published documents, or an unreadable published document get and delete on the topology GET /builder/topologies/{topology}/document Read the diagram that builder-doc names, from the store or the file get on the topology

These routes need only builder use:

Route Notes GET /schemas/builder/v1, /schemas/builder/templates/v1, /schemas/builder/package/v1, /schemas/builder/layersets/v1 JSON Schemas of the Builder document, template file, package and layer set file GET, POST /builder/drafts The list has drafts (latest change first), damaged and limits.drafts GET, DELETE /builder/drafts/{draft} DELETE also works on a damaged draft GET, POST /builder/drafts/{draft}/snapshots POST saves a new version GET, DELETE /builder/drafts/{draft}/snapshots/{snapshot} You can't delete the current snapshot PATCH /builder/drafts/{draft}/cursor Undo and redo: choose the current snapshot POST /builder/cleanup See Cleaning Up Storage GET, POST /builder/icons The list has no images, but gives maxIcons and an etag for If-None-Match (304 while unchanged) GET, PUT, DELETE /builder/icons/{icon} GET also works with an old name. PUT renames an uploaded icon, keeping at most 16 old names GET /builder/templates The library (templates, collections), builtins and the server collections (preloaded) POST /builder/templates/items, PUT /builder/templates/items/{template} Add templates (with collection, in a new collection), or replace one POST /builder/templates/collections, PUT /builder/templates/collections/{collection} Add or replace a collection POST /builder/templates/delete Delete templates and collections GET, POST /builder/layersets Built-in sets first, then by name, with defaultId, defaultEtag, damaged and the limits GET, PUT /builder/layersets/default "id": null clears the default GET, PUT, DELETE /builder/layersets/{layerset} Not for a built-in set (PUT, DELETE)

These requests need an If-Match header with the item's etag from the last response: each change to an existing draft, PUT and DELETE of a layer set, PUT of a template or collection, PUT /builder/layersets/default, and DELETE of an icon or a published topology. Without it, the request answers 400. An older tag answers 412 (template.item.stale, layerset.stale or request.stale) with the current ETag, so read the item again, check it, and resend. POST /builder/templates/delete takes each item's etag in the body ({"templates": [{"id": "…", "etag": "\"3\""}]}), and answers 412 and deletes nothing if any of them changed.

Use the etag in the body of draft responses rather than the ETag header, which a compressing proxy can change. Templates, collections, layer sets and icons carry createdBy and updatedBy; an item that no user added, such as a built-in template, has no createdBy.

With authentication enabled, send a token in the X-Phenix-Auth-Token header as Bearer <token> (see Generating User Authentication Tokens). A refused request answers with a JSON body whose code names the failure, such as publish.topology.exists (see Errors of the REST API).

docs.title: Response Headers
docs.text: Every Builder response, the schema routes included, has X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Cache-Control: no-store, so no browser or proxy keeps a copy. The icon responses also have Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
These examples use the example lab and jq. Set the server and your token first:

PHENIX=http://localhost:3000
TOKEN='your-token'   # a token from the Users page

List the drafts:

curl -s -H "X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer $TOKEN" "$PHENIX/api/v1/builder/drafts" \
  | jq '.drafts[] | {title, createdBy, id, etag}'

{
  "title": "Riverside Water",
  "createdBy": "darrow",
  "id": "6290aef3-24a3-4126-b90a-308cbf561f17",
  "etag": "\"10\""
}

Make a document from the stored topology riverside-water, as Import does. POST /builder/generate writes nothing:

curl -s -X POST -H "X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"source":"Topology/riverside-water"}' "$PHENIX/api/v1/builder/generate" > generated.json
jq '{name: .document.metadata.name, source: .source.fullName, warnings}' generated.json

{
  "name": "riverside-water",
  "source": "Topology/riverside-water",
  "warnings": [
    "The Builder added 2 nodes from included topology corp-services (2 nodes). The diagram shows them read only. Edit them in their own topology. Publishing keeps includeTopologies and does not copy them."
  ]
}

Store the document as a draft. The sourceToken connects the draft to its topology, so the draft can publish back to riverside-water:

jq '{title: .document.metadata.name, sourceToken: .source.fullName, document}' generated.json \
  | curl -s -X POST -H "X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d @- "$PHENIX/api/v1/builder/drafts" > created.json
jq '{id, createdBy, title, etag}' created.json

To keep the name of an uploaded file (the Inspector's Source file), send sourceFile beside document: a plain file name of at most 255 bytes, with no / or \. The answers to creating and saving a draft have no document; they give createdBy, createdAt, updatedBy and updatedAt as stamp (see Who made and last saved a diagram).

Convert a legacy Builder diagram, as Upload does. content is the XML of the diagram, or a Topology config that holds it in builder-xml, and name names a diagram that has no topology. The answer has the same form as for POST /builder/generate:

jq -Rs '{content: ., name: "plant"}' plant.xml \
  | curl -s -X POST -H "X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d @- "$PHENIX/api/v1/builder/legacy" > converted.json
jq '{name: .document.metadata.name, warnings}' converted.json

Delete the draft with its current ETag. The delete answers 204, or 400 without If-Match:

ID=$(jq -r .id created.json)
ETAG=$(curl -s -H "X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer $TOKEN" "$PHENIX/api/v1/builder/drafts/$ID" | jq -r .etag)
curl -s -X DELETE -H "X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "If-Match: $ETAG" \
  "$PHENIX/api/v1/builder/drafts/$ID"

Read the diagram of the topology pump-station (see Builder Documents in Files), without the document itself:

curl -s -H "X-Phenix-Auth-Token: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "$PHENIX/api/v1/builder/topologies/pump-station/document" | jq 'del(.document)'

{
  "source": "file",
  "digest": "sha256:1c92d3b0c95588fbb20926c1e58bb0452903c4e2cb0ffbf12fcdc19f72717732",
  "size": 6517,
  "target": "pump-station",
  "kind": "Topology",
  "config": "Topology/pump-station",
  "path": "/phenix/topologies/pump-station/pump-station.builder.json"
}

digest is the value to write beside path (see Pinning the File with a Digest). For a file, the answer has "topologyDiffers": true when the stored topology isn't what the document publishes. For a published document, source is store, and the answer has id, createdBy and createdAt instead of path.

docs.title: Compressed Files
docs.text:
The UI build writes a Brotli and a gzip copy of the large Builder scripts, and phēnix sends the one the browser accepts, with a one-year cache (a changed file gets a new name). PHENIX_BROTLI_QUALITY sets the Brotli quality of the UI build: a whole number from 0 to 11, by default 9. Higher is smaller and slower to build, and any other value stops the build. The Docker and Podman images (docker/Dockerfile, which make docker and make deb use unless PHENIX_BUILD_IMAGE names another image) build with quality 11.

cd src/js
PHENIX_BROTLI_QUALITY=11 npm run build

# or, for the Docker image
docker build --build-arg PHENIX_BROTLI_QUALITY=9 -t phenix -f docker/Dockerfile .

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: The problems an administrator can fix, such as a missing permission, a Builder file that phēnix can't use, or a proxy that blocks the layout engine, are in Troubleshooting, with the steps for each.

docs.title: Checks and Preflight: Details
docs.text:
Info

This page goes deeper than the short guide: The Editor.

docs.title: Checks and Warnings
docs.text:
Go to on an issue about a network goes to its switch. An issue about the whole diagram, or about a network with no switch, has no Go to. The Publish diagram dialog shows the warnings that block publishing as errors (see What blocks publishing). For the code and default severity of each issue, see Codes.

Devices from included topologies get no warnings, because they belong to their own topology. A hostname that an included device also uses is still an error, though, and an address that it also uses is a warning.

When the server doesn't list its disk images, the dialog says The Builder does not check drive images, because the server did not list its disk images. Otherwise, a drive image that the server doesn't have is a warning.

docs.title: Rulesets and Addresses
docs.text:
phēnix accepts these settings, but they don't work the way the diagram shows them. None of these warnings blocks publishing. Publish and the Topology YAML download list them too.

Warning Code Go to opens A device that isn't a Router or a Firewall has firewall rulesets, or an interface that names one. The vrouter app ignores them. device.rulesets.ignored The Type of the device An Inbound ruleset or Outbound ruleset of an interface names no ruleset of its device, so the vrouter app applies no firewall to that interface. interface.ruleset.unknown The ruleset field An interface's address isn't a host address of its network's subnet. interface.ip.outside-subnet The Address No interface on a network has the network's gateway address. Interfaces of external devices and of included topologies count. network.gateway.unowned The Gateway of the network The subnets of two networks overlap. network.subnet.overlap The Subnet of the network

Overlapping subnets are a problem only when the networks connect, for example through a router. If you reuse a subnet on purpose in isolated enclaves, you can ignore this warning.

docs.title: Device Settings
docs.text:
phēnix apps don't apply these device settings the way the diagram shows them. The Inspector shows these warnings at the field, and Publish and the Topology YAML download list them too. Three of them block publishing.

Devices from included topologies and external devices get none of these warnings (phēnix still reads the ntp-server label of an external device). A device whose phenix/default-apps annotation is false isn't configured by the phēnix apps, so it gets no warning about its OS type, interfaces, OSPF or vrouter/enable-ssh. It still gets the others.

Warning Code Go to opens A device has no drive under Drives. phēnix needs a drive to start it. This blocks publishing. device.drives.none Add drive under Drives A Router or Firewall has an OS type other than vyatta, vyos or minirouter, so phēnix doesn't configure its routing or firewall. phēnix still configures linux as Vyatta, but this is deprecated. device.router-os.unsupported OS type A device that isn't a Router or Firewall has static interfaces, and an OS type other than linux, rhel, centos or windows, for example other. phēnix writes no interface configuration for it. device.interfaces.unconfigured OS type A device has serial interfaces, but its OS type isn't exactly linux, the only one on which phēnix sets them up. device.serial.unconfigured OS type A device has file injections or deletions, but Snapshot is off, or the Inject partition of its first drive is 0, so phēnix doesn't apply them. device.injections.unapplied Snapshot, or the Inject partition of the drive A Vyatta or VyOS router (OS type vyatta, vyos or linux) has an ospf interface but no network.ospf. The experiment doesn't start. This blocks publishing. device.ospf.missing The Protocol of the interface An ospf interface of a minirouter has an address in no area network of its network.ospf, or the device has no network.ospf. The interface is in no OSPF area. interface.ospf.outside-area The Address of the interface An area network of a minirouter holds the address of none of its ospf interfaces, so minirouter doesn't advertise it. device.ospf-network.unused The area network A minirouter has network.ospf, but no ospf interface. device.ospf.unused network.ospf The ntp-server label names no interface of its device, or one with no IP address. The experiment doesn't start. This blocks publishing. device.ntp-server.invalid The value of the label More than one device has the ntp-server label. phēnix uses only the first one, in the order of the diagram. device.ntp-server.ignored The value of the label The diagram has Vyatta or VyOS routers, and the ntp-server device has no interface on VLAN mgmt (in any case). The routers get no NTP server, unless an ntp app of the scenario names one. device.ntp-server.no-mgmt The value of the label The vrouter/enable-ssh annotation of a Vyatta or VyOS router isn't an IP address or the name of an interface with an IP address, so phēnix doesn't enable SSH. No other device reads this annotation. device.enable-ssh.invalid The value of the annotation An entry of the phenix/startup-autotunnel annotation isn't "port", "port:dport" or "port:host:dport" with ports from 1 to 65535 (a dport of VNC, in any case, permits an empty host). phēnix skips each bad entry, and opens no tunnel when the value isn't a list of texts. device.autotunnel.invalid The value of the annotation The phenix/default-apps annotation isn't true or false, for example the text "false". phēnix runs its default apps. device.default-apps.invalid The value of the annotation The phenix/startup-set-hostname annotation is not true or false, for example the text "false". phenix sets the hostname. device.set-hostname.invalid The value of the annotation

phēnix matches interface names in any case, so ETH0 names eth0. In the Inspector, the values of the ntp-server label and the vrouter/enable-ssh annotation suggest the device's interface names.

docs.title: Fixing an Issue in One Step
docs.text:
Some issues have a Fix button that says what it does, for example Fix: Rename web-01 to web-01-2. The dialog stays open, and Undo reverts each fix as one step.

Issue Code What Fix does Two devices have the same hostname node.hostname.duplicate Renames the device to the next free hostname, such as web-01-2. When the other device is from an included topology, Fix renames the one in this diagram. Interfaces on one network use the same IP address interface.ip.shared Gives the interface the first free address of the subnet, with the same gateway rules as Assign addresses. Interfaces on one network use the same MAC address interface.mac.shared Clears the MAC address of the interface, so phēnix makes one when the experiment starts.

There's no Fix when the draft is read only, or when the device is from an included topology, which has to fix it. For an IP address, there's no Fix when the interface is on no network, its network has no subnet, or the subnet has no free address. Set a Subnet for the network, or type a new address in the Inspector. A router keeps the gateway address, so its interface gets no Fix. When several routers have the gateway address, the first one keeps it, and Fix gives each other router a free address.

docs.title: Preflight
docs.text:
The steps to run Preflight are in the guide.

Check What it compares Host capacity The hardware.vcpus and hardware.memory of each device that isn't external, against the free resources of the schedulable cluster hosts. Unset values count as 1 vCPU and 512 MB. Each device must fit on one host, and too little free memory fails the check. Too few free CPUs is only a warning, because VMs can share CPUs. Networks The VLANs of the devices and the VLAN aliases of the networks, against the VLAN range of the experiment that you name, if it sets one. The aliases, against the VLANs of the running experiments. The bridges of the interfaces and the experiment's default bridge (phenix without an experiment), against the bridges of the schedulable hosts. A missing bridge is only a warning, because minimega creates it when the experiment starts. Disk images Each drive image, by file name, against the disk images of the server. The kind must agree: a VM or ISO image for a kvm device, a container image for a container. A new image can take up to 10 seconds to show up. Scenario apps Each app that the diagram's scenarios run, against the default apps, the built-in apps and the user apps on the server's PATH. Disabled apps don't count.

The report gives a total, for example Preflight: 3 passed, 1 unavailable. Each issue has its code, and an issue about a device or a network has Go to. The report stays until the diagram changes.

A check is Unavailable when Builder couldn't do all of it, and Builder still does the other checks. The issue gives the cause:

  • Your role doesn't have the permission the check needs (see What each task needs).
  • Builder can't connect to minimega.
  • The server lists no disk images, or doesn't list them within 10 seconds.
  • The check took longer than 20 seconds.

  • Publishing: Details: what blocks publishing, and what publishing writes.

docs.title: Building a Diagram: Details
docs.text:
Note

This page goes deeper than the short guide: Diagrams.

The examples use the Riverside Water draft of the example lab. Icons, Layers and Scenarios and Included Topologies have their own pages.

docs.title: Adding Devices
docs.text:
Clicking an item under Nodes & Objects drops the device in free space on the visible canvas and selects it. For what Device and the five built-in templates set, see Built-in templates. The built-in templates are read only; to change one, duplicate it into the server's template library (see Node Templates).

For a VyOS router such as edge-rtr, set OS type to vyos and the drive's Image to vyos.qc2. The vrouter app configures the interfaces, routes and rulesets of a Router or Firewall (see vrouter App).

docs.title: Adding Switches and Networks
docs.text:
A new switch comes with a new network named EXP, then EXP-2 and so on. A network's fields are all optional:

  • VLAN alias, from 1 to 4094. When you publish with an experiment, it becomes the network's entry in vlans.aliases (see Publishing a topology and an experiment).
  • Subnet, an IPv4 network in CIDR form such as 10.1.0.0/24.
  • Gateway, the address of the router on the network. It must be a host address in the subnet, such as 10.1.0.1 in 10.1.0.0/24.

Type # in the command palette to find a network. A network can have more than one switch (after a paste, for example), and Remove network in the command palette deletes it with all its switches and connections.

Deleting the last switch of a network deletes the network too, unless an unconnected interface's VLAN still names it. In that case the checks warn that the network has no switch; add a switch, change the VLAN, or use Remove network. A diagram that you open or upload keeps all its networks.

docs.title: Subnets and Addresses
docs.text:
Builder gives addresses only to static interfaces (Interface kind Static or OSPF) that have none. It never changes an existing address, or a device from an included topology.

An assigned address is the next free host address in the subnet: not the gateway, and not used by another interface on the network. The interface also gets the subnet's prefix length as its Mask, and the network's gateway if it has no Gateway of its own. With 10.1.0.0/24 and gateway 10.1.0.1, the first interface gets 10.1.0.2, mask 24 and gateway 10.1.0.1.

Routers (devices of type Router or Firewall) get their addresses first and never get a Gateway of their own:

  • If no interface on the network has the gateway address, the first router interface gets it.
  • If the network has no gateway, the first router interface gets the next free address, which becomes the network's Gateway in the same step.
  • Other router interfaces get the next free addresses.

The suggested subnet of a new network is the first 10.N.M.0/24 that overlaps no subnet and holds no interface or gateway address of the diagram, so in an empty diagram it's 10.1.0.0/24. A network that you import or upload keeps its own subnet, or has none.

Builder assigns addresses when you connect a static interface to a switch (including by pasting or duplicating a device with its switch), and when you click Assign addresses. Turning off the Assign addresses on connect setting (in the Editing section of Settings) stops the first case only.

When Builder gives no address on connect, it says why, such as "No address set: network CORP has no subnet." or "No address set: subnet 10.1.0.0/30 of network SCADA is full." A static interface without an address stops Apply of its device.

docs.title: Connecting Interfaces
docs.text: Dragging from one device to another adds a switch between them, with a new network named EXP and a suggested subnet. You can't connect two switches, since each switch is a network. A published diagram and an included device have no + handle.

docs.title: Add a Connection Without Dragging
docs.text: Add connection in the Inspector header, or Add a connection… in the command palette, opens a dialog with the selection filled in. Pick the Device, the Interface (Add a new interface or one with no connection) and the Switch, then click Connect. The command has no default key (see Customizing shortcuts).

docs.title: Type the VLAN in the Inspector
docs.text:
Applying a network's name in an interface's VLAN field connects the interface to that network's switch, as the quick start does for ws-03:

The VLAN matches a network name in any letter case, and the name of another network moves the connection. A renamed interface keeps its connection as long as its VLAN names the same network. If you remove one interface and add another in the same Apply, the new one doesn't inherit the old connection; it connects only if its VLAN names a network.

Under Connection points, Disconnect, Add connection point and Remove connection point take effect at once, without Apply. A disconnected interface blocks publishing (see What blocks publishing).

docs.title: Hiding Connections
docs.text: Hide connections in the command palette, or Alt+Shift+C (⌥+⇧+C on macOS), hides the connections on your canvas only; run it again, or use the Show connections switch in Settings, to show them. The diagram keeps every connection, so the checks, Publish and the PNG and SVG downloads still include them. While they're hidden you can't select a connection, but dragging from a connection point still connects it.

docs.title: Editing Device Settings
docs.text:
See Editing a node for the Inspector and the Node Editor. An interface's Interface kind is Static or OSPF (an address you give, or Builder assigns), DHCP or manual (from DHCP or set inside the VM), or Serial. A new interface is Static or OSPF with Mask 24, and an external device's interfaces are always static. Changing the kind asks first, and Switch and clear empties every field of the interface, Name and VLAN included.

The eye button beside Description hides the description on the canvas (see Hiding descriptions on the canvas). Generate a random MAC address, beside MAC address, writes a locally administered unicast address that no other interface in the diagram uses; click Apply to keep it.

miniccc commands, under More settings, lists the commands that phēnix gives miniccc to run in the VM, such as exec df -h.

docs.title: Duplicating a Device
docs.text: Duplicate pastes a copy of the selected nodes next to them, with every setting, addresses included, but no connections. The unconnected interface is a warning, and once the copy is on the same network, so is the shared address. Give the copy its own hostname and address (see Example: Riverside Water expansion).

docs.title: Drive Images
docs.text: When Builder can list the server's disk images, a drive's Image suggests them, and an image the server doesn't have is a warning. When the server lists no images, the checks skip images.

docs.title: Routes and Rulesets
docs.text: An interface's Inbound ruleset and Outbound ruleset suggest the device's rulesets, including unapplied ones. The vrouter app applies rulesets only on a Router or Firewall, and skips a ruleset name the device doesn't have; the checks warn about both (see Rulesets and addresses).

docs.title: Labels and Annotations
docs.text:
Each label or annotation under More settings is a Name and a Value, as on web-01:

Builder reads an annotation value as YAML: true, false and numbers become those values, and ["8080:80"] is a list. Apps read annotations to configure a node (see Apps).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: A note also has a Color. Resize a selected note the same way as a group.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
A new group is named "Group" ("Group 2" and so on if that's taken). Its Description shows on one line under the title, its Border pattern is Dashed (the default), Solid, Dotted or Double, and its Icon is the container icon by default. Only Title and Description wait for Apply.

Group under Nodes & Objects adds an empty group. To move a node into a group, select it, click Move to group in the Inspector header (or pick Move to a group… in the command palette), pick the group, and click Move. Pick No group to take a node out of its group.

To resize a selected group or note, drag its handles, or press Alt+Shift (⌥+⇧ on macOS) with an arrow key. A group is never smaller than its members need.

docs.title: Shapes, Icons and Lines
docs.text:
Drawings can also be added from the command palette. Layouts don't move a drawing, but one in a group moves with the group, and a layout that makes the group smaller still keeps the drawing inside it.

  • A rectangle or circle fills its box (so a circle in a box that isn't square is an ellipse). It's see-through until you give it a Fill Color.
  • An icon shows a built-in or custom icon scaled to its box.
  • A line joins no node or network. It has arrowheads and 2 to 64 Points, and a new line is 160 pixels long.

Some fields take effect at once (see Fields that take effect at once); the others wait for Apply. Rectangles, circles and lines always stay under devices and switches, so they never hide a device or its connection points.

Resize a rectangle, circle or icon like a group. To reshape a line, drag the handles on its ends and bends, and double-click the line to add a bend. A clicked handle also moves with the arrow keys, and Delete removes its point. Without a mouse, edit the Points in the Inspector.

docs.title: Auto-group
docs.text:
Two of the choices have a rule of their own:

  • By network puts a device on several networks with the smallest one.
  • By name leaves switches out.

Auto-group only groups devices and switches that are in no group, and only the selected ones if anything is selected. A group needs at least two members. Afterwards, Auto-group arranges the diagram with the draft's layout so the groups don't overlap, and Undo removes the groups.

docs.title: Grouping by a Name Pattern
docs.text:
1. In Auto-group, pick By name pattern….
  2. Type a JavaScript regular expression in Name pattern.
  3. Click Group.

The pattern is matched against each device hostname and switch name, ignoring case. Names with the same matched text go into one group named after that text, or after the first parenthesized part when there is one. For example:

  • ^[a-z]+ puts web-01 and web-02 in group web, and db-01 and db-02 in group db.
  • ^(\w+)-(east|west) groups by the part of the name before the site.
  • -(\d)\d$ groups by the tens digit of the number at the end.

A pattern has at most 200 characters, only the first 255 characters of a name are matched, and a group's name is cut to 80 characters. A pattern that takes more than 2 seconds is stopped with "This pattern takes too long to match. Use a simpler one." The dialog remembers your last pattern in this browser until you log out; it isn't saved in the diagram or sent to the server.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text:
Where Field What it colors Values Switch Edge Color The network: its connections, and the outline of its switches Any CSS color Connection Color This connection, in place of its network's color Any CSS color Device, switch Outline Color The node's border #rrggbb only Device, switch Fill Color The node's background #rrggbb only Note, group Color The note or the group Any CSS color Rectangle, circle Outline Color, Fill Color The shape's border and inside #rrggbb only Line Color The line and its arrowheads #rrggbb only

The swatch button before a color field offers suggested colors, Custom color and No color. A #rrggbb field takes no color names, short forms or transparency. A switch's Outline Color and Fill Color belong to that switch, so two switches of one network can differ.

A device's or switch's outline uses the first of these that applies: its own Outline Color, its layer's color (when the diagram colors outlines by layer, see Layer outlines), and, for a switch, its network's color. A new network gets the suggested color that the fewest networks use.

docs.title: Line Styles
docs.text: On a connection, Auto follows its network. The Auto choice names the pattern it picked, for example "Auto (Solid)". A pattern can repeat on several networks, but a connection's label and switch still name its network.

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text:
The layout menu shows the layout that last arranged the draft, or Default if none has. Imported, uploaded and blank drafts start at Default; an import puts its devices in rows on a grid with the switches below them.

In Network cards, the devices in each card are grouped by name, and ELK layered puts a device on several networks with its smallest one. A layout gives the same result every time for the same diagram and selection, and keeps group members inside their group and other nodes out. Restore previous layout stays in the menu until you make some other change.

Auto layout in the command palette runs the draft's layout again. On a draft at Default, Auto layout and Auto-group use the Default layout setting (see Settings), which is ELK layered unless you change it.

Publishing and a Topology YAML download ignore positions and layouts.

Here's Metro Campus (metro-campus.topology.yaml), 42 devices on 7 networks, after the import and then after ELK layered:

docs.title: By Layer
docs.text:
By layer stacks the diagram by layer, highest ID at the top. Only IDs count, so an ID that isn't in the diagram's layer list works too. Each connection runs down from the higher layer to the lower.

  • A device or switch without a layer goes to the layer of the nearest connected node that has one (the higher one on a tie).
  • A connected node that no layer reaches goes below every layer, and an unconnected node, such as a note, goes at the bottom.
  • A group sits at the layer of its highest member, with its members in layer order inside it.

When no device or switch has a layer, and within a single layer, the layout starts from a top node and puts every other node below the node that leads to it. The top node is the selected device or switch, else a firewall, else a router, else the switch with the most connections. Firewalls and routers are found by icon or node type. An external device is a top node only when you select it, since hardware such as a PLC usually sits low in a plant.

docs.title: Arranging by Hand
docs.text: Nodes moved with Shift and an arrow key don't snap to the grid, and holding the keys down makes one Undo step. A move by hand doesn't change the layout shown in the layout menu.

docs.title: The Grid
docs.text:
Grid size, in the Inspector with nothing selected, is the spacing of the grid: a whole number of pixels from 4 to 200, 16 for a new diagram.

Snap to grid (in the Editing section of Settings, or in the command palette) is off by default. When it's on, nodes that you drag, drop or add, and the points of lines that you drag or add, go to the nearest grid point. It's a per-browser setting, so other users have their own.

docs.title: Copy, Paste, Duplicate and Delete
docs.text:
Each has a key (see Keyboard shortcuts). Copy and Paste use Builder's own clipboard, not the system clipboard, and work between drafts that you open one after another in the same tab. Duplicate copies and pastes in one step without touching that clipboard.

  • A paste lands 40 pixels down and right of the original, and each further paste 40 pixels more.
  • A pasted device gets a free hostname, such as server-2, and keeps its settings.
  • A connection is pasted or duplicated only with both of its nodes, so Duplicate with only connections selected does nothing.
  • Copying a group copies the nodes in it.

docs.title: Undo and Redo
docs.text:
Each change is a snapshot of the draft on the server, so Undo moves the draft itself back. Undo and Redo reach only the changes since you opened the draft in this tab, or since your last restore; to go back further, use Draft History.

Warning

After an undo, a new change removes the snapshots you undid, including any that other users saved after them (see Newer snapshots).

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• The Editor: the Inspector, Node Editor and settings.
  • Publishing: Details: what blocks publishing and what a publish writes.
  • Checks and Preflight: Details: the warnings and errors a diagram can show.

docs.title: Drafts: Details
docs.text:
Info

This page goes deeper than the short guide: Drafts.

docs.title: The Drafts Page
docs.text:
The theme, Settings, Help and Focus mode buttons work as they do in the editor. The Node Templates tab is the template library, the Icons tab is the icon library, and damaged drafts come last on the Drafts tab.

"Updated" on a draft card, for example "Updated Sep 29, 2026, 1:02 PM by alice", counts any activity on the draft: an edit, an undo, a restore, a deleted snapshot or a publish. That's why it can differ from Last edited in the Inspector, which shows when the content was saved.

docs.title: Filtering the Lists
docs.text:
Filter drafts and Filter published diagrams match the name, or the user who created or last changed the item. Filter layer sets matches the name or description, and Filter templates matches the name and whatever t: finds in the command palette (see The Node Templates tab).

Filters match the way the command palette does: each word you type must appear in the name or a user name, in any case, or the letters must appear in the name in order (pmpst finds "Pump station"). Select all, Download selected and Delete selected act only on the cards that show, and a filter that hides a selected card clears its selection.

docs.title: Creating a Draft
docs.text: Blank diagram names the new draft "Untitled topology", or "Untitled topology 2" and so on when a draft of any user already has that name (see Renaming the diagram). Import names the draft after its config (see Importing a topology or experiment), and Upload always makes a new draft. Edit on a Builder topology on the Configs page works like Edit as a draft (see Editing a published topology).

docs.title: Opening a Draft
docs.text: In the command palette, open draft lists the published diagrams as well as the drafts.

docs.title: Links to a Draft
docs.text: A link to a draft looks like <phenix-address>/builder?draft=<draft-id>. The address bar shows it while the draft is open, so a reload opens the same draft.

docs.title: Publishing from the Drafts Page
docs.text: Publish on a card opens the Publish diagram dialog without the editor (see Publishing). If the diagram has errors, the dialog lists them and won't publish; click Open draft to fix them. Closing the dialog doesn't stop a running publish, and pending changes keep saving.

docs.title: How Drafts Save
docs.text: Each saved change is a snapshot in Draft History. Besides sending pending changes, Save now applies the valid Inspector changes that you haven't applied with Apply. For every save state, see Save states.

docs.title: Working Offline
docs.text: Unsent changes stay in this browser even after you close the tab, and Builder sends them the next time you open the draft in the same browser. Logging out deletes them.

docs.title: Draft History
docs.text: Draft History in the toolbar lists the snapshots, newest first. Each row shows the snapshot's number (1 is the draft as Builder made it), a name that says what the change did, such as "Added device", and the date and user. You can't restore or delete the current snapshot. The tooltip on each other Restore says how many newer snapshots your next change after that restore removes. If the server doesn't move the draft to the snapshot, for example while you're offline, the page says so and the draft stays as it was. Undo and Redo skip a deleted snapshot (see Undo and redo).

docs.title: Newer Snapshots
docs.text:
While you're on an older snapshot, the notice above the toolbar reads like "Your next change removes 2 newer snapshots (latest by bob, Oct 26, 2026, 10:00 AM)."

  • After Undo, Return to latest works like Redo and keeps your undo steps. Otherwise it restores the newest snapshot.
  • Save newer history as a new draft copies the newest snapshot to a new, unpublished draft, for example "Riverside Water (copy)". Like a duplicate, it publishes as a new topology.

docs.title: Automatic Snapshots
docs.text: When you leave, publish or download a draft with Inspector changes that you didn't apply, Builder applies and saves them. The snapshot is named after the node, for example "Saved unapplied changes to Device web-01", and marked Automatic.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
The server holds at most 2,000 drafts across all users. At that limit, delete drafts or click Clean up… in Settings, which deletes every user's published, unchanged drafts (see Cleaning up storage).

A draft keeps at most 50 snapshots and 50 MiB of them, and Builder deletes the oldest past either limit. A published diagram and a diagram read from a file have no draft history; to keep one, edit the diagram as a draft.

docs.title: Published Diagrams
docs.text:
The cards show the topology name, and the publish time for a topology that Builder published. A published diagram records who made it and who last edited it, taken from the draft at publish time.

After the first Edit as a draft by any user, the button opens the draft that published the diagram or was made from it instead of making another one (see Publishing again).

docs.title: Opening the Experiment
docs.text: When a diagram was published with an experiment (see Publishing a topology and an experiment), Exp on its card and in the editor toolbar, or Open experiment in the command palette, opens the experiment page in the same tab. Exp shows only while the experiment exists and you may view it, and it follows a renamed experiment. It doesn't show for an experiment that you made from the topology yourself. When one publish made several experiments, Exp opens one of them.

docs.title: Diagrams Read from a File
docs.text:
An administrator can point a topology at a Builder file on the phēnix server as its diagram, without a publish (see Builder documents in files). The card shows the tag File and the file path, and has no Delete; to delete the topology, use the Configs page.

Open reads the file. If the stored topology isn't what the diagram in the file would publish, the notice says so, and a draft made from it can publish only as a new topology. Edit as a draft reopens the same draft as long as the file holds the same diagram, and makes a new one after the file changes. Such a draft can update the topology (see Publishing to a topology that names a Builder file). If the file changes between Open and Edit as a draft, Builder makes no draft, so open the diagram again. When phēnix can't use the file, the page says why (see When the file cannot be used).

docs.title: Deleting a Published Topology
docs.text:
1. Click Delete on the card.
  2. Click Delete topology.

If another user published or changed the topology after Builder read the list, Builder deletes nothing and reloads the list, so check the topology and try again. A draft that published the topology, was imported from it, or was opened from its published diagram creates the topology again the next time it publishes to that name.

docs.title: The Layers Tab
docs.text:
A layer set is a named list of layers and their options. Show Layers in the command palette opens this tab from the drafts page, and in a diagram, Edit layers… applies a copy of a set to the diagram.

New layer set opens the layers editor on a new set with the 7 placeholder layers, and Upload layer set… adds a set from a layer set file. On the cards:

  • Edit opens the layers editor (see Editing the layers). Each save gives the set its next version.
  • Duplicate adds a copy with a number after its name, such as "Purdue Model (2)".
  • Download saves a layer set file.
  • Delete can't be undone. Diagrams keep their copies of the set's layers.
  • Set default makes the set the server's default (Clear default undoes it). Any Builder user can change the default.

The built-in Purdue Model set is read only and can't be deleted. Each Blank diagram starts with a copy of the default set, linked to it, or with the placeholder layers when there's no default. A library template also offers the default set's layers in the template editor.

If another user changed the set or the default after the tab read the library, Delete, Set default and Clear default change nothing and the tab reloads the library, so try again. If another user saved the set after you opened it, Save fails; close the editor and open the set again.

The tab doesn't list sets that the server can't read, such as sets saved by a newer phēnix version, but it says how many there are. The library holds at most 200 sets plus the built-in one (see The libraries).

docs.title: Selecting Several Layer Sets
docs.text: Selection works as it does for drafts, except that Download selected also saves the built-in set and Delete selected skips it.

docs.title: Duplicating a Draft
docs.text:
Duplicate draft… in the command palette works like Duplicate on a card. In the editor it copies the open draft once its changes are saved; on the drafts page it asks which draft to copy.

When a name ending in "(copy)" is taken, the copy gets "(copy 2)", "(copy 3)" and so on, so a copy of "Pump station (copy)" is "Pump station (copy 2)". You're the copy's creator, and it still includes the topologies that the original included. A read-only published diagram has no Duplicate, so click Edit as a draft first.

docs.title: Deleting a Draft
docs.text: If another user has the draft open, their next save fails. A delete during a publish of the draft waits until the publish is done.

docs.title: Selecting Several Drafts
docs.text: A card has a checkbox when Download selected or Delete selected can act on it: every card on Drafts, the cards on Published Diagrams (for Delete selected, only those you can delete, and none for a diagram read from a file), and each icon on Icons (see The Icons tab). Each tab keeps its own selection.

docs.title: Selecting with the Keyboard
docs.text:
The cards of a tab are one stop for the Tab key, which lands on the card you were last on.

Key What it does Arrow keys Move to the next or previous card, also to the card above or below Home, End Move to the first or last card Space Select the focused card, or clear it Shift+Space, Shift and an arrow key Select the cards from the card you last selected or cleared to the focused card, also when you cleared that card ⌘A (macOS), Ctrl+A Select every card Escape Clear the selection Delete (Backspace on macOS too) Ask to delete the selected cards, where Delete selected can

Shift-clicking a checkbox gives every card from the one you last selected or cleared to that checkbox its new state. After Select all, ⌘A or Escape, it changes only that card.

docs.title: Downloading Several Drafts
docs.text: Download selected saves one Builder JSON file per card, with its custom icons, as Download in the editor does. Each file holds the draft as the server has it, or on Published Diagrams, the published diagram. Your browser may ask you to allow the page to download several files.

docs.title: Deleting Several Drafts
docs.text:
1. Select the cards.
  2. Click Delete selected.
  3. Click Delete 2 drafts (the number of selected drafts).

When some items can't be downloaded or deleted, a summary under the row lists each one with the reason, and failed deletes stay selected. If the server can't be reached partway through, Builder stops and lists the rest as "Not attempted."

docs.title: Damaged Drafts
docs.text: A draft that this phēnix server can't read, for example one that a newer phēnix version saved, has no Open. Open it with the version that saved it, or delete it. Any Builder user can delete a damaged draft.

docs.title: Logging Out
docs.text: Logging out, or signing in as another user in the same browser, deletes your Builder data from the browser at once: unsent changes, recent commands, the last Auto-group name pattern and the Preflight checks you last selected. Download keeps a copy of a draft that hasn't finished saving. phēnix logs you out the same way when your session ends (see Troubleshooting) or after a long idle time. Your preferences stay: theme, column widths, minimap size, keyboard shortcuts and settings (see Storage).

docs.title: Same Draft in Multiple Tabs
docs.text:
When a draft is open in more than one browser tab, each tab shows a notice under the header:

If more than one tab holds unsaved changes, for example after offline work, Builder can save only one tab's changes, so it opens the Choose which changes to save dialog:

  1. Under Version to save, choose a version, for example "This tab: 1 change, last at Sep 29, 2026, 1:01:26 PM". Download saves this tab's version as a file.
  2. Click Save this version.

Builder saves each other version as a new draft with " (local copy)" after its name, and the tab with that version switches to it. Decide later closes the dialog without sending anything, and Choose which to save in the notice opens it again.

docs.title: Draft Merging
docs.text:
When someone saves a newer version of the draft before your changes reach the server, Builder merges their changes with yours, field by field, and the save state says "Merging your changes with the server version…".

  • A change that only one of you made stays, even on different fields of one device: if alice moves router-1 and you rename it, router-1 is moved and renamed.
  • Items either of you added stay. An item one of you deleted is deleted, unless the other changed it or added a connection to it.
  • An interface that one of you renamed keeps the other's changes.
  • Scenarios that either of you added or removed are added or removed.
  • Your zoom and position on the canvas don't change.

When nothing clashes, Builder saves the merged diagram on top of the newer version and says "Merged alice's changes with yours." Draft History lists it as "Merged changes from alice", and Undo goes back to alice's version.

These changes clash:

  • A field you both changed to different values. A device's name, its hostname and the hostname in its settings are one choice, as are the new names of one interface (the diagram keeps one interface) and the whole link of a linked template.
  • An item one of you deleted while the other changed it or connected to it. The choices read like Keep theirs: delete ws-01 and drop your connection to it and Keep mine: keep ws-01 with your connection.
  • A group one of you deleted or ungrouped while the other put a node in it. If the group goes, the node moves to the group that held it, as Ungroup does, or to no group.
  • A node one of you put in a group while the other put that group in the node. The choices name the groups, such as Keep mine: Site and Keep theirs: no group. If your choices still nest two groups in each other, Builder moves one of them out.

Builder tells you about each connection it drops and each node it moves.

When something clashes, or the merged diagram has an error such as two devices with one hostname, the This draft changed on the server panel opens under the header. Your unsaved changes stay on this device, and new edits don't save until you choose:

  • Review and merge opens the Merge changes from alice dialog.
  • Save my history as a new draft saves your version as a new draft, for example "Riverside Water (local copy)", and opens it. If that save stops partway, Builder deletes the incomplete draft.
  • Discard mine and load the server version asks first, then drops your changes for good. If Builder can't read the newer version, it keeps your changes.

In the dialog, pick Keep mine or Keep theirs for each clash, or click Keep all mine or Keep all theirs. Save merged saves the result, with every change that doesn't clash, on top of the newer version.

  • If the result has an error, the dialog lists it and stays open. When the dialog opened only because of such an error, Save merged is unavailable: click Cancel, then save your history as a new draft or discard it.
  • If yet another version arrives while Builder saves, it saves nothing and merges again.
  • If the save fails, the dialog keeps your choices, so click Save merged again.

Merging needs the version your changes started from. The panel says "Merging is not available", with no Review and merge, when the server no longer keeps that version (a draft keeps its last 50 snapshots), when Builder can't read it, or when the server doesn't send it within 15 seconds. If the merge fails, the panel says "Merging failed" with the reason and offers the same choices.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Troubleshooting: problems with saving, merging and offline work.
  • Publishing: what publishing a draft writes and replaces.
  • Administration: permissions, storage and cleanup.

docs.title: The Editor: Details
docs.text:
Info

This page goes deeper than the short guide: The Editor. The examples use the Riverside Water draft of the example lab.

docs.title: Header
docs.text: The guide lists what the header holds.

docs.title: Selecting by Kind
docs.text:
Click a count in the header to replace the selection with every item of that kind. For example, 12 devices selects the 12 devices.

  • The networks count selects the networks' switches, because the canvas shows each network as its switch.
  • While a device or a switch is at a layer, there's also a layers count. It includes the placeholder layers, and selects each device and switch that's at a layer, whether chosen for the node or matched by its fields (see Layers).
