The Node Templates tab says the same, but still lists the built-in templates and the server collections. Open the library with the phēnix version that saved it.

Builder reads the library again when it reads the drafts lists, when a draft opens, when you come back to the editor's window, and after each change you make to it, so another user's change shows up then.

docs.title: Making a Diagram Template
docs.text:
New device template is also in the command palette. A template made from a device empties the VLAN of each interface, and takes in the Inspector changes that you haven't applied yet. A template made with no device selected starts from a plain device (hostname device, image ubuntu.qc2) with no name. When the diagram holds 50 templates, the + does nothing, and its tooltip says that the diagram is full.

Save to library first sends the diagram's own copy of the template's custom icon, if it has one, to the server's icon library (see The Diagram and Its Icons). If that fails, Builder still saves the template and tells you why.

docs.title: The Template Editor
docs.text:
Template Name (required) and Template Description are one line each: a pasted line break or tab becomes a space. Two templates can share a name, but the field then shows a note.

Node fields has the Inspector's fields, with the same checks (see Editing a Node), and the rarely used ones are under More settings. Hostname is the name that new devices start from. A few fields work differently:

  • Icon size Diagram default uses the size of the diagram that the device goes into. In a diagram template it names that size, for example "Diagram default (Large)".
  • Layer offers the diagram's layers for a diagram template. For a library template it offers the default layer set, or the placeholder layers when the server has no default set (see The Layers Tab).

The device of a template can be at most 16 KiB as JSON.

docs.title: Linked Templates
docs.text:
A diagram gets a linked template when you add a device from a library or server template, or when you click Save to library. Builder compares it with its source when a draft opens and each time it reads the library, and marks it when something changed:

Mark What it means Button on the mark Update available The library has a newer version. For a server template, an administrator changed the template file and restarted the server. Update Deleted from library A user deleted the library template. Unlink Removed from server The server collection no longer has the template. Unlink

With nothing selected, the Inspector lists them under Template updates (see With Nothing Selected).

An update gives the diagram template the name, description and device fields of its source, as one change that Undo can reverse. Update all (there when two or more templates have an update) asks once, with an Update templates button. Unlink doesn't ask, and is also one change. You can change a linked template in the diagram and keep the link, but an update replaces your changes.

docs.title: The Template Library
docs.text: The server keeps one template library, which no user owns. Every Builder user sees the same templates and collections, and can add, change and delete them (see The Libraries). Only the built-in templates and the server collections are read only.

docs.title: The Node Templates Tab
docs.text:
The command palette has Open Node Templates library in the editor and Show Node Templates on the drafts page. c: shows a collection, and t: opens a template in the template editor.

Filter templates finds a template by its name, by the fields that t: finds, and by its source (Library, Server or Built-in). The text stays when you change Show (see Filtering the Lists).

New template opens the template editor on a plain device with no name. When a save fails, the editor stays open with the reason, for example "Could not save the template. A library holds at most 200 templates." If someone changed the template after you opened it, the editor tells you: click Save again to replace their version, or Cancel to keep it.

Delete removes the template from the library and from its collections, and you can't undo it. If someone changed the library after the tab read it, Delete, Delete collection and Delete selected delete nothing and the tab shows the library as it is now. Check it, then delete again.

docs.title: Missing Disk Images
docs.text:
The tab compares each template's drive images with the server's disk images by file name, with the same case, like the drive image check of a diagram (see Checks and Warnings). A card with a missing image says, for example, The server has no disk image named "ubuntu.qc2". Built-in and server templates get the warning too, but Templates with missing images in Show lists only library templates.

The tab reads the disk images when you show it, and again when you come back to it after 30 seconds or more. When your role can't list disk images, or the server lists none, no card shows the warning and Show doesn't offer Templates with missing images. If the images become unknown while that list shows, the choice stays, marked "(disk images unknown)", with an empty list, until the tab can read them again.

docs.title: Built-in Templates
docs.text: The five built-in templates (see Built-in Templates) are read only for everyone, administrators included, and a device made from one adds no template to the diagram. Duplicate, or Duplicate to library in the editor that View opens, adds a copy to the library that you can change.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text: New collection… in the Add to collection menu makes a collection from the selected templates, and Remove from collection takes them out of the collection that shows. Deleting a collection keeps its templates in the library, and deleting a template takes it out of every collection.

docs.title: Selecting Several Templates
docs.text:
The row above the cards acts on the checked cards. For the library it has Add to collection (and Remove from collection while a collection shows), Download selected and Delete selected, which asks once. For the built-in templates and a server collection, it has Duplicate selected and Download selected.

Changing Show clears the selection. The keys of the drafts page also select cards (see Selecting With the Keyboard).

docs.title: Downloading and Importing Templates
docs.text: A download writes the same format that Import templates and the phēnix server read, so you can import it on another server, or put it in the template directory of a server (see Server Collections).

docs.title: Downloading Templates
docs.text:
Each download saves a YAML file of one collection: Download on a card makes a collection named after the template, Download selected one named after the list (such as "Library"), and Download collection keeps the collection's name and description. The file name comes from that name, for example plant-floor.templates.yaml.

The file carries a copy of each custom icon that its templates name, from the server's icon library, and Builder names any icon that the library doesn't have. Template names in a file must differ in more than case, so when the library holds "PLC" and "plc", the download keeps the first and numbers the others, such as "plc (2)".

This short file is only an illustration. The example file node-templates.yaml has three templates and no icons.

$schema: https://phenix.sandia.gov/schemas/builder/templates/v1
name: Plant floor
description: Devices of the plant's control network.
templates:
  - name: PLC
    description: Programmable logic controller
    device:
      iconKey: server
      icon: plc-icon
      spec:
        type: VirtualMachine
        general:
          hostname: plc
          vm_type: kvm
        hardware:
          os_type: linux
          drives:
            - image: ubuntu.qc2
icons:
  plc-icon:
    data: iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAYAAAAfFcSJAAAADUlEQVR42mNkYPhfDwAChwGA60e6kgAAAABJRU5ErkJggg==
  • $schema (required) names the format. The server serves its JSON Schema at /api/v1/schemas/builder/templates/v1.
  • name (required) and description describe the collection, each on one line.
  • templates (required): each has a name, an optional description, and a device with the fields that the template fills in. Templates have no IDs: the place that keeps a template gives it one.
  • icons (optional) holds copies of custom icons by name, each a PNG in base64. A template can also name an icon that the file doesn't carry, which the server's icon library must then hold.

YAML anchors and aliases (&name, *name) aren't allowed. For the size limits, see Limits.

docs.title: Importing
docs.text:
For a file that it can't import, the Import templates dialog lists each problem and where it is in the file. The new collection takes the file's name and description, with a number when the library already has that name, such as "Plant floor (2)", and the dialog tells you before you import.

The file's custom icons go to the server's icon library first (see The Diagram and Its Icons). If an icon can't go there, the import continues and the dialog tells you what happened. An import is refused when the library already holds 50 collections, or when the file would take the library past 200 templates.

docs.title: Server Collections
docs.text:
An administrator can give everyone on a server the same templates: phēnix reads each template file in the server's template directory at startup, as one collection (see Template Files on the Server). Server collections are read only for everyone, administrators included, so duplicate a template to change it. When an administrator changes a template file and restarts the server, the linked copies of its templates show Update available.

Here the template directory holds the example file node-templates.yaml:

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: A diagram holds at most 50 templates, and the library 200 templates in at most 50 collections. Names and descriptions are one line each. For every limit of templates, collections and template files, see Limits.

docs.title: From a Script
docs.text:
• Scripts list, add, change and delete library templates and collections through the REST API (see REST API). Each template and collection names the user who added it (createdBy) and the user who last changed it (updatedBy).
  • --base-dir.builder-templates sets the template directory of the server collections.
  • Diagram templates are part of the Builder document, so a Builder file can hold them. A linked template keeps its link in source (see Builder JSON and YAML). Publish never writes diagram templates into a Topology config.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Adding Devices: the other ways to add a device.
  • Custom Icons: the icon library that templates use.
  • Schema: the node spec that a template's device holds.

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text: Every phenix command, generated from its source. Each top-level command has its own page, and the options of phenix itself are global flags that every command accepts.

docs.title: phenix
docs.text:
A cli application for phēnix

phenix [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--base-dir.builder-templates string   directory of the Builder template files phenix ui reads at start (default: <base-dir.phenix>/builder/templates)
      --base-dir.injects string             base directory for staged workflow injects (default: <base-dir.phenix>/injects; workflow apply uses the server's value unless this flag is given)
      --base-dir.minimega string            base minimega directory (default "/tmp/minimega")
      --base-dir.phenix string              base phenix directory (default "/phenix")
      --base-dir.topologies string          base directory for topology directories (default: <base-dir.phenix>/topologies)
      --bridge-mode string                  bridge naming mode for experiments ('auto' uses experiment name for bridge; 'manual' uses user-specified bridge name, or 'phenix' if not specified; a phenix ui in 'auto' mode overrides it) (options: manual | auto) (default "manual")
      --color string                        when to color the output: 'auto' colors only a terminal, and not when NO_COLOR is set or TERM is dumb. JSON and YAML output never have color (options: auto | on | off) (default "auto")
      --deploy-mode string                  deploy mode for minimega VMs (options: all | no-headnode | only-headnode)
      --experiment.disk-check string        what a start does when a VM disk image or CD-ROM image is missing or its backing chain is broken ('error' refuses the start, 'warn' starts with a warning, 'off' does not check) (options: error | warn | off) (default "error")
  -h, --help                                help for phenix
      --hostname-suffixes string            hostname suffixes to strip (default "-minimega,-phenix")
      --log.console string                  output for console logs (text format) (stderr, stdout, or file path) (default "stderr")
      --log.level string                    level to log messages at (default "info")
      --log.system.max-age int              maximum number of days to retain old log files (default 90)
      --log.system.max-backups int          maximum number of old log files to retain (default 3)
      --log.system.max-size int             maximum size in megabytes of the log file before it gets rotated (default 100)
      --log.system.path string              path to system log (JSON format) (default: /var/log/phenix/phenix.log as root, $HOME/phenix_logs/phenix.log otherwise)
      --minimega.read-connections int       most read-only commands sent to minimega at once, 3 to 64; 2 are kept for reads of the head node (default 16)
      --mount-dir string                    base directory for VM filesystem mounts (default: <base-dir.phenix>/mounts)
      --store.endpoint string               BoltDB store endpoint (bolt://<path>) (default: bolt:///etc/phenix/store.bdb as root, bolt://$HOME/.phenix.bdb otherwise)
      --unix-socket string                  phēnix unix socket to listen on (ui subcommand) or connect to (default "/tmp/phenix.sock")
      --use-gre-mesh                        use GRE tunnels between mesh nodes for VLAN trunking

docs.title: phenix admin
docs.text: Every command on this page also accepts the global flags.

docs.title: phenix admin
docs.text: Administration of users, roles and API tokens

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Administration of users, roles and API tokens

  The list and get commands read the store. The commands that change users,
  roles or tokens call the running phenix server over its unix socket
  (--unix-socket), as the user global-admin. The server then closes the
  websockets of a user whose role changes, revokes the capture grants of a
  deleted user, and signs tokens with its JWT signing key.

phenix admin [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text: -h, --help   help for admin

docs.title: phenix admin role
docs.text: List, get, create, update, or delete roles

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
List, get, create, update, or delete roles

  A role is a list of policies. A policy gives verbs on resources, and
  optionally only on some resource names. Give a policy as
  resources=<list>;verbs=<list>[;names=<list>], each list separated by
  commas. Only custom roles change: a built-in role cannot. A role cannot
  give more than the user global-admin of the unix socket holds, and no
  custom role may give roles create, patch or delete.

phenix admin role [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text: -h, --help   help for role

docs.title: phenix admin role create
docs.text: Create a custom role

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Create a custom role

  Creates a role with the policies that --policy gives. The config name is
  --config-name, or else the role name in lower case with a "-" for each run
  of other characters. Give the role to a user with phenix admin user
  update <username> --role <role name>.

phenix admin role create <role name> [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: phenix admin role create "Lab Viewer" --policy 'resources=experiments,vms;verbs=list,get;names=lab-*'

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--config-name string   Config name of the role (default from the role name)
  -h, --help                 help for create
      --policy stringArray   Policy of the role, as resources=<list>;verbs=<list>[;names=<list>] (repeatable)

docs.title: phenix admin role delete
docs.text: Delete a custom role that no user has

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Delete a custom role that no user has

  --dry-run reads the store: it checks that the role exists, is not built
  in, and that no user has it, and does not call the server. The server
  also refuses a role that its settings name, such as in ui.users.

phenix admin role delete <role name> [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--dry-run   Show what the command would change, and change nothing
  -h, --help      help for delete

docs.title: phenix admin role get
docs.text: Show the policies of a role

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Show the policies of a role

  The role name is its name or its config name. -o json and -o yaml print
  the role with the fields of GET /roles/{name} and its config name
  (configName).

phenix admin role get <role name> [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
-h, --help            help for get
  -o, --output string   Output format (table, json, yaml) (default "table")

docs.title: phenix admin role list
docs.text: List the roles

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
List the roles

  -o json and -o yaml print each role with the fields of GET /roles and its
  config name (configName), sorted by config name.

phenix admin role list [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
-h, --help            help for list
  -o, --output string   Output format (table, json, yaml) (default "table")

docs.title: phenix admin role update
docs.text: Replace the policies of a custom role

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Replace the policies of a custom role

  Replaces all policies of the role with those that --policy gives. Each
  user with the role gets the new policies, with the resource names that
  the user had, and the websockets of those users close.

phenix admin role update <role name> [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: phenix admin role update lab-viewer --policy 'resources=experiments;verbs=list,get'

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
-h, --help                 help for update
      --policy stringArray   Policy of the role, as resources=<list>;verbs=<list>[;names=<list>] (repeatable)

docs.title: phenix admin token
docs.text:
Create API tokens

phenix admin token [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text: -h, --help   help for token

docs.title: phenix admin token create
docs.text: Create an API token for a user

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Create an API token for a user

  The running phenix server signs the token with its JWT signing key
  (ui.jwt-signing-key) and adds it to the tokens of the user. The command
  writes the token to stdout and its expiry to stderr. Send the token in the
  X-Phenix-Auth-Token header. The token is valid until it expires or the
  user signs out with it. --lifetime is a duration, such as 12h, or a whole
  number of days.

phenix admin token create <username> [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix admin token create alice
TOKEN=$(phenix admin token create ci-bot --lifetime 30 --description "CI runner")

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--description string   Description of the token (default "manually generated" and the time)
  -h, --help                 help for create
      --lifetime string      How long the token is valid: a duration or a whole number of days (default "24h")

docs.title: phenix admin user
docs.text:
List, get, create, update, or delete users

phenix admin user [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text: -h, --help   help for user

docs.title: phenix admin user create
docs.text: Create a user

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Create a user

  Creates a user with the role --role. --resource-names limits the role to
  those resource names, such as my-exp/*. The command asks for the password
  twice on the terminal, or reads it from the first line of stdin with
  --password-stdin. The password must meet the password settings. The user
  may get and update their own user.

phenix admin user create <username> [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix admin user create alice --role experiment-user --resource-names 'lab-*'
printf '%s\n' "$PASSWORD" | phenix admin user create bob --role global-viewer --password-stdin

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--first-name string        First name of the user
  -h, --help                     help for create
      --last-name string         Last name of the user
      --password-stdin           Read the password from the first line of stdin
      --resource-names strings   Resource names that the role applies to (comma list)
      --role string              Role of the user, by its name or its config name

docs.title: phenix admin user delete
docs.text: Delete a user

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Delete a user

  Deletes the user, closes the websockets of the user, and revokes the
  capture grants given to the user. --dry-run reads the store: it checks
  that the user exists and is not global-admin, and does not call the
  server.

phenix admin user delete <username> [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--dry-run   Show what the command would change, and change nothing
  -h, --help      help for delete

docs.title: phenix admin user get
docs.text: Show a user and the policies of its role

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Show a user and the policies of its role

  -o json and -o yaml print the user with the fields of GET /users/{username}.

phenix admin user get <username> [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:

docs.title: phenix completion
docs.text: Generate completion script

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
To load completions:

Bash:

  # Requires the bash-completion package, available from your OS package
  # manager.
  $ source <(phenix completion bash)

  # To load completions for each session, execute once:
  # Linux:
  $ phenix completion bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/phenix
  # macOS:
  $ phenix completion bash > /usr/local/etc/bash_completion.d/phenix

Zsh:

  # If shell completion is not already enabled in your environment,
  # you will need to enable it.  You can execute the following once:

  $ echo "autoload -U compinit; compinit" >> ~/.zshrc

  # To load completions for each session, execute once:
  $ phenix completion zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_phenix"

  # You will need to start a new shell for this setup to take effect.

Fish:

  $ phenix completion fish | source

  # To load completions for each session, execute once:
  $ phenix completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/phenix.fish

PowerShell:

  PS> phenix completion powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression

  # To load completions for every new session, run:
  PS> phenix completion powershell > phenix.ps1
  # and source this file from your PowerShell profile.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Configuration file management

  This subcommand is used to manage the different kinds of phenix configuration
  files: topology, scenario, experiment, or image.

phenix config [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text: -h, --help   help for config

docs.title: phenix config apply
docs.text: Create or update configurations from files

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Create or update configurations from files

  This subcommand creates each configuration in the given JSON or YAML files
  that is not stored, updates each stored configuration that is different,
  and does not change a configuration that is the same. Give the files as
  arguments, with -f, or both. Each one is the path of a file with the
  extension .json, .yaml or .yml. A directory is an error. To read the files
  of a directory, let the shell give them: "phenix config apply DIR/*".

  The command applies Topology configurations first, then Scenario, then
  Experiment, then Image and Role configurations, because a scenario and an
  experiment refer to a topology. It does not apply User configurations,
  because their files do not hold the password hash and the tokens.

  A comparison looks at the apiVersion, kind, name, annotations and spec. It
  ignores the fields that phenix sets: created, updated, revision, status and
  the experiment name. "phenix config diff" shows the differences. phenix
  adds values to an experiment configuration when it stores it. Thus, apply
  an experiment file that "phenix config get" wrote, or the file is always
  different.

  An update goes through the same checks as config edit. phenix refuses to
  update the configuration of a running experiment, and refuses an update
  when the configuration changes while the command runs. The command prints
  one line for each configuration. It tries all configurations, and then
  exits with an error if one or more failed.

  With --dry-run, the command checks each configuration as for an apply,
  shows the configurations that it would create or update, and changes
  nothing.

  The command fills in the ${NAME} and ${NAME:default} placeholders of each
  file before it reads the file. A value comes from -e, else from an env
  file of --env-file, else from the shell. The shell gives no PHENIX_
  variable unless -e NAME names it. A placeholder with no value and no
  default is an error, and so is a -e variable that no file uses: the
  command then changes nothing. Write ${NAME:} for an optional variable and
  $${NAME} for the literal text ${NAME}.

phenix config apply <file>... [-f <file>]... [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix config apply topology.yml scenario.yml
phenix config apply -f topology.yml -f scenario.yml
phenix config apply ./configs/* --dry-run
phenix config apply topology.yml -e NODES=3 --env-file site.env

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--dry-run                Show what the command would change, and change nothing
  -e, --env stringArray        set a variable for the ${NAME} placeholders: NAME=value, or NAME to copy the value from the shell (repeatable)
      --env-file stringArray   read variables from an env file of NAME=value lines; a relative path starts at the working directory (repeatable)
  -f, --filename stringArray   Configuration file to apply (repeatable); the same as an argument
  -h, --help                   help for apply
      --skip-validation        Skip schema validation of new configurations (updates are always validated)

docs.title: phenix config create
docs.text: Create a configuration(s)

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Create a configuration(s)

  This subcommand is used to create one or more configurations from JSON or
  YAML file(s). Each argument is the path of a file with the extension
  .json, .yaml or .yml. A directory is an error. To read the files of a
  directory, let the shell give them: "phenix config create DIR/*".

  A Builder document (the Builder's JSON or YAML export), a Builder
  template file, a Builder package and a Builder layer set file are not
  configurations. The command refuses such a file. Use the Builder in the web
  UI, or the Builder REST API below /api/v1/builder/, for these files. Upload
  a document and publish it to create its topology. Use Import templates to
  add the templates of a template file. Use Upload to open a package. Use
  Upload layer set on the Layers tab to add a layer set file.

  The command fills in the ${NAME} and ${NAME:default} placeholders of each
  file before it reads the file. A value comes from -e, else from an env
  file of --env-file, else from the shell. The shell gives no PHENIX_
  variable unless -e NAME names it. A placeholder with no value and no
  default is an error, and so is a -e variable that no file uses: the
  command then changes nothing. Write ${NAME:} for an optional variable and
  $${NAME} for the literal text ${NAME}.

  The command reads every file and checks every variable before it stores a
  configuration.

phenix config create </path/to/filename> ... [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix config create topology.yml scenario.yml
phenix config create ./configs/*.yml
phenix config create topology.yml -e NODES=3 --env-file site.env

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
-e, --env stringArray        set a variable for the ${NAME} placeholders: NAME=value, or NAME to copy the value from the shell (repeatable)
      --env-file stringArray   read variables from an env file of NAME=value lines; a relative path starts at the working directory (repeatable)
  -h, --help                   help for create
      --skip-validation        Skip configuration spec validation against schema

docs.title: phenix config delete
docs.text: Delete a configuration(s)

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Delete a configuration(s)

  This subcommand is used to delete one or more configurations. With
  --dry-run, it shows the configurations that it would delete, and deletes
  nothing.

  A name can contain the wildcard *, which matches zero or more characters.
  For example, topology/cm-* selects each topology whose name starts with
  "cm-". Put quotation marks around a pattern, so that your shell does not
  expand it. The kind cannot contain *. The pattern <kind>/* does the same
  as "delete all <kind>", and */* does the same as "delete all". Another
  pattern that selects no configuration is an error. Before phenix deletes
  the configurations that a pattern selects, it shows their names. A pattern
  does not delete the configuration of a running experiment.

  When phenix cannot delete a configuration, it continues with the other
  ones. Then it exits with an error that names each failure.

phenix config delete <kind/name> ... [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix config delete topology/foo
phenix config delete topology/foo scenario/bar
phenix config delete 'topology/cm-*'
phenix config delete 'topology/cm-*' --dry-run

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--dry-run   Show what the command would change, and change nothing
  -h, --help      help for delete

Delete all configurations

  experiment. With --dry-run, it shows the configurations that it would
  delete, and deletes nothing.

phenix config delete all [kind] [flags]

docs.title: Examples

docs.title: phenix config diff
docs.text: Show how configuration files differ from the stored configurations

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Show how configuration files differ from the stored configurations

  This subcommand prints a unified diff from each stored configuration to the
  configuration of the same kind and name in the given JSON or YAML files. It
  prints "new" for a configuration that is not stored. It prints nothing for a
  configuration that is the same. Each argument is the path of a file with
  the extension .json, .yaml or .yml. A directory is an error. To read the
  files of a directory, let the shell give them: "phenix config diff DIR/*".

  The diff shows the apiVersion, kind, name, annotations and spec, as YAML
  with sorted keys. It ignores the fields that phenix sets: created, updated,
  revision, status and the experiment name. A configuration that config diff
  shows as the same is one that config apply does not change.

  The command exits with 0 when no configuration differs, 1 when one or more
  differ, and 2 when it cannot read or compare a configuration.

  The command fills in the ${NAME} and ${NAME:default} placeholders of each
  file before it reads the file. A value comes from -e, else from an env
  file of --env-file, else from the shell. The shell gives no PHENIX_
  variable unless -e NAME names it. A placeholder with no value and no
  default is an error, and so is a -e variable that no file uses: the
  command then changes nothing. Write ${NAME:} for an optional variable and
  $${NAME} for the literal text ${NAME}.

phenix config diff <file>... [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix config diff topology.yml
phenix config diff ./configs/*
phenix config diff topology.yml -e NODES=3 --env-file site.env

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
-e, --env stringArray        set a variable for the ${NAME} placeholders: NAME=value, or NAME to copy the value from the shell (repeatable)
      --env-file stringArray   read variables from an env file of NAME=value lines; a relative path starts at the working directory (repeatable)
  -h, --help                   help for diff

  it only when the new backing image holds the same data. Give --independent
  in place of <backing> to copy all data into <disk> and remove its backing
  image.

# Make the image independent of its backing image

docs.title: phenix doctor
docs.text: Check the phenix configuration without a running server

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Check the phenix configuration without a running server

  Prints the phenix and minimega versions, every setting with its value and
  source, one row for each check (pass, warn, fail or skip), and a summary
  with a hint for each failure (and each warning with --strict). The checks look at the config files, the
  environment, the store, phenix ui, minimega, the host tools, the disk images
  and the apps. doctor changes nothing. Run it as the user, and with the flags
  and environment, of the phenix command you are checking. It exits 1 when a
  check fails, or with --strict when one warns. For each check and its fix,
  see https://phenix.sceptre.dev/latest/doctor/.

phenix doctor [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# As JSON, waiting up to 10 seconds for minimega
phenix doctor -o json --timeout 10s

# Without minimega or the settings list, failing on any warning
phenix doctor --skip minimega -x --strict

# Only the problems
phenix doctor -p -x

# Output to paste into a bug report, with host data replaced
phenix doctor --report

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
-h, --help                help for doctor
  -x, --no-print-settings   leave out the settings list
  -o, --output string       Output format (text, json) (default "text")
  -p, --problems-only       show only the checks that warn or fail (the summary still counts every check)
      --report              print the output in a fenced block to paste into a bug report, with host names, addresses, user names and secrets replaced
      --skip strings        checks or groups of checks to skip, comma-separated or repeated (such as minimega or ui.jwt-signing-key)
      --strict              exit 1 when a check warns, not only when one fails
      --timeout duration    how long to wait for each answer of minimega, phenix ui or ovs-vsctl, for the store lock, and for each check that reads many files, such as disk-chains, leftovers and image-locks (default 3s)

docs.title: See Also

docs.title: phenix experiment create
docs.text: Create an experiment

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Create an experiment

  Used to create an experiment from existing configurations; can be a
  topology, or topology and scenario, or paths to topology/scenario
  configuration files (YAML or JSON). (Optional are the arguments for
  scenario or base directory.)

  The command fills in the ${NAME} and ${NAME:default} placeholders of each
  file before it reads the file. A value comes from -e, else from an env
  file of --env-file, else from the shell. The shell gives no PHENIX_
  variable unless -e NAME names it. A placeholder with no value and no
  default is an error, and so is a -e variable that no file uses: the
  command then changes nothing. Write ${NAME:} for an optional variable and
  $${NAME} for the literal text ${NAME}.

phenix experiment create <experiment name> [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix experiment create <experiment name> -t <topology name or /path/to/filename>
phenix experiment create <experiment name> -t <topology name or /path/to/filename> -s <scenario name or /path/to/filename>
phenix experiment create <experiment name> -t <topology name or /path/to/filename> -s <scenario name or /path/to/filename> -d </path/to/dir/>
phenix experiment create <experiment name> -t <topology name or /path/to/filename> -s <scenario name or /path/to/filename> --disabled-apps "app1,app2"
phenix experiment create <experiment name> -t <topology name> --node-annotation phenix/default-apps=false --annotation phenix.workflow/tags=nightly

docs.title: Synopsis

Reconfigure an experiment

  Used to rerun the 'configure' stage of all the apps (both default and user)
  for the given experiment (as long as it's not running). Using 'all' instead
  of a specific experiment name will reconfigure all non-running
  experiments.

  This differs from 'phenix experiment trigger <experiment name> configure'
  in that it re-runs config validation and any registered config hooks, and
  always applies to all apps. Use this after editing an experiment's stored
  topology, scenario, or deployment settings. Use 'trigger configure' to
  manually re-run a specific app's (or apps') configure hook on demand for
  debugging; note it does not validate the config, run config hooks, or
  guard against running experiments the way 'reconfigure' does.

docs.title: phenix experiment restart
docs.text: Restart an experiment

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Restart an experiment

  Used to restart a running experiment, using 'all' instead of a specific
  experiment name will include all running experiments; dry-run will do
  everything but call out to minimega.

  Before phenix stops the experiment, it checks the disk images and CD-ROM
  images of the VMs as 'phenix experiment start' does. A missing file
  refuses the restart, and the experiment continues to run. When the
  scenario has a user app, the app can change the disks, so this check
  only shows warnings, and the check before the start can still refuse it.

  The stop of the experiment takes the flags of 'phenix experiment stop'
  (--force and --keep-injection-snapshots), and its start takes the flags
  of 'phenix experiment start'. With --treat-mm-errors-as-warnings, the
  check before the stop shows the problems as warnings.

  NOTE: passing the --honor-run-periodically flag will prevent the CLI from
  returning. If Ctrl+c is pressed, the experiment will continue to run but
  the running stage will no longer continue to be triggered for any apps
  configured (via the scenario) to have their running stage triggered
  periodically.

phenix experiment restart <experiment name> [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--dry-run                       Do everything but actually call out to minimega
  -f, --force                         Mark the experiment stopped even if minimega cannot kill its VMs
  -h, --help                          help for restart
      --honor-run-periodically        Periodically trigger running stage in apps if configured in scenario
  -K, --keep-injection-snapshots      Keep VM injection snapshots after stopping
      --treat-mm-errors-as-warnings   Treat errors from minimega as warnings instead of failing
      --vlan-max int                  VLAN pool maximum for this start (1-4094; 0 keeps the maximum of the experiment)
      --vlan-min int                  VLAN pool minimum for this start (1-4094; 0 keeps the minimum of the experiment)

docs.title: phenix experiment scorch
docs.text: Start a Scorch run for experiment

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Start a Scorch run for an experiment

  Used to start the Scorch run that --run selects (0 when not given) for the
  given experiment, and to wait until it ends. The command prints the
  progress of the run, and exits with an error when the run fails.

  When phenix ui is running, the server executes the run, so the web UI
  shows it and can cancel it. Ctrl+C cancels the run on the server. When
  phenix ui is not running, this command executes the run in its own
  process. The web UI does not show that run.

  The --status, --cancel, --cleanup and --clear flags need phenix ui. Each
  acts on the run that --run selects, and only one can be given:

    --status   shows the status of each stage and component of the run
    --cancel   cancels the run on the server
    --cleanup  runs only the cleanup stage of the run, and waits for it
    --clear    clears the status of a run that is not executing

  -o/--output sets the output format of --status. With --cancel or --clear,
  --dry-run checks that the server has the run, shows what phenix would
  request, and requests nothing.

phenix experiment scorch <experiment name> [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Run Scorch run 1 and wait until it ends
phenix experiment scorch exp1 --run 1

# Show the status of Scorch run 1
phenix experiment scorch exp1 --run 1 --status

# Cancel Scorch run 1 on the server
phenix experiment scorch exp1 --run 1 --cancel

# The status of Scorch run 1 as JSON
phenix experiment scorch exp1 --run 1 --status -o json

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--cancel          Cancel the run on the server (needs phenix ui)
      --cleanup         Run only the cleanup stage of the run (needs phenix ui)
      --clear           Clear the status of the run (needs phenix ui)
      --dry-run         Show what the command would change, and change nothing
  -h, --help            help for scorch
  -o, --output string   Output format (text, json, yaml) (default "text")
  -r, --run int         ID of the Scorch run to act on (defaults to 0)
      --status          Show the status of the run (needs phenix ui)

docs.title: phenix experiment start
docs.text: Start an experiment

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Start an experiment

  Used to start a stopped experiment, using 'all' instead of a specific
  experiment name will include all stopped experiments; dry-run will do
  everything but call out to minimega.

  Before minimega launches a VM, phenix checks that each disk image and
  CD-ROM image of the VMs exists, and that the backing chain of each disk
  image is complete. A missing file refuses the start and lists each VM,
  disk and missing file. With --dry-run or --treat-mm-errors-as-warnings,
  phenix shows the problems as warnings. The experiment.disk-check setting
  changes this for every start: warn shows the problems as warnings, and
  off skips the check.

  NOTE: passing the --honor-run-periodically flag will prevent the CLI from
  returning. If Ctrl+c is pressed, the experiment will continue to run but
  the running stage will no longer continue to be triggered for any apps
  configured (via the scenario) to have their running stage triggered
  periodically.

phenix experiment start <experiment name> [flags]

      --treat-mm-errors-as-warnings   Treat errors from minimega as warnings instead of failing

docs.title: Synopsis

Stop an experiment

  Used to stop a running experiment, using 'all' instead of a specific
  experiment name will include all running experiments. An experiment whose
  VMs minimega cannot kill stays running; --force marks it stopped anyway.

phenix experiment stop <experiment name> [flags]

docs.title: phenix experiment trigger
docs.text: Trigger lifecycle stage for app(s) in experiment

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Trigger an app lifecycle stage in an experiment

  Used to manually trigger the "configure", "pre-start", "post-start", "running",
  or "cleanup" stage of an app (or apps) for the given experiment on demand.
  Using 'all' instead of a specific experiment name triggers the stage for the
  given app(s) in all experiments. Providing no apps triggers the stage for all
  apps in the experiment(s). The "running" stage is skipped for stopped
  experiments.

  Triggering the "configure" stage is not the same as
  'phenix experiment reconfigure': this command does not validate the
  experiment config, run config hooks, or guard against running
  experiments. Use 'phenix experiment reconfigure' after
  editing an experiment's stored topology, scenario, or deployment settings.

  This command runs the stage in its own process. Ctrl+C stops a trigger
  that this command runs. --cancel stops the triggers that phenix ui runs,
  which the web UI or the REST API started: give no lifecycle with it, and
  give app names to stop only those apps. Without app names, --cancel also
  ends the scheduled runs of the running stage that phenix ui runs after a
  start (the experiments.periodic job). --cancel needs phenix ui. With
  --cancel --dry-run, phenix shows the cancels that it would request, and
  requests none.

  The old argument order, <lifecycle> <experiment name> [<app name> ...],
  is deprecated. It still works, with a warning, when no experiment has the
  lifecycle as its name.

  Valid lifecycles and shorthands: configure (config), pre-start (pre), post-start (post), running (run), cleanup (clean).

phenix experiment trigger <experiment name> <lifecycle> [<app name> ...] [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Run the configure stage of every app of exp1
phenix experiment trigger exp1 configure

# Run the running stage of the soh app in every experiment
phenix experiment trigger all running soh

# Stop the soh trigger that phenix ui runs for exp1
phenix experiment trigger exp1 --cancel soh

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--cancel    Stop the triggers that phenix ui runs for the experiment (needs phenix ui)
      --dry-run   Show what the command would change, and change nothing
  -h, --help      help for trigger

docs.title: phenix healthcheck
docs.text: Check the health of the phenix UI server

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Check the health of the phenix UI server

  Requests the server's liveness endpoint (/healthz), or with --ready its
  readiness endpoint (/readyz), and exits 0 when it answers 200 and 1
  otherwise. The URL comes from ui.listen-endpoint and ui.tls-key/tls-cert
  (the config file or PHENIX_UI_* environment variables), with a wildcard
  host replaced by loopback; --url overrides it. Flags given only on the
  phenix ui command line are not seen here: pass --url, or set
  PHENIX_UI_LISTEN_ENDPOINT, PHENIX_UI_TLS_KEY and PHENIX_UI_TLS_CERT.

  Unlike other subcommands, healthcheck opens no store, unix socket or log
  file, so it is cheap enough for a container health check.

phenix healthcheck [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Liveness, as the Docker and Podman health checks run it
phenix healthcheck

# Readiness (minimega, store, disk space, ...), with every check
phenix healthcheck --ready -o json

# A server listening elsewhere
phenix healthcheck --url https://phenix.example.com/readyz

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
-h, --help               help for healthcheck
  -o, --output string      Output format (text, json) (default "text")
      --ready              check readiness (/readyz) rather than liveness (/healthz)
      --timeout duration   how long to wait for an answer (default 5s)
      --url string         URL to check, instead of the one derived from the UI settings

docs.title: phenix image delete
docs.text: Delete one or more image configurations

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Delete one or more image configurations

  When phenix cannot delete an image configuration, it continues with the
  other ones. Then it exits with an error that names each failure.

  A name can contain the wildcard *, which matches zero or more characters.
  For example, cm-* selects each image configuration whose name starts with
  "cm-", and * selects all of them. Put quotation marks around a pattern, so
  that your shell does not expand it. Before phenix deletes the image
  configurations that a pattern selects, it shows their names. Another
  pattern that selects no image configuration is an error.

  With --dry-run, phenix shows the image configurations that it would
  delete, and deletes nothing.

phenix image delete <configuration name>... [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix image delete ubuntu
phenix image delete ubuntu kali-mini
phenix image delete 'cm-*'
phenix image delete 'cm-*' --dry-run

docs.title: phenix image inject-miniexe
docs.text: Inject a minimega executable into a disk image

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Inject a minimega executable into a disk image

  Used to add a minimega executable (miniccc, protonuke, or minirouter) and
  relevant boot scripts into an existing disk image. The disk operating system
  is guessed based on the provided agent's extension. When specifying the path
  to the disk to modify, the partition to inject into can optionally be included
  at the end of the path using a colon (for example, /phenix/images/foo.qc2:2).
  If not specified, partition 1 will be assumed.

  In a Windows disk image, the minimega executable will be injected into
  C:\minimega\[miniccc,protonuke]. A scheduler command will be placed into the
  Windows Startup directory for miniccc if '--init-system=startup' is provided,
  but not for protonuke, since protonuke's command line arguments are dynamic.
  Users or apps wishing to leverage protonuke on Windows hosts need to inject
  their own scheduler command in the Windows Startup directory or use miniccc to
  start protonuke.

  In a Linux disk image, the minimega executable will be injected into
  /usr/local/bin and the service file and symlinks will be injected into the
  appropriate locations, depending on which init system is being used. For
  systemd, they will be injected into /etc/systemd/system, and for sysinitv they
  will be injected into /etc/init.d and /etc/rc5.d. The protonuke service will
  only start if a file is present at /etc/default/protonuke, and that file
  should contain a single line setting the PROTONUKE_ARGS variable to a set of
  protonuke command line arguments. The minirouter service expects the miniccc
  service to be injected, and injecting minirouter will automatically cause
  miniccc to be injected as well.

phenix image inject-miniexe <path to exe> <path to disk> [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
-h, --help                 help for inject-miniexe
      --init-system string   Linux init system to generate boot scripts for (Linux: systemd, sysinitv; Windows: startup) (default "systemd")

  server (bulk VM actions, experiment file archives, disk clones), over its
  unix socket (--unix-socket), which acts as Global Admin and sees every

  VMs in progress; archive and clone jobs stop at once and leave no file. Use

  the cancel that it would request, and requests nothing.

docs.title: phenix mm
docs.text: Send commands, or attach, to minimega

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Send commands, or attach, to minimega

  Sends a command to minimega and prints the response, or attaches to the
  interactive minimega console. Exits non-zero if minimega reports an error.

  Flags must come before the minimega command. Everything after the first
  minimega argument, including arguments that start with "-", is passed to
  minimega unchanged, and arguments are quoted for minimega as needed. A

docs.title: phenix util scorch-json
docs.text: Print SCORCH component JSON input for given experiment to STDOUT

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Print SCORCH component JSON input for given experiment to STDOUT

  Prints the JSON that the program of a SCORCH user component
  (phenix-scorch-component-<type>) gets on stdin in a SCORCH run of the
  stored experiment. The command uses the code of a SCORCH run that starts
  from the web UI, the REST API or phenix experiment scorch, and it stores
  nothing. With -o json (the default), the output is the exact bytes that
  the component gets, with a newline at the end.

  --run, --loop and --stage select where the run starts the component. Loop
  0 is the run, loop 1 is the loop of the run, and so on. When you do not
  give them, the command uses the first place that runs the component.
  --count is the pass of that loop, from 0. Only the arguments change with
  the stage and the count.

  A SCORCH run picks a random value for each replacement (replace) at each
  pass of a loop. The command picks the values in the same way. --replace
  KEY=VALUE sets a value. The command reads VALUE as JSON when it is valid
  JSON, and as text when it is not.

  --runtime adds the cluster hosts and the VMs of the experiment (hosts and
  vms). A component gets them when an external app ran before the scorch
  app in the same app stage.

  On stderr, the command prints the program, its arguments, the PHENIX_*
  variables that phenix adds, the replacement values and warnings. When you
  give -o json, it prints only the warnings.

phenix util scorch-json <experiment name> <component name> [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix util scorch-json my-exp capture
phenix util scorch-json my-exp capture --run 1 --loop 1 --stage stop --count 2
phenix util scorch-json my-exp capture --replace '{{DURATION}}=30' -o json \
  | phenix-scorch-component-tcpdump start capture 0 0 0

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--count int             Pass of the loop, from 0
  -h, --help                  help for scorch-json
      --loop int              Depth of the loop, 0 for the run (default: the first loop that runs the component)
  -o, --output string         Output format (json, yaml) (default "json")
      --replace stringArray   Value of a replacement as KEY=VALUE, read as JSON when it is valid JSON
      --run int               Index of the SCORCH run (default: the first run that runs the component)
      --runtime               Add the cluster hosts and the VMs of the experiment
      --stage string          Stage: configure, start, stop, cleanup (default: the first stage that runs the component)

docs.title: phenix vlan alias
docs.text: View, pin or unpin VLAN aliases

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
View, pin or unpin VLAN aliases

  With no arguments, lists the VLAN aliases of every experiment. With an
  experiment name, lists that experiment's VLAN aliases. With an experiment
  name and an alias name, prints the VLAN ID of that alias. With a VLAN ID as
  well, pins the alias to that VLAN ID. With --unpin, clears the pin of the
  alias, so minimega gives it an ID when the experiment starts.

  The experiment must be stopped to pin or unpin an alias, and the alias must
  be in the experiment. A pin is refused when another experiment or a
  minimega namespace uses the VLAN ID, when minimega blacklists it, or when
  minimega does not answer. Use --force to pin it anyway.

  -o json and -o yaml print each alias as an object with its experiment,
  alias and VLAN ID; an alias lookup prints one object. --dry-run with
  --unpin checks the unpin and changes nothing.

phenix vlan alias [experiment name] [alias name] [vlan id] [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix vlan alias
phenix vlan alias <experiment name>
phenix vlan alias <experiment name> <alias name>
phenix vlan alias <experiment name> <alias name> <vlan id>
phenix vlan alias <experiment name> <alias name> --unpin

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--dry-run         Show what the command would change, and change nothing
  -f, --force           Pin the alias even when another experiment or namespace uses the VLAN ID, minimega blacklists it, or minimega does not answer
  -h, --help            help for alias
  -o, --output string   Output format (table, json, yaml) (default "table")
      --unpin           Clear the pin of the alias, so minimega gives it an ID at start

docs.title: phenix vlan check
docs.text: Check VLAN pins and a VLAN range of an experiment against the cluster

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Check VLAN pins and a VLAN range of an experiment against the cluster

  Starts from the VLAN pins and the VLAN range that the experiment has, pins
  each --alias, and replaces the range with --range. Then it lists the issues
  that the experiment would have in the cluster: duplicate pins, blacklisted
  pins, range overlaps and pins outside the range. The command changes
  nothing. The experiment does not have to exist. An --alias with the VLAN
  ID 0 has no pin. -o json and -o yaml print the body of POST /vlans/check.

phenix vlan check <experiment name> [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix vlan check my-exp
phenix vlan check my-exp --alias EXP_1=101 --alias EXP_2=102
phenix vlan check my-exp --range 100-199

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--alias stringArray   Pin a VLAN alias to a VLAN ID, as <alias>=<vlan id> (repeatable)
  -h, --help                help for check
  -o, --output string       Output format (table, json, yaml) (default "table")
      --range string        Replace the VLAN range, as <min>-<max>

List the VLAN IDs of the cluster

      --vlan string         Show only the rows of this VLAN ID

docs.title: phenix vlan range
docs.text: View, set or clear the VLAN range of an experiment

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
View, set or clear the VLAN range of an experiment

  With no arguments, lists the VLAN range of every experiment. With an
  experiment name, lists the VLAN range of that experiment. With a range
  minimum and maximum as well, sets the VLAN range of the experiment and
  replaces its current range. With --clear, clears the VLAN range of the
  experiment.

  The experiment must be stopped to set or clear its range. A range that
  leaves out a pinned alias is refused. A range that overlaps the VLAN range
  of another experiment is refused. Use --force to set it anyway.

  -o json and -o yaml print each range as an object with its experiment,
  minimum and maximum. --dry-run with --clear checks the clear and changes
  nothing.

phenix vlan range [experiment name [range minimum range maximum]] [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix vlan range
phenix vlan range <experiment name>
phenix vlan range <experiment name> <range minimum> <range maximum>
phenix vlan range <experiment name> --clear

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--clear           Clear the VLAN range of the experiment
      --dry-run         Show what the command would change, and change nothing
  -f, --force           Set the range even when it overlaps the VLAN range of another experiment
  -h, --help            help for range
  -o, --output string   Output format (table, json, yaml) (default "table")

docs.title: phenix vm commit
docs.text: Create a backing image from the disk of a running VM

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Create a backing image from the disk of a running VM

  Writes the first disk of the VM as it is now, with the changes in its
  snapshot, to a new image that has no backing image. phenix shuts down the
  VM while it writes the image, and then starts the VM again. It also starts
  the VM again if the operation fails.

  The image name must be a bare file name, with no folder. Without an image
  name, phenix names the image after the base image of the VM and the time,
  for example ubuntu_20261106120000.qc2. phenix writes the image in
  <base-dir.phenix>/images on the head node, copies it to the other cluster
  nodes, and prints its name. The VM can run on any cluster node.

  The experiment and the VM must run, and the VM must have its snapshot flag
  set. For a VM with more than one disk, the image holds only the first disk.
  The other disks do not change.

phenix vm commit <experiment name> <vm name> [image name] [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: phenix vm commit my-exp web web-configured.qc2

docs.title: Options
docs.text: -h, --help   help for commit

docs.title: phenix vm cp
docs.text: Copy a file into or out of a running VM

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Copy a file into or out of a running VM

  Copy one file between the local host and a running VM through the VM's
  miniccc agent, as scp does. Name the VM side as <vm name>:<path>, with an
  absolute path in the VM. Exactly one of <src> and <dst> must name the VM.
  A path that ends with "/" is a folder, and the file keeps its name.

  To copy into the VM, phenix puts a staging copy in the experiment's folder
  of the minimega files directory. It sends the copy with "cc send" and then
  moves it to the path in the VM. To copy out of the VM, phenix gets the file
  with "cc recv". This works only for a VM on the headnode, and for a Unix
  path with no glob characters. phenix removes the staging copy and the
  received copy when the copy is complete. A file copied out of the VM gets
  the permissions 0600. The VM must run the miniccc agent.

phenix vm cp <experiment name> <src> <dst> [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix vm cp myexp ./setup.sh host-01:/root/setup.sh
phenix vm cp myexp ./setup.sh host-01:/root/
phenix vm cp myexp host-01:/var/log/syslog ./syslog

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
-h, --help               help for cp
      --timeout duration   How long to wait for the VM to complete the copy (default 1m0s)

docs.title: phenix vm exec
docs.text: Run a command in a running VM

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Run a command in a running VM

  Run a command in a running VM through its miniccc agent, as the minimega
  command "cc exec" does, and print the stdout and stderr of the command.
  The command exits with the exit code of the command in the VM when minimega
  reports it.

  miniccc runs the command without a shell. To use pipes or redirects, run a
  shell, such as "sh -c '...'". Put "--" before a command that has flags.
  phenix refuses an argument that minimega would change on the host: an
  argument with a "$" variable, or a file:, http:, https: or tar: URL. The VM
  must run the miniccc agent.

phenix vm exec <experiment name> <vm name> [--] <command> [args...] [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix vm exec myexp host-01 hostname
phenix vm exec myexp host-01 --timeout 5m -- ls -la /tmp
phenix vm exec myexp host-01 -- sh -c 'ps aux | grep nginx'

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
-h, --help               help for exec
      --timeout duration   How long to wait for the command to complete (default 1m0s)

docs.title: phenix vm forward
docs.text: List, add, or remove the port forwards of a VM

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
List, add, or remove the port forwards of a VM

  A port forward is a minimega tunnel from a cluster port to a port that the
  VM reaches, which phenix-tunneler serves on the computer of its owner. The
  running phenix server holds the forwards, so these commands call it over
  its unix socket (--unix-socket). The server takes a request from the socket
  as the user global-admin, so a forward that the CLI adds has that owner,
  and the CLI removes only the forwards of that owner.

phenix vm forward [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text: -h, --help   help for forward

docs.title: phenix vm forward add
docs.text: Add a port forward to a VM

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Add a port forward to a VM

  Opens a minimega tunnel from a cluster port to the destination port on
  --host, as the cluster node of the VM reaches it. With vnc, the forward
  goes to the VNC console of the VM. --source-port is the port that
  phenix-tunneler listens on; it defaults to the destination port. An owner
  has at most one forward to each host and port of a VM.

phenix vm forward add <experiment name> <vm name> <destination port|vnc> [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix vm forward add my-exp web 22
phenix vm forward add my-exp web 80 --host 10.0.0.5 --source-port 8080
phenix vm forward add my-exp web vnc

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
-h, --help                 help for add
      --host string          Destination host, as the cluster node of the VM reaches it (default "127.0.0.1")
      --source-port string   Port for phenix-tunneler to listen on (default the destination port)

docs.title: phenix vm info
docs.text: Table of virtual machine(s)

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Table of VM(s)

  Used to display a table of virtual machine(s) for a specific experiment;
  VM name is optional, when included will display only that VM.

  Filter the output by repeating --filter with a COLUMN=VALUE expression.
  Multiple filters are combined with AND semantics. Column names and values
  are case-insensitive. Supported columns are HOST, NAME, RUNNING, DISK,
  INTERFACES, UPTIME, MEMORY, VCPUS, OS_TYPE, and TAPS. DISK values may be
  full paths, filenames, or filenames without extensions. For example:

    phenix vm info my-experiment --filter RUNNING=true
    phenix vm info my-experiment --filter RUNNING=true --filter OS_TYPE=linux
    phenix vm info my-experiment --filter DISK=jammy

  Repeat --host to list only the VMs running on any of the named cluster
  hosts, named exactly as minimega reports them. --host combines with the VM
  name or --label, and with --filter: a VM must match each of them. For
  example:

    phenix vm info my-experiment --host compute1 --host compute2
    phenix vm info my-experiment --host compute1 --label role-web

  -o json and -o yaml print each VM with the fields of the API, as
  GET /experiments/{exp}/vms gives them.

phenix vm info <experiment name> [vm name] [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
-f, --filter stringArray   Filter output by column value (COLUMN=VALUE); may be repeated
  -h, --help                 help for info
      --host stringArray     Cluster host to filter VMs by, named exactly as minimega reports it; may be repeated
  -l, --label stringArray    Label to filter VMs (supports glob patterns); use 'all' to select every VM
  -o, --output string        Output format (table, json, yaml) (default "table")
  -t, --taps                 Include tap interface names in the table

docs.title: phenix vm set
docs.text: Set configuration value(s) for VM(s)

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Set configuration value(s) for VM(s)

  Used to set one or more configuration values for virtual machine(s) in an
  experiment. Only flags that are explicitly provided will be applied.

  While the experiment is running, you can change only the labels
  (--label-changes, --append-labels), the annotations (--annotation) and the
  VLAN of an interface (--interface). Apps read the new annotations when the
  experiment starts again. --interface changes only a VM of a running
  experiment.

  --annotation replaces all of the annotations of the VM with the given ones.
  The values true and false become booleans, and a JSON list or object keeps
  its type. Other values, numbers too, stay text.

  --interface <index>=<vlan> connects the interface with that index to a VLAN
  alias or ID. --interface <index>= disconnects the interface.

  --partition 0 turns off disk injection for the VM, so the startup app sends
  its scripts through miniccc.

phenix vm set <experiment name> [vm name] [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix vm set <experiment name> <vm name> --cpu 2 --mem 4096
phenix vm set <experiment name> <vm name> --host compute1
phenix vm set <experiment name> <vm name> --annotation phenix/default-apps=false
phenix vm set <experiment name> <vm name> --interface 0=EXP_1
phenix vm set <experiment name> <vm name> --interface 1=
phenix vm set <experiment name> --label role=server --label-changes tier=web --append-labels

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--annotation stringArray      VM annotation in key=value form (may be repeated; replaces all of the annotations of the VM)
      --append-labels               Append the provided labels to the VM's existing labels instead of replacing the labels
  -c, --cpu int                     Number of VM CPUs (1-16 is valid)
  -d, --disk string                 VM backing disk image file
      --do-not-boot                 Set the do-not-boot flag for the VM
  -h, --help                        help for set
      --host string                 Cluster host to run the VM on (an empty value lets the scheduler choose the host)
      --interface string            Connect an interface to a VLAN alias or ID as <index>=<vlan>, or disconnect it as <index>= (running experiments only)
  -l, --label stringArray           Label to filter VMs (supports glob patterns); use 'all' to select every VM
  -L, --label-changes stringArray   VM label(s) to add or edit in key=value form (may be repeated)
  -m, --mem int                     Amount of memory in megabytes (a multiple of 512 from 512 to 131072)
  -p, --partition int               Partition of the first disk to inject files into (0 turns off disk injection)
      --snapshot                    Set the snapshot (non-persistent) flag for the VM

docs.title: phenix vm snapshot
docs.text: List, create, restore, and delete VM disk and memory snapshots

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
List, create, restore, and delete the snapshots of a VM

  A snapshot holds the disk and the memory state of a VM in a running
  experiment. Restore a snapshot to return the VM to that state. For an ELF
  memory dump, use phenix vm memory-snapshot.

  To create or restore a snapshot, the VM must have its snapshot flag set and
  exactly one disk. phenix refuses a VM with more than one disk, because a
  snapshot holds only the first disk (sandialabs/sceptre-phenix#145).

  phenix keeps the snapshot files on the cluster node that runs the VM, in
  <base-dir.phenix>/images/<experiment name>/files. The list shows the
  snapshots on all nodes. A restore of a VM on a node other than the head
  node can fail if minimega on that node runs with the -headnode flag:
  minimega then gets the snapshot files from the head node, which does not
  have them (sandialabs/sceptre-phenix#153).

phenix vm snapshot [flags]

docs.title: Options
docs.text: -h, --help   help for snapshot

docs.title: phenix vm snapshot create
docs.text: Create a snapshot of a running VM

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Create a snapshot of a running VM

  Saves the disk and the memory state of the VM as a snapshot. The snapshot
  name must be a bare file name, with no folder. phenix removes an extension
  from the name, and names the snapshot <vm name>__<snapshot name>. The
  command prints that name.

  minimega pauses the VM while it saves the snapshot, and then resumes the VM.
  The command waits up to one hour for the save. The experiment and the VM
  must run.

phenix vm snapshot create <experiment name> <vm name> <snapshot name> [flags]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: phenix vm snapshot create my-exp web before-update

docs.title: Options
docs.text: -h, --help   help for create

docs.title: phenix vm snapshot delete
docs.text: Delete one of the snapshots of a VM

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Delete one of the snapshots of a VM

  Deletes the memory state and the disk of the snapshot from the experiment's
  files directory on every cluster node. Give the snapshot name as phenix vm
  snapshot list prints it. The experiment does not have to run. phenix
  refuses a snapshot whose disk a running VM uses, as it does after a
  restore.

phenix vm snapshot delete <experiment name> <vm name> <snapshot name> [flags]

List the snapshots of a VM

  Prints the name of each snapshot of the VM, one name on each line, in sort
  order. Give one of these names to phenix vm snapshot restore. The
  experiment does not have to run. -o json and -o yaml print the names as a
  list.

phenix vm snapshot list <experiment name> <vm name> [flags]
